A review group had called the process "error prone" and "not easily scalable"; the automation that was promised "was never automated"; and an error in the spreadsheet "likely had the effect of muting volatility by a factor of two" (p.186). Halving the measured volatility halves the risk the limit sees, which is the risk number's version of marking at 79. Hal's bank has a ticket to automate the desk's own nightly risk load. It was opened three years ago. Chapter 27 is about why that ticket is the most dangerous object on the floor.

> **View From Another Seat.** *The dealer desk, in dealers' own public words.* To this seat Halvorsen is an inventory line that is expected to earn its balance sheet. Fred Orlan, Jefferies' global head of fixed income, described a mid-size dealer's economics to The DESK (26 Oct 2023): "It's hard for investment banks to run large balance sheets in this environment because it isn't making a lot of money," and "You're really making your money trading with and helping clients, which requires good ideas and good execution." At the largest banks the binding limit is often capital rather than conviction: JPMorgan's CFO, Jeremy Barnum, called the G-SIB surcharge "a significant disincentive to a particular type of business, in particular some markets business" (Q1 2026 earnings call, 14 Apr 2026). And flow franchises live on turnover, which moves with rates: Bank of America's CFO, Alastair Borthwick, said that when rates jump, "Clients tend to slow their activity" (Q3 2026 earnings call, 14 Oct 2026). A dealer holding \$6 million of a lender-call bond is warehousing it until a client wants it, at a cost the desk feels daily in its balance-sheet charge. Chapter 4-C, §4C.1, puts the seat under a Friday 2:58 p.m. RFQ.

*Builds on:* §1B.3 (the same cancelled print, from the reporting side). *Used in:* Chapter 8-C and §8C.7 (the explain, the true-up, and the whale's explain), §8B.9 (tolerances and limits), §8.1, §18.7 (the RFQ log as hit-ratio data), §2.5 and Appendix C (the lunch hour), Chapter 3 and §3B.6 (the cultural bridge and the twelve mistakes), Chapter 27 (the spreadsheet that stayed a spreadsheet).

## 1B.5 Friday. The Distressed Fund: "Information Has a Legal State"

*Fictional composite: a distressed-debt fund. The mechanics of confidentiality, restriction and big-boy letters follow Stephen Moyer's* Distressed Debt Analysis *(printed pp.62–64); the sourcing remarks are from a published podcast transcript. Sol Ferreira, his fund, its general counsel and its positions are invented.*

The cell is still green at 6:45. By 11:00 it will be red, and Sol knows it, because on Sunday night Halvorsen's advisers asked his fund to join a group of unsecured noteholders and on Thursday his PM said yes. The fund owns \$25 million of the 7.25s, bought at 88 in the spring *(illustrative)*, so the decision was less about whether to be in the room than about how long to stay out of it.

Moyer's book describes the architecture. Joining a bondholder group that will receive the company's private information means signing a confidentiality agreement, "generally referred to as signing 'confi'," which "can result in the holder becoming 'restricted'" (p.62). To "maximize the time period members remain unrestricted, the receipt and analysis of confidential information initially can be limited to the financial advisors and counsel" (p.62). And once members receive the information they "cannot become unrestricted until the information becomes public, usually through the filing of a Form 8-K, 10-Q, or 10-K, or the information becomes nonmaterial" (p.63). The group's advisers have had Halvorsen's numbers since Tuesday. This morning the company wants the members themselves to see a cash-flow forecast before it proposes anything, and so the members are coming over the wall.

At 10:00 the fund's general counsel holds a call to decide who goes. Sol goes; the PM goes; the trader stays outside and so does everyone else. The general counsel reads the confi aloud in the voice of someone who has read many, and at 10:40 Sol signs. At 10:52 the restricted-list cell for Halvorsen turns red for every security the company has issued, not only the notes. That catches the fund's loan sleeve, which had a standing order to sell \$3 million of Halvorsen's term loan, a position nobody on the call was thinking about. The order can still be done, but now only with a "big-boy letter," which Moyer describes as an acknowledgment by the other side that it knows the seller holds nonpublic information and a waiver of the claims it might otherwise bring, its execution "typically arranged by a broker-dealer intermediary" (p.63). The trader cancels the order instead. Nobody wants to sell a term loan in a lender-call week by announcing that they know something.

> **[SOURCE EXTRACTION]** *Moyer, Distressed Debt Analysis, pp.63–64:* "Assume that a group of bettors are at an off-track betting salon segregated in a room where there is no information about the outcome of any races. A man walks into the room and announces that he has just watched the third race at Santa Anita and offers to sell his winning ticket on the number six horse for 50% of the amount of the wager. Would anyone be foolish enough to buy it?"
>
> **Annotation.** A big-boy letter protects the seller legally and destroys him commercially, because it announces his state. On a 2026 desk the same logic reaches the screen without any letter: when the best-informed holders of a bond stop trading, the silence is itself a print. §3.6 builds a detector on it, and §3.6.3 argues that the wall is a feature the model is obliged to respect, not a signal it gets to exploit.

At 11:00 the Ad Hoc Group forms. It is, as ever, represented by counsel.

At 11:30 a private-equity sponsor calls about a different company entirely, a portfolio company in which Sol's fund holds a slice of the term loan. The sponsor would like to add debt to pay itself a dividend, and would the fund like to participate? Sol listens, asks four questions and passes. The pass goes into a log with a date, a reason and the price at which the deal eventually clears, because the fund learned years ago that its passes are as informative as its trades and much more numerous. Milwood Hobbs, who runs sourcing at Oaktree, described the economics of that log on *Odd Lots* ("How Oaktree's Head of Sourcing Finds the Next Great Deal," 28 Nov 2024): "the relationship is getting the first call," and "out of 20 deals, I only care about the last two. So how do I pass 18 times?" On dividend deals specifically, he said a sponsor who calls its main lenders first can "take me from violently upset to mildly annoyed." A systematic desk would give a great deal for a clean, dated, reasoned record of eighteen passes per two trades. §3.5 calls that record the Edge Ledger.

At 1:00 an email arrives from someone Sol met on a conference panel: Kaz Lind, the model builder on a systematic credit desk across town. Their liquidity score for Halvorsen fell sharply on Thursday and Friday, they write, and nothing in the public record explains it. Does Sol have a view? And, in a postscript, Kaz has heard the phrase "big-boy letter" this week from a distressed PM named Mags and would like to know whether there is a small-boy letter, and which one applies to a fund under a billion dollars.

Sol forwards the email to the general counsel without reading the postscript twice. The general counsel replies to Kaz, from the compliance mailbox, with the fund's standard sentence: *we do not comment on any issuer or security.* Kaz reads it, thinks about it, and writes back to their own desk that Sol's fund is probably restricted on Halvorsen. Then they look at the sentence again and delete the message, because they have just noticed what the general counsel already knew.

> **Math, Gently.** *Conditional probability, told through a silence.* A conditional probability is the chance of one thing given that you have seen another, written $\mathbb{P}(A \mid B)$. Kaz's question is: given that Halvorsen's best-informed holders have gone quiet, how likely is it that they are restricted in private talks? Suppose, across 1,000 high-yield issuers in a year, 50 are in private talks with a holder group *(illustrative)*. In 40 of those 50, the biggest holders stop trading. Among the 950 issuers not in talks, holders go quiet anyway in 95 cases, for holidays, redemptions or boredom. A two-by-two table does the rest. There are $40 + 95 = 135$ quiet names, of which 40 are in talks, so
>
> $$\mathbb{P}(\text{talks} \mid \text{quiet}) = \frac{40}{40 + 95} \approx 30\%.$$
>
> The prior was 5%; the silence multiplied it by six. Now take the compliance reply. If the fund sends the identical sentence about every issuer, restricted or not, then the chance of receiving it is 100% in talks and 100% out of talks, the ratio of the two is one, and the posterior equals the prior. The general counsel's boring sentence is boring on purpose: a reply that is the same in every state of the world carries no information about which state you are in. A fund that answered "no comment" only about restricted names would be publishing its restricted list one email at a time. The full version, with the base-rate trap that catches nearly everyone, is §3.4 and §3.4.3; the sequential detector built on silences is §3.6.2.

![Figure 1-B.5: Silence is evidence and a uniform reply is not: when the biggest holders go quiet, 40 of the 135 quiet names are in private talks (about 30%, against a 5% prior: the odds rise eightfold, from 50:950 to 40:95), but a fund that sends the same "no comment" about every issuer leaves the 5% untouched. Illustrative: the box's table of 1,000 issuers (50 in talks, 40 of them quiet; 95 of the other 950 quiet).](../assets/figures/ch01b_silence_odds.png)

Kaz's last email of the day, to their own desk, proposes modelling "restricted" as Gaussian. It is not answered.

From 2:00 to 5:00 nothing trades in Halvorsen at Sol's fund, because nobody who knows anything may trade it, and the people who know nothing have been told not to ask. Sol reads the cash-flow forecast twice and builds his own version of it on a tab he has kept since his first job, a week-by-week runway of cash against the next interest payment. At 3:15 Mags calls him about something else and asks, without asking, how his Friday is going. "Back in my day," she says, "the restricted list was a Post-it on the Bloomberg and the confi was a handshake." A pause. "And that was worse. And I miss it."

The 8-K that would cleanse everyone is expected after the close. At 4:30 there is nothing on EDGAR. At 5:00 there is nothing. At 5:45 the Ad Hoc Group speaks for the only time this week, in unison and through counsel, to ask whether anyone has seen the 8-K. Nobody has. The fund will stay restricted over the weekend, and Sol, who has watched Halvorsen since 88, will spend two days unable to do anything about a bond he now understands better than anyone who can trade it.

> **View From Another Seat.** *The opportunistic buyer, in its own published words.* To the distressed seat Halvorsen is a document first, a price second and a possible restricted interval third, and the interval is part of the price: a fund that joins the group trades liquidity for information, and the trade is priced in weeks of being unable to sell. The other side of that trade is the buyer with patient capital and no obligation to be anywhere in particular. The cleanest public account of the seat comes from structured credit rather than corporate distress. D. E. Shaw's research note *Assessing U.S. Mortgage-Backed Credit Stress in 2020* reports that over March and April 2020 "we purchased in excess of \$400 million in CAS and STACR bonds at a significant discount to par," from sellers who "were put under stress by redemption requests and margin calls." Wednesday's systematic seat sees a liquidity score falling; this seat sees a forced seller's discount and the possibility that somebody else's constraint is about to become its week. Chapter 4-C walks the full set of seats; Chapter 12-B gives the restructuring itself its state machine.

*Builds on:* §1B.3 (the liquidity score that fell without a public reason), Chapter 3-B §3B.5 (the wall, from Theo's side). *Used in:* §3.4 (the Bayesian 8-K), §3.5 (the Edge Ledger), §3.6 (who at this table knows about the LMT), Chapter 12-B (the restructuring as a state machine), Chapter 13 (the restricted interval as a dated feature in the Priming Risk Score), Chapter 25 (reading the 8-K when it finally arrives), Chapter 4-C (the opportunistic seat).

## 1B.6 Which Room Is Yours?

At 5:30 on Friday Priya closes the week's last page. The vendor has answered Monday's ticket with an apology and a second restatement, and the second restatement has gone into quarantine beside the first, each with the minute it arrived. Dov's x-ray is grey, his distance to the line is a little longer than it was on Tuesday, and the lender of his Halvorsen bonds has not yet asked for them back. Ngozi's pull request passed Thursday's review; the April ticket is closed, after 187 days. Hal's Friday email went out at 4:41 and tied, and his shadow column has no rows in it, which is the only state in which a shadow column is good news. Sol is restricted until an 8-K that did not come, reading a forecast he cannot act on.

The only number that rose steadily all week was the age of the tickets. Fourteen months for Dov's roll sync. Three years for Hal's risk load. Sol's fund has no ticket. It has a binder.

On Sunday, Theo Marsh, three weeks into his own first year on a systematic desk, writes up his week for Ines, who asks every new hire for the same thing: a log of who touched which number, when, and on whose authority. Halfway down the page he notices that the log has the shape of every week he spent at his old firm. A market maker who saved what it knew when it knew it, a pod whose hedge was right for the bonds it used to have, a manager whose rank moved because the past was edited, a bank with two prices for one bond, and a fund that could not trade because it knew too much. Five businesses. One question underneath all of them, and it was not *what is this worth?* It was *who is responsible for this number, and can they prove where it came from?* His USB stick is in his pocket. Sol, he will learn at the next poker game, keeps a 13-week model too, a week-by-week runway of cash against the next coupon. It is a survival curve that Sol does not call a survival curve, and Chapters 5 and 6 will call it one for him.

Which room is yours is a real question, and the first year in each looks different. In the market maker it is a rota and a toolchain. In the pod it is a mandate and a line. In the systematic manager it is a tape and a ticket. On the bank desk it is a mark and an email. In the distressed fund it is a confi and a log. Chapter 3-B follows Theo through his first year in one of these rooms, and Chapter 4-D is about getting a seat in any of them. (The Priya and Dov of this chapter are not the Priya and Dov of Chapter 28. Credit has more CUSIPs than first names.)

The week looked like five different jobs. It was one: the custody of a number. Who marked it, which feed it came from, whether yesterday's version of it still exists, and who is allowed to know it today. A restructuring banker has been doing that job since the first 13-week cash flow they ever tied out.

*Builds on:* Chapter 1 (the Halvorsen RFQ). *Used in:* Chapter 3-B (the first year), Chapter 4-C (the seats in full), Chapter 4-D (getting the seat), Chapters 5 and 6 (the survival curve the 13-week model becomes).

## 1B.7 The Week Log

### Specification for AI Implementation

*The problem it solves, at this point in the story.* Every room this week ran on clocks, and the clocks came in three kinds. Some were set by regulation: the fifteen-minute TRACE report, the quarterly best-execution review, the annual market-access certification. Some were sourced practice, routines that real firms have described in public: the support rota, the morning x-ray, the end-of-day reflection. And some were composite, invented for the story. Each event also had two times, the moment it happened and the moment the shop learned the version it acted on, which is what Monday's vendor file and Wednesday's cancelled print were both about. A desk that wants to learn from its own weeks needs those events in one table, with the clock type and the source attached, so that a later reader can tell a regulation from a habit from a story.

*What it computes, and why it is built this way.* The listing defines one immutable row type, `WeekEvent`, and two functions. Each row carries a logical `event_id` (a correction is a new row with the same id, not an edit), the shop type, a task class, the clock type, `occurred_at`, `known_at`, an optional interval end, an optional ticket-opened date and a `source`. The constructor refuses a regulation or sourced-practice row without a source, which is the chapter's labelling discipline enforced in code. `as_known` returns the latest version of an event that the shop knew at a given time, the bitemporal read of §27.2. `to_calendar_row` emits the row shape that Chapter 3-B's `desk_calendar.py` already ingests (event id, date, known-at date, source), so no new library is needed.

*Inputs and outputs.* In: events typed or parsed from tickets, load logs, compliance calendars and the restricted list. Out: validated rows, a point-in-time view of any event, ticket ages in days, and calendar rows for 3-B's module.

*When to use it, and when not.* It is a record of what happened and when it was known, useful for post-mortems, for the week-in-review, and for back-tests that want to know what the desk knew. It is not a compliance system and it does not decide whether anyone may trade; the restricted list stays the authority for that.

*The edge case that bites.* Two versions stamped with the same `known_at`, as when a cancel and its re-report arrive in the same minute. The listing breaks the tie by order of arrival in the list, which is arbitrary; a production version carries a sequence number from the feed. A second, gentler trap: a restricted interval whose end is unknown. The listing stores it as an open interval, with no end, because "next 8-K" is not a date.

*The full python listing is [Listing 1-B.1 in Appendix F](#code-1b-1).*

## 1B.8 Desk Debrief

The week's ideas, in the order the rooms taught them. A point-in-time archive is a back-test's alibi: Priya could open on Friday's original file only because her firm had saved it with the minute it arrived. A trade not done still has a markout, and a desk that logs only its fills is grading itself on the hands it chose to play. A hedge ratio built on DTS is right for the bonds a pair used to hold; when the idiosyncratic view pays, the ratio drifts, and a pair left alone turns quietly into a market position, while the jump it was not designed to hedge becomes the risk that matters. A return is a ratio of two prices, either of which the tape can retract, and one bad print makes two fake returns of opposite sign. A mark is a choice inside the bid-ask, and a tolerance is a budget for honest disagreement that can be spent one basis point at a time. Information has a legal state with timestamps, and even a silence carries a likelihood ratio unless someone has made it carry none. Underneath all of it sits one job, the custody of a number, and the one figure that rises reliably every week is the age of the ticket to automate the thing everyone does by hand.

### The Spec You Hand the Robot

*Vague version:* "log what happens each week." *What ROBO built from it:* a table with one column, `what_happened`, populated from every Bloomberg chat on the floor, including Thursday's discussion of where to get lunch, each row timestamped with the moment ROBO read it rather than the moment it happened. ROBO did exactly what was asked. *The precise version:* one immutable row per event version with `event_id`, `shop`, `task_class`, `clock_type` in {regulation, sourced practice, composite}, `occurred_at`, `known_at`, optional `ends_at` (open intervals allowed), optional `ticket_opened`, optional `instrument_id` (a surrogate key, not a CUSIP), and a `source` that is mandatory unless the row is composite; corrections as new rows, not edits; a point-in-time read by `known_at` with a feed sequence number to break ties; export rows in the shape Chapter 3-B's `desk_calendar.py` ingests.

### Exercises

**1. The river on a passed trade.** Priya's engine passes on an RFQ to buy \$3mm of a bond that trades at 80 with someone else; an hour later the composite is 81.50. What is the markout of the trade the engine did not do, and what would you want to see before calling the pass a mistake? *Solution.* Had it bought at 80, the markout would be $(81.50 - 80) \times 3{,}000{,}000/100 = +\$45{,}000$, so the pass cost \$45,000 of opportunity. One pass proves little: the market may have rallied, so the beta-adjusted (IDO) markout of §3.3.3 is the fairer number, and a month of passes set against a month of fills is the real test (§3.3.5).

**2. A pair that keeps working.** Suppose Kestrel's leg stays at a market-value DTS of about 70,200 and Halvorsen falls to 70, with a spread of 1,800 bp and a spread duration of 2.0. What face amount of Halvorsen short keeps the pair DTS-matched? *Solution.* Solve $N \times 0.70 \times 2.0 \times 1{,}800 = 70{,}200$, so $N \approx \$27.9$mm, down from \$39mm. As the short leg's view pays, its DTS rises and the matched size shrinks; an unrebalanced pair becomes a market short. The rematch does nothing about the jump risk of an exchange offer.

**3. The PM's option.** A platform pays 20% of positive P&L. Strategy A makes or loses \$5mm with equal odds; strategy B makes or loses \$20mm. What is the PM's expected pay under each, and the platform's expected P&L under B with and without a stop at a \$12mm loss? *Solution.* PM: $0.5 \times 0.2 \times 5 = \$0.5$mm and $0.5 \times 0.2 \times 20 = \$2.0$mm. Platform under B without a stop: $0.5 \times 16 - 0.5 \times 20 = -\$2.0$mm; with the stop: $0.5 \times 16 - 0.5 \times 12 = +\$2.0$mm, provided the loss arrives gradually enough for the stop to bind.

**4. One bad print.** A bond closes Friday at 95. Monday's last print is reported at 88, Tuesday's at 94.50; Tuesday evening the Monday print is corrected to 94.80. What are Monday's and Tuesday's returns before and after the correction, and which pair belongs in a back-test? *Solution.* Before: $88/95 - 1 = -7.4\%$ and $94.50/88 - 1 = +7.4\%$, a fake reversal. After: $94.80/95 - 1 = -0.2\%$ and $94.50/94.80 - 1 = -0.3\%$. A back-test that reproduces decisions uses the as-known version; a performance measurement uses the corrected one; the archive keeps both (§27.2).

**5. Leaning inside the tolerance.** A desk holds twelve high-yield bonds, \$40mm of face in total, and the valuation group's tolerance is 0.75 points. How much P&L can be moved without breaching a single tolerance, and why does the valuation group look at the signs of the deviations as well as their sizes? *Solution.* Up to $0.75 \times 40{,}000{,}000/100 = \$300{,}000$ if every mark leans the same way. Honest marking errors fall on either side of mid; all twelve on the favourable side has probability $0.5^{12} \approx 0.02\%$ if the errors are honest coin flips, which is a much louder alarm than any single breach.

**6. Kaz's small-boy letter.** Suppose the fund's general counsel used the standard "no comment" reply 90% of the time for restricted names and 60% of the time otherwise. With a 5% prior that a name is in private talks, what does receiving the reply do to the probability? *Solution.* The likelihood ratio is $0.9/0.6 = 1.5$. Prior odds $0.05/0.95 \approx 0.053$ become $0.079$, a posterior of about 7.3%. A reply used for every name, in every state, has a ratio of one and moves nothing; there is, alas, no small-boy letter.

# Chapter 2: The Revolutions in Credit Trading

*Tuesday, 20 October 2026, week five, 3:41 p.m. Nineteen minutes to the index mark. The desk smells like burnt espresso and somebody else's DV01.*

The ticket on Theo Marsh's screen is the first one that is entirely his: **buy \$4mm, Halvorsen Packaging 7.25% senior notes due 2029, B3,** sent all-to-all. (Halvorsen is fictional. The chime is not.) Responders get two minutes. In the old world Theo would have called three dealers, waited for two of them to call back, and spent the wait rereading the restricted payments covenant. In this world eleven responses arrive before he has found the covenant: four banks, two non-bank market makers, three asset managers, a hedge fund, and something whose name is a string of capital letters.

He lifts the best offer. The cover, the second-best response, is three-eighths of a point behind. Done in forty seconds.

"Back in my day," says Marguerite "Mags" Dunleavy, without looking up, "I priced these by phone and by grudge. You called Steve, Steve gave you a number that punished you for something you did in 1997, and the print showed up on the tape whenever it felt like it, if it showed up at all."

Ines Okafor rolls her chair over and studies the eleven rows the way she once studied a final table. "Eleven players. Nice pot, tight cover. Now tell me which one of them just got off a lender call."

Theo knows exactly what a lender call does to an offer, and he reaches for the indenture out of habit. "But what does the credit agreement say about electronic trading?"

"Nothing, Theo." Dr. Kasimir "Kaz" Lind keeps typing. "The bond doesn't know how it was traded. The dataset does."

Theo finds the forty seconds oddly satisfying, the way a closing dinner is satisfying, and he sits back to enjoy it. Then, because a month on a systematic desk has taught him that nothing has happened until it shows up somewhere as a row, he opens the TRACE window to watch his own trade arrive in public.

It is not there.

He refreshes at 3:43. The Halvorsen line shows the morning's prints and an odd lot from lunchtime. He refreshes at 3:47, and again at 3:50, and nothing on the screen looks like four million bonds changing hands at 3:41.

"It isn't broken," says Kaz, who has not looked up but has apparently heard him refresh. "Rule 6730. The reporting side has 'as soon as practicable, but no later than within 15 minutes of the Time of Execution.'" Kaz pronounces the quotation marks, with the small relish of someone quoting a rulebook they have actually read. "Most people report in seconds. Some people use the whole fifteen."

"Fifteen minutes," says Mags. "Luxury. In July 2002 it was seventy-five minutes, and by the end of that year the tape covered about five hundred and twenty bonds, none of which I owned. The regulator gave us transparency the way a casino gives you a free drink. TRACE was a newspaper that only reported the weather in towns I didn't live in."

At 3:56 the print lands. Theo reads it twice. The price is his, to the sixteenth. The times are his: executed 15:41, reported 15:56, the counterparty having taken every one of its fifteen legal minutes. The size is not his. Where Theo bought \$4mm, the tape says `1MM+`.

"That's not what I bought."

"That's what the public is allowed to know you bought," Kaz says. "Halvorsen is B3. A high-yield trade over a million prints as `1MM+`; in investment grade the cap is `5MM+`. The idea is to protect whoever is left to go and find your bonds before the whole street knows the size."

"So my own trade is a lower bound."

"Your own trade is a lower bound to everyone except you, your counterparty and FINRA."

Theo scrolls up the Halvorsen line, because a restructuring banker never reads a page without reading the page before it. At 2:38 p.m., an hour and three minutes before his fill, there is another print: `1MM+`, a customer selling to a dealer, about half a point below where he has just paid *(illustrative)*. He did not see it when it happened. He was rereading the restricted payments covenant. He cannot really see it now, either. The tape tells him that somebody sold at least a million Halvorsen bonds to a dealer an hour before he bought, and it declines to say whether that somebody sold one million or forty.

"Who was that?"

"Could be anyone," Ines says. "A mutual fund rebalancing. A CLO trimming its bucket. Someone who just got off a lender call. Or a dealer's customer, and then the same dealer offered those bonds back out to you on the all-to-all, three-eighths through the cover." She shrugs, the way she used to shrug at a river card. "Which one it was changes what you paid."

Theo looks at the two `1MM+` rows, his own and the ghost's, a screen apart. He has three questions, and he asks them in the order a banker would. "What did I actually pay for that bond? Who knew it before I did? And could a machine have told me in advance?"

"Better than the question you came in with," Ines says. "Here's the answer in one line, and the rest of the week is evidence. Every basis point off a ticket buys more tickets, and more tickets is more edge." She starts to count the evidence on her fingers, the way she counts outs, and stops at one. "The math is at the end. The evidence is the seven changes that built this screen."

"And the ghost?"

"The ghost," says Ines, "is the last page."

That exchange is the whole chapter. A bond's *value* lives in its documents. Its *tradability* lives in its data exhaust: how many prints it gets per day, how many dealers answer an RFQ for it, how far the cover sits from the winner, whether it sits in an ETF redemption basket, and which of its trades the public tape refuses to show you. Theo's three questions are the trader's version of a historian's one. **The question this chapter answers: what changed in the plumbing of credit trading between 2002 and 2026, how big was each change, and why did those changes, rather than any new factor, make systematic credit possible?**

The answer arrives in three movements. The tape (§2.2) made the cost of a trade knowable after the fact, and then censored exactly the trades Theo cares about. The wire (§2.3 to §2.8) made cost knowable at the moment of the trade and turned every fill, and every miss, into a labeled data point. The payoff (§2.9) is Ines's one line made precise: a lower cost per ticket buys more breadth, so the same signal becomes a better strategy, and the optimal net alpha scales like $1/c$.

A housekeeping note for Kaz: every expectation in this chapter is under the physical measure $\mathbb{P}$, the weather forecast rather than the price of rain insurance. A fill rate or a count of RFQ responses records what traders actually did and carries no price of risk (Chapter 1's risk-neutral box draws the difference; $\mathbb{Q}$ becomes a main character in Chapter 6).

## 2.1 The Desk View: Execution Certainty and a Modelable Cost

Seen from a market maker's chair, a systematic credit book looks like this. A quant credit strategy is a function from data to target weights. Every day, or every hour, it says "own more of these 400 bonds and less of those 300." The optimizer behind those targets makes an assumption it never states: that the bonds can actually be traded, at a cost it can predict.

For most of its history, credit broke that assumption. Man Group's systematic team put the barrier plainly:

> **[SOURCE EXTRACTION]** *Man_Revolutions_in_Credit_Trading_2023 p.2:* "The greatest barriers to systematic approaches breaking through in credit have traditionally been execution and the ability to model transaction costs and liquidity within decades-old manual processes."
>
> **Annotation.** Notice what is *not* on the list: signals. By 2023, credit factors (value, momentum, quality, low risk) had more than a decade of published evidence behind them (Chapters 9–12). What was missing was a way to turn a target weight into a fill. The sentence recasts the history of quant credit as a history of plumbing, and that is this chapter's frame. Where the 2026 desk departs: in liquid IG, "manual processes" no longer bind, because most small tickets are electronic and many are auto-executed. They still bind for high-yield blocks, stressed names and anything near a liability-management transaction (Chapters 13–14): the barrier moved down the credit curve, into Theo's old neighborhood, where §2.8 ends up.

On the next page of the same paper, Man named the two conditions a systematic strategy needs:

> **[SOURCE EXTRACTION]** *Man_Revolutions_in_Credit_Trading_2023 p.4:* "Two of the key challenges for such systematic techniques are having a high certainty of execution and having a relatively good sense of the likely transaction costs, as quantitative approaches depend on being able to model accurately which securities can be traded and at what cost."
>
> **Annotation.** These are the two inputs a portfolio optimizer cannot do without. One is a *feasible set*: which bonds can be traded. The other is a *cost function*: at what price. Write them as $\Pr(\text{fill}\mid x)$ and $\mathbb{E}[c \mid \text{fill}, x]$, where $x$ is a vector of ticket features such as size, rating, age, recent prints, and the number of dealers who answered the last RFQ. Every revolution in this chapter improves one or both, and each section closes by saying which. The modern departure is that by 2026 both quantities are *forecast*, not just measured, and §2.5 shows them feeding a router rather than a spreadsheet.

Man's earlier paper explains why this matters to an optimizer. The subject of the sentence is the optimizer's solution:

> **[SOURCE EXTRACTION]** *Man_Quantitative_Credit_Alpha_Early_Mover_2022 p.19:* "is no longer really optimal if that bond is not available for purchase. In addition, unfilled orders can lead to unintended and potentially unmodelled risk exposures."
>
> **Annotation.** An optimal portfolio you cannot buy is not optimal, and an unfilled order is not a zero. It is an *unintended position*. If you sold the bond you meant to swap out of but failed to buy its replacement, you are now short beta you never chose. The desk motto applies to execution as much as to alpha: *IDO or it didn't happen*. A backtest that assumes every target fills is reporting the alpha of a market that does not exist.

Theo reads the three extractions and objects, which is how he learns. "At PJT we never had a fill problem," he says. "Nobody ever failed to buy a bond. When a client needed to own the fulcrum, they owned the fulcrum by Friday. We always got filled. We just paid."

"How much?" Ines asks.

He opens his mouth, and closes it. He knows roughly where the claims traded the week the plan went effective. He knows what the client's average cost was, because it was in the fund's letter. What he does not know, and has never known, is how far each of those purchases sat from what the bonds were worth at the moment they were bought, because nobody at the table ever wrote that number down. There was a price, and there was a story about the price, and the story was usually told by the dealer who had sold it.

"'Paid' was never written down," Ines says, "so it could never be a variable. You can't optimize against a number nobody records. That's the whole revolution, really. Not that people started getting filled. That somebody started writing down what it cost."

At PJT the unit of analysis was a document and a process, and the only liquidity information was whatever Steve said. A systematic desk needs liquidity to be a *variable*, measured for every bond every day and comparable across 10,000 CUSIPs; the rest of this chapter dates the process that made it one, sizes it, and shows where it has still not reached.

Mags, who has been listening with the expression she keeps for sell-side research, does not let the variable stand unchallenged. "Write down what my last exit cost, then. Five positions, each a few percent of an issue. When I want out, I don't want the probability it fills. I want a name: the other holder in the group, the sponsor buying back paper at a discount, the fund that wants the fulcrum. Your regression trained on ten thousand IG tickets has never met him." Ines concedes the point the way she concedes a pot she was never going to win. A book of 700 IG lines rebalanced monthly lives in the variable's world: a fill probability ten points off on one \$1mm BBB ticket is one error among hundreds, and next month's labeled RFQs correct it. Mags's book lives in the relationship's world, and a high-yield book of 150 names is a hundred lines of the first kind and a dozen of the second. "So ask the model how many comparable fills it has seen," Ines says. "In the thousands, it's a variable. In the dozens, it's Steve again."

So before any of the revolutions, the two numbers looked like this: $\Pr(\text{fill})$ was close to one for anyone willing to pay, and $\mathbb{E}[c]$ was not small so much as unknowable. The story of the next seven sections is the second number being written down.

## 2.2 Revolution 0: TRACE, or the Dataset Appears

Before you can trade a bond on a model, the model needs training data. For US corporates that data is TRACE, FINRA's Trade Reporting and Compliance Engine. It underlies everything that follows, so we call it Revolution 0. It did not change how bonds traded. It changed what anyone could *know* about how they traded.

> **[SOURCE EXTRACTION]** *Bohn_Stein_Active_Credit_Portfolio_Management p.91:* "In the past, credit markets have been hampered by lack of transparency in pricing, making it difficult to mark a portfolio to market let alone hedge or trade a particular exposure."
>
> **Annotation.** Bohn and Stein wrote when TRACE was a few years old, and their footnote 6 on the same page dates its origin: in September 1998 the SEC asked the NASD (now FINRA) to provide more transparency in corporate debt. The sentence lists three uses in rising order of difficulty: mark, hedge, trade. A systematic desk needs all three every day for every bond in its universe. Where the 2026 desk departs: transparency is no longer the scarce input for the liquid half of the market. The scarce input is *clean* transparency, meaning duplicate prints, processed voice trades and capped sizes have all been dealt with. That is the subject of the rest of this section.

### 2.2.1 The dissemination timeline

TRACE did not arrive all at once. FINRA phased it in by issue size and rating and cut the reporting clock in steps. The dates below come from the FINRA TRACE Fact Book (2025 edition) and FINRA's reporting-timeframes page. The one-minute saga comes from SEC and FINRA releases.

> **Trend Watch.** **The reporting clock, 2002–2026: a twenty-four-year countdown that stopped at fifteen minutes.**
>
> | Date | Change | Source |
> | :-- | :-- | :-- |
> | Sept 1998 | SEC asks NASD for corporate-debt transparency | `Bohn_Stein p.91`, fn. 6 |
> | July 1, 2002 | TRACE launches with 75-minute reporting. Phase I disseminates IG issues of \$1bn or more plus the "FIPS 50" HY names: about 520 securities by end-2002 | FINRA TRACE Fact Book 2025 |
> | Mar 3 and Apr 14, 2003 | Phase IIa (AAA/AA/A issues of \$100mm or more) and Phase IIb (120 BBB plus 50 HY names): about 4,650 bonds | Fact Book |
> | Oct 1, 2003 | Clock cut to 45 minutes | Fact Book |
> | Oct 1, 2004 | Phase IIIa; clock cut to 30 minutes | Fact Book |
> | Feb 7, 2005 | Phase IIIb: about 99% of public transactions and 95% of par value disseminated immediately | Fact Book |
> | July 1, 2005 | Clock cut to 15 minutes | Fact Book |
> | Jan 9, 2006 | Immediate dissemination of all public TRACE-eligible corporates | Fact Book |
> | June 30, 2014 | Rule 144A corporate trades disseminated | Fact Book |
> | May 15, 2023 | Portfolio-trade modifier required on corporate bond reports | Fact Book; FINRA RN 22-12 |
> | Jan 11, 2024 | FINRA files SR-FINRA-2024-004 to cut the 15-minute outer limit to one minute | SEC Rel. 34-101121 |
> | Sept 20, 2024 | SEC approves the one-minute rule | SEC Rel. 34-101121 |
> | Early 2025 | FINRA signals it will not set an effective date | Mayer Brown, *Free Writings*, Feb 10, 2025 (as reported); FINRA RN 25-17, fn. 9 |
> | Dec 4, 2025 | FINRA "is not moving forward"; the 15-minute standard stays | FINRA RN 25-17 |
> | June 8, 2026 | Optional aggregate allocation reporting begins | FINRA RN 25-17 |
> | Aug 31, 2026 | Expanded affiliate-principal indicator becomes available on a voluntary basis (mandatory Aug 2, 2027) | FINRA RN 26-16 |
>
> **What it means for the desk.** The headline clock (75, then 45, 30 and 15 minutes) understates how fast the market actually is. FINRA's own statistics, summarized in the SEC's 2024 approval order, show that in 2022, 82.9% of trades executed between 8:00 a.m. and 6:15 p.m. ET were already reported within one minute, and 90.6% within three. The rule would have accelerated "up to 16.4% of current annual trading volume, or up to 6.1 million trades and 20 trillion dollars in par value" (SEC Rel. 34-101121). So FINRA spent 2022 to 2025 trying to make the market report in one minute, found that 83% of it already did, and dropped the rule. It was the most TRACE-like thing TRACE has ever done: the information arrived, late, and changed nothing. For a quant, the interesting number is the remaining 17%. The trades that still report slowly are the manual ones, and manual trades are where blocks and distressed names live.

Mags's seventy-five minutes and Theo's fifteen are the outer limits. The interesting object is what happens inside them, and it needs one idea from statistics first.

> **Math, Gently.** *A mixture: two queues poured into one bag.* Picture the arrivals hall of an airport with two passport queues. One is the row of automated gates: scan, beep, through in seconds. The other is the human desk, where an officer reads every page and the wait runs to minutes. Stand at the exit with a stopwatch, time every passenger, and draw the histogram (Chapter 1's box says what a distribution is). This one has two humps, a tall narrow one near zero and a low wide one out at several minutes, and two humps are the signature of a **mixture**: two distributions in one bag, with a weight $\pi$ on the first and $1-\pi$ on the second. If almost every gate passenger is out within a minute and almost no desk passenger is, then the share of *all* passengers out within a minute is approximately $\pi$ itself. A tiny number: if 60 of every 100 passengers use the gates and the desk never takes less than three minutes, then 60% are out within one minute, and a single count has told you $\pi \approx 0.6$. TRACE's print delays are the same hall: straight-through electronic reports are the gates, manually booked voice trades are the desk. Chapter 5 builds mixtures properly, starting with the survive-or-jump mixture inside every bond price (§5.1).

Written down, the print delay $\ell$ is a two-component mixture:

$$
\Pr(\ell \le u) = \pi\,F_{\text{fast}}(u) + (1-\pi)\,F_{\text{slow}}(u), \qquad 0 \le u \le 15 \text{ min}.
$$

Here $F_{\text{fast}}$ is the delay distribution of straight-through electronic reports (seconds), $F_{\text{slow}}$ is the delay distribution of manually booked voice trades (minutes), and $\pi$ is the weight on the electronic component. FINRA's 2022 statistic pins down one point of the mixture: $\Pr(\ell \le 1\text{ min}) = 0.829$. What matters for feature design is that $\pi$ is *not constant across bonds*. It is lowest exactly where the information is richest: large, stressed, voice-traded tickets. So a feature like "minutes since last print" means different things in different bonds. In an IG bond a stale print means nobody traded. In a CCC bond it may mean somebody traded big and the ticket is still being booked.

The airport also has a third queue, and it closes at night. A trade executed after the 6:30 p.m. ET close, or in the last fifteen minutes before it, is not disseminated when it happens; it is reported after the next business day's open and marked "as/of" (Rule 6730; Farshid Abdi, with Marco Rossi and Botao Wu, "Overnight Corporate Bond Trading," The Microstructure Exchange, 15 Sept 2026). In the mixture above, that regime is a third component parked entirely outside the 0-to-15-minute window, at "tomorrow, after the open," which is why the SEC's 82.9% is quoted only for trades between 8:00 a.m. and 6:15 p.m. A "minutes since last print" feature computed at 8:05 a.m. therefore blends three situations: bonds nobody traded, voice tickets still being booked, and bonds that changed hands while New York slept. A timestamp has a regime, and the regime belongs in its own column.

### 2.2.2 The caps: censoring as a data problem

The two strings Theo met at 3:56, `5MM+` and `1MM+`, matter more to a credit quant than any others in the feed. The cap is the bond market's version of "a source familiar with the matter": you know something big happened, but not how big.

> **Math, Gently.** *Censored, missing and truncated are three different things.* Picture a bathroom scale that only goes up to 300 pounds. A heavy friend steps on and the display says "300+". That reading is **censored**: it is not a blank, and it is not 300. It is a lower bound, and a lower bound is information. Now picture a different problem: the scale's battery died on Tuesday, so Tuesday has no reading at all. That observation is **missing**, and it tells you nothing about anyone's weight, only about the battery. And picture a third: a gym that only lets people under 300 pounds through the door, so the heavy friend never appears in the log in the first place. That sample is **truncated**: the big values are not hidden, they are absent, and nothing in the data warns you. TRACE's `5MM+` is the first kind. Dropping it treats a lower bound as a dead battery; replacing it with 5 treats a lower bound as a measurement. Both understate. To see how much they understate, it helps to know a trick for averages. The mean of any nonnegative quantity equals its survival probabilities stacked up: the chance it exceeds 0, plus the chance it exceeds 1, plus the chance it exceeds 2, and so on. A tiny number: if a trade size is equally likely to be 1, 2 or 3, the chance it exceeds 0 is 1, exceeds 1 is $2/3$, exceeds 2 is $1/3$, and exceeds 3 is zero. Stack them: $1 + 2/3 + 1/3 = 2$, which is exactly the mean, $(1+2+3)/3$. Now cap the sizes at 2. The stack loses its top layer, the $1/3$ above the cap, and the average capped size is $5/3$. The stack is the picture behind every number in this section. The full version is the derivation at the end of it.

> **[SOURCE EXTRACTION]** *Ben_Dor_Quantitative_Credit_Portfolio_Management p.162 (note 3):* "disseminates trade-by-trade corporate bond execution information within 15 minutes to all market participants. At this time, TRACE data are censored at \$5 million for investment grade and \$1 million for high-yield securities."
>
> **Annotation.** The Barclays authors use the right word: *censored*, the bathroom scale's "300+", not its dead battery. The caps have not moved since this was written. FINRA still disseminates `5MM+` for IG and `1MM+` for HY, and RN 25-17 applies the same caps to the new allocation reports. The *ticket* has moved: average trade size fell from about \$560k to about \$360k over the four years to 2024 (IFR, citing MarketAxess data), so a larger share of trades now prints uncapped. The capped minority is the part of the market an RSSG veteran knows best.

A capped size keeps every layer of the stack below the cap and loses every layer above it, so turnover summed from the tape comes out low. Ben Dor and coauthors flag exactly this:

> **[SOURCE EXTRACTION]** *Ben_Dor_Quantitative_Credit_Portfolio_Management p.364 (note 8):* "TRACE truncates the sizes of large transactions at \$1 million and \$5 million for high-yield and investment-grade bonds, respectively, which may cause our estimates of turnover to be downward biased."
>
> **Annotation.** The same note then gives the fix. Capped trades are assigned larger sizes, chosen so that the sum of individual trades matches TRACE's aggregate volume figures, which "yields higher transaction limits of \$4 million and \$12.5 million for high-yield and investment-grade bonds, respectively." That is a moment-matching estimator. Where the modern desk departs: academic and enhanced TRACE files with uncapped sizes are released with a lag (Appendix B), so a backtest can use true sizes, but a live model sees only the capped feed. Train on what you will see at decision time. Otherwise your turnover feature is look-ahead bias in a lab coat.

The imputation can be made to tell us something, and it is worth watching Kaz find out what. Kaz reads the note, gets as far as "\$4 million and \$12.5 million," and stops. "Those are averages of the trades above the cap. If I knew the shape of the tail, I could get the average from the cap. So if I know the average, I get the shape."

So Kaz runs the arithmetic backwards. Suppose block sizes above the cap follow a Pareto tail, the standard model for the giants: the chance of a block at least twice as big falls by the same fraction however big you start, and a single tail index $\alpha$ sets how fat the tail is. (The body of the size distribution, many \$200k tickets and few \$2mm ones, is closer to lognormal; Chapter 1 met fat tails, and §5.7 fits them properly.) Then the average capped trade is a fixed multiple of the cap, $\alpha/(\alpha-1)$, and a published average pins down $\alpha$. For investment grade, an average of 12.5 against a cap of 5 means the tail index is 5/3, about 1.67. For high yield, 4 against a cap of 1 means 4/3, about 1.33. Two numbers in a footnote, written to fix a turnover estimate, turn out to contain a structural fact about how large trades are distributed.

Read that slowly, because it is the book's first quant "aha" for an RSSG reader. Both tail indices are below 2, so the implied block-size distribution has *infinite variance*: however many trades you average, one block keeps showing up large enough to dominate, and the sample mean never settles the way a normal's would. (Kaz, who was going to assume Gaussian, now regrets it.) The HY tail is also fatter. Relative to its cap, the average hidden HY block is four times the cap, against two and a half times in IG, so `1MM+` hides proportionally more of HY than `5MM+` hides of IG. The trades the tape conceals most completely are large HY and stressed trades, the ones where knowing who sold, and how much, is worth the most. The RSSG skill set is most valuable exactly where the data exhaust is thinnest.

#### The Full Derivation: the tail index from one moment

Every TRACE-based turnover model rests on the following identity. Let $X$ be the true size of a trade, with CDF $G$, and let the cap be $c$. TRACE shows $\tilde X = \min(X, c)$. For any nonnegative random variable, $\mathbb{E}[X] = \int_0^\infty \Pr(X > x)\,dx$, so

$$
\mathbb{E}[\tilde X] = \int_0^{c} \big(1 - G(x)\big)\,dx, \qquad \mathbb{E}[X] - \mathbb{E}[\tilde X] = \int_c^{\infty} \big(1 - G(x)\big)\,dx \;\ge\; 0 .
$$

Volume summed from capped prints therefore biases turnover *down*, by the area under the size distribution's tail beyond the cap.

Next, the imputation. Suppose block sizes above the cap follow a Pareto tail, the standard model for heavy-tailed sizes:

$$
\Pr(X > x \mid X > c) = \left(\frac{x}{c}\right)^{-\alpha}, \qquad x \ge c,\quad \alpha > 1 .
$$

Then the mean size of a capped trade is

$$
\mathbb{E}[X \mid X > c] = c + \int_c^\infty \left(\frac{x}{c}\right)^{-\alpha} dx = c + \frac{c}{\alpha - 1} = \frac{c\,\alpha}{\alpha - 1}.
$$

Ben Dor's imputed limit $m$ is this conditional mean. Set $m = c\alpha/(\alpha-1)$ and solve for the tail index:

$$
\hat\alpha = \frac{m}{m - c}.
$$

For IG, $c = 5$ and $m = 12.5$, so $\hat\alpha = 12.5/7.5 = 5/3 \approx 1.67$. For HY, $c = 1$ and $m = 4$, so $\hat\alpha = 4/3 \approx 1.33$.

(A caveat for the exercises: a Pareto tail fitted from one moment is a sketch, not an estimate. Chapter 22 fits the tail directly from the uncapped academic file.)

Kaz once asked whether a "riskless principal" trade involved a principal with no risk, "like a tenured professor." It is a dealer who buys from one customer and sells to another at nearly the same moment, so one economic trade can print twice, and affiliated desks reporting to each other add more echoes. What the echoes do to a dashboard is a story about plumbing.

> **Shop Life: the TRACE loader.** *A fictional composite; the dates and rule changes are real.* A systematic asset manager, the kind with four hundred bonds in a book and nine people in a room called "Data." Wednesday, 7 October 2026, 8:20 a.m. The portfolio manager's morning dashboard has a chart called *IG market activity*, and on Tuesday's bar the chart has dipped. The PM has written one line in the team channel: "Why is Tuesday's IG volume 9% below Monday's? Tuesday was much busier. Three new deals and the index rebalance." The line is addressed to nobody, which on a data team means it is addressed to the most junior person, who this year is Femi, eleven months out of a statistics master's and still young enough to find the question interesting.
>
> Femi starts where everyone starts, by assuming the market is right and the code is wrong. He pulls Tuesday's raw TRACE file and counts rows: more prints than Monday, not fewer. He sums par in the raw file by hand, in a notebook, the way his manager says to do it once before trusting any pipeline, and Tuesday comes out *above* Monday. So the loss is inside the loader. He diffs the loader's commits and finds a tidy pull request merged on Monday evening by a colleague who was cleaning up warnings. The old code read the size column as text and had a special case for `5MM+` and `1MM+`. The new code casts the column to a number with errors coerced, which turns `5MM+` into a blank, and four steps later a `dropna()` removes the blanks. Nobody wrote "drop the biggest trades." The code simply stopped knowing what the biggest trades were. Tuesday, being the busier day, had more blocks above the cap, so Tuesday lost more volume. The capped prints were not treated as lower bounds or even floored at the cap. They were treated as dead batteries.
>
> That explains most of the gap, and Femi could stop. He does not, because the dashboard's other chart, month over month, has been bothering him for a week. September's high-grade TRACE volume on the dashboard looks soft against June's. He goes to the platforms' monthly reports to cross-check and finds Tradeweb's September 2026 report, published that Tuesday, with a footnote: the affiliate-principal change "lowered reported U.S. High Grade TRACE volumes," and "TRACE and Tradeweb have not restated prior periods and therefore these amounts may not be comparable." He reads it twice. FINRA's expanded affiliate-principal indicator became available on a voluntary basis on 31 August 2026; when a dealer flags the inter-affiliate leg of a trade, TRACE suppresses it and disseminates only the trade with the outside customer. So September is cleaner than June, not quieter. And June was dirtier than it looked: MarketAxess had reported duplicate trade reports inflating US high-grade volume by up to 8% that month. The dashboard was comparing a month with echoes to a month with fewer echoes and calling the difference a market. Nobody can say exactly how big the break is, because the footnote does not size it, and the indicator stays voluntary until August 2027, so each dealer flips its own switch on its own day.
>
> By now it is 11:40, and Femi has the slightly dangerous feeling of someone on a roll. He opens the feature store to see what else touches TRACE and finds the portfolio-trading share feature, which the cost model uses. Before 15 May 2023 it is exactly zero, every day, for every bond. FINRA only began requiring the portfolio-trade modifier on 15 May 2023, so before that date the tape cannot say which trades were in portfolio trades. A zero claims to know there were none, in 2021, the year dealers were bidding baskets most aggressively. The honest value before the modifier exists is "unknown," a NaN, and a model that sees NaN can be told to ignore the feature for those years instead of learning that 2021 had no portfolio trading.
>
> The fix takes forty minutes and is almost insultingly small. The loader gets back its special case, now written as a flag: `size_capped = True` and `size = cap`, so a downstream model can choose to floor, impute or censor-model the block as it likes. The table gets one new column, `trace_regime`, with three values: before the portfolio-trade modifier, after it, and after the affiliate indicator. The schema document gets one paragraph that begins "TRACE sizes are censored, not missing." Femi reruns Tuesday. It is now 4% above Monday *(illustrative)*, which is what the PM had assumed all along. No model was retrained. No signal changed. At the Friday meeting the PM says "good catch" in the voice people use for plumbing, and moves on to the agenda item about the new office chairs. It is, by any measure that matters to a systematic fund, the most valuable thing anyone on the floor did that week.

Last, a period piece from the shelf, included because it explains why some of Mags's habits survive:

> **[SOURCE EXTRACTION]** *Moyer_Distressed_Debt_Analysis p.416 (note 62):* "However, most of the securities required to be posted do not constitute distressed securities."
>
> **Annotation.** Moyer was writing in TRACE's phased-in early years, when dissemination mostly covered larger issues, and the same note expands the acronym as "Trade Reporting and Comparison Entry Source," an artifact of its vintage. For the distressed investor of that era, the new tape was something that happened to other people. Today every public TRACE-eligible corporate is disseminated, stressed ones included. But the caps and the slow manual component from §2.2.1 still make distressed trading the least transparent corner of a transparent market. That is why Mags still prices some things by grudge, and why she is still, irritatingly, right about some of them.

So Revolution 0 left $\Pr(\text{fill})$ exactly where it was and made $\mathbb{E}[c]$ estimable after the fact, for every trade except the large ones, which it recorded only as lower bounds.

## 2.3 Revolution 1: From Phone to RFQ

Mags has a war story for every protocol, and this one begins with a run. "A run," she tells Theo, who has received several hundred and never been told what one is, "is a dealer's list of bonds and levels. It goes out at 8 a.m., is stale by 8:05, and binds nobody. It's a menu where every price says 'market.'"

Man's 2022 paper describes the market the electronic RFQ was built to replace:

> **[SOURCE EXTRACTION]** *Man_Quantitative_Credit_Alpha_Early_Mover_2022 p.19:* "the bond market is structured around a Request for Quotation (RFQ) process that has hardly changed for decades. Corporate bond bid/ask prices are indicated by dealer runs that are not firm and actionable"
>
> **Annotation.** Two phrases carry the weight. "Hardly changed for decades" means the protocol still runs request, quote, accept. Electronification did not abolish the RFQ. It put it on a wire, sent it to many dealers at once and timestamped every answer. "Not firm and actionable" separates an *indication* from a *price*. A run is an indication. A TRACE print is a fact about a trade somebody else already did. Neither is a firm price for the trade you want now. An electronic RFQ is: $n$ dealers answer the same question at the same moment, each answer is binding for the response window, and the client can execute against the best one or walk away. Where the 2026 desk departs: the RFQ is now being split into variants (request-for-market, session-based auctions, streaming, one-click). Buy-side panelists at FILS Europe in 2026 predicted that the RFQ "in its current form" would become obsolete (The DESK, Oct 2026). If that happens, the request-quote-accept structure will have lasted most of a century. It would be the most durable thing in this chapter.

> **View From Another Seat.** *The dealer desk (a generic bank seat; no bank is named).* From the dealer's chair the run and the RFQ are two halves of one business, and they feel nothing alike. The run is advertising. A flow trader sends it at 8 a.m. to a few hundred clients so that, when one of them has a bond to move, the bank's name is the first one they think of. The RFQ is the moment a client asks the bank to stand behind its advertising, in size, for two minutes, against rivals it cannot see. That is the asymmetry the dealer lives with all day. The client sees eleven answers. Each dealer sees its own answer and, afterward, whether it won. The client learns the market eleven numbers at a time; the dealer learns it one bit at a time. The published run data in §2.4 is humbling for anyone who thinks the tightest quote takes the trade: usually it does not, because relationships, timing and the client's own constraints all get a vote. A dealer desk reads that two ways at once. It is a reason to keep sending runs, because a quote helps the client just by being present, and presence is how a bank stays on the client's list. It is also a reason not to spend capital being the tightest name on every line. And when Theo lifts the best of eleven offers, the dealer that wins learns one thing: it was the most aggressive of a crowd it never saw. That is exactly the news a dealer least wants, and §2.3.2 turns it into the winner's curse.

Here is why a pre-RFQ quant could not build the obvious cost model directly from TRACE:

> **[SOURCE EXTRACTION]** *Ben_Dor_Quantitative_Credit_Portfolio_Management p.120:* "Although it is possible to capture transaction spread data via TRACE, for most bonds the time between a broker-dealer buy and sell transaction for a given CUSIP can be very long, so it is difficult to calculate an accurate bid-ask spread using TRACE."
>
> **Annotation.** A bid-ask spread is a statement about two prices *at the same moment*. TRACE gives you two prices at *different* moments, a dealer buy on Tuesday and a dealer sell on Friday, with three days of spread moves mixed into the difference. Measured that way, a bond's "spread" is mostly volatility. This is why Barclays built its Liquidity Cost Score from trader quotes (§2.9.1), and why RFQ data is the better cost instrument: an RFQ records competing quotes for the same bond within the same two-minute window. Where the 2026 desk departs: composites such as MarketAxess CP+ and Tradeweb Ai-Price (which covers about 30,000 US corporates, per Tradeweb's FY2025 10-K) now provide a continuous estimated mid. The remaining problem is not getting a mid. It is checking whether the composite deserves your trust (§2.3.2).

The first large academic look at the new protocol is Hendershott and Madhavan (2015), *Click or Call? Auction versus Search in the Over-the-Counter Market* (*Journal of Finance*). They study every US corporate bond transaction from January 2010 to April 2011, about 4.6 million trades. Electronic auctions account for 467,614 trades in 5,528 bonds and voice for 4,153,611 trades in 11,122 bonds, so about one trade in ten was electronic. Auctions lasted 5 to 20 minutes, and they turned out to be a workable source of liquidity even in bonds that rarely trade. The paper also carries a warning this book repeats often: traders choose the venue. Easy tickets go electronic and hard tickets go to the phone, so a raw comparison of "electronic cost" with "voice cost" flatters the wire. Every venue-choice model in Chapter 19 inherits that selection.

> **Trend Watch.** **Electronic share of US corporate bond trading, 2015–2026: IG crossed the halfway line, HY parked at a third.**
>
> | Period | US IG e-share | US HY e-share | Source and definition |
> | :-- | :-- | :-- | :-- |
> | 2015 | ≈20% | ≈6% | Coalition Greenwich (McPartland, June 10, 2025); notional *(approx.; as reported, not independently verified)* |
> | 2021 | ≈34% | ≈25% | Greenwich, *U.S. corporate bond trading in 2024 by the numbers* (Jan 2025); chart reading |
> | 2022 | ≈41% | ≈31% | Same; chart reading |
> | 2023 | 45% | 33% | Same |
> | Feb 2024 | 45% | 29% | Greenwich via The DESK (Mar 19, 2024) |
> | 2024 (full year) | 48% | 33% | Greenwich (Jan 2025); overall 44%, ADNV \$46.2bn, 125,723 trades/day, average ticket \$381k |
> | Feb 2025 | n/a | 30% | Greenwich Data Spotlight (Mar 17, 2025) |
