> | 2023 / 2024 / 2025 | ≈45% / 50% / 60% | ≈30% each year | MarketAxess 10-K estimates, as reported (company definition, above Greenwich's; not independently verified) |
>
> Protocol mix inside US e-volume: disclosed RFQ was 48.3% (2021), 42.3% (2022), 47.2% (2023) and 44.0% (2024) (Greenwich, Jan 2025). One systematic shop's own order flow shows the same shift more sharply. Man moved from "roughly 30% of our order flow in high yield and 60% in investment grade going through electronic venues, to over 90%" as of May 1, 2023 (`Man_Revolutions_in_Credit_Trading_2023 p.3`).
>
> **What it means for the desk.** IG crossed the halfway line on at least one definition in 2025, while HY has been stuck near a third for four years. The gap between them is the structural fact. Everything else in the table is an exercise in reading definitions, and the desk works through it below.

Theo's first instinct with a table like this is a banker's: find the biggest number and put it on a slide. Ines takes the mouse away from him. "Read it like a hand history, not a headline. Start with the gap." She points at the two columns. "IG went over half on somebody's definition in 2025. HY has sat around a third since 2022, four years. That isn't a slow adopter. That's a ceiling, and you want to know why before you draw a line through it."

"Fine. IG is 48%."

"Or about 60%. Or around half. Which?" She scrolls to the source column. Greenwich says 48% for full-year 2024. MarketAxess's own 10-K estimates, on the company's definition, say about 50% for the same year and about 60% for 2025. Barclays, as reported in September 2025, puts it around or above half on broader definitions. "Same market, same year. The difference is the word 'electronic.'" She counts its meanings on her fingers. *Fully electronic*: negotiated and executed on a venue. *Processed*: negotiated by voice or chat, booked electronically afterward. *Auto-executed*: no human touched it at all. "And then the denominator: notional, ticket count or customer volume. A ticket-count share runs higher than a notional share, because the wire got the small tickets first. Bondwave divides portfolio trading by *customer* volume; a platform quotes its share of TRACE, interdealer prints included. Splice two of those into one series and your fitted growth rate partly measures the change of definition. Kaz won't touch a series until somebody has written on it which 'electronic' it means and what it divides by. This week, that somebody is you."

Theo looks at the HY column again. 29% in February 2024, 30% in February 2025, against 33% for full-year 2024. "So HY went backwards?"

"HY went *harder*. When trading gets difficult the hard tickets go back to the phone, so the e-share falls. A monthly HY number is partly a difficulty indicator. That makes it useful for a router, and it makes it a terrible input to an adoption curve, which is why Kaz fits those on annual points only." She hands the mouse back. "Now you can put a number on a slide."

### 2.3.1 The adoption S-curve, with an honest ceiling

Asked to "project HY electronic share to 2030," ROBO fit a constant growth rate to the move from 6% (2015) to 33% (2024), compounded it six more years and returned
$$
0.33 \times \left(\frac{0.33}{0.06}\right)^{6/9} \approx 1.03,
$$
so 103% of HY would trade electronically by 2030. Nobody told it that $K \le 1$. ROBO has discovered a market in which more bonds trade electronically than trade.

The honest model is a logistic with a ceiling, and the intuition behind it is older than any bond market.

> **Math, Gently.** *Odds and the S-curve.* Picture a rumor loose in a school of 1,000 pupils. On the first morning ten of them know it. Each one who knows passes it on at a steady rate, but only to pupils who have not heard it yet. So at the start the rumor spreads slowly, because there are few tellers, and at the end it spreads slowly, because there is almost nobody left to tell. It spreads fastest when half the school knows, and a plot of "share who know" against time is an S. The top of the S is the size of the school, not infinity. There is a ceiling, $K$, and in a bond market the ceiling is set by the tickets that will never leave the phone. (ROBO's 103% is what happens when a model forgets the school has walls.) The trick that tames the S is to stop watching the share and watch the **odds**: those who know divided by those still to be told, $e/(K-e)$. On a logistic S-curve the odds grow by the same *percentage* every year, so their logarithm, the **log-odds**, rises in a straight line, and a straight line can be drawn with a ruler and two points. A tiny number: if a share climbs from 20% to 50% in ten years with $K = 1$, the odds go from $0.20/0.80 = 0.25$ to $0.50/0.50 = 1$, multiplying by 4. That is a growth rate of $r = \ln 4/10 \approx 0.139$ a year, and odds growing at that rate double every $\ln 2/r \approx 5$ years. The derivation below runs the real IG and HY points.

Two things sit inside the arithmetic, and both matter more than the projections.

*The ceiling is not identified from two points.* Each choice of $K$ gives a different line through the same two observations. Redo the fit with $K = 0.80$, roughly the ceiling Barclays has suggested for electronic execution (via The DESK, Jan 2025), and the fitted slope *rises* while the 2030 projection falls (the derivation below has the numbers). A lower ceiling means a *faster* implied adoption rate, because the same observed share is closer to the ceiling than it looked. You need curvature to estimate $K$, meaning at least three points with the curve visibly bending. The only bend in the US IG series is 2024 to 2025 (48% to 48%), a single year that could just as well be noise. In practice, $K$ comes from outside evidence, and §2.8's is blunt: at the end of 2023 about nine block trades in ten still went by phone or chat.

*Fit the right object.* If you fit all three parameters by least squares on the levels, an optimizer given the IG points $\{0.20, 0.48, 0.48\}$ is free to set $K$ at about 0.48, make $r$ as steep as its bounds allow and report that US IG electronification was over by about 2017. The fit is perfect, and meaningless. Kaz tried this. Kaz now treats a fitted ceiling equal to the latest observation as a diagnostic, not a result, and the code in §2.9 prints a warning when it happens. A ceiling also has a shelf life: portfolio trading (§2.6) put blocks on the wire as baskets, which moved $K$ itself, and a logistic with a fixed $K$ has no way of noticing.

#### The Full Derivation: fitting a ceiling from two points

Let $e_t \in (0, K)$ be the electronic share of notional in a segment at time $t$ (years):

$$
e_t = \frac{K}{1 + \exp\{-r\,(t - t_0)\}}, \qquad 0 < K \le 1,\; r > 0 .
$$

Here $K$ is the ceiling, the share that will eventually trade electronically (blocks that never leave the phone keep it below 1), $r$ is the adoption rate per year, and $t_0$ is the midpoint, where $e_{t_0} = K/2$. (This $r$ is an adoption rate, not the interest rate; the context never mixes them, but we flag it once.) Rearranging,

$$
\frac{e_t}{K - e_t} = \exp\{r\,(t - t_0)\} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad z_t(K) \equiv \ln\frac{e_t}{K - e_t} = r\,(t - t_0).
$$

For a fixed $K$, the generalized logit $z_t(K)$ is *linear in time*. Two dated observations therefore give a closed-form slope and midpoint:

$$
\hat r(K) = \frac{z_{t_2}(K) - z_{t_1}(K)}{t_2 - t_1}, \qquad \hat t_0(K) = t_1 - \frac{z_{t_1}(K)}{\hat r(K)} .
$$

Since $e_t/(K-e_t)$ is the odds of "electronic" relative to the ceiling, and those odds grow like $e^{rt}$, they double every $\ln 2/\hat r$ years.

Now plug in Greenwich's 2015 and 2025 numbers with $K = 1$. For IG, $z = \ln(0.20/0.80) = -1.3863$ in 2015 and $\ln(0.48/0.52) = -0.0800$ in 2025, so $\hat r_{IG} = 1.3063/10 = 0.131$ per year and the odds double every $0.6931/0.131 = 5.3$ years. For HY, $z = \ln(0.06/0.94) = -2.7515$ and $\ln(0.32/0.68) = -0.7538$, so $\hat r_{HY} = 0.200$ per year, with odds doubling every 3.5 years. Projected to 2030 with $K=1$, IG reaches $1/(1+e^{-0.573}) = 64\%$ and HY reaches $1/(1+e^{-0.245}) = 56\%$. These are *illustrative extrapolations*, not forecasts.

The ceiling-sensitivity fit works the same way. With $K = 0.80$, the IG slope rises to $\hat r_{IG}(0.8) = [\ln(0.48/0.32) - \ln(0.20/0.60)]/10 = 0.150$, and the 2030 projection falls to $0.8/(1 + e^{-1.158}) = 61\%$. HY becomes $\hat r = 0.211$ with a 2030 value of 53%.

### 2.3.2 The RFQ as an auction: why eleven anchored dealers are worth about two

Back to the cold open. Theo got eleven responses, and the instinct is that eleven is great. Order statistics say how great, and then say why the instinct is too generous.

> **Math, Gently.** *Order statistics, and the effective number of dealers.* An **order statistic** is what you get when you sort a handful of random draws and keep one of them by its rank: the smallest, the second smallest, the largest. The best offer in an RFQ is the smallest of the dealers' distances from fair value, and the cover is the second smallest. Picture eleven friends each guessing the fair price of a used car, and you get to buy at the lowest guess. More friends help, because with more draws one of them is likelier to land low; with independent guesses of the kind used below, doubling the friends roughly halves how far the best guess sits from the true price. But that only works if the friends guess independently. If all eleven have just read the same online listing, their guesses cluster around the listing, the listing's own error is shared by everyone, and no number of extra friends removes it. Eleven friends reading one listing are worth only a few independent ones, and the arithmetic that says how few gives the **effective number** of guessers. One more property makes the cover easy to think about. If the distances are *exponential*, the shape with no memory that Chapter 1 met as the wait for a phone to ring, then once you know the best quote, each of the others sits above it by a fresh exponential amount with the same mean as before. So the cover is to the winner what the winner is to mid: the gap from winner to cover is, on average, about as big as the winner's own distance from fair. A tiny number: five responders whose quotes share an anchor worth a quarter of their average distance from fair ($\phi = 0.25$) count as $5/(1 + 4 \times 0.25) = 2.5$ independent ones. Theo's eleven are worked in the derivation.

#### The Full Derivation: best-of-$n$ with a common anchor

Let $\delta_j \ge 0$ be dealer $j$'s quote distance from fair mid, for $j = 1, \dots, n$. For Theo's buy order this is the dealer's offer minus fair mid, in points of price. Suppose first that the $\delta_j$ are i.i.d. with CDF $F$ on $[0, \infty)$. The best quote is the minimum, $\delta_{(1)} = \min_j \delta_j$. It exceeds $x$ only if every quote exceeds $x$, so $\Pr(\delta_{(1)} > x) = \big(1 - F(x)\big)^n$, and by the tail-integral identity used in §2.2.2,

$$
\mathbb{E}\big[\delta_{(1)}\big] = \int_0^\infty \big(1 - F(x)\big)^n \, dx .
$$

For exponential distances with mean $\theta$, $1 - F(x) = e^{-x/\theta}$, so $(1-F(x))^n = e^{-nx/\theta}$ and

$$
\mathbb{E}\big[\delta_{(1)}\big] = \frac{\theta}{n}.
$$

The *cover* is the second-best quote, $\delta_{(2)}$. Because the exponential is memoryless, once the best quote is known the other $n-1$ quotes exceed it by i.i.d. exponential amounts with mean $\theta$. The gap from winner to cover is the minimum of those $n-1$ excesses:

$$
\mathbb{E}\big[\delta_{(2)} - \delta_{(1)}\big] = \frac{\theta}{n-1}, \qquad \frac{\mathbb{E}[\delta_{(2)} - \delta_{(1)}]}{\mathbb{E}[\delta_{(1)}]} = \frac{n}{n-1}.
$$

In this model the expected cover gap is about as large as the winner's own distance from mid. Theo's three-eighths cover suggests his winner was also roughly three-eighths from fair, which is plausible for a B3 bond *(illustrative)*. The best quote improves like $1/n$, which is the arithmetic behind every platform's claim that more responders means better prices.

Now the correction. In 2026 most dealers that answer a small RFQ do so with an auto-quoter, and every auto-quoter starts from a composite mid. Write each quote distance as a common part plus an idiosyncratic part:

$$
\delta_j = A + \varepsilon_j, \qquad A \ge 0,\;\; \mathbb{E}[A] = \phi\,\theta, \qquad \varepsilon_j \overset{\text{i.i.d.}}{\sim} \text{Exp}\big(\text{mean } (1-\phi)\,\theta\big),
$$

with $A$ independent of the $\varepsilon_j$ and $\phi \in [0,1]$ the *anchoring share*: the fraction of the average quote distance shared by every responder, such as the composite's own error or a common hedging cost. The minimum of $A + \varepsilon_j$ is $A + \min_j \varepsilon_j$, so

$$
\mathbb{E}\big[\delta_{(1)}\big] = \phi\,\theta + \frac{(1-\phi)\,\theta}{n}, \qquad \mathbb{E}\big[\delta_{(2)} - \delta_{(1)}\big] = \frac{(1-\phi)\,\theta}{n-1}.
$$

Competition can only compete away the idiosyncratic part. Define the *effective number of dealers* $n_{\text{eff}}$ as the number of independent dealers ($\phi = 0$) that would give the same expected best quote, so $\theta/n_{\text{eff}} = \phi\theta + (1-\phi)\theta/n$:

$$
n_{\text{eff}} = \frac{n}{1 + (n-1)\,\phi}, \qquad \lim_{n \to \infty} n_{\text{eff}} = \frac{1}{\phi}.
$$

This is the same formula as the effective number of independent bets in an equicorrelated portfolio, and the resemblance is not a coincidence. Set $n = 11$ and $\phi = 0.45$: $n_{\text{eff}} = 11/(1 + 4.5) = 2$. Eleven responders anchored to one composite at $\phi \ge 0.45$ are worth no more than two independent ones, and no number of responders gets you past $1/\phi$, about 2.2.

Anchoring also explains why a bad morning can look milder in the count than it was. On 9 April 2025 half the responders to a US high-grade RFQ vanished (§2.9.3 has the numbers). Independent dealers would have doubled the best quote's expected distance; anchored at $\phi = 0.45$, $n_{\text{eff}}$ fell only from about 2.0 to about 1.9, so the damage had to come from $\theta$, the scale of every quote, or from $\phi$ itself moving as the composites stopped deserving trust. The desk argues about which, live, in §2.9.3.

The cover gap is a weaker witness than it looks, because it measures only the idiosyncratic part. Tradeweb's median distance to cover hit a record low in 2024 (The DESK, Jan 29, 2025), which is what more competition predicts and *also* what more anchoring predicts; only the winning quote measured against an independent fair value can tell them apart. A dealer who declines to quote is a censored observation, the `5MM+` lesson again: it says $\delta_j$ exceeded what that dealer was willing to show, and Chapter 18 models response jointly with the quote. And the auction has a common value, which Ines puts better than the algebra.

> **Poker Table.** She says it in a sentence: "Eleven responders is a big table. Order statistics say the best quote improves like $1/n$. The winner's curse says the one guy who knows you just left a lender call improves it like minus $1/n$." This is the common-value auction. When the bond's value is uncertain and the request itself carries information, each dealer has to ask what the bond is worth *given that it won*, and winning against more rivals is worse news. A rational dealer facing a possibly informed client shades more as $n$ grows, so on toxic flow the best quote can *worsen* with competition. The hand history is the markout: compare the fill to the composite five minutes, one hour and one day later, grouped by $n$. If markouts against the winner grow with $n$, the table is telling you who is informed. In most cases that is the client. Chapter 3 builds this as a counterparty-type model. Her version for Theo is shorter: "If the name is anywhere near a liability-management transaction, those aren't eleven opinions. They're eleven people deciding how much they believe you."

So the RFQ on a wire did two things to the desk's numbers. It made $\mathbb{E}[c]$ measurable at the moment of the trade, as a winner and a cover inside the same two minutes, and it turned every request, filled or not, into a labeled observation of $\Pr(\text{fill})$.

## 2.4 Revolution 2: All-to-All, or the Buy Side Learns to Quote

Kaz reads "all-to-all" as graph theory and asks, with real interest, whether the corporate bond market is now a complete graph. "It's a graph where the edges have prices," says Ines, "and half the nodes are lying about their degree." That is a fair one-line summary of what all-to-all trading changed. Anyone on the platform can respond to an RFQ, not only the dealers the client invited, and the anonymity that makes that safe for responders also hides which nodes are informed.

MarketAxess launched Open Trading, the largest all-to-all pool, in 2013 according to its own FY2025 10-K. Several slide decks you will see on the desk say 2012. The protocol is simple. A client's RFQ goes to its chosen dealers *and* to an anonymous pool of other participants, including asset managers, hedge funds, non-bank market makers and other dealers, and the platform stands between the two sides so neither has to take the other's credit. The effect was to turn the buy side from price takers into occasional price makers, and quants were among the first to take the other side:

> **[SOURCE EXTRACTION]** *Man_Quantitative_Credit_Alpha_Early_Mover_2022 p.6:* "larger players in quant credit have begun to make markets on the all-to-all electronic platforms, meaning that they are price makers as well as price takers."
>
> **Annotation.** This sentence changes what a quant credit fund *is*. A price taker needs a cost model. A price maker needs an *adverse-selection* model, because every time it answers an RFQ it is selling an option to whoever sent it. Man's primer put the scale at \$116.5bn of quant-fund volume on Open Trading in the first three quarters of 2020, up 150% year on year (Man, *Quant Credit: A Primer*, 2021). Where the 2026 desk departs: all-to-all has settled as a large structural minority, not a takeover. Open Trading carried 35.2%, 35.0% and 37.0% of eligible MarketAxess credit volume in 2023, 2024 and 2025, with about 1,800 participating firms (MarketAxess 10-Ks), and all-to-all was about 11% of total US market volume in April 2025 (Greenwich). The quant that answers RFQs is now an ordinary participant. What remains open is whether its quotes are smart enough to survive the RFQs it would rather not have answered.

The economics show up in two places. For liquidity *takers*, MarketAxess estimates 2025 price improvement on Open Trading of \$324.9mm, plus \$171.6mm for liquidity *providers*, \$496.4mm in total, measured against its CP+ composite (FY2025 10-K). The comparable totals were \$701.9mm in 2023 and \$488.8mm in 2024. For the market as a whole, Kozora, Mizrach, Peppe, Shachar and Sokobin (2020), *Alternative Trading Systems in the Corporate Bond Market* (NY Fed Staff Report 938), find that dealer participation on ATSs lowers customer trading costs by 24 to 32 bp, and that ATS trades are smaller, more often IG, and concentrated in older, less active issues. The last finding matters: all-to-all helps most in exactly the bonds where the dealer you invited was least interested.

And there is direct evidence that quotes from outside the relationship move prices. Hendershott, Li, Livdan, Schürhoff and Venkataraman (2026), *Quote Competition in Corporate Bonds* (*Journal of Finance* 81(4)), study dealer runs on about 24,000 bonds. A dealer's quote improves client execution by 6 to 7 bp just by being present. The best-quoting dealer wins only 15% of trades, and 16% to 40% of trades print worse than the best available quote. Non-relationship dealers handle 23% of trades when they quote, against 11% when they do not. The authors call quoting "not a zero-sum game." For a systematic desk, the 16%–40% trade-through range is a reminder that a best quote on a screen is not a fill, which is why §2.5 trains on fills.

Which brings the chapter to Ines's favorite object.

> **Math, Gently.** *A markout is a hand history.* After a poker hand, a serious player replays it: what did I know, what did they know, and what did the cards that came afterward say about who was right? A markout is the same replay for a trade. When you provide liquidity, you take a small edge at the moment of the fill, the price improvement you charged against the composite. Then you watch where the composite goes over the next five minutes, hour or day. If it moves against you, the person who traded with you knew something, or was early to something, and the move is what you paid for not knowing it. Your expected profit is the edge minus the expected adverse move, and both halves are averages over many hands, not a verdict on any single one. A tiny number: a provider buys at 3 bp better than the composite, and an hour later the composite has fallen 4 bp. The provider showed an edge of 3 and played a hand worth $3 - 4 = -1$ bp. It paid one basis point to be told, an hour late, what the other side already knew. Repeat that across a thousand fills and the platform's "price improvement" statistic will still report the 3. In symbols, it is one line.

The hand history, written down for a liquidity provider: let $h$ be the edge at the fill, the provider's price improvement relative to the composite, in bp of price. Let $m_H$ be the adverse markout at horizon $H$, how far the composite moves against the provider in the $H$ after the fill. The provider's expected P&L per unit notional, before hedging costs and under $\mathbb{P}$, is

$$
\mathbb{E}\big[\Pi^{\text{LP}}\big] = \mathbb{E}[h] - \mathbb{E}[m_H].
$$

The \$171.6mm in the 10-K is $\sum h$ summed over all provider fills. It is the edge the provider showed, not the hand it played. A provider whose markouts eat that edge has paid 1,800 firms for the privilege of being the last one to learn what they knew. Chapter 3 conditions $\mathbb{E}[m_H]$ on counterparty type and RFQ timing, which is where Theo's lender-call instinct becomes a feature.

> **View From Another Seat.** *The systematic fund as liquidity provider, in its own published words.* Put a systematic credit manager on the far side of Theo's all-to-all ticket and the RFQ looks like one row in a very long table. It arrives anonymous, with a size, a rating, an age and a time since the last print, and the fund's quoting engine prices it on those features within the response window, or declines. That seat also knows its limits, and the clearest public account comes from Man Numeric's Robert Lam and Paul Kamenski on Man's *Long Story Short* podcast ("Extra Credit: Algorithmic Advantage," recorded March 2024; quotations from the machine-generated transcript). Between them they describe execution as a daily choice of "venue selection" and "high touch or low touch," and Kamenski is explicit that there remain "circumstances where the best course of action is to trade voice." Lam takes up size: a 10–50 million block sent through a single dealer "might not be the optimal way"; the alternative is to "slice it" and route each piece to "the best venue and the best protocol." Read from Theo's chair, that is a warning as much as a description. The fund quoting tight on his \$4mm Halvorsen ticket may be the same fund slicing a block in Halvorsen across three venues that afternoon, and its quote on his RFQ is one of the slices. The anonymity that let it answer him is the anonymity that kept him from knowing.

> **Desk Myth vs. Desk Reality.** *Myth:* All-to-all means the dealer is dead. *Reality:* Dealers are among the most active responders in all-to-all pools, disclosed RFQ to chosen dealers still carried 44% of US e-volume in 2024 (Greenwich), and the client still picks dealers by hand: more than two-thirds of buy-side traders hand-pick their RFQ dealers, and about 80% say relationships drive venue choice (Greenwich, Dec 2023). All-to-all added nodes. It did not delete the relationships, and it gave them a measurable price.

All-to-all, then, raised $\Pr(\text{fill})$ for small tickets in exactly the bonds the invited dealers liked least, and it put the buy side on the other side of $\mathbb{E}[c]$, where one firm's cost of a fill is another firm's edge minus its markout.

## 2.5 Revolution 3: Automation, or Algos Answering Algos

Theo's eleven responses came back in under two minutes, and several came back in about a second. "Those weren't traders," says Ines. "They were parameters. Somebody set a size limit, a spread tolerance around the composite and a list of names to stay away from, and then went to lunch."

Automation is the revolution hidden inside the word "electronic." On the buy side, about 60% of credit participants used some form of automated execution by late 2024, up from about 40% (Barclays survey via The DESK, Jan 2025; Man's 2025 *Systematic Credit: A New Frontier* cites the same 60%). MarketAxess counted 204, 245 and 261 client firms using its automated and algorithmic tools in 2023, 2024 and 2025, and dealers sent 32.5 million algorithmic responses in 2023 and 40.9 million in 2024 (10-Ks). On Trumid, 75% of RFQs executed "no-touch" in Q4 2024 (The DESK, Jan 10, 2025), and 88% of eligible RFQ line items did by September 2025 (The DESK, Oct 8, 2025). Tradeweb's AiEX handled more than 40% of its institutional trades in 2025, against 30% in 2021 (FY2025 10-K). Vanguard automates about 70% of its traded volume, up from about 40%, and still sends nothing without a trader watching (The DESK, Oct 2026). FINRA's within-a-minute count from §2.2.1 is the regulator's view of the same thing: a print that arrives in seconds was never touched by a human booking clerk.

What automation needs is a router that decides, for each line, which protocol to try and in what order. Man described the inputs to theirs:

> **[SOURCE EXTRACTION]** *Man_Revolutions_in_Credit_Trading_2023 p.5:* "We can see whether a security is actually available for RFQ, filtering to only high-quality RFQ participants as well as on the frequency of RFQs, the rate of completed trades, and whether a given trade size is digestible in RFQ form."
>
> **Annotation.** Read it as a feature list. "Available for RFQ" is the feasible set from §2.1. "High-quality RFQ participants" is a dealer-level score built from response rates, quote quality and markouts. "Frequency of RFQs" and "rate of completed trades" are a bond-level fill-rate history. "Digestible" trade size is a size-dependent fill probability. Every item is estimated from venue logs, and none of them existed before the venues did. Where the 2026 desk departs: in 2023 this was a filter that removed bad candidates before a trader decided. On a 2026 desk, the same features feed a model that *chooses* the protocol and the order of attempts. It still keeps a human on the kill switch, because the parameters that work on a calm Tuesday are not the ones you want on a gap day.

Man also named the dataset that makes the router trainable:

> **[SOURCE EXTRACTION]** *Man_Revolutions_in_Credit_Trading_2023 p.4:* "Electronic venues give us greater insight into these imbalances – such as realised prints, bid/ask spreads, or trades that were attempted but not executed – and thus greater confidence in identifying and quantifying liquidity and costs."
>
> **Annotation.** The key phrase is "trades that were attempted but not executed." A voice market records only the trades that happened. An electronic market also records the ones that failed: the RFQ nobody answered, the quote that was too wide, the order that was pulled. Those failures are the negative labels a fill-probability model needs. Without them you are fitting $\Pr(\text{fill})$ on a sample in which every trade filled, which gives you a model that is always optimistic.

### 2.5.1 The router as a cost-minimization problem

Ines pulls one line from the morning's rebalance to show Theo how the router thinks, on the theory that a formula is easier to trust once you have watched it decide something. The line is \$2mm of a 7-year BBB *(all numbers illustrative)*. The router has several doors it could knock on, and the notation indexes them by $p$: an all-to-all RFQ, a disclosed RFQ to chosen dealers, a session or mid-match, inclusion in a portfolio trade, or voice.

For each door it asks three questions about the line, whose features are collected in $x$. The first is how likely the door is to open: the fill probability $\pi_p(x) = \Pr(\text{fill} \mid x, p)$. Ines points at the all-to-all column, which says 0.55. "Logistic model, fitted on attempted-and-failed labels. The table everybody tries to drop because it has no trades in it." The second is what it costs if the door does open: $c_p(x) = \mathbb{E}[c \mid \text{fill}, x, p]$, the expected one-way cost given a fill, in bp of price relative to fair mid. All-to-all shows 4 bp. The disclosed RFQ to dealers shows 7 bp, with a 90% fill rate. The third question is the one every new trader forgets: what does it cost if the door stays shut? That is $\kappa(x)$, the cost of *not* filling: the expected cost of the next attempt plus the price of carrying the unintended position from §2.1 until then. A simple form is $\kappa = c^{\text{next}} + \tfrac{\gamma}{2}\,\sigma_\epsilon^2\, T^{\text{wait}} + \alpha^{\text{decay}}$, with $\gamma$ risk aversion, $\sigma_\epsilon^2$ the line's residual variance per year, $T^{\text{wait}}$ the expected wait in years, and $\alpha^{\text{decay}}$ the signal lost while waiting. On this line the router has $\kappa$ at 20 bp.

"Why does waiting cost anything," Theo asks, "if the bond's expected return is the same next week?"

Kaz answers before Ines can. "Because the bond doesn't sit still while you wait. Its residual wanders like a random walk, so the variance piles up in proportion to the wait, and a risk-averse desk charges itself for variance." (Chapter 1's drunk and lamppost is the picture; §6.1.1 does it properly.) "Two percent a year of residual vol, two weeks' wait, risk aversion ten: $\tfrac{10}{2} \times 0.02^2 \times 2/52$, about 0.8 bp. Small. Most of the twenty is the next attempt and the signal going stale."

All expectations are under $\mathbb{P}$. The expected all-in cost of a single attempt is

$$
J_p(x) = \pi_p(x)\,c_p(x) + \big(1 - \pi_p(x)\big)\,\kappa(x),
$$

and the one-shot router picks $p^\star = \arg\min_p J_p(x)$. For the disclosed RFQ on its own, that is $0.90 \times 7 + 0.10 \times 20 = 8.3$ bp.

Real routers try doors in sequence, though, and a failed attempt has a price of its own: information leakage, $\chi_p \ge 0$, the adverse move caused by showing the order and not trading. Showing this line anonymously and failing costs about 1.5 bp. Is it worth knocking on the cheap door first? The answer has the shape of a bet, which is why Ines likes it. Trying all-to-all first pays when the *odds* of filling exceed the ratio of what failure leaks to what success saves. Success saves $8.3 - 4 = 4.3$ bp; failure leaks 1.5 bp; so the threshold odds are $1.5/4.3 = 0.35$. The fill odds are $0.55/0.45 = 1.22$, comfortably above, so the router tries all-to-all first, at an expected cost of 6.6 bp against 8.3 bp for going straight to dealers.

Then Ines changes one thing. She retypes the line as a stressed HY credit two weeks before an exchange offer. $\chi_A$ jumps, because the anonymous pool is full of people who read the same 8-K; $\pi_A$ falls; and the inequality flips. The router sends it to a trader. It turns out the formula agrees with Mags, and Mags, from across the desk, says the formula took its time.

"So when do I stop trusting it?" Theo asks.

"It's for the lines you'd never have looked at anyway," Ines says. "Three hundred small IG tickets in a rebalance, each one a near-repeat of thousands of labeled attempts. It doesn't beat you on the hard line. It gives you the afternoon back for the hard lines." She taps the corner of the screen where the no-touch fill rate sits. "And the first thing that tells you it's broken isn't a loss. It's the auto-ex fills drying up, an hour before the P&L notices. By the time the cost model looks wrong, it's been wrong for a while."

#### The Full Derivation: the sequential router

Trying all-to-all first and falling back to disclosed RFQ costs

$$
J_{A \to R} = \pi_A c_A + (1 - \pi_A)\big(\chi_A + J_R\big).
$$

Subtract this from $J_R$ and rearrange. Trying all-to-all first is better if and only if $\pi_A (J_R - c_A) > (1 - \pi_A)\chi_A$, or, assuming $J_R > c_A$,

$$
\frac{\pi_A}{1 - \pi_A} \;>\; \frac{\chi_A}{J_R - c_A}.
$$

The odds of filling must exceed the ratio of leakage cost to savings. On the BBB line ($c_A = 4$, $\pi_A = 0.55$, $J_R = 8.3$ and $\chi_A = 1.5$, all in bp), $J_{A\to R} = 2.2 + 0.45 \times 9.8 = 6.6$ bp, the number Ines read off the screen.

> **Ways This Blows Up.** *Fair-weather parameters.* Every number in the router was estimated on 2023–2025 data, mostly in calm markets. In stress, dealers widen their algorithm parameters or switch them off, fill rates fall and leakage rises, and all of it happens at once. At FILS Europe in 2026, a Vanguard trader recalled that in the Russia–Ukraine shock "a lot of algos and PT execution got turned off," whereas in April 2025 they "stayed there," and a Swiss Life Asset Managers trader said platforms and electronic liquidity providers "help more in quiet markets or normal market conditions" (The DESK, 15 Oct 2026). In March 2026, median EUR IG bid-ask rose to 64% above its January average, and it took 4 weeks (EUR IG), 6 (US HY), 8 (US IG) and 13 (EUR HY) to normalize (MarketAxess data via The DESK, Oct 1, 2026). A router trained on the calm sample will be most confident on exactly the day it is most wrong. Condition $\pi_p$, $c_p$ and $\chi_p$ on a stress regime variable (§2.7 offers one: the ETF–NAV basis), and give the kill switch to a human.

Automation, then, pushed $\Pr(\text{fill})$ on small, calm lines close to a constant, and it turned $\mathbb{E}[c]$ from a measurement into a forecast: a forecast that is good in exactly the weather it was trained in.

## 2.6 Revolution 4: Portfolio Trading

"A portfolio trade," says Mags, "is a mystery box, except the dealer gets to look inside before paying, and the index closes at four so everyone gets to be surprised at the same time."

A portfolio trade (PT) is one negotiation and one price for a basket of many bonds, sometimes hundreds of lines and sometimes a mix of buys and sells, executed all-or-none with a single dealer. The dealer prices the basket as a whole, hedges its systematic risk at once (a Tradeweb executive described a 1,000-line PT hedged with at most seven Treasury trades; The DESK, Jan 29, 2025) and works off the idiosyncratic residue over days. Tradeweb says it offered the first corporate-bond PT in 2019 (FY2025 10-K). FIMSAC recommended a TRACE flag for portfolio trades in February 2020. FINRA's portfolio-trade modifier became mandatory on May 15, 2023, for trades between two parties, in at least ten unique issues, at a single basket price (FINRA RN 22-12). Before that date nobody could measure PT share from public data. After it, everybody could, and everybody used a different denominator.

Man's account of the first boom:

> **[SOURCE EXTRACTION]** *Man_Revolutions_in_Credit_Trading_2023 p.2:* "We found that orders attracted high fill rates as competition for trades proliferated, not only among what we would consider tier-one counterparties but also those in the second tier, with aggressive pricing offered."
>
> **Annotation.** This describes 2021, which Man called "the year of portfolio trading." For a systematic book, high fill rates on a basket solve the §2.1 problem at once: a 300-line rebalance either fills completely or does not fill at all, so there is no half-executed portfolio to carry. The second-tier dealers matter too, because they meant more effective competitors in the sense of §2.3.2. Where the 2026 desk departs: the boom did not last, and §2.6.2 tells the reversal. Fill rates are a property of dealer balance sheets, and balance sheets change.

### 2.6.1 What a dealer bids for a basket

A dealer pricing a 300-line basket at 3:15 p.m. starts from fair value, subtracts what each line would cost to trade alone, adds back a credit, $\Pi(w)$, for the lines that net against inventory or go straight into an ETF creation basket (the cheapest exit a bond ever gets), and charges, at its risk aversion $\gamma$, for the residue left after hedging the basket's market exposure, which will take days to work off. That last term is where baskets beat blocks, and it is built out of covariance.

> **Math, Gently.** *Covariance, and the quadratic form.* Variance measures how much one thing wobbles. **Covariance** measures how much two things wobble *together*. A basket's risk is not the sum of its lines' risks, because their wobbles partly cancel, and the bookkeeping that adds up every pair's covariance is called a **quadratic form**, written $w^\top \Sigma\, w$: the notionals $w$ on both sides, the covariance matrix $\Sigma$ in the middle, every pair of lines counted. The intuition is a crowd. Fifty people shouting at random do not produce an average shout fifty times as wild as one person's; the shouts partly cancel, and the average of 50 independent voices has $1/50$ of the variance of a single voice. Now suppose each voice follows a conductor a little, with a correlation of 0.2. The conductor's part does not cancel, so however large the crowd grows, its average is never quieter than a fifth of one shout. A tiny number: for 50 voices with correlation 0.2, the average carries $(1 + 49 \times 0.2)/50 = 10.8/50 = 0.216$ of one voice's variance, against $1/50 = 0.02$ with no conductor at all. A dealer's basket is the crowd, the residual correlation between its lines is the conductor, and the basket's risk charge scales with that fraction. The dealer's version follows.

Mags's mystery box is the term the formula leaves out, which is adverse selection. The client knows which lines it most wants to get rid of, and a basket priced on average line costs invites the client to stuff it with the worst ones. Dealers respond by pricing line by line and adding a charge for the basket's composition. Chapter 19 estimates that charge. Theo's instinct, which Chapter 13 turns into the Priming Risk Score, is to screen the lines before anyone prices them: a 150-line HY basket can hide two or three liability-management candidates, and spotting them is an RSSG skill.

#### The Full Derivation: what a basket's risk charge nets

Let $w$ be the vector of signed notionals in the basket ($w_i > 0$ if the dealer buys line $i$), $P_i^{\text{mid}}$ each line's fair mid, and $c_i^{\text{line}}$ its standalone half-spread. A skeleton for the dealer's bid, with the full engine in Chapter 19, is

$$
B_{\text{PT}} = \sum_i w_i P_i^{\text{mid}} \;-\; \sum_i |w_i|\, c_i^{\text{line}} \;+\; \Pi(w) \;-\; \frac{\gamma}{2}\, T_{\text{liq}}\; w^\top \Sigma_\epsilon\, w .
$$

The first term is fair value. The second is the sum of single-line costs. $\Pi(w) \ge 0$ is the *netting credit*: the value of being able to net lines against existing inventory or deliver them into an ETF creation basket. The last term is the risk charge on the residual after the hedge, with $\gamma$ the dealer's risk aversion, $T_{\text{liq}}$ the liquidation horizon in years and $\Sigma_\epsilon$ the residual covariance of returns per unit notional per year.

Here is why baskets are cheaper than blocks. Take $N$ equal lines of notional $w$, total $M = Nw$, with residual variance $\sigma^2$ per line and a common residual correlation $\rho_\epsilon$. Then $w^\top \Sigma_\epsilon w = w^2\sigma^2\,[N + N(N-1)\rho_\epsilon]$, and the risk charge per dollar of basket is

$$
\frac{\gamma}{2}\,T_{\text{liq}}\,\sigma^2 M \cdot \frac{1 + (N-1)\rho_\epsilon}{N}.
$$

A single-name block of the same size $M$ carries the factor 1 in place of the fraction. So a \$100mm, 200-line basket with uncorrelated residuals carries $1/200$ of the idiosyncratic risk charge of a \$100mm block in one bond *(illustrative)*. The fraction $(1 + (N-1)\rho_\epsilon)/N$ is $1/n_{\text{eff}}$ from §2.3.2 again. Diversification across lines, like competition across dealers, cannot get past the common component. With $\rho_\epsilon = 0.1$, no basket goes below one-tenth of the block charge.

### 2.6.2 Case Study: The Portfolio-Trading Cycle, 2021–2026

*A Thursday in 2026, 2:50 p.m. The monthly rebalance is 312 lines, and for the first time Theo has been asked to decide how it goes out. The desk, its rebalance and its dialogue are invented; the dated market facts and the quoted words of real people come from the sources cited.*

Theo's first draft is one basket. It seems obvious: one negotiation, one price, all-or-none, nothing half-executed to carry overnight, and the four o'clock index mark to hide in. He posts the draft in the desk channel with the word "Proposed," which on this desk is an invitation to be argued with.

Mags reads it first. "One basket. Very elegant. In 2021 that would have been free money." She swivels her chair, which means a story is coming. "I was running distressed then, so I watched from the cheap seats, and from the cheap seats it looked like a fire sale in reverse. Every dealer on the street was bidding baskets like they were giving them away. Second-tier banks I had never once seen quote a CCC were sending tight levels on two-hundred-line lists. You handed them a basket full of bonds nobody wanted and they took it a couple of basis points inside what the lines would have cost you one at a time."

"Why would they?"

"Because they could get rid of them. The ETFs were growing, the banks had built algorithms to price every line, and a bond you could push into an ETF creation basket had an exit nobody needed to negotiate. I asked a salesman once why his desk was being so generous. He said, 'We're not generous. We're fast.'" She shrugs. "Then 2022 came, and they stopped being fast."

"So what did you do?" Theo asks.

Nobody answers at once, because the honest answer is that it depended on what you looked at first. Ines types the question into the channel instead, and leaves it there for him.

#### Decision point: February 2022

*Last month your 300-line basket priced 2 bp over mid. Today the same kind of basket prices at 9. Do you pay, unbundle it into 300 RFQs, or wait a week? And what would tell you that this is a regime and not a bad week?*

Theo's instinct is a banker's: wait. Markets have bad weeks, and nobody refinances into a bad week. Kaz's instinct is a quant's: unbundle, or at least price it both ways. If the summed all-in costs of 300 single-line RFQs, $\sum_i J_{\text{RFQ},i}$, come in under $J_{\text{PT}}$, then the basket is simply the wrong protocol this month and there is nothing to wait for. Ines's question is the one that decides between them. "Which term moved?" If it is a bad week, it is mostly the risk charge: dealers' $\gamma$ spikes for a few days and comes back. If it is a regime, it is $\Pi(w)$. The netting credit is structural; it rests on the ETF plumbing and on dealer inventory, and it does not come back until they do. The tell is the gap between portfolio-trade costs and RFQ costs on comparable lines, measured by markouts rather than by quotes, together with whether ETF creation activity is falling alongside it. In early 2022 both were moving the same way, and they kept moving for months. A week of waiting would have bought a slightly worse basket.

Here is what actually happened, in dated order.

**2021, the boom.** Mags's fire sale in reverse. Man moved most of its order flow from voice into portfolio trades (`Man_Revolutions p.2`).

**H1 2022, the reversal.** Rates rose and spreads widened. Kaz reads it in the four terms of §2.6.1: two moved at once. The netting credit $\Pi(w)$ collapsed, because the custom ETF baskets that made it cheap to recycle bonds went away, and $\gamma$ rose as every bank pulled balance sheet. Smaller $\Pi$, bigger $\gamma$: a lower bid, with nothing about the bonds inside the basket changed (`Man_Revolutions pp.2–3`). Man Numeric's Paul Kamenski later recalled on Man's *Long Story Short* podcast that 2021 "was the year of portfolio trading," and that in 2022 changes to ETF creation and redemption made it "harder for those desks to recycle risk," while "transaction costs generally went up substantially" ("Extra Credit: Algorithmic Advantage," recorded March 2024; machine-generated transcript). It was a bad year for the strategy class as a whole: eVestment data cited by IFR show systematic credit funds down about 15% on average in 2022, with assets down 27% to about \$52bn, and transaction costs more than doubled (IFR, "Quant credit rebounds after tough period"). Man's response was to move more than 90% of flow onto electronic venues, mostly as single-line RFQs:

> **[SOURCE EXTRACTION]** *Man_Revolutions_in_Credit_Trading_2023 p.5:* "The vast majority of our trades are now sent as RFQs, leading to significant savings in transaction costs versus portfolio trades."
>
> **Annotation.** This is the router of §2.5.1 run on a whole book. When $\Pi(w)$ collapses and $\gamma$ rises, $J_{\text{PT}}$ climbs above $\sum_i J_{\text{RFQ},i}$, and a cost-minimizing desk unbundles the basket. Note what Man did *not* conclude: it did not decide that PT was a fad. It changed protocol because the costs changed, and the same logic sends flow back to PT when the costs reverse. Where the 2026 desk departs: today the PT-versus-RFQ decision is made line by line and day by day, inside the router. In 2023 it was an allocation decision made by people.

**2023–2026, the resurgence.** The TRACE modifier made PT measurable from May 2023. Costs fell: MarketAxess's median IG bid-ask went from 0.19 points in 2022 to 0.11 in 2024 (IFR). PT share then climbed through every denominator in the Trend Watch at the end of this section.

The resurgence did not wait for calm markets, either: baskets carried a real share of the April 2025 tariff week, which §2.9.3 replays. By 2026, 78% of institutions were using portfolio trading, five points more than a year earlier (Greenwich, via The DESK, May 15, 2026). The basket had become infrastructure, which is not the same thing as being cheap.

**How it would have traded.** A systematic desk with Ines's tell would have routed each rebalance by $\min\{J_{\text{PT}}, \sum_i J_{\text{RFQ},i}\}$ every day, sweetened baskets with liquid lines the dealer prices cheaply, pulled the illiquid lines that raise $\gamma$, and treated protocol share as **regime-switching, not a trend**: a two-state model driven by dealer balance sheet and ETF-basket economics fits 2021–2026 better than any S-curve.

Theo's 312 lines go out, in the end, as two things: a basket of 260 lines whose basket price beats their summed RFQ costs, and 52 lines that do not, which the router takes one at a time *(illustrative)*. Mags observes that in 2021 the dealers would have taken all 312 and thanked him. Kaz observes that 2021 was a regime, and that the point of a regime model is not to be nostalgic about one. Ines says nothing, and adds a column to the rebalance log: the PT-minus-RFQ markout gap, one number a month, the regime variable the desk did not have in February 2022.

> **Trend Watch.** **Portfolio trading, 2021–2026: from novelty to infrastructure, measured with at least three denominators.**
>
> | Period | Measure | Value | Source |
> | :-- | :-- | :-- | :-- |
> | 2021 → 2022 | PT share of US e-volume (protocol mix) | ≈7% → ≈10% | `Man_Revolutions p.4`, Fig. 4, Greenwich MarketView; chart reading |
> | 2023 | PT share of TRACE | ≈7–8% | Tradeweb's Ted Husveth, via The DESK (Jan 29, 2025) |
> | 2023 | PT share of *customer* volume | ≈5% | Bondwave, "A Market Transformed" (May 20, 2026) |

> **What it means for the desk.** "PT is about 11–12% of the market" and "PT is about 20% of the market" are both true. The first uses TRACE, which includes interdealer prints, as the denominator. The second uses customer volume. Pick one and label it. Index-time clustering is now a structural feature: nearly half of PT volume prints at or after the index pricing time (Bondwave), so cost models need a time-of-day term, and a backtest that fills rebalances at the 4 p.m. mark is assuming the most crowded fill of the day. The basket arbitrage is also compressing. Bondwave's PT execution-quality percentile drifted from 57.3 (May 2023) to 50.3 (February 2026), toward the median, which is what competition does to an edge.

Portfolio trading, then, created fills for baskets that no single-bond RFQ could absorb, turning $\Pr(\text{fill})$ for a whole rebalance into one or zero, and it made $\mathbb{E}[c]$ a function of dealer balance sheets and ETF plumbing, which is to say a regime variable.

## 2.7 Revolution 5: ETFs as the Liquidity Backbone

Bond ETFs did something the cash market could not do for itself. They gave credit an exchange-traded, continuously priced, penny-wide instrument whose underlying is a basket of bonds that might not trade all week. Global bond ETF assets went from under \$10bn in 2009 to more than \$1.2tn in 2020 (Todorov, *BIS Quarterly Review*, March 2021) and about \$2.6tn at the end of 2024, when ETFs took about 40% of fixed-income fund flows (iShares, Apr 23, 2025). US bond ETFs held \$1.8tn at end-2024, 17% of US ETF assets (ICI 2025 Fact Book). BlackRock projects \$6tn globally by 2030, which is a forecast by the largest issuer, and reads like one.

The structural change was regulatory. The SEC adopted Rule 6c-11 on September 26, 2019 (press release 2019-190), allowing ETFs to use *custom* creation and redemption baskets under written policies. That turned the ETF into a tool for moving baskets of bonds. An authorized participant (AP) can now assemble a creation basket from bonds it wants to get rid of, or accept a redemption basket of bonds a dealer wants to buy. (Kaz, meeting the phrase for the first time, took an authorized participant to be someone who had been given permission to participate, and asked who else was there without permission. "Everyone else," said Ines, which is closer to the truth than it sounds: an AP is one of a short list of firms with a contract to create and redeem shares directly with the fund, and everyone else trades the shares on the exchange.) The result is what Todorov's anatomy shows: US corporate-bond ETF creation baskets cover only about 20% of holdings and redemption baskets about 35%, the holdings' bid-ask is about 17 times the ETF's (against about 5 times for equity ETFs), and for the largest bond ETF a basket can be as small as about 3% of holdings. Koont, Ma, Pástor and Zeng (NBER w30039; *RFS* 2025 with Sialm) show that ETFs actively manage these baskets, trading off index tracking against liquidity transformation, and that basket inclusion improves a bond's liquidity, except when creation or redemption imbalances are large.

### 2.7.1 The ETF discount as the price of immediacy

> **Math, Gently.** *No-arbitrage bands, and a NAV that is wrong.* Picture a gift card for a shop that is shut for the week. The card says \$100. Nobody will pay you \$100 for it today, because the only way to turn it into goods is to wait until the shop reopens, and waiting costs something, so the card trades a little below face, by the cost of waiting. It cannot trade *far* below face, though, because anyone could buy it cheap, wait, and spend it in full. The range between where the card can drift and where someone steps in is a **no-arbitrage band**: the price can wander inside it, and its edges are set by what the arbitrage costs to do. Now add a rumor that the shop's stockroom flooded. The card trades below face by the cost of waiting *plus* whatever you heard about the shop, and the \$100 printed on it is not exactly wrong, just out of date. A bond ETF is the card, its NAV is the printed face, and the authorized participant is the person who can hand back shares for the underlying bonds and sell them. A tiny number: NAV is 100 and liquidating the redemption basket costs 2, so the arbitrage floor is 98; below 98 an AP buys shares, redeems, sells the bonds and keeps the difference. If the ETF prints at 95 and the 2 is honest, the AP's arithmetic says the price cannot be there unless the NAV itself is wrong. The 3 points below the floor are the market saying the marks are 3 points stale. The AP's two trades, in symbols, come next.

#### The Full Derivation: the arbitrage band with stale marks

Let $P^{\text{ETF}}_t$ be the ETF's price, $\mathrm{NAV}_t$ its published net asset value per share (built from evaluated bond prices, often at the bid), $\mathcal{C}^{\text{red}}_t$ and $\mathcal{C}^{\text{cr}}_t$ the AP's per-share cost of liquidating a redemption basket or assembling a creation basket, and $f$ the fixed fee per share. An AP who buys a share, redeems it and sells the basket earns $\mathrm{NAV}_t - \mathcal{C}^{\text{red}}_t - f - P^{\text{ETF}}_t$. An AP who buys a basket, creates and sells the share earns $P^{\text{ETF}}_t - \mathrm{NAV}_t - \mathcal{C}^{\text{cr}}_t - f$. With no arbitrage, both are nonpositive, which gives the band

$$
\mathrm{NAV}_t - \mathcal{C}^{\text{red}}_t - f \;\le\; P^{\text{ETF}}_t \;\le\; \mathrm{NAV}_t + \mathcal{C}^{\text{cr}}_t + f .
$$

The band assumes $\mathrm{NAV}_t$ is the true value of the basket. It is not. Evaluated prices lag, so write true basket value as $\mathrm{NAV}_t + \eta_t$, where $\eta_t$ is the information the ETF price has and the stale marks do not. Under selling pressure, the price sits at the lower edge of the band around the *true* value:

$$
P^{\text{ETF}}_t - \mathrm{NAV}_t \;\approx\; -\,\mathcal{C}^{\text{red}}_t \;+\; \eta_t \qquad (\text{with } f \text{ absorbed}).
$$

In a sell-off both terms push the same way. Liquidating the redemption basket is expensive, and the marks have not caught up with a falling market, so a measured discount is partly the price of immediacy and partly the NAV being wrong. Neither is a free lunch for the buyer: the first is a cost you are paid to bear, and the second goes away when the marks catch up. That makes the discount the cleanest real-time stress variable a credit desk has. It is observable every second, it combines the cost of immediacy with information about stale marks, and it is the regime input the router in §2.5.1 was asking for. On a calm day the ETF is an inexpensive hedge; on a stressed day it is where prices are discovered, as the March 2020 scene below and the April 2025 replay in §2.9.3 both show. Chapter 20 builds the full engine. As a share of cash bond volume, though, credit ETFs *shrank* in calm markets: the ETF-to-cash ratio fell from 23.2% in 2022 to 16.6% in 2024 (Greenwich), as portfolio trading took over part of the basket risk transfer. ETFs, PTs and cash bonds are now three routes for the same basket risk, and credit index futures are becoming a fourth (Cboe iBoxx futures block trades topped \$1bn a month in mid-2026; The DESK, Oct 2026).

> **View From Another Seat.** *The ETF market maker, and the opportunistic lender.* Two seats look at the bond ETF from opposite ends of the credit market. The first is the ETF liquidity provider, the firm quoting the share on the exchange all day and, when the share drifts from fair, deciding whether to create or redeem. A public account of that seat is the *ETF Central Podcast*, "Episode 19: Ugo Egbunike, Fixed Income Specialist at Jane Street Capital" (10 Jan 2024), on how ETF liquidity providers price products against one another across asset classes, and on why creation and redemption matter to anyone launching a fund. Described generically, that seat runs the band above in real time, every afternoon. The second seat is nowhere near an exchange. Apollo's John Zito, speaking at Bloomberg Invest on 4 March 2026, described a financing need that "requires very bespoke, long-duration capital that's not traditional to the CUSIP market" (Apollo, *Private Credit, Now in an ETF*, text dated 15 May 2026). For a seat like that, the electronic market this chapter describes is the edge of the map, the ceiling $K < 1$ of §2.3.1 seen from the other side: the cheaper the CUSIP market becomes to trade, the clearer it is which credit risks it cannot carry, and those are the risks the second seat is built to originate.

#### The Week the ETF Was the Only Price

*Thursday, after the close. Theo has spent the afternoon with Todorov's BIS article and the New York Fed's SMCCF page, and he has a question that is not in either of them. The dialogue and the cast's March 2020 seats are invented; the dates, discounts, facility milestones and research findings come from the sources cited, and no real person speaks.*

"Where were you all," he asks, "in March 2020?"

The desk has replayed that month before, on the whiteboard of §1.8. Theo is asking for something else: what the week felt like from the seats each of them actually had. They were scattered across three kinds of shop, and each remembers a different piece of the same week, like witnesses to an accident who were standing on different corners.

Ines goes first, because her corner was closest to the crash. In March 2020 she was running an investment-grade market-making book at a dealer. "Monday the ninth was the first day it felt wrong. Oil had collapsed over the weekend, everything was down, and the RFQs came in faster than we could price them. That part was normal, for a bad day. What wasn't normal was Wednesday and Thursday. Clients were calling to sell investment-grade bonds, good ones, ten-year paper from companies everybody has heard of, and we couldn't show a bid in size. Not wouldn't. Couldn't. The risk limits were full, the balance sheet was full, and every bond we bought at ninety we'd be marking at eighty-nine by the close."

"So what did you do?"

"We stopped being principal and became a phone book." She means it nearly literally. "A client calls to sell ten million. In February, I buy it, put it on my sheet and work it out over a week. In March, I say, 'Let me see who wants it,' and I ring round, and if I find a buyer I cross the two of them and take a small fee for the introduction. Nothing on my books. Agency." The academic account of her week is Kargar, Lester, Lindsay, Liu, Weill and Zúñiga (2021, *RFS*), who measured exactly that shift: trades moved from risky-principal to agency as dealers stopped committing capital, and customers' willingness to pay for immediacy rose by about 200 bp at the peak. MarketAxess later put the average US high-grade bid-ask at the COVID peak at 44.62 bp (MarketAxess, *AxessPoint*, 14 July 2025), in bonds that on an ordinary day trade a few basis points wide. "Two hundred basis points to trade *now* instead of next week," Ines says. "That's what immediacy cost. Most people paid it, because next week was the frightening part."

Mags remembers the same days from a dealer's distressed desk, which in March 2020 meant a desk that suddenly had very interesting things to buy and no idea what any of them were worth. "My first thought was opportunity. My second thought was: opportunity compared to *what*? I'd ask for a level on an IG bond, just to calibrate, and the answer would come back as a number and an apology." What she remembers most is the inversion. "The safe stuff was the stuff nobody could sell. You'd think high yield would be the disaster, and it was a disaster, but the investment-grade ETFs were trading at bigger discounts than the high-yield ones. Everybody who needed cash sold what they thought was liquid, and it turned out everybody thought the same thing was liquid." The published version is Haddad, Moreira and Muir (2021, *RFS*): safer bonds and IG ETFs were discounted *more* than HY, the inverted ranking you would expect if dealer balance sheet, not credit risk, was the scarce input.

Kaz was not on any desk at all. "I was finishing my thesis," they say, "on a problem in stochastic filtering that had nothing to do with bonds, and I was watching markets on a laptop in a university library, because that month everyone was watching something." What Kaz watched was LQD. On Thursday, 12 March 2020, the largest investment-grade corporate bond ETF closed at a 5.0% discount to its net asset value, and the Vanguard and SPDR intermediate corporate funds, VCIT and SPIB, closed at discounts of 3.2% and 3.1% (WealthManagement.com, 16 Mar 2020, as in §1.8.3). "Five percent. On the most liquid credit product in the world. I emailed a friend at a fund with the subject line 'free money?' Buy LQD, short the basket of bonds inside it, wait for the gap to close. A textbook arbitrage."

"Who sells you the basket?" says Ines.

"That," says Kaz, "was more or less the reply."

"It would have been me," Ines says. "I'm the one who'd have had to sell you that basket and deliver bonds I didn't own, in a market where I couldn't buy them either. I wasn't selling. Nobody was."

"And at what price?" says Mags. "At NAV? The NAV was a rumor. A rumor with four decimal places, computed at four o'clock by a pricing service from bonds that hadn't traded since Tuesday." She does not say it unkindly. She says it the way she says "adjusted EBITDA."

Theo is quiet for a moment, because his own corner of March 2020 was very different. He was ten weeks into the job at PJT, and that month nobody there watched bond prices. Everybody watched cash. "We were building thirteen-week cash flow models for every client that had just drawn its revolver," he says. "Thirty of them, maybe more. Every model asked the same question: how many weeks until the money runs out?" He pats the pocket with the USB stick in it. "I never once asked what the bonds were trading at. I assumed somebody knew."

"Somebody did," says Ines. "The ETF knew."

That sentence is what the BIS later spent a quarterly review establishing. Todorov's study of bond-ETF arbitrage (*BIS Quarterly Review*, March 2021) measured tracking errors above 200 bp in March 2020, against a historical average of 0.7 bp. The band of §2.7.1 had not broken. Its two terms had exploded at once. The cost of liquidating a redemption basket, $\mathcal{C}^{\text{red}}_t$, was enormous, because nobody could sell the bonds, and $\eta_t$, the gap between the stale marks and the truth, was large and negative, because the evaluated prices behind the NAV were still describing February. The 5% was both at once, and nothing on the screen said how much of each.

Some of the market did keep answering, and not the part anyone expected. "The people still responding to RFQs that month weren't all banks," Ines says. "Some were funds with models that said the bonds were cheap and no risk manager telling them the balance sheet was full." The numbers bear her out: §2.4's quant-fund volume on Open Trading grew 150% in the first three quarters of 2020. MarketAxess's own count points the same way, with the algorithmic share of the prices on its platform falling from 60% to 50% during 2020 (*AxessPoint*, 14 July 2025), a loss of machine presence that April 2025 did not repeat (§2.9.3). That is the paradox §2.9.3 takes up in Man's own words.

The rest of the spring belonged to the Fed, and Mags tells that part with something close to admiration. The Secondary Market Corporate Credit Facility, announced on 23 March and expanded on 9 April, was allowed to buy IG bonds and US-listed ETFs giving broad exposure to IG corporates. The New York Fed's "certain" purchases began on 12 May, and they were ETFs; the "additional" purchases, the individual bonds, followed on 16 June. For about five weeks the most powerful central bank on earth was trading credit through the same ticker as a dentist in Scottsdale. Purchase authority expired on 31 December 2020, ETF sales began on 7 June 2021 and bond sales on 12 July 2021, and by 31 August 2021 every holding had been sold or had matured (New York Fed SMCCF page). "The day the Fed said 'ETFs,'" Mags says, "I knew the ETF had won the argument. When the lender of last resort decides the fastest way into your market is a ticker symbol, the ticker symbol is the market." Haddad, Moreira and Muir's finding is the dry version: the announcements did most of the work, and the discounts closed well before the Fed had bought much of anything.

Ines writes one line on the whiteboard and leaves it there for Theo.

#### Decision point: 3:30 p.m., 12 March 2020

*Thursday. Your model says buy 40 IG bonds, and its signal has never been stronger. LQD is 5% below a NAV you do not believe. Do you send the 40 RFQs, buy the ETF instead, or sit on your hands, and why?*

Theo starts to answer. Ines shakes her head. "You've got one of the three tools. The band tells you what the 5% is made of. You haven't met the other two yet." The question stays on the board until §2.9.3.

ETFs, then, gave credit a fill when the bonds themselves had none, raising $\Pr(\text{fill})$ for basket risk at exactly the moment single-bond fills vanished, and they made the price of immediacy, $\mathbb{E}[c]$ for the whole market, a number on a screen that updates every second.
