## 7-B.6 The Statistical Bootstrap: Block, Stationary and Cluster

### The plug-in principle

You want the sampling distribution of a statistic $\hat\theta$ (a Sharpe ratio, an AUC, a default rate) and you have one sample. Efron's (1979) idea is to treat the empirical distribution as if it were the population: draw $n$ observations with replacement, recompute $\hat\theta^{*}$, repeat $B$ times, and use the spread of $\hat\theta^{*} - \hat\theta$ as a stand-in for the spread of $\hat\theta - \theta$. Percentile intervals are the simplest. Studentized (bootstrap-$t$) intervals, which resample a pivot $(\hat\theta^{*} - \hat\theta)/\widehat{\text{se}}^{*}$, are more accurate, and the extra computation is cheap next to a wrong answer.

### Why the i.i.d. bootstrap lies on credit data

Resampling single observations destroys dependence, and credit data are made of dependence. For an AR(1) series with autocorrelation $\rho$, the variance of the sample mean is approximately $\frac{\sigma^2}{T}\cdot\frac{1+\rho}{1-\rho}$; the i.i.d. bootstrap reports $\sigma^2/T$. Stale marks with $\rho = 0.3$ hide a factor of 1.86 in variance. Across issuers it is worse, because correlated defaults make one cohort close to one observation.

> **[SOURCE EXTRACTION]** *Bohn_Stein_Active_Credit_Portfolio_Management p.443:* "Thus, about half of the time, even with infinite data, we would mistake the default probability for 20 bps when it was actually 200 bps."
>
> **Annotation.** Bohn and Stein's setting is a portfolio with uniform asset correlation 0.25 and a true PD of 2%. Because defaults share a factor, the realized default rate of even an infinitely large portfolio is one draw from the distribution of the systematic factor, and that draw is often benign. Their next page describes the Hanson–Schuermann bootstrap, which resamples *firms*, and warns that multiyear bounds are hard "due to the dependence induced in the sample from year 1 to year 2" (p.444). The 2026 desk takes both warnings literally. Resample *years* (whole cross-sections), in blocks long enough to keep a cycle's persistence, never firms one at a time. And accept the limit no resampling scheme removes: twenty years of data hold two or three credit cycles, and the bootstrap never shows you a crisis you did not have. It only reshuffles the ones you did.

### Block and stationary bootstraps

The **moving block bootstrap** (Künsch 1989) resamples blocks of $\ell$ consecutive observations and concatenates them, so dependence within a block survives. The circular version wraps the series end to start so every observation is equally likely to be drawn. The **stationary bootstrap** (Politis and Romano 1994) draws block lengths from a geometric distribution with mean $1/p$: at each step, with probability $p$ start a new block at a random date, otherwise take the next date (circularly). The resampled series is itself stationary, which fixed-length blocks are not. Block length should grow like $T^{1/3}$; the Politis–White (2004) rule picks it automatically, and for overlapping returns it must be at least the overlap $h$.

### Panels: resample the unit that is independent

- **Dates, with the cross-section intact.** To keep both serial and cross-sectional dependence, resample blocks of months and carry every bond in each month along. Resample months, not bonds.
- **Issuers, with their history intact.** For issuer-level dependence, the cluster (pairs) bootstrap resamples issuers with replacement, each with all its bonds and months. This is the bootstrap analogue of (7B.2).
- **Few clusters.** With a dozen sectors, use the wild cluster bootstrap: keep $X$ fixed, multiply each cluster's residual vector by an independent random sign, rebuild $y^{*} = X\hat b_0 + u^{*}$ under the null, and refit (Cameron, Gelbach and Miller 2008).
- **Sharpe ratios.** To compare two strategies' Sharpe ratios, use a studentized circular block bootstrap of the difference (Ledoit and Wolf 2008), then deflate for the number of trials (§7.8, Law 12).

*Used in:* §7.6 (the sequential bootstrap for bagging over overlapping labels), §7.8 (Sharpe-ratio inference), §11.5 (confidence bands on AUC and hit rates), §14.2 (cohort uncertainty in cumulative incidence), §28.2 and §28.6 (breadth and drawdown confidence); collision with curve bootstrapping (§6.8) recorded in Appendix A §A.3.


## 7-B.7 Tree Ensembles in One Section

**A tree** partitions feature space by recursive binary splits. At each node it picks the feature $j$ and threshold $c$ that most reduce impurity (squared error for a return, Gini $\sum_k p_k(1 - p_k)$ or entropy for a default flag) and predicts the leaf average. Trees find thresholds and interactions a logit cannot ("distance to default below 1.5 *and* runway under 13 weeks"), and they are invariant to monotone transformations of features, so a leverage ratio needs no winsorizing. A single deep tree is also a high-variance estimator that memorizes its training set.

**Bagging** averages $B$ trees grown on bootstrap samples. If each tree's prediction has variance $\sigma^2$ and any two have correlation $\rho$, the average has variance

$$
\operatorname{Var}\Big(\frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^{B} f_b\Big) = \frac{1}{B^2}\big[B\sigma^2 + B(B-1)\rho\sigma^2\big] = \rho\,\sigma^2 + \frac{1 - \rho}{B}\,\sigma^2 ,
$$

which falls to $\rho\sigma^2$, not zero, as $B \to \infty$. This is Law 2 again, inside the model: forty-seven correlated trees are about one tree. Random forests (Breiman 2001) lower $\rho$ by letting each split consider only a random subset of features.

**Boosting** (Friedman 2001) builds the model in stages, $F_m(x) = F_{m-1}(x) + \nu\, h_m(x)$, where each small tree $h_m$ is fitted to the negative gradient of the loss at $F_{m-1}$ and $\nu \in [0.01, 0.1]$ is a learning rate. With log loss and $F$ in log-odds, the negative gradient is $y_i - p_i$, exactly the score contribution of §7-B.3. Boosting on log loss is a logistic regression that grows its own features. XGBoost (Chen and Guestrin 2016) adds second-order steps and regularization.

**What credit adds to the recipe.** (1) Cross-validate with purged, embargoed, parent-grouped folds (§7.7): trees can identify an issuer from a coupon-and-maturity pair and will happily learn the issuer instead of the economics. (2) Impose monotone constraints where the economics is not in doubt: PD non-decreasing in leverage, non-increasing in distance to default and in runway. (3) Recalibrate the output (§7-B.3); boosted log-odds are overconfident in the tails. (4) Remember that trees do not extrapolate. A tree has never heard of anything worse than the worst thing it has seen, so an issuer at 12× leverage scores like the most-levered leaf in training. (5) Rank features by permutation importance computed on held-out purged folds, not by in-sample impurity, which favors continuous, high-cardinality features. Measured honestly, the gain is real where the signal is nonlinear: on walk-forward bankruptcy prediction, trees lift AUC well above a linear logit using distance to default alone (§11.4.4). Where events are few, as with roughly a hundred LMTs, a logit with a prior still wins (§13.8).

*Used in:* §7.0 and §7.5 (the secondary model in meta-labeling), §7.6 (the sequential bootstrap), §7.7 (grouped CV), §11.4.4 (the bankruptcy horse race), §14.1 (PD models trained on the wrong labels), §26.7 (an agent's trials are your trials).


## 7-B.8 Monte Carlo as a Method: Standard Errors, Variance Reduction and the Brownian Bridge

### The estimator and its error

To compute $\theta = \mathbb{E}[g(X)]$, under a stated measure, draw $X_1, \ldots, X_n$ and average: $\hat\theta_n = \frac{1}{n}\sum_i g(X_i)$. The central limit theorem gives $\sqrt n(\hat\theta_n - \theta) \to \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_g^2)$, so the standard error is $\hat s_g/\sqrt n$ in any dimension. That is Monte Carlo's virtue and its tax: halving the error costs four times the paths.

### Where every tolerance in this book comes from

Every reference implementation in this book asserts that a simulated number matches a closed form within a tolerance. The tolerance is not a matter of taste. For an assertion $|\hat\theta_n - \theta| < \text{tol}$ to fail by chance with probability $\alpha$, set $\text{tol} = z_{\alpha/2}\,\hat s_g/\sqrt n$; to reach a target error $\varepsilon$, you need

$$
n \ge \Big(\frac{z_{\alpha/2}\,\sigma_g}{\varepsilon}\Big)^2 .
$$

The book's convention is four standard errors, a two-sided false-alarm rate of $6.3 \times 10^{-5}$ per assertion, with a fixed seed so that the test is deterministic. A tolerance tuned until the test passes is a p-hack with a seed.

Tails are expensive. For a probability $p$, $\sigma_g = \sqrt{p(1-p)}$ and the *relative* standard error is $\sqrt{(1-p)/(np)}$. A 0.1% tail event estimated from 100,000 paths carries a 10% relative error. Quantiles are worse: the standard error of the sample $\alpha$-quantile is $\sqrt{\alpha(1-\alpha)/n}\,/\,f(q_\alpha)$, and the density $f$ in the far tail is tiny.

> **[SOURCE EXTRACTION]** *Bolder_Credit_Risk_Modelling p.508:* "The standard error for this brute-force estimator is extremely small for lower levels of confidence, but increases significantly as we reach the extreme part of the tail of the default-loss distribution."
>
> **Annotation.** Bolder's report card for the one-factor Gaussian threshold model compares raw simulation at 10 million and 100,000 iterations with importance sampling at 3,000, and finds that the variance-reduced estimator's error grows much more slowly as the quantile moves into the tail. The desk lesson is a reporting rule: every simulated VaR, CVaR or tail probability ships with its Monte Carlo standard error, computed at the quantile that is reported, and a 99.9% number without one is unlabeled (Law 11). Where the modern desk departs from the book is scale: a portfolio of correlated credits with jump-to-default is now routinely simulated on a GPU, which shrinks the cost of brute force but not the $1/\sqrt n$ law. A GPU buys you paths; it does not repeal the square root.

### Seeds, streams and common random numbers

Seed one `numpy.random.Generator` per experiment and derive independent streams from it with `SeedSequence.spawn`, never by adding 1 to a seed. When you compare two strategies, two parameter values, or a bumped and an unbumped price, use **common random numbers**: the same draws for both. Since $\operatorname{Var}(\hat\theta_A - \hat\theta_B) = \operatorname{Var}\hat\theta_A + \operatorname{Var}\hat\theta_B - 2\operatorname{Cov}(\hat\theta_A, \hat\theta_B)$, positively correlated estimates make the difference far more precise than either level. A finite-difference Greek without common random numbers is mostly noise.

### Variance reduction: three tools that earn their keep

- **Antithetic variates.** Pair each normal draw $Z$ with $-Z$. The pair average has variance $\frac{\sigma_g^2}{2}(1 + \rho)$ with $\rho = \operatorname{Corr}(g(Z), g(-Z))$, which is negative for any monotone $g$, so monotone payoffs (most bond and loss payoffs) get cheaper.
- **Control variates.** If $Y$ has known mean $\mu_Y$, use $\hat\theta_c = \hat\theta - c(\bar Y - \mu_Y)$. The optimal $c^{*} = \operatorname{Cov}(g, Y)/\operatorname{Var}(Y)$ cuts the variance by the factor $1 - \rho_{gY}^2$. Price a Black–Cox bond with the Merton bond as control, or a portfolio loss with its analytic expected loss.
- **Importance sampling.** Draw from $q$ instead of $p$ and reweight by the likelihood ratio: $\hat\theta = \frac{1}{n}\sum_i g(X_i)\,p(X_i)/q(X_i)$. In a one-factor threshold model, shift the systematic factor to $Z \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, 1)$ with $\mu < 0$ so bad states are sampled often, and weight each path by $p(z)/q(z) = \exp(-\mu z + \mu^2/2)$. This is the technique behind Bolder's 3,000-path estimator above.

### Discretisation, and the bias that first passage adds

Simulate log-normal quantities exactly in logs, so that the grid introduces no error at the grid points. Between the grid points is another matter. A path-dependent payoff that depends on whether a barrier was ever touched (Black–Cox default, a covenant trip, a drawdown stop) misses every crossing that happens between grid points and comes back, and this bias shrinks only like $\sqrt{\Delta t}$. Broadie, Glasserman and Kou (1997) show that a discretely monitored barrier behaves like a continuous one shifted away by a factor $e^{0.5826\,\sigma\sqrt{\Delta t}}$. For a driftless log asset 0.30 above its barrier with $\sigma_V = 0.25$, the one-year continuous hitting probability is $2\Phi(-1.2) \approx 23.0\%$; monitoring monthly behaves like a barrier at distance $0.30 + 0.5826 \times 0.25 \times \sqrt{1/12} \approx 0.342$, or $2\Phi(-1.37) \approx 17.1\%$ *(approx., via the continuity correction)*. The monthly grid misses about a quarter of the defaults.

### The Brownian-bridge correction, derived

The exact fix needs one fact about Brownian motion. For a standard Brownian motion $W$ started at 0 and a level $a > 0$, the reflection principle says that a path that touches $a$ and ends at $y \le a$ is matched one-for-one by its reflection after the touch, which ends at $2a - y$. Hence the joint density of "touched $a$" and "$W_t \in dy$" is $\phi_t(2a - y)$, where $\phi_t$ is the $\mathcal{N}(0, t)$ density, and dividing by the density of $W_t$ at $y$ gives

$$
\mathbb{P}\Big(\max_{s \le t} W_s \ge a \;\Big|\; W_t = y\Big) = \frac{\phi_t(2a - y)}{\phi_t(y)} = \exp\!\Big(-\frac{(2a-y)^2 - y^2}{2t}\Big) = \exp\!\Big(-\frac{2a(a - y)}{t}\Big).
$$

Now take the log asset $X$ over one step of length $\Delta t$ with volatility $\sigma_V$, starting at $x_i$ and ending at $x_{i+1}$, both above a log barrier $b$. Reflect so that "down to $b$" becomes "up to $a$": the distance to the barrier is $a = x_i - b$, the displacement toward it is $y = x_i - x_{i+1}$, so $a - y = x_{i+1} - b$, and the variance is $\sigma_V^2\Delta t$. Then

$$
p_i = \mathbb{P}\Big(\min_{[t_i, t_{i+1}]} X \le b \;\Big|\; x_i, x_{i+1}\Big) = \exp\!\Big(-\frac{2\,(x_i - b)\,(x_{i+1} - b)}{\sigma_V^2\,\Delta t}\Big) ,
\tag{7B.9}
$$

the formula §6.5.4 uses. It holds for any constant drift, because the Girsanov density that adds a drift depends on the path only through its endpoint, so conditioning on the endpoint cancels it. The corrected algorithm simulates exact log endpoints on a coarse grid, records a hit if an endpoint is at or below $b$, and otherwise records a hit with probability $p_i$ (Beaglehole, Dybvig and Zhou 1997; Glasserman 2004). Better still, do not flip the coin: carry the path's survival probability $\prod_i (1 - p_i)$ as its weight. The mean is the same and the variance is lower, because you integrated the coin out analytically. Figure 7-B.5 sets the grid, the bridge and the exact answer side by side.

![Figure 7-B.5: Probability that a driftless log asset 0.30 above its barrier, with volatility 0.25, touches it within one year. Checking only on a grid understates the exact 23.0% by 5.4 points at monthly dates and closes the gap only like the square root of the step, while the Brownian-bridge crossing probability (7B.9) recovers 23.0% on any grid, even a single annual step. Illustrative: Monte Carlo, 200,000 paths per point, from the model of §7-B.8.](../assets/figures/ch07b_first_passage_bridge.png)

## 7-B.9 Case Study: Theo's Runway, Re-Audited

A week after the cold open, Theo ran the runway signal through every tool in this chapter. All numbers are *illustrative*; the sequence is the lesson.

| Treatment | Unit of independence | t-statistic |
| :--- | :--- | :---: |
| Classical OLS (what ROBO did) | bond-month | 6.1 |
| White (HC1) | bond-month, unequal variances | 5.6 |
| Clustered by ultimate parent | issuer (206) | 2.4 |
| Two-way: parent and month | issuer and month | 2.1 |
| Fama–MacBeth, Newey–West on slopes ($L = 4$) | month (36) | 2.2 |
| Wild cluster bootstrap, p-value | issuer | 0.04 |

Then the second error bar. Across 24 defensible specifications (runway capped at 13 or 26 weeks, a one- or two-month knowledge lag on lender reporting, IDO or plain excess returns, ex-ante trimming at three thresholds), the coefficient ranged from 0.4 to 1.9 bp per week of runway, against a clustered standard error of 0.5. The non-standard error was about the size of the standard error, which by the Trend Watch's measure is normal for credit and still uncomfortable. The Cox fit of §7-B.4 told the same story on a different clock, a hazard ratio near 3 for issuers inside thirteen weeks.

"So it's real," Theo said, "but it's one real thing, not six."

"It's a hand worth playing at a quarter of the size you wanted," Ines said. "Which is usually what a real edge looks like."

*Used in:* §11.4.2 (runway as a hazard covariate), §13.8 (runway inside the PRS), §28.9 (the dashboard's runway column).


## 7-B.10 The Credit Statistics Module: A Reference Implementation

### Specification for AI Implementation

**What ROBO built from the vague version.** Theo's first spec said: "Estimate default probabilities for the practice cohort. Use clean data." ROBO dropped every issuer without an observed outcome, as instructed, and reported a 75% three-year PD for six issuers that §7-B.4 shows have a 60% product-limit PD with a 22-point standard error. "Clean" had meant "censored," and nobody had said so. The precise spec below names the unit of independence, the censoring rule and the error bar for every estimator.

**The Spec You Hand the Robot.** Build `creditstats.py` (NumPy and SciPy only; no `statsmodels`, `lifelines` or `sklearn`, so every estimator is auditable against this chapter's equations). Every random function takes an explicit `numpy.random.Generator`; experiments spawn independent streams with `SeedSequence.spawn`.

**The functions.** `ols` and `vcov` (classical, hc1, cluster on the ultimate parent, two-way, Newey–West; equations 7B.1, 7B.2, 7B.4) with `nw_lags`; `logit_fit` (IRLS, optional ridge on slopes, issuer-clustered sandwich) and `platt_calibrate`; `kaplan_meier` (Greenwood, Nelson–Aalen, entry times for left truncation; 7B.5–7B.6) and `cox_ph` (Breslow ties and baseline; 7B.7); `ledoit_wolf` (7B.8), `mp_edge` and `residual_pca`; `stationary_bootstrap_indices` and `block_bootstrap` (stationary, moving-block, i.i.d.); `mc_estimate`, `control_variate`, `bridge_hit_prob` (7B.9), `first_passage_mc` and `first_passage_exact`. Shapes: `y (n,)`, `X (n, K)` with the constant in column 0, returns panels `(T, N)`; times in months or years as the caller states; $\sigma_V$ annualized decimal.

**Edge cases ROBO must handle, not guess.** Cluster on the ultimate parent, never the CUSIP; flag fewer than 50 clusters in `info`. Two-way covariances that are not positive semidefinite are eigenvalue-clipped and the clipping is logged. `nw` requires one time-ordered row per period. A logit that has not converged in 50 Newton steps raises an error that names separation, rather than returning the last iterate. Probabilities are clipped to $[10^{-6}, 1 - 10^{-6}]$ before any logarithm. Kaplan–Meier counts an issuer censored at an event time as at risk at that time, and an issuer with an entry time only after entry (left truncation). Distressed exchanges are events, never censoring, and the caller passes them as such. PCA loadings are sign-normalized so they sum to a positive number, and the count of "real" components uses the Marchenko–Pastur edge with a 10% margin for finite samples. Every Monte Carlo result returns its standard error and its 4-s.e. tolerance.

The first block is the module, saved as `creditstats.py`; the second is its acceptance test. Both are seeded; neither touches the network or the disk.

By Friday Theo had nine estimators, each with a paragraph on how it lies and a footnote on why you use it anyway. A list of estimators is not a tool. The trouble with a standard error is that a wrong one looks exactly like a right one: the runway signal printed a t-statistic of 6.1 or 2.4 depending on a single argument, and nothing in the output blushed. A desk that will run these estimators thousands of times across Chapters 8 through 15 cannot have every researcher re-derive the sandwich from memory and hope the degrees-of-freedom correction survived the trip. So the estimators live in one module, written once against this chapter's equations, small enough for Kaz to audit in an afternoon and strict enough that ROBO cannot quietly improve it.

The listing is `creditstats.py`, seven parts in the chapter's order, importing only `numpy` and `scipy`. For regression, `ols` returns coefficients and residuals, and `vcov` turns them into a covariance by wrapping a "bread", the inverse of $X'X$, around a "meat" built from scores, each row of $X$ scaled by its residual. The `kind` argument picks the meat: the pooled residual variance for `classical`, row-by-row outer products for `hc1`, scores summed within each group first for `cluster` (so eleven sibling bonds count as one draw), parent plus month minus their intersection for `twoway`, and Bartlett-weighted lagged cross-products for `nw`, with `nw_lags` choosing the window. The returned `info` carries the cluster count and a flag under 50. The logit is Newton's method from the sample log-odds, with a ridge that spares the constant, and `platt_calibrate` fits a two-parameter logit on a holdout and hands back a function. `kaplan_meier` and `cox_ph` walk the distinct event times and count who is still at risk at each; the first returns the product-limit curve with Greenwood variance and the Nelson–Aalen hazard, the second a Breslow-ties coefficient, its covariance and a baseline hazard. The rest serves panels and simulation: `ledoit_wolf` shrinks toward a scaled identity and returns the weight, `residual_pca` counts eigenvalues above 1.10 times the Marchenko–Pastur edge, `block_bootstrap` resamples whole dates so the cross-section travels together, and `mc_estimate`, `control_variate`, `bridge_hit_prob` and `first_passage_mc` report every simulated number with its standard error, with `first_passage_exact` as the closed-form referee.

Use it as the reference your faster code is checked against, and as the daily driver at the scale of this book's panels. Do not use it as a cure for few clusters: under 50, `vcov` raises the flag and nothing more, and the wild cluster bootstrap of §7-B.6 is not in the module. The survival loops are plain Python over event times, fine for thousands of issuers and slow for millions. The edge case that bites is `nw`, which lags rows, not dates. `nw_meat` slides down the score matrix and assumes each row is the next period. Hand it a bond-by-month panel stacked bond after bond and it will cheerfully correlate one bond's last month with the next bond's first, then return a confident, wrong standard error without a murmur. Collapse to one time-ordered row per period first, as with the Fama–MacBeth slopes.

*The full listing is [Listing 7-B.1 in Appendix F](#code-7b-1).*

A statistics module has a peculiar failure mode: it runs. A sandwich with the wrong small-sample factor, a Kaplan–Meier curve that drops a censored issuer from the risk set one period early, a bridge probability with the wrong sign in the exponent: each hands back a plausible number, and plausible numbers go into position sizes. The only defense is to make the code answer questions whose answers we already know, and to write the tolerance down before running it. Mags, who distrusts anything labeled "adjusted," would approve of the principle. A function earns its place by reproducing a result you could have worked out on the back of a docket.

The acceptance test draws six independent streams from one `SeedSequence(707)`, so that editing one experiment cannot move another, then runs one check per section of the chapter. The structural checks use bands derived from theory. A panel of 200 issuers with 11 bonds each and sibling correlation 0.6 should show a clustered-to-classical standard error ratio near $\sqrt{1+(m-1)\rho}$, about 2.65; the run gives 2.66. Twelve-period overlapping sums of white noise should return Newey–West multipliers near 8.0 at $L = 11$ and 10 at $L = 23$, against a truth of 12, so the test asserts the shortfall instead of hiding it. The six-issuer practice cohort must return survival of 0.8, 0.6 and 0.4 and a Greenwood variance of 0.048, which is the 60% PD and its 22-point error bar. The statistical checks use four standard errors: the logit recovers its three coefficients, and its fitted probabilities sum to the observed defaults; the Cox fit recovers a log hazard ratio of 1.1 under independent censoring; a million-draw tail probability lands on the normal. Shrinkage must stay invertible with more bonds than months, and one planted factor must clear the Marchenko–Pastur edge while pure noise must not. The block bootstrap must see the AR(1) dependence the i.i.d. bootstrap misses. The last block sets a monthly grid against the exact first-passage probability, 0.230: the naive grid gives 0.176, the bridge gives 0.230, and a drifted case on four steps confirms that drift cancels.

Run it after every edit to the module and every upgrade of NumPy or SciPy. It proves only that the code reproduces cases generated by its own assumptions; it cannot tell you the world is stationary. The edge case that bites is the shared stream. `r_mc` feeds the bootstrap, Monte Carlo and bridge checks in sequence, so the results are deterministic only for this exact order of draws. Insert one assertion above them and every later draw changes; a four-standard-error band then fails by luck about once in sixteen thousand tries per assertion, and the temptation is to widen the tolerance. Don't. Give the new experiment its own stream.

*The full listing is [Listing 7-B.2 in Appendix F](#code-7b-2).*

*Used in:* imported by Chapters 8–12, 14 and 15 (`from creditstats import vcov, logit_fit, kaplan_meier, ledoit_wolf, first_passage_mc`); its asserts are the tolerance convention for every reference implementation in the book.


## 7-B.11 Desk Debrief

On Friday Theo taped one sheet beside the monitor where the t-statistic of six had lived. Ines read it, crossed out every "always," and handed it back.

- **The coefficient is cheap; the error bar is the claim.** OLS is unbiased under almost any dependence, and its standard error is whatever you assumed about $\Omega$. On a bond panel that means clustering on the ultimate parent, adding the month when the market shock sits in the residual, and bootstrapping when clusters are few. (Laws 2, 11)
- **The Moulton factor and effective breadth are one formula.** $1 + (m-1)\rho_x\rho_u$ charges issuer-level signals in full; extra CUSIPs add rows, not information. (Law 2)
- **Overlap divides your sample by $h$.** Newey–West at $L = h - 1$ still misses about a third of the variance; $1.5h$ to $2h$ lags, shown beside the $h$ non-overlapping subsamples, is the honest pair. (Law 12)
- **Every probability on the desk is one logit.** Evidence adds in log-odds, the intercept carries the base rate, and calibration is free in sample and earned on a holdout. (Laws 5, 11)
- **Censoring is the signal.** Kaplan–Meier gives each censored issuer the credit it earned: calls censor the healthy, distressed exchanges are events, late entrants join on entry, and event types go to §14.2. (Laws 7, 13, 14)
- **Every covariance you invert is a shrinkage estimator, chosen or not.** Ledoit–Wolf weighs noise against misspecification, DTS supplies the market loading, and a principal component is noise until it clears Marchenko–Pastur. (Laws 3, 9)
- **Resample the unit that is independent.** Months travel with their cross-section, issuers with their history, and no bootstrap shows you a crisis you did not have. (Laws 2, 14)
- **A simulated number ships with its standard error, and a barrier with its bridge.** More paths make a biased grid more precise, never more right. (Laws 4, 11)

Mags read it over his shoulder. "Back in my day the error bar was the PM's mood," she said. "At least that was clustered properly. One mood a week, and every trade that week shared it."

> **View From Another Seat.** *The CLO manager's other 4%.* §7-B.3 asks whether a 4% PD comes true 4% of the time. A CLO manager needs that answer and one more, because the vehicle's tests never read the desk's model. They read agency ratings, mapped through a fixed table into a weighted-average rating factor, and a CCC bucket whose excess is carried at a haircut in the overcollateralization test (§21.4). A loan fairly priced at a 4% PD can still cost the CLO money if a downgrade pushes it over the bucket limit. So that seat calibrates twice, to realized defaults for the credit view and to the agencies for the tests, and treats the gap between them as a risk of its own. The systematic fund on the other side of the resulting sale reads the same gap as a supply schedule it can forecast (Law 15).

**The Spec You Hand the Robot.** "Implement `creditstats.py` per §7-B.10, NumPy and SciPy only: `vcov` (classical, HC1, parent-clustered, two-way with logged eigenvalue clipping, Newey–West); an IRLS `logit_fit` that raises on separation, and `platt_calibrate`; `kaplan_meier` with Greenwood, Nelson–Aalen and entry times; Breslow `cox_ph`; `ledoit_wolf`, `mp_edge` and sign-normalized `residual_pca`; bootstraps over months or issuers, never bonds; Monte Carlo helpers that return a standard error and a 4-s.e. tolerance; `first_passage_mc` with bridge weights. Every random function takes a `Generator`. Tests: the Moulton ratio; Newey–West multipliers near 8 and 10 out of 12; the practice cohort's $\hat S = 0.400$ with variance 0.048; one planted factor above the Marchenko–Pastur edge and none in pure noise; bridged first passage within four standard errors of the exact value."

### Exercises

1. *(More CUSIPs.)* An issuer-level signal has a classical t-statistic of 4.0 on 300 issuers with five bonds each and sibling residual correlation 0.5. Theo adds every issuer's loans, doubling $m$ to 10 at the same correlation. Find the clustered t before and after, and the most any number of extra rows could deliver. *Solution.* Before, the factor is $1 + 4(0.5) = 3$ and $t \approx 2.31$. After, the classical t is $4\sqrt2 \approx 5.66$, the factor 5.5, the clustered t about 2.41. The true variance is proportional to $(1 + (m-1)\rho_u)/m$, which falls from 0.6 to a floor of 0.5, so the ceiling is $2.31\sqrt{0.6/0.5} \approx 2.53$. The sample is 300 issuers, whatever ROBO counts.
2. *(A rumor repeated six times.)* A six-month-return signal sampled monthly for fifteen years shows a naive t of 3.0. Treating it as the sample-mean case of §7-B.2, find the honest t and the Newey–West t at $L = 5$ and $L = 11$. *Solution.* Honest: $3/\sqrt6 \approx 1.22$. At $L = 5$ the multiplier is $1 + 2\sum_{k=1}^{5}(1 - k/6)^2 = 1 + 110/36 \approx 4.06$, so $t \approx 1.49$. At $L = 11$ the weights $1 - k/12$ meet autocorrelations $1 - k/6$, giving $1 + 2(145/72) \approx 5.03$ and $t \approx 1.34$.
3. *(The fallen angel's missing years.)* Add to the practice cohort a fallen angel that enters at month 18 and is alive at 36. Compute $\widehat{\text{PD}}(36)$ with left truncation, then counting it from month 0, and give the Greenwood standard error of the first. *Solution.* The risk sets at the three events are 5, 5 and 4, so $\hat S = 0.8 \times 0.8 \times 0.75 = 0.48$ and $\widehat{\text{PD}} = 52\%$. From month 0 they are 6, 5 and 4, so $\hat S = 0.50$: the entrant is credited with surviving month 14, when it could not have failed in the sample. Greenwood gives $0.48^2(\tfrac1{20} + \tfrac1{20} + \tfrac1{12}) \approx 0.042$, about 21 points. In a panel of thousands the standard error shrinks; the bias does not.
4. *(One factor per coffee.)* A residual panel of 250 bonds over 60 months has top correlation eigenvalues 14.1, 8.7 and 6.2, and Kaz announces three factors, one for each coffee he drank this morning. How many clear Marchenko–Pastur with a 10% margin, and how many eigenvalues are zero? *Solution.* $q \approx 4.17$, the edge is $(1 + 2.04)^2 \approx 9.25$, or 10.2 with the margin: one factor. The 8.7 may be real, but this panel cannot tell, so check its stability across windows. Rank is at most 59, so at least 191 eigenvalues are zero, and an optimizer handed the raw matrix will find 191 riskless portfolios that are not.
5. *(A tolerance with a pedigree.)* The one-year first-passage probability of §7-B.8 is 23.0%. How many paths give a 4-s.e. tolerance of 0.5 points? ROBO runs 200,000 on a monthly grid without the bridge; by how much does the test fail? *Solution.* $n \ge (4\sqrt{0.23 \times 0.77}/0.005)^2 \approx 113{,}000$. The grid converges to about 17.1%, with a standard error of about 0.084 points at 200,000 paths, so the 5.9-point bias is about 70 standard errors. More paths drew a tighter circle around the wrong number.
6. *(The base-rate oracle.)* Kaz's model gives every issuer 2% in a cohort that defaults at 2%. Decompose its Brier score. *Solution.* Reliability and resolution are both zero, so the score is the uncertainty, $0.02 \times 0.98 = 0.0196$, and the AUC is 0.5: perfectly calibrated, no ranking at all, like a forecaster who reads out London's average rainfall every morning. An intercept-only logit builds this model for free (§7-B.3), so that is what it is worth.

# Part III: Isolating Idiosyncratic Alpha (IDO), Factors & Trend

*Chapters 8–12*

Picture a mixing desk. A bond's return comes in on a dozen tracks at once: a rates track, a carry track, a credit-beta track, a few factor tracks (value, momentum, quality, low-risk, size), a liquidity track, and somewhere underneath, if you are lucky and the issuer is interesting, a track that is only this bond. Everyone who has ever pitched a credit has pointed at the mix and said "listen to that." Part III teaches you to press mute on every track but one and find out what is actually there.

The first time Theo did it, the solo channel was silent. The bond he loved, the one whose capital structure he could draw from memory, had returned 9 percent over the year, and every basis point of it was duration and carry. The desk motto was taped to his monitor by the following morning: *IDO or it didn't happen.*

**Chapter 8, Stripping Beta to Isolate Pure IDO,** is the mute button. It decomposes a bond's return with the signs right ($-D\,\Delta y$, not $+$), separates OAS carry from yield carry, and explains the most useful empirical fact in high yield: measured duration is much shorter than analytical duration, and for CCC bonds it turns negative, because spreads and rates move against each other. It covers DTS, the betas you compute when prices are stale (Dimson and Scholes–Williams lag sums), and the hedge matrix across CDX, Treasury futures, HYG and JNK, and equity puts, which is a constrained least-squares problem so ill-conditioned that ridge regularization is a safety feature rather than a style choice. The 2022 rates sell-off is the case study, because it was the year everyone's duration hedge was wrong in the same direction.

**Chapter 9, Factor Investing in Corporate Credit,** is the factor tracks: value, momentum, quality, carry, low-risk, size and liquidity, and the "informed investor" factor from Man Group's 2022 framework. The chapter is about construction more than discovery, because in credit the construction is the alpha: neutralization within rating, sector, and maturity buckets, DTS-neutral versus market-value-neutral portfolios, long-only constraints, liquidity cost scores that eat the paper return, crowding, and the 2019–2026 debate over whether published credit factors replicate.

**Chapter 10, Trend-Following & Time-Series Momentum in Credit (TREND),** is the track that is itself a trend, and the one readers who came for trends should turn to first. It applies the time-series-momentum framework to CDX, iTraxx, and credit excess returns, studies the equity-to-credit lead–lag that makes cross-asset trend work, combines trend with carry, scales by volatility, and looks hard at the crisis years, 2008, 2020, and 2022, where trend's drawdown behavior is the entire reason anyone allocates to it. It also asks what trend does in a market where returns jump, which is a polite way of describing the LMT era.

**Chapter 11, Defensive Systematic High Yield,** follows BlackRock's framework: default avoidance, downside mitigation, the CCC problem (where most of the index's defaults and most of its negative convexity live), quality and low-risk tilts, the arithmetic of upside and downside capture, and the capacity question that decides whether any of this scales.

**Chapter 12, Multi-Asset Credit Allocation,** zooms out to Nuveen's framework for rotating across high yield, loans, emerging-market debt, preferreds, securitized credit, and private credit: regimes, valuation per unit of default loss and per unit of volatility, risk budgets, and liquidity tiers, so that the allocation can be unwound in the order the market will let you.

The trend that defines this part is that systematic credit has grown a track record. Factor and trend strategies in credit used to be backtests in white papers; they now have live performance through two full drawdowns, and the sourced figures in these chapters let you judge them. Mags remains unconvinced. "Back in my day we had one factor. It was called 'I know the CFO.'" Then she asks to see the momentum chart again.

# Chapter 8: Stripping Beta to Isolate Pure IDO


## 8.0 Cold Open: Thirty-Seven Cents

*The bond, the afternoon and its headline are illustrative; the desk and everyone on it are fictional.*

At 2:58 p.m. on the Friday before a lender call, Theo's screen showed two numbers that refused to agree. He was long \$40mm of a B3 first-lien secured bond at +620. The 10-year had sold off 18 bp since lunch. The bond was down thirty-seven cents.

"Analytical duration 4.1," Kaz said, without looking up. "You're long \$16,400 of DV01. ROBO is sizing the hedge now. Two hundred thirty-two TY contracts, short."

"The bond only lost thirty-seven cents," Theo said. "Your duration says it should have lost seventy."

"Then it outperformed. That's alpha." Kaz kept typing. "Congratulations."

Ines rolled her chair over, holding a coffee she had clearly been nursing since the open. "What's the pot? If rates are selling off because the data says growth is fine, this bond tightens. Short two hundred thirty-two futures against it and your Treasury hedge isn't a hedge. It's a second position, with worse liquidity than the first one had at 9 a.m."

"So I hedge less?"

"So you find out how much this bond actually cares about rates before you sell something to protect yourself from them."

From across the aisle, without turning around, Mags said: "In '94 the desk I joined two years later hedged its B paper by buying the long bond. Flight to quality, they were told. Lost on both. By phone. They were still paying for it when I got there."

Theo opened his old 13-week cash flow model, the one on the USB stick, the way other people touch a lucky coin. "This thing has a duration of thirteen weeks and an empirical duration of zero. Nothing in it has ever moved with Treasuries."

Kaz lit up. "So it's a CCC bond."

Nobody laughed, mostly because it was correct.

It was Theo's fourth Friday on the desk, and he had learned one thing about the place for certain: when two numbers disagree, somebody has a reconciliation, and nobody has read it. At PJT the reconciliation was the sources-and-uses tab, and the person who had not read it was usually the client. Here it was a button in the risk system labeled EXPLAIN, which nobody pressed because the same report arrived by email every evening at 6:40 whether anyone wanted it or not.

He pressed it. Ninety seconds later the email arrived, laid out by someone who had once been shown a spreadsheet and had taken against it:

*HY-FL1 B3 \$40mm. P&L today: −\$148,000 (−37¢). Explained: −\$132,000 (−33¢). Unexplained: −\$16,000 (−4¢).*

The word "Unexplained" was blue and underlined. Theo clicked it. The drill-down page took eleven seconds to load and contained one line, "Residual = Total − Σ(Explained)," and, at the bottom, a view counter that some optimistic engineer had installed when the system went live. It read 1. The 1 was him.

"Four cents," he said. "Who owns four cents?"

"Nobody," Kaz said. "It's the plug. Plugs are orphans by construction."

"At PJT the plug had an owner. Usually me, at two in the morning, before the client call."

"Here it has an owner too," Ines said. She had not rolled her chair back. "You. But four cents is the small problem. The thirty-three cents of 'explained' is the big one, because it was explained with Kaz's duration, and Kaz's duration assumes something about this afternoon that none of us knows." She turned her coffee cup a quarter turn on the desk, the way other people tap a table before a bet. "Serious question, before anybody sells anything. Why did rates sell off since lunch?"

Nobody answered. Kaz looked at the rates screen as if it might volunteer. Mags, across the aisle, said "Hm," which from Mags was a paragraph.

Theo opened the news pane and scrolled from noon. Between 12:00 and 2:58 there was exactly one headline that a bond market could have traded on. At 12:47 a Federal Reserve governor, speaking at a lunch, had said the committee could afford to be patient on further cuts because the economy was "proving resilient."

"There," Kaz said. "Resilient. Growth. The bond tightened nine basis points because growth is good for credit. Rates sold off because growth is bad for bonds. It's one story."

"Or," Ines said, "patient because inflation isn't done. That's a different story, and in that one your bond doesn't tighten on the news. It widens with the ten-year, a month from now, when everyone has read the transcript."

"Or," Mags said, still facing her own screens, "somebody large had to sell ten-years at one o'clock, and the headline is the excuse the tape found afterwards. Happens every week. Nobody writes a book about it."

Theo wrote the three on his notepad as if they were bidders in a process: *growth, inflation, somebody had to sell.* Under growth he wrote "bond tightens: hedge less." Under inflation, "bond widens with rates: hedge more, or hedge the spread." Under the forced seller, "bond doesn't care: hedge the duration, nothing else."

"So the hedge ratio depends on which one it was," he said.

"The hedge ratio *is* which one it was," Ines said. "Kaz's two hundred thirty-two contracts assume the bond moves like a Treasury whatever the reason. A smaller number assumes it was growth. A bigger one assumes inflation. Every number on that screen is somebody's guess about why the ten-year moved, written down as if it were arithmetic."

"The bond tightened," Kaz said. "That's evidence."

"That's the bond. It might have tightened for its own reasons on a day the ten-year sold off for its. You don't get to use the answer to grade the question." She stood up. "Find out what this bond has done on days like this, and on days that only looked like this. Then tell me what you'd short."

Theo looked at the three words on the notepad, then at the four cents nobody owned, then at the thirty-four cents Kaz had already called alpha. He wrote the question on a sticky note and put it on his monitor: *Of the thirty-seven cents this bond moved today, how much was the bond?*

By the end of this chapter you will be able to split a bond's move into the parts you did not choose and the one part you did, to hedge each part with the instrument that actually owns it, and to say what is left precisely enough that a coding agent computes the same number you would.

## 8.1 The Subtraction: Return Decomposition With the Right Signs

Every restructuring banker has built a sources-and-uses table, and every one of them knows the rule: if the columns do not foot, somebody is about to be embarrassed in front of a client. A bond's daily return is a sources-and-uses table for performance. The uses side is one number, the realized total return. The sources side is a list of things you did not choose (Treasury carry, the curve, the rate move, the market's spread move, convexity) and one thing you did: the idiosyncratic residual you were paid to find. The desk calls that residual IDO, and the desk motto, "IDO or it didn't happen," is a statement about accounting before it is a statement about skill. Until the sources foot, you do not know whether you made money or the Federal Reserve made it for you.

### Deriving the decomposition

Kaz's seventy cents came from one number, the 4.1 on the risk screen, and the number has a picture behind it that is worth having before any algebra.

> **Math, Gently.** *A curve, its tangent, and the bend.* Draw the bond's price against its yield and you get a hillside seen from the side: yield runs left to right, price runs up and down, and the ground slopes downhill because a higher yield means a lower price. Stand on the hill at today's yield. Duration is the steepness of the ground under your feet, the slope of the straight line (the *tangent*) that just touches the hill where you stand, quoted per dollar of price. Take a small step to the right and the tangent tells you roughly how far you drop. Convexity is how quickly that steepness changes as you walk. A bond's hillside is bowl-shaped, so the straight line always overstates the fall when yields rise and understates the gain when they drop, and the correction is half the bend times the *square* of the step. Theo's bond has a slope of 4.1 and the afternoon's step was 18 bp: $4.1 \times 0.0018 = 0.74\%$, about seventy cents on a \$95 price. The bend is about 20, so the correction is $\tfrac12 \times 20 \times (0.0018)^2 \approx 0.003\%$, a third of a cent, which is why the table below shows 0. Squares of small numbers are tiny. That is why a straight-line hedge works on a quiet afternoon, and why it stops working on a loud one. The formal version, a second-order Taylor expansion with the yield split into its Treasury and spread parts, is next.

In words, then: a bond's day is carry, minus its duration times the Treasury move, minus its spread duration times the spread move, plus the bend, plus whatever is left. Take away a matched Treasury portfolio and what remains of the credit part is DTS times the *relative* spread change. Take away what the whole market did through a factor model, and only what survives both subtractions has earned the name IDO.

#### The Full Derivation: from Taylor to the excess return

Write the bond's price as a function of its yield and time, $P(y,t)$, and split the yield into a Treasury part and a spread part, $y = y^{\text{TSY}} + s$. For a callable bond read $y$ as the option-adjusted yield and $s$ as the OAS. Over a short interval $\Delta t$ in which the issuer does not default, a second-order Taylor expansion gives

$$
\frac{\Delta P}{P} \approx \frac{1}{P}\frac{\partial P}{\partial t}\,\Delta t + \frac{1}{P}\frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\,\Delta y + \frac{1}{2}\,\frac{1}{P}\frac{\partial^2 P}{\partial y^2}\,(\Delta y)^2 .
$$

Define modified duration $D^{\text{mod}} = -\frac{1}{P}\frac{\partial P}{\partial y}$ and convexity $C = \frac{1}{P}\frac{\partial^2 P}{\partial y^2}$. Add the coupon accrual to the price change to get total return. At an unchanged yield, price pull plus coupon accrual earns the yield, so the time terms collapse to yield carry $y\,\Delta t$ (two parts with two different owners, split in the table below) plus a roll-down term when the curve is sloped. Now split $\Delta y = \Delta y^{\text{TSY}} + \Delta s$ and allow the spread sensitivity to differ from the rate sensitivity. For a fixed-rate bullet they are equal; for a floater, a callable, or a bond trading to a call date they are not. The result is

$$
R^{\text{tot}} \approx \underbrace{y\,\Delta t}_{\text{carry}} + \underbrace{\text{roll}}_{\text{curve}} \;-\; D^{\text{mod}}\,\Delta y^{\text{TSY}} \;-\; D^{\text{spr}}\,\Delta s \;+\; \tfrac{1}{2}\,C\,(\Delta y)^2 \;+\; \epsilon .
$$

Every symbol carries units. $R^{\text{tot}}$ is a decimal return. $y$ and $s$ are decimal annual rates. $\Delta t$ is in years under the bond's day count (30/360 for US corporates). $D^{\text{mod}}$ and $D^{\text{spr}}$ are in years. $\Delta y^{\text{TSY}}$ and $\Delta s$ are decimal changes, so an 18 bp sell-off is $0.0018$, not $18$. The residual $\epsilon$ collects the Taylor remainder, pricing noise, and anything specific to the issuer.

The index convention isolates the credit part by subtracting a portfolio of par Treasuries whose key-rate durations match the bond's. To the same order, that portfolio returns $y^{\text{TSY}}\Delta t + \text{roll} - D^{\text{mod}}\Delta y^{\text{TSY}} + \tfrac12 C^{\text{TSY}}(\Delta y^{\text{TSY}})^2$. Subtracting it leaves the excess return:

$$
R^{\text{xs}} \equiv R^{\text{tot}} - \sum_k w_k R^{\text{TSY}}_k \approx s\,\Delta t \;-\; D^{\text{spr}}\,\Delta s \;+\; (\text{convexity cross-terms}) \;+\; \epsilon .
$$

The carry is now OAS carry, $s\,\Delta t$, not yield carry. The rate term is gone by construction, and that is exactly what the index excess return is designed to do. Finally, rewrite the spread term in relative-change form, because (as §8.4 shows) relative spread changes are the quantity that is stable across credits:

$$
-D^{\text{spr}}\,\Delta s \;=\; -\,\underbrace{D^{\text{spr}}\,s}_{\text{DTS}}\,\cdot\,\frac{\Delta s}{s} .
$$

That is the whole chapter in one line. The accounting identity hands you $\Delta s$, the bond's own spread change. It does not tell you how much of $\Delta s$ was the market. Stage two of the subtraction is the factor model

$$
R^{\text{xs}}_{i,t} = \sum_{k} \beta_{i,k}\,F_{k,t} + \epsilon_{i,t},
$$

with factor returns $F_{k,t}$, loadings $\beta_{i,k}$, and residual $\epsilon_{i,t}$. IDO is what survives *both* stages. The decomposition residual is a bookkeeping error term; the factor residual is the asset.

*Assumptions and measure.* The expansion assumes small moves, no default inside $\Delta t$, and option-adjusted durations for callables. The decomposition is accounting and needs no probability measure. Two things built on it do. The *expected* excess return is a $\mathbb{P}$ object, because it is what you forecast. The OAS is a $\mathbb{Q}$-consistent spread, because it is what discounts the bond's cash flows to its price. (The one-sentence version: a $\mathbb{Q}$ spread is the number that makes the discounted cash flows equal today's price, and a $\mathbb{P}$ return is the number you forecast and are later paid, or not paid, on. Chapter 5 and Chapter 6-B own risk-neutral pricing; nothing here needs more than the distinction.) OAS includes compensation for expected default loss, so "the bond yields +620 over Treasuries" is not "the bond is expected to beat Treasuries by 620 bp a year." The gap is the expected loss, and Chapter 5 priced it.

### The thirty-seven cents, itemized

Apply the decomposition to Theo's bond *(illustrative inputs)*: price \$95, $D^{\text{mod}} = 4.1$, $D^{\text{spr}} = 4.0$, yield 11.1%, a coupon of 10% (about what the price, yield and duration imply), one day of 30/360 carry. The 10-year sold off $\Delta y^{\text{TSY}} = +0.0018$, and the bond's OAS tightened 9 bp, $\Delta s = -0.0009$.

| Source | Formula | Return | Cents on \$95 |
| :--- | :--- | ---: | ---: |
| Carry | $y\,\Delta t = 0.111/360$ | +0.031% | +3 |
| *of which coupon accrual (custodian)* | $\dfrac{c\,\Delta t}{0.95} = \dfrac{0.10/360}{0.95}$ | +0.029% | +2.8 |
| *of which pull-to-par (model)* | $y\,\Delta t - \dfrac{c\,\Delta t}{0.95}$ | +0.002% | +0.2 |
| Rates | $-D^{\text{mod}}\Delta y^{\text{TSY}} = -4.1 \times 0.0018$ | −0.738% | −70 |
| Spread | $-D^{\text{spr}}\Delta s = -4.0 \times (-0.0009)$ | +0.360% | +34 |
| Convexity | $\tfrac12 C (\Delta y)^2$, $C \approx 20$ | +0.000% | 0 |
| Residual | plug | −0.043% | −4 |
| **Total** | | **−0.390%** | **−37** |

The two italic lines split the carry row and add back to it. They are not extra sources, and the total foots on the headline rows alone. They are separate because they have different owners. The coupon accrual is a fact: the custodian's records of accrued interest confirm it to the cent, and if the books disagree, someone has misbooked a coupon. Pull-to-par is a forecast: the model's projection of where a discount bond's price drifts if the yield stays where it is, and it is wrong the moment the yield moves. On this bond the forecast is 0.2 of a cent, so folding the two into one carry line costs nothing today. On a bond trading far below par it would not be small, and a missing coupon would hide inside it. Product control keeps the lines apart for that reason. Chapter 8-C does the same split for a whole book every morning, in the meeting where the four cents behind the EXPLAIN button stop being an orphan and become a line somebody is paid to own.

Kaz's "alpha" was the 34 cents of spread tightening. The question for the next three sections is whether those 9 bp of tightening belonged to the bond or to the rate move. If high-yield spreads systematically tighten when yields rise for growth reasons, the 34 cents is beta wearing a disguise, and a hedge of 232 futures would have converted a modestly hedged position into a short rates bet with a spread rider.

> **[SOURCE EXTRACTION]** *Ben_Dor p.298:* "Barclays Capital reports excess returns that equal the difference in total return between a bond and a portfolio of hypothetical par Treasury bonds matching the bond's key rate duration exposures."
>
> **Annotation.** This sentence is the industry's definition of the first subtraction, and it carries two hidden choices. First, the hedge is *key-rate* matched, not single-duration matched, so a 30-year bond's excess return is not polluted by 2s10s steepening. Second, the hedge portfolio is *hypothetical*: par Treasuries at each key rate, rebalanced costlessly. A desk that hedges with actual futures earns the index's excess return minus the futures-cash basis, roll costs, and the cheapest-to-deliver switch (§8.6). On a 2026 desk the definition matters for a second reason: the excess-return series you download from an index provider is already a hedged P&L under a hedge you did not choose. Any empirical duration you estimate on *excess* returns is a duration *relative to that hedge*. Estimate $D^{\text{emp}}$ on total returns, then subtract.

> **[SOURCE EXTRACTION]** *Man_2022 p.14:* "ICE BofAML excess returns taken as total returns less key rate duration matched sovereign return."
>
> **Annotation.** Two index families, one convention. That is convenient and slightly dangerous, because it lets people forget that "excess return" is a model output. Asvanunt and Richardson (2017), *The Credit Risk Premium*, make the point that the measured credit premium is biased if the term component is mis-hedged; the definition you choose leaks into every Sharpe ratio built on it. For a systematic desk the operational rule is to store total returns, Treasury key-rate returns, and the hedge weights separately, and to compute excess returns in your own code. Then, when the index provider restates history, your backtest does not silently change its mind.

Kaz keeps the next list taped inside a desk drawer, one item for each morning it has cost somebody.

> **Ways This Blows Up.** (1) *The sign.* $-D\,\Delta y$ has a minus sign. ROBO, given the formula without it, will report that a rate sell-off made the book money, and the P&L explain will foot perfectly because the residual absorbs twice the error. (2) *Units.* $D \cdot \Delta y$ needs $\Delta y$ in decimal. Feed it 18 instead of 0.0018 and a 4-year bond loses 7,200% on a quiet afternoon. Assert $|\Delta y| < 0.05$ per day as a data-error trap. (3) *Yield carry versus OAS carry.* Yield carry belongs to total return and OAS carry to excess return. Mixing them double-counts the Treasury leg, roughly 5% a year in 2026, and hands you a mysterious, very stable "alpha." (4) *Callable HY.* Much of a high-yield index is callable, and a bond priced to a call date has a spread duration set by the call, not the maturity. Some of what looks like OAS carry is the short call decaying. When the bond crosses the call price, duration-to-worst jumps. Any rolling regression that treats that jump as a rate response will invent a structural break.

## 8.2 Empirical vs. Analytical Duration: One Formula, Three Regimes

Analytical duration answers a question nobody asked: what happens to the bond's price if Treasury yields move *and nothing else does*. On a desk, nothing else moving is the one scenario that never occurs. Empirical duration answers the question Ines asked: when yields move, what tends to happen to this bond, given that its spread tends to move too?

The RSSG reader already knows the limit case. A name in restructuring trades on dollar price, and every bond at the same seniority converges to the same recovery regardless of maturity. Its sensitivity to the 10-year is roughly zero. Empirical duration is the continuum between that limit and par.

Ines's instruction at the end of the cold open, find out what this bond has done on days like this, is a request for a cloud of dots and the line through it. Before the algebra, here is what that line is.

> **Math, Gently.** *What a regression slope is, and why it equals $\rho\,\sigma_s/\sigma_y$.* **Part one, the slope.** Put one dot on a page for every trading day. The dot's distance to the right is that day's change in the 10-year yield; its height is the same day's *relative* change in a B bond's spread (a move from 500 bp to 510 bp is +2%). A thousand days make a cloud. The regression slope is the tilt of the line that runs through the middle of the cloud, and it answers one question: when the yield moves one unit to the right, how far up or down do I expect the spread to move? The tilt factors into two pieces you can see. How tightly the dots hug a line is the correlation, $\rho$, between −1 and +1. How tall the cloud is relative to how wide is the ratio of the two volatilities, $\sigma_s/\sigma_y$. Multiply them and you have the slope. In the margin, with Ben Dor's numbers for B bonds: $\rho = -0.56$, $\sigma_s = 2.2\%$ a day, $\sigma_y = 6.4$ bp a day, so each 1 bp of yield rise comes with $-0.56 \times 2.2\% / 6.4 \approx -0.19\%$ of relative spread change. A 10 bp sell-off predicts a spread 1.9% tighter, about 10 bp off a 500 bp bond. **Part two, the miss.** No real day sits on the line. On a day the yield rose 10 bp and the spread fell 3%, the line predicted −1.9%, so the day *missed* by −1.1%. That vertical miss is the "part orthogonal" that the derivation calls $u_i$. The line is drawn so that the misses have no correlation at all with the yield change; if they had any, you could tilt the line and miss less. So everything in the bond's spread that the 10-year can explain sits on the line, and everything it cannot sits in the miss. The derivation that turns this slope into a hedge ratio is in the next subsection.

### The two-factor derivation

Put the rate leg and the spread leg of §8.1 together, let the spread lean on the yield by the slope in the box, and the fraction of analytical duration worth hedging comes out in one line: $H_i = 1 + s_i\,\rho_{y,s}\,\sigma_s/\sigma_y$. Everything that matters in this chapter is visible in it. The correlation alone decides whether $H$ sits above or below one, because the spread and both volatilities are never negative. The spread level multiplies whatever the correlation says, so the same correlation that shaves 5% off an IG bond's duration can erase a B bond's. And nothing stops the answer from going negative.

Call the slope the *linkage factor*, $\ell \equiv \rho_{y,s}\sigma_s/\sigma_y$, so $H = 1 + \ell s$. Ben Dor's 1998–2009 sample has $\sigma_y = 6.4$ bp a day and relative spread volatilities of 1.6% to 2.5% a day. For B-rated bonds, $\rho = -0.56$ and $\sigma_s \approx 2.2\%$ (the box's cloud) give $\ell \approx -0.56 \times 0.022/0.00064 \approx -19$ per unit of decimal spread. That is a loss of 0.19 of hedge ratio for every 100 bp of spread, so a B bond at 500 bp has $H \approx 0.03$, and Theo's bond at 620 bp comes out slightly below zero. Under the 1998–2009 parameters, every one of Kaz's 232 contracts was a second position. Under the 2026 parameters in the Trend Watch below, most of them were a hedge. That is the problem.

#### The Full Derivation: the two-factor hedge ratio

Start from the excess-return identity of §8.1, put the Treasury leg back, and keep only first-order terms. Let $x_i \equiv \Delta s_i / s_i$ be bond $i$'s relative spread change. Then

$$
R_i \approx -D_i\,\Delta y - D_i\,s_i\,x_i ,
$$

where $\Delta y$ is the Treasury yield change and, for a bullet bond, $D_i = D^{\text{mod}}_i = D^{\text{spr}}_i$. Decompose the relative spread change into the part linearly predictable from the yield change and a part orthogonal to it:

$$
x_i = \rho_{y,s}\,\frac{\sigma_s}{\sigma_y}\,\Delta y + u_i, \qquad \mathrm{Cov}^{\mathbb{P}}(u_i,\Delta y) = 0 .
$$

Here $\rho_{y,s}$ is the correlation between yield changes and relative spread changes, $\sigma_s$ the volatility of relative spread changes, and $\sigma_y$ the volatility of yield changes, all measured over the same horizon. The coefficient $\rho_{y,s}\sigma_s/\sigma_y$ is the population OLS slope of $x$ on $\Delta y$. Substituting and taking the conditional expectation under $\mathbb{P}$:

$$
\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{P}}[R_i \mid \Delta y] = -D_i\,\Delta y\left(1 + s_i\,\rho_{y,s}\,\frac{\sigma_s}{\sigma_y}\right).
$$

Empirical duration is the negative of the slope of this expectation in $\Delta y$:

$$
D^{\text{emp}}_i = D_i\left(1 + s_i\,\rho_{y,s}\,\frac{\sigma_s}{\sigma_y}\right), \qquad H_i \equiv \frac{D^{\text{emp}}_i}{D_i} = 1 + s_i\,\rho_{y,s}\,\frac{\sigma_s}{\sigma_y} .
$$

$H_i$ is the *hedge ratio*: the fraction of analytical duration that minimizes the variance of a Treasury-hedged position. (We write $H$ rather than $h$ because $h$ is reserved for the hedge-weight vector in §8.6.) The three properties stated above the derivation follow by inspection.

*The estimable form.* Theory gives the shape; the numbers come from data. With a panel of bond returns, regress

$$
R_{i,t} = \beta\,(-D_{i,t}\,\Delta y_t) + \gamma\,(-D_{i,t}\,s_{i,t}\,\Delta y_t) + \epsilon_{i,t},
\qquad H(s) = \beta + \gamma\,s ,
$$

with $\gamma < 0$ expected. The first regressor is the analytical rate exposure; the second is that exposure scaled by spread. If the two-factor model were exact, $\beta = 1$ and $\gamma = \ell$. In data, $\beta < 1$ for HY even at low spreads, which is the puzzle of §8.3.

*Assumptions and failure modes.* (i) Horizon: daily, weekly, and monthly $\rho$ differ, and daily HY marks are stale (§8.5); Dynkin p.436 runs the pooled regression on monthly, carry-adjusted returns for exactly this reason. (ii) Extrapolation: $H(s)$ is linear in $s$ inside the sample and nowhere else. Ben Dor p.196 tests 2005–2009 spreads that lay outside the fitting range. (iii) The min-variance hedge also hedges your spread view (see the Poker Table below). (iv) In distress, price is pinned to recovery and $D \to 0$ whatever $\rho$ is: a second route to zero duration that this formula does not contain. (v) Price level matters: discount bonds respond asymmetrically (§8.3). On measures: $\rho$ and the $\sigma$'s are $\mathbb{P}$ sample moments, while $D_i$ is the derivative of a $\mathbb{Q}$-consistent price. The gap between $D$ and $D^{\text{emp}}$ is comovement, not mispricing. Nobody is wrong; the bond is just never alone.

> **[SOURCE EXTRACTION]** *Ben_Dor p.191:* "If this correlation is negative, the empirical duration would be lower than the analytical one and may even end up being negative."
>
> **Annotation.** The sentence is conditional, and the condition is the whole game. In Ben Dor's 1998–2009 sample the correlation was reliably negative, because rates mostly moved on growth news and Fed easing, and spreads moved against them. The book treats the sign as a fact about the sample. A 2026 desk must treat it as a state variable. In 2022 the condition failed, $\rho > 0$ and $H > 1$, and the replay in §8.7 sits the desk down at that table. The formula held. The parameter moved. Any production system that hard-codes $H$ from a pre-2020 table is a 2022 loss waiting for a calendar.

> **[SOURCE EXTRACTION]** *Dynkin p.437:* "When rates fall, bond prices increase. Due to this negative correlation, however, spreads tend to widen, and thus the bond prices do not increase by as much as would have been expected based on analytical duration alone."
>
> **Annotation.** The plain-English version, and the one to read aloud to a PM who asks why the hedged book lost money on a rally. Note the asymmetry the sentence implies for convex payoffs. On a rally, a long credit position under-earns its duration *and* a full Treasury short loses its full duration, so the hedged book bleeds from both sides. The pooled monthly IG regression in the same chapter (Dynkin p.438–439, January 1992 to April 2014, 737,506 bond-months) finds a base hedge ratio of 0.97 that falls by 0.13 per 1% of spread. That is gentler than daily estimates, which is partly the stale-price effect of §8.5 washing out at monthly horizons.

### Three regimes

The formula $H = 1 + s\,\ell$ has one sign switch, so there are three regimes worth naming. Ines names them the way she would name the tables in a card room. "Three tables," she told Theo, tapping the formula on his screen with the cap of a pen. "Flight, nobody, inflation. Find out which one you're sitting at before you buy chips."

The flight table is where Ben Dor's sample sat for eleven years, August 1998 to November 2009, and where the market went back for one week in March 2023 (§8.7). Rates are moved by growth news and by a Fed that eases into trouble, so when spreads widen, yields fall: $\rho < 0$. Then $H < 1$ for everything, and $H \le 0$ for single-B and below. A Treasury short on a high-yield bond at this table is not a hedge but a second bet, and it loses on the days the bond loses.

The nobody table is 2026 so far. Rates and spreads move on unrelated news, $\rho \approx 0$, and $H \approx 1$ even for high yield. Analytical duration is the right hedge by accident, and the desk that uses it looks wise for reasons it did not earn. The FRED computation in the Trend Watch at the end of this section puts 2026 year-to-date here.

The inflation table is 2022. The same news pushes yields up and spreads wider, so $\rho > 0$ and $H > 1$: high yield carries *more* rate sensitivity than its analytical duration, the opposite of what Table 8.1 recommends. The replay in §8.7 sits Theo down at this table with Table 8.1 in his hand.

> **Poker Table.** Ines draws it on a napkin. "Two hands. In the first, you're long a Ba bond because you think spreads tighten when the economy is strong, which is also when rates rise. You hedge at the empirical ratio, $H = 0.4$. Rates rise 50 bp, spreads tighten 30 bp, exactly what the correlation predicted, and the hedge and the bond net to zero. You were right, and you got paid nothing. The minimum-variance hedge saw your view in the correlation and hedged it away, because a view is variance. In the second hand you hedge the full analytical duration. Rates rise, the futures pay, spreads tighten, the bond pays. Now you got paid for the view, and you also carried the risk of the view. Pick the hedge that matches the bet you meant to make. If you have a view that spreads tighten when rates rise, the empirical hedge pays you nothing for being right."

Theo had spent six years watching clients sign documents that did something other than what they meant, and he recognized the shape of Ines's napkin. Ben Dor asks the same question in one line, almost in passing.

> **[SOURCE EXTRACTION]** *Ben_Dor p.219:* "An empirical hedge, reduced to reflect this known correlation, would exactly offset both of these market effects. Is this what the investor intended?"
>
> **Annotation.** This is the most important question in the chapter, asked as a rhetorical aside. A hedge ratio is a choice of objective, not a fact. Minimum total variance gives you $H$. "Zero rate exposure, keep the spread beta" gives you $H = 1$ plus a separate decision about spread. "Zero exposure to both" gives you a different instrument set altogether. ROBO cannot choose among these. The spec must name the objective, and §8.9 makes that a required field.

Every argument in this section assumes the reader wants to get rid of rate risk. There is a seat in credit that does not, and it holds a great deal of the market.

> **View From Another Seat.** *The insurer, who wants the duration.* An annuity writer reads this section backwards. Its liabilities are long, fixed-rate promises to policyholders, so it does not ask how much Treasury duration to strip out of a bond; it *wants* the duration, matched against those liabilities, and the question it asks of a bond is whether the spread over Treasuries beats the capital charge the bond attracts under risk-based capital rules and its ratings. The seat is large. Athene, Apollo's retirement-services business, reported net invested assets of \$292B at year-end 2025 and a blended net spread, excluding notable items, of 120 bp in the fourth quarter (Jim Zelter, Apollo's president, on the 9 February 2026 earnings call). For a balance sheet built that way, $H > 1$ in 2022 was not the disaster it was for a hedged trading book. The bonds fell in market value, but an insurer holding them to maturity against long fixed-rate liabilities records most of that fall as an accounting event rather than a realized loss, and the same rise in yields let it put new premiums to work at higher rates. How any particular insurer hedges is its own business, and nothing here infers Apollo's policy. What this seat worries about is what the chapter's hedges cannot see: a default that turns a spread into a loss, and a capital charge that jumps when a bond is downgraded across a line, Alltel-style (§8.3).

Mags put it more briefly, to nobody in particular. "Every basis point of duration this desk sells ends up on somebody's balance sheet. The biggest balance sheets in credit buy it on purpose."

> **Trend Watch: The Correlation That Changed Sides, 2018–2026.** *What changed.* For two decades the stock–bond correlation was negative or near zero (rolling three-year correlations, November 2000 to 2020, per Morningstar's diversification research as reported in secondary summaries; approx.). It turned positive in 2021 and was roughly 0.58 for full-year 2022 (approx.; secondary summaries of Morningstar's data, which differ on 2023). The rate–spread correlation $\rho_{y,s}$ is a cousin of that number: when inflation drives rates, it drives both. *How big.* In 2022 the 10-year rose from 1.52% to 3.88% and the 2-year from 0.73% to 4.41% (FRED, DGS10/DGS2, year-end closes). The Bloomberg US Corporate High Yield index returned about −11.2% and the IG Corporate index about −15.8% (approx.; secondary data summaries). Apollo's Torsten Slok noted on December 3, 2022 that the HY total-return index was "down 10% so far in 2022" and attributed it mainly to duration. High yield, the asset class with "negative empirical duration," lost money on rates. *What happened next.* Our computation on FRED daily data (ICE BofA OAS by rating against DGS10; relative OAS changes; $H = 1 + \bar s\rho\sigma_s/\sigma_y$; computed 2026-10-17, index level, correlation route only):
>
> | Window | $\rho$: HY / BB / B / CCC / IG | Implied $H$: HY / BB / B / CCC / IG |
> | :--- | :--- | :--- |
> | 2024 (249 days) | −0.34 / −0.39 / −0.29 / −0.22 / −0.38 | 0.65 / 0.64 / 0.66 / 0.61 / 0.92 |
> | 2025 (248 days) | −0.35 / −0.38 / −0.31 / −0.31 / −0.32 | 0.42 / 0.47 / 0.42 / 0.14 / 0.90 |

> In 2024–2025 high yield behaved like the textbook: 0.4 to 0.65 of analytical duration, and the rolling 60-day CCC hedge ratio touched −0.78 in the window ending May 23, 2025. In 2026 so far, daily rate and spread moves have been nearly uncorrelated, and HY's empirical duration is roughly its analytical duration. IG never left the band [0.79, 1.04] on a rolling 60-day basis. *What it means for the desk.* The hedge ratio is a time series, and its sign has changed twice in five years. Re-estimate monthly, monitor a rolling $\rho$ daily, and treat a zero crossing as a regime alarm (§8.7). One more data-infrastructure fact: FRED's ICE BofA OAS pages state that starting in April 2026 the series include only three years of observations, so the free history now begins in October 2023. A desk that wants Ben Dor's 1998 start date must build its own spread history from TRACE (Appendix B).
