## 12.8 Tactical Overlays and the Turnover Budget

The strategic allocation answers "what should we own over five years?" The tactical overlay answers "what should we change this year?", which Nuveen frames as a shorter, one-year horizon applied to the same framework (Nuveen pp.3 and 7). The engineering question is how much the overlay may move the book, and that question starts with how to count a move.

> **Math, Gently.** *Turnover is a sum of absolute moves.* Picture the book as a row of jars, one per sector, and the tactical overlay as permission to pour between them. Move 3% of NAV out of HY and 3% into CLO BBB and you have poured twice, once out and once in. Turnover counts both, so the tilt uses $|{-3\%}| + |{+3\%}| = 6\%$ of the budget. That is why turnover is measured with absolute values, the "$\ell_1$ norm" in the jargon, and not by adding signed moves, which would net to zero and call the trade free. Each pour also costs half a round trip: $3\% \times \text{LCS}_{\text{HY}}/2$ on the way out and $3\% \times \text{LCS}_{\text{CLO}}/2$ on the way in. With round trips of 1 point on HY and 2 points on CLO BBB *(illustrative)*, the tilt costs $0.03 \times 0.5\% + 0.03 \times 1\% = 4.5$ bp of NAV before it has earned anything. Absolute values are awkward for an optimizer, so the engine splits every move into two non-negative pieces, an amount poured in and an amount poured out, like the two pans of a kitchen scale. The budget limits the total weight on both pans, and because each pan charges its own cost, the optimizer never loads both pans for the same sector. In symbols, next.

Write the tilt budget as an $\ell_1$ constraint, $\|w - w^{\text{SAA}}\|_1 \le \kappa$, and linearize it with split variables: $w = w^{\text{SAA}} + d^{+} - d^{-}$ with $d^{\pm} \ge 0$ and $\mathbf{1}^{\top}(d^{+} + d^{-}) \le \kappa$. Because each unit of $d^{+}$ and $d^{-}$ also costs $\text{LCS}_i/2$ in the objective, the optimizer never sets both positive for the same sector, so $d^{+} + d^{-} = |w - w^{\text{SAA}}|$ at the solution and the constraint is exactly the turnover budget.

Three signals feed the overlay's expected returns, and they disagree in exactly the months that matter.

*Carry.* Across sectors, carry is the yield-minus-expected-loss term of (12.1) and it has a long record as a premium.

> **[SOURCE EXTRACTION]** *Man_2022 p.26:* "Koijen et al. find that the Carry factor has, on average, positive returns, with Sharpe ratios between 0.4 and 0.5. Over the long run, Carry appears to offer a significant premium, but with incredibly high volatility of returns."
>
> **Annotation.** Koijen, Moskowitz, Pedersen and Vrugt (2018) measured carry across asset classes, including credit; the MAC application is cross-sector carry per unit of DTS (Ratio 2 of §12.3). "Incredibly high volatility" is the regime problem in two words: carry pays steadily in calm and gives it back in a stress month, because high-carry sectors are high-DTS sectors. The modern desk scales the carry tilt by the filtered calm-state probability, which is a regime hedge bought at the price of being a month late.

*Mean reversion.* The OU forecast of §12.3 buys after spreads widen. Blackstone's systematic credit description says it plainly (Blackstone p.1): "When credit spreads widen aggressively (often due to market panic rather than fundamental deterioration), the model algorithmically increases credit exposure."

*Regime.* The HMM of §12.4 does the opposite in the same month: the stress probability rises and the regime-mixture means in (12.2) fall.

The reconciliation is about timing, and the sign of the error matters. In the first weeks of a widening, the regime signal is right and the mean-reversion signal is early. After the peak, the reversion signal is right and the regime filter, still reading stress, is late. BlackRock's warning about defensive tilts is the cost of being late (BlackRock p.5): "In many cases, these managers gave up more excess return in subsequent 'Very Positive' regimes than was mitigated on the downside during 'Very Negative' regimes." A practical overlay therefore uses the regime probability to *size* the tilt budget (smaller $\kappa$ in stress, so that neither signal can move the book much while it is least reliable) and the valuation signal to *direct* it. Equity momentum in credit, which Dynkin and coauthors found positive in both drawdown and recovery regimes (§12.4; Dynkin p.617), is the one signal in the set that does not need the reconciliation.

The cleanest recent test of that reconciliation lasted about five weeks, and its numbers, which the replay in §12.9 uses, are these.

> **Trend Watch: April 2025 as a Transition Test.** *What happened:* a regime transition in about 26 trading days of drawdown (February 28 to April 7). The HY OAS moved from 259 bp (January 22) to 461 bp (April 7); peak-to-trough total returns were HY −3.83% (February 28 to April 7), CCC −7.80%, B −4.21%, BB −2.83%, IG −3.03% (March 3 to April 11), EM corporate −2.37% and EM HY corporate −3.79% (ICE BofA indices via FRED). HY mutual funds and ETFs saw −\$10.9bn of flows in April and +\$18.5bn from May to September, and by the end of September 2025 the HY spread-to-worst was 299 bp, "only 22 bps wider than the post-2008 tights reached earlier in 2025," after 12 straight quarterly gains, the longest run since 1997 (MacKay Shields, *High Yield 4Q 2025 Outlook*, October 2025). *What it means for the desk:* the drawdowns lined up by DTS and quality, as (12.3) predicts, and the snap-back was faster than any monthly regime filter. A book that de-risked on the filtered stress probability in mid-April would have sold near the wides and paid round-trip LCS to own less of the recovery. The private-credit sleeve's marks did not move at all, by construction, which made it look like the best diversifier of the quarter. That is the desmoothing lesson of §12.5, delivered in real time.

## 12.9 Case Studies: Three Stress Tests of the Framework

### Case Study A: April 2025, a Regime Transition in 25 Trading Days

#### Long Scene: Twenty-Five Days (a replay, cut off at the close on 7 April 2025)

*(A replay. The sleeve as it stood in 2025, its overlay and rebalance rule, the desk's runs and blotter, the cards and every line of dialogue are fictional. Spreads, volumes, flows, ETF premiums and dates are public and cited.)*

On Friday afternoon, 16 October 2026, Ines made Theo build the replay folder himself, on the theory that whoever builds the folder learns the most from it. It was a remembered week. Everyone at the desk knew how April 2025 had ended, so Ines's rule for remembered weeks applied: the cards are graded against what was knowable at the cut-off and against the desk's own blotter from the time, not against hindsight. Theo had spent the tariff week at PJT refreshing liquidity runways for clients whose names he still could not say, which meant he remembered April 2025 as a set of revolver questions, not as a tape. His memory of the week was a conference room, a chief financial officer asking whether the revolver banks would still fund a draw if the tariffs stuck, and a partner asking for the runway "with and without the overseas supplier" by Thursday. Nobody in that room had mentioned a spread. That was the difference between the seats, Ines had told him in his first week: the banker's clock runs in weeks of cash and the desk's runs in basis points per hour, and a replay was the only way to put both clocks on one page. Building the tape was the point.

**Beat 1: the tape, and a filter that eats months.** The folder opened on the year's tights. The HY OAS was 259 bp on 22 January 2025, and it had drifted to 355 bp by the end of March (ICE BofA via FRED). The HY total-return index had been falling since 28 February. After the close on Wednesday 2 April came the tariff announcement. By Friday the 4th the HY OAS was 445 bp. On Monday the 7th, the cut-off, it closed at 461 bp, with B at 486, CCC at 1,137, BB at 306 and IG at 120; the VIX closed at 46.98 (FRED). That day about \$99bn of fixed-income ETFs changed hands, roughly 60% of it in iShares funds (Coalition Greenwich, reported by The DESK), which on a stress day is what the bond market looks like when the bonds themselves are hard to trade.

The last page was the sleeve's regime overlay, as it had run that Monday morning. The monthly filter, fed the March month-end, put the stress probability at 0.21 *(the desk's fictional run)*.

"Two hundred basis points in eleven weeks, and the filter says one in five," said Theo.

"The filter eats months," Kaz said. "April has not finished. It cannot have an opinion about a month that does not exist yet." Kaz did not sound happy about it. "And when April does finish, the filter will see one month-end print, not the day the spread peaked."

**Beat 2: the rebalance that sells what has a price.** The sleeve rebalanced to its risk budgets every Monday (§12.6), and Theo had put that Monday's trade list in the folder exactly as the engine produced it. It sold HY, loans, CLO mezzanine and EM corporates, and it added to the BDC through a subscription at the last reported NAV. The engine's reasoning was correct arithmetic on the numbers it had. The EWMA covariance had learned the stress quickly for every public sector, their volatilities had jumped, and their contributions to risk had blown through their budgets. The BDC's reported volatility was still 1.9%, its NAV unchanged since December, its return for the quarter the best on the sheet. In the engine's terms the private sleeve had outperformed and become a smaller share of the risk, so restoring the budgets meant selling public credit and buying more of the one asset that had not reported anything. The list was not small. HY's EWMA volatility had gone from about 4% to about 7% annualized in five weeks, CLO mezzanine's further, and the public sleeves' share of the risk budget had risen from 62% to 78% *(all illustrative)*. To restore the budgets the engine sold 5% of NAV of public credit, bought 2% of the BDC and parked the rest in cash. Kaz checked the arithmetic twice and found nothing wrong with it, which was the problem: every number was right, and one of the inputs was a December appraisal.

"It didn't outperform," said Theo. "It didn't report." He drew two columns on the whiteboard, one headed *has a price* and one headed *has a NAV*, and an arrow from the first to the second. "This rebalance sells what has a price, at the wides, to buy what doesn't, at a mark from December. I spent four weeks this month learning why that mark is a valuation committee with a deadline. I'm not trading against it."

**Beat 3: three signals and a table with no chips on it.** Then the overlay's three signals, which disagreed exactly as §12.8 says they do. The OU forecast saw HY roughly two standard deviations wide of its long-run mean and wanted to buy. Theo did the leash arithmetic of §12.3 on the back of the folder: with a two-year half-life, a 300 bp gap closes by about 89 bp over a year, and by about 9 bp over the next month *(illustrative)*. "The leash pulls," he said, "but it pulls in years, and the panic is in days." The regime model, or Kaz's eye, which on this Monday was quicker, wanted to sell. And the dealers, Ines pointed out, were not offering much of a market for either view. Her own blotter from that week (the desk's, and fictional), which she had added to the folder without being asked, showed RFQs answered by fewer dealers and at wider prices than any week since 2022.

"So count the pot," Ines said. "Not the expected return. The pot. If you buy here and you're right, you collect the reversion. If you buy here and need to sell next month, you pay the round trip twice, at a bid-ask that's twice what it was in March." She tapped the ETF number. "And look at who's on the other side. When the ETF trades at a discount to its NAV, somebody is selling the whole basket in a hurry. That's someone else's forced seller. That's the only player at this table I want to play against. Part of the discount is a clock, because the NAV is struck from evaluated prices that lag on a day like this (Chapter 20). The rest is a person who has to sell."

*It is the close on 7 April 2025. Write three things: whether you rebalance to the risk budgets, de-risk on the regime, or buy the widening; how much of the tilt budget $\kappa$ you use; and which number on the page you refuse to act on.*

Kaz's card de-risked, using the full tilt budget to cut HY, CCC-heavy sleeves and CLO mezzanine, and refused to act on the OU z-score: "A leash is a model of calm. Nobody has shown me the leash is still attached." Mags's card bought, with half of $\kappa$, and with a date on it: "the second week, not the first." She explained it before anyone asked. "The first week, you're buying from people who are scared. The second week, you're buying from people who are *forced*: the fund outflows have hit, the redemptions settle, the ETFs trade at discounts because somebody has to deliver cash. Scared is expensive. Forced is cheap. And it's Monday of the second week." "Back in my day the second week was when the phone started ringing with people who had to sell, instead of people who wanted to. You could hear the difference in their voices. Now you can see it in the ETF discount, which is better, because it doesn't lie about being calm." Her refused number was the BDC's NAV. Ines used a quarter of $\kappa$, only in the sectors where an ETF discount said a forced seller was on the other side, and refused the monthly filter's 0.21, which was the right answer to a question from March. Theo's card said no rebalance, a small tilt, and refused the BDC's weight in the sleeve, "because it is a weight computed from a price nobody paid."

Ines opened the second half of the folder.

**Beat 4: the snap-back.** On Tuesday 8 April the VIX closed at 52.33, its highest close of the episode, one day after the spread had peaked (FRED). US credit traded a then-record \$89.7bn, 12% of it through portfolio trades (Coalition Greenwich, 14 April 2025), and HYG closed at a 0.66% discount to its NAV (iShares). The average number of dealer prices a US high-grade RFQ received on MarketAxess fell from 13.2 to 6.6 on 9 April, and was back to 11.3 within a week (MarketAxess, July 2025). That was what full balance sheets look like in a statistic. Ines read the desk's own hand history for the 8th aloud: it had made markets all day, been hit far more often than lifted, and closed the session longer than it wanted to be *(fictional)*, "which nobody enjoyed until Wednesday." On Wednesday 9 April came the 90-day pause on most of the new tariffs, and HYG closed that day at a 1.49% premium to NAV, a swing of more than two percentage points of premium in one session. The month-end print on 30 April was 394 bp, so a monthly sample of the episode never saw 461 at all. The fund flows and the September tights are in the Trend Watch at the end of §12.8: out in April, back in by more from May to September, and a spread-to-worst within 22 bp of the post-2008 tights by the end of September.

Kaz's card was graded first. De-risking with the full budget on the close of the 7th sold within a day of the wides, paid the round trip at the widest bid-ask of the year, and owned less of a recovery that began two sessions later. "The regime was real," Kaz said. "It was also over before my trades settled." The BlackRock sentence in §12.8 is this card's grade, in someone else's words. Mags's card scored best, and not because of the tariff pause, which nobody at the cut-off could have known. The forced selling she wanted to buy from arrived on schedule on the 8th, in record volume and at an ETF discount, and her trades would have been paid by September whether or not the pause came on the 9th. Ines's quarter of $\kappa$ was right-sized and right-signed. Theo's refusal to rebalance was the cheapest decision in the folder, because the trade it refused would have sold public credit near the wides to buy a sleeve that never marked down. The reader's card is graded on the third line: a card that refused the monthly filter or the BDC's NAV-based weight read the page correctly, whatever it did next.

While Ines graded, Kaz reran the regime filter the way the answer would have wanted it, on weekly data and on the BB, B and CCC vector instead of the index. In that run the stress probability crossed one half in the third week of March *(the desk's fictional run)*, three weeks before the peak, while the CCC bucket was widening faster than the index and the headline was still in the 300s. Kaz looked at it for a long time. "Same model. Different clock, different ruler. It saw the start."

Then Ines read the answer paragraph she had written in 2025, which had no trade on it at all, only what the desk's own engine had gotten wrong. The filtered stress probability rises only after the first bad month has printed, so a monthly filter with a one-month action delay acts in May, after the trough; a weekly filter on the BB/B/CCC vector would have acted in mid-March, near the start, as Kaz's rerun had just shown. The covariance, by contrast, was right: cross-sector correlation went to one exactly as the DTS-scaled factor model predicts, because with (12.3), doubling the factor variance raises every pairwise correlation toward one without any change to $\Omega$'s structure, so the model's stress covariance was right before the fact and only its *probability* was late. And the private-credit sleeve did not move, so a desk that rebalanced to its targets in April mechanically *sold* public credit near the wides to keep its private-credit share, because private credit had "outperformed." The repair is to rebalance on desmoothed weights and risk, or not at all, inside a stress regime. Figure 12.4 shows the tape and what a month-end sample of it looks like.

Source: ICE BofA US High Yield OAS and total-return indices via FRED (BAMLH0A0HYM2, BAMLHYH0A0HYM2TRIV, BAMLHYH0A1BBTRIV, BAMLHYH0A2BTRIV, BAMLHYH0A3CMTRIV), pulled October 18, 2026; losses run from each index's high since February 1 to its April 7 low.](../assets/figures/ch12_april_2025_daily_vs_month_end.png)

### Case Study B: First Brands, Tricolor and the First BDC Redemption Cycle

This case is told once, as the replay in §12.7 ("Long Scene: The Queue"): First Brands and Tricolor in September and October 2025, the OBDC II merger that was announced and withdrawn in November, the par loan sale and the \$3.80 tender in the spring of 2026, and the first quarter in which the gate bound for everyone at once. Its lesson for this section is the one the scene grades: the hit to private credit came through the gate, not through the marks.

### Case Study C: The 2026 CCC/BB Split

*(Live, not a replay. The desk's model runs, Hana's dispersion run and every line of dialogue are fictional; the spreads, returns and quotations are public and cited.)*

By October 15, 2026, the HY index OAS was 323 bp, unremarkable. Inside it, CCC was at 1,278 bp and BB at 197 bp, a 1,081 bp gap; CCC returned −5.21% year to date against +0.33% for BB (FRED). That was Thursday of the week the PM's spreadsheet arrived, and the evening marks came in while the desk was still arguing about the BDC.

Kaz's regime model, the one fitted to the HY *index*, had run at six. It read calm, with a stress probability of 0.08 *(the desk's fictional run)*, and it was not wrong about what it measured. An index-level MAC engine reads "HY at 323, fair, hold the strategic weight," because 323 bp is close to the index's own recent average and its month-to-month moves had been small since the summer. The index's volatility was low, its correlation with the other public sectors was ordinary, and nothing in the eleven tabs was moving together.

Hana had run something else. After the August refresh she had started a notebook that fitted the same two-state model to the *vector* of BB, B and CCC excess returns instead of the index, with each state allowed its own idiosyncratic variance, and she had been running it every Thursday since, mostly to see whether it would ever disagree with the production model. On this Thursday it did. The common factor's volatility was low, but the variance of the buckets around it, the part that belongs to each bucket alone, had been rising since June, and the model had moved most of its weight onto a state the production model did not have: quiet market, loud dispersion *(the desk's fictional run)*.

"It's the same market," Kaz said, looking at the two outputs. "Two models, one says calm and one says something is happening."

"It's two markets," said Mags. "You fitted the first one on the average of them." She pointed at the CCC line in Figure 12.5's data. "Break-even default rate on that bucket is about twenty percent a year at a thirty-five recovery. We did that an hour ago." (§12.3; the recovery is *illustrative*.) "On the BB bucket it's about three. Those aren't one asset with one regime. That's two assets that happen to share an index."

Hana added a number she had computed for herself, because the composition argument of §12.3 had stuck with her. Holding the bucket spreads at their 15 October levels and putting back the index weights of December 2024, the headline OAS came out at about 377 bp, not 323 *(the desk's computation from the FRED bucket series)*. Roughly 54 bp of the index's calm was its mix: fewer CCCs in it than there used to be, and those that remained much wider. The CCC spread stood at almost four times the index's. At the April 2025 peak, in the replay the desk would run the next day, it had been about two and a half times.

Theo's question was where the CCC risk entered the sleeve, because the sleeve held no CCC tab. The expected-loss term of (12.1) for the CCC bucket depends almost entirely on which issuers enter liability management transactions and at what recovery (Chapter 13), and that risk had two back doors into the PM's eleven tabs. CLO BBB to B tranches are levered to the CCC bucket through the overcollateralization tests (typical documents haircut CCC holdings above about 7.5% of the pool to market value), so a wave of downgrades to CCC reaches the mezzanine tranche through the waterfall before any loan defaults. And the Fed's May 2026 report put software at the top of private-credit sector exposure, which is the BDC's tab. "So the CCC problem is in the sheet twice," Theo said, "and it isn't labeled CCC either time."

The same day, on Bloomberg Intelligence's *The Credit Edge*, TCW's chief investment officer Bryan Whalen described the order in which borrowers break: the CCCs are "the weakest borrower, and they cry uncle first," then the single-Bs, then the double-Bs (*The Credit Edge*, 15 October 2026). Mags played the clip twice, which for her is applause.

> **View From Another Seat.** *The CLO manager: seven numbers and a 7.5% line.* For the manager of a broadly syndicated CLO (described generically), the CCC split is not a valuation question but a covenant one. Every month the trustee report checks seven numbers against their limits: the CCC share, the weighted average rating factor, the diversity score, the weighted average spread, the weighted average life, and the overcollateralization and interest-coverage cushions. The first is the sharp one. In the words of a European Systemic Risk Board study, "a CLO faces a limit on loans rated CCC/Caa1 or below, typically set to 7.5%. The loans in excess of this percentage are marked at the lowest market value of the loans in the CCC/Caa1 bucket," and "the median CLO operates within 4% of the most stringent covenant threshold" (Kundu, ESRB Working Paper 141, March 2023). One CLO-equity investor's letter put market-wide CCC exposure at 4.3% and junior OC cushions at 3.9% early in 2026 (Eagle Point Income Co., letter of 18 February 2026). So a manager near the line does not wait to see whether a downgraded loan defaults. It sells, and Kundu's finding is that the lowest-price haircut pushes managers to sell their *higher*-priced CCC loans first, because the cheap ones set the haircut either way. From this seat, a CCC spread of 1,278 bp is partly a default forecast and partly the price of being the buyer when the CLOs are the sellers. For the MAC desk, the CLO BBB tab in the PM's spreadsheet is a position in this manager's cushion, and the cushion is what the CCC bucket is eating.

Theo wrote the response to the PM at 7:40 that evening, three sentences long, because the PM had asked for efficiency and he had decided to take it literally. "We would split the HY sleeve into BB, B and CCC sub-sleeves, each with its own loss term, because the index average is hiding two markets. We would price the CLO tranche off the CCC bucket and its overcollateralization cushion rather than off its rating. And we would fit the regime model on the bucket vector, where a dispersion regime shows up as rising idiosyncratic variance even while the index is calm, which is what it is doing today." He read it to Ines before sending it.

"No numbers," she said.

"The numbers are in the attachment. The PM reads three sentences." He sent it. Figure 12.5 was the attachment.

Source: ICE BofA US High Yield OAS and total-return indices via FRED (BAMLH0A0HYM2, BAMLH0A1HYBB, BAMLH0A2HYB, BAMLH0A3HYC; BAMLHYH0A0HYM2TRIV, BAMLHYH0A1BBTRIV, BAMLHYH0A2BTRIV, BAMLHYH0A3CMTRIV), pulled October 18, 2026; returns from December 31, 2025.](../assets/figures/ch12_ccc_bb_split.png)

## 12.10 The MAC Engine: A Reference Implementation

### Specification for AI Implementation

**The Spec You Hand the Robot.** What ROBO built from the vague version ("maximize Sharpe across our credit sectors"): a portfolio at the 35% direct-lending bound, a claimed volatility it computed from appraisal marks, and an EM sovereign allocation sized on an index yield that included a defaulted country. It never complains and never guesses; it did exactly what it was asked. The precise version follows.

*Inputs.* Sector table, one row per sector: `{sector: str, yld, pd, rec: decimal, dmod, dspr: years, spread: decimal, dspread_h: decimal change over the horizon, tier in {HL, ML, LL, IL}, days: float, lcs_bp: float, w_min, w_max: decimal}`. Return panel `R: (T, n)` monthly excess returns (decimal), relative spread changes `U: (T, n)`. Horizon `h` in years. All rates are decimals per year; the code raises if anything looks like a percent.

*Pipeline.* (1) forward returns by (12.1) with physical PD and seat-level recovery; (2) desmooth any appraisal-marked series (GLM weights, invertibility check) or build its risk from a proxy via `smoothed_view`; (3) $\Omega$ by EWMA on relative spread changes, shrunk to a one-factor target, then $\Sigma$ by (12.3); (4) two-state HMM on the bucket-level excess-return vector, filtered probabilities only; (5) regime-mixture moments by (12.2); (6) strategic allocation by mean-variance with the tiers of (12.4), with shadow prices of the binding constraints reported; (7) tactical tilt with an $\ell_1$ budget and LCS costs.

*Edge cases and guards.* Log-space densities with a max-shift before exponentiating; ridge $10^{-10}$ on regime covariances; label alignment after every fit; refuse non-invertible smoothing weights; feasibility check on bounds before optimizing; every optimizer output is re-checked against every constraint by assert, not trusted from the solver's success flag.

The five blocks run in order in one interpreter; each ends in asserts that are the acceptance tests.

At a quarter to eight on Tuesday, Theo's pencil had tied Nuveen's five numbers on the first pass and failed to tie their labels (§12.2). Block 1 is that pencil, made permanent. Every allocation engine begins with a table nobody enjoys typing. Theo's has eleven rows, one per sector, and a dozen columns that each mean something different: a yield, a physical default probability, a recovery, two durations, a spread, an expected spread move, a liquidity tier, days to liquidate, a round-trip cost and a pair of weight bounds. In a spreadsheet this table is right on Monday and wrong by Friday, when someone pastes 6.97 into a column that wanted 0.0697 and the optimizer discovers a sector yielding 697%. The desk automates this first step for the dullest reason there is: the forward return is the number every later block inherits, so a unit error here is a unit error everywhere, and it is cheapest to catch before anything has been optimized.

Block 1 turns the table into the two vectors the rest of the chapter runs on. The inputs are illustrative decimals per year, durations in years, and weight bounds read from Nuveen's Figure 5. Three small functions implement (12.1) term by term. `expected_loss` multiplies the physical default probability by one minus recovery. `mtm_drag` multiplies a duration by an expected yield or spread change over the horizon and divides by the horizon, so a 50 bp rise over five years costs a 3.2-duration sector 32 bp a year. `forward_return` subtracts those drags from the yield. Spread duration drives the spread term and modified duration drives the rates term, which is why loans, CLOs and direct lending carry a quarter-year of rate duration and three to four years of spread duration. The outputs are `MU`, the forward return by sector (3.62% for HY corporates and 6.53% for CLO BBB to B on these inputs), and `DTS`, spread duration times spread, which Block 3 uses to scale risk.

The asserts are the acceptance tests. Feeding the function Nuveen's own HY inputs must return 3.56%. The six portfolios of Figure 6 must each imply a cash rate between 3.60% and 3.75% when computed as return minus Sharpe times volatility, which checks that the vendor's table is at least consistent with itself. The CCC break-even must come out near 19.7%, and a spread duration of two at 200 bp must carry the same DTS as four at 100 bp.

It is the front door for any sector-level forecast, though not where yields move along a clearly nonlinear path: `mtm_drag` is the plain $D\Delta/h$ of Nuveen's identity and leaves out the reinvestment offset of §12.2, so it overstates the drag a little. The trap is in the unit guard itself. `_decimal` raises when any magnitude exceeds 1.0, which catches 6.97 but waves through 0.75 typed for 75 bp, a perfectly legal 75% a year.

*The full listing is [Listing 12.1 in Appendix F](#code-12-1).*

Block 2 desmooths (§12.5). The planted profile $\theta = (0.5, 0.3, 0.2)$ has $\xi = 0.38$.

Listing 12.2 is the thermometer of §12.5 run backward: it is the block that turned Kaz's 1.9% into about 5.7% on the day Mags asked who had measured it. Here is the problem as Kaz meets it. The direct-lending sleeve reports a return every month, but the return is a sequence of appraisals: it moves a little, it moves late, and each month's change is correlated with the previous month's for reasons that have nothing to do with the economy. Mags would ask whether the number was measured by the fund or by the fund's lawyer. An optimizer fed that series concludes the sleeve is nearly riskless and buries the book in it. The cure of §12.5 is to estimate how much averaging the appraisals are doing and undo it. A desk automates the cure because it has to be re-run every quarter on every appraisal-marked series, and because the one way it fails, an unstable inverse, produces garbage that looks exactly like data.

The listing has four working parts. `acf` computes sample autocorrelations at lags one through k. `_ma_rho` computes the autocorrelations that a given weight vector would produce if the true returns were serially uncorrelated. `fit_smoothing` finds the weights that make the second match the first, searching over an unconstrained vector passed through `_softmax`, which forces the weights to be nonnegative and to sum to one, the Getmansky–Lo–Makarov constraints, so the search never has to enforce them. It returns the weights and $\xi=\sum_j\theta_j^2$, the share of true variance that survives in the reported series; reported volatility divided by $\sqrt{\xi}$ is the true volatility. `desmooth` inverts the averaging one period at a time: take the reported return, subtract the weighted true returns already recovered, divide by $\theta_0$. `ar1_profile` supplies the truncated geometric weights of the AR(1) smoothing model for when you would rather assume a persistence than estimate one.

The test is a planted-parameter test. It builds 6,000 months of true returns at 2% monthly volatility, smooths them with weights $(0.5, 0.3, 0.2)$, drops the first ten months as burn-in, and demands that the fit recover $\xi$ near 0.38 (it prints 0.379), recover the true volatility within 10%, reproduce the true series to $10^{-10}$ when handed the true weights, and give $\xi=(1-\phi)/(1+\phi)$ for the AR(1) profile.

It belongs on a NAV series sampled at the frequency of the appraisals, with enough history to pin down k autocorrelations; the listed share price stays out, for the reason Theo gave on Friday (§12.5, "The listed twin"). The subtler trap is the mirror image: a weight vector and its reverse have identical autocorrelations, but only one of them inverts stably. The decreasing starting point steers the search toward the invertible one, which is a heuristic and not a guarantee, so `desmooth` checks the roots of the weight polynomial and raises rather than return a series that explodes.

*The full listing is [Listing 12.2 in Appendix F](#code-12-2).*

Block 3 builds the DTS covariance, the smoothed view an optimizer would see, and a synthetic regime panel: 3,000 months, which is 250 years, longer than the HY market by about two centuries, because a planted-parameter test needs power that real history does not have.

At 8:15 on the morning of the August refresh, Hana's run stopped on a minimum eigenvalue of $-1.0 \times 10^{-7}$ after a vendor backfill (§12.4); the asserts at the end of this block are the ones that stopped it. A covariance matrix is the quietest way for an allocation engine to go wrong. Eleven sectors have 66 distinct covariances, a few years of monthly data supply roughly one effective observation per parameter, and an optimizer handed that sample matrix will find the noise and bet on it. The structural answer of §12.5 is to stop estimating eleven volatilities and estimate one covariance of relative spread changes instead, scale it by each sector's spread duration times spread, and shrink what remains toward a one-factor shape. A desk automates this because the matrix is rebuilt every month, and because somebody has to build, beside it, the matrix an optimizer would see for the appraisal-marked sleeve, so the investment committee can see for itself what the smoothing hides.

The listing does three jobs. `dts_cov` implements (12.3): the elementwise product of the outer product of `DTS` with $\Omega$, the covariance of relative spread changes, plus $\sigma_y^2$ times the outer product of modified durations for the Treasury factor. That rates block is the independent base case, $\rho_{y,s}=0$; the cross term and the per-regime $\rho_k$ of §12.5 are the extension, and the listing does not include them. The "true" $\Omega$ is built from per-sector volatilities and a one-factor correlation with loadings `B_LOAD`, and the yield volatility is 80 bp. The second job, `smoothed_view`, rewrites row and column $i$ the way a GLM-smoothed sector would report: covariances with every other sector are scaled by $\theta_0$ and the own variance by $\theta^\top\theta$. With the AR(1) profile at $\phi=0.8$ the direct-lending volatility prints 6.30% true against 2.10% reported. The third job is the simulation of the regime panel: a two-state Markov chain with persistence 0.95 and 0.80, a common spread factor whose mean and volatility switch with the state, sector loadings on that factor, and idiosyncratic noise that is also larger in stress. Monthly excess returns are the spread divided by 12 minus DTS times the relative spread change.

The estimator comes last. `ewma_cov` runs the recursion at $\lambda=0.97$, seeded with the first 24 months and assuming zero mean. `one_factor_target` builds the factor matrix from an equal-weighted market portfolio, keeping the sample diagonal. `lw_delta` computes the Ledoit–Wolf intensity with the diagonal-$\rho$ simplification flagged in §12.5. The final $\hat\Omega$ blends the EWMA with its target on the last 300 months, annualizes by 12, and goes back through `dts_cov` to give `SIGMA_HAT`. The asserts require the intensity to lie in $[0,1]$, the matrix to be positive semidefinite, and the DTS scaling to hold for the first sector's spread-only volatility.

The number to watch is the intensity itself. On this planted panel `delta` prints 1.000, the ceiling, because the data really are one-factor and the target is the truth. On a real panel an intensity pinned at 1 means the target is doing all the work, which is the cue to check the window length before trusting the matrix.

*The full listing is [Listing 12.3 in Appendix F](#code-12-3).*

Block 4 is the regime engine (§12.4): log-space forward–backward, EM, label alignment, and the mixture moments of (12.2).

Hana's worst find in August was a sign: the June re-fit had swapped the labels, and the overlay had leaned the wrong way for two months before anyone looked (§12.4). Listing 12.4 aligns the labels after every fit because of mornings like that one. Spreads do not wander; they lurch. Between January 22 and April 7, 2025, the HY OAS went from 259 bp to 461 bp (§12.9), and a covariance matrix estimated on the quiet months before it said nothing about the loud ones after. Ines would put it simply: the table changed, and your estimates were fitted to a different game. A regime model asks the one question an allocator can act on, which state are we in right now, and it has to answer using only what had printed by today. The desk automates this because the answer is a probability that must be updated after every print, and because the arithmetic fails silently, with eleven-dimensional densities rounding to zero and the likelihood quietly turning into nonsense.

`mvn_logpdf` evaluates a multivariate normal log density through a Cholesky factor, which gives the quadratic form and the log determinant in one pass. `forward_backward` takes a T-by-2 array of log densities and subtracts each row's maximum before exponentiating, the underflow guard. Its forward pass is the filter: the filtered probabilities $\xi_{t\mid t}$ use data to date and nothing later. Its backward pass produces the smoothed probabilities $\gamma_t$, which use the whole sample, and the expected transition counts; it also returns the log-likelihood, with the shifts added back. `hmm2_em` is the fit. It starts from the worst 20% of months by cross-sectional average return, then alternates weighted means and covariances (with a $10^{-10}$ ridge) with a forward-backward pass, updates the transition matrix from the expected counts, and stops when the likelihood gain falls below tolerance. States are then sorted by average mean return so that label 0 is calm. `stationary` solves $\pi P=\pi$ by least squares. `regime_cma` is (12.2): it rolls the current state probabilities forward, averages them over the horizon, and returns the mixture mean and the mixture covariance, which is the probability-weighted regime covariances plus the spread of regime means around the mixture mean.

The asserts require the fitted diagonal of $P$ to sit within 0.05 of the planted one and filtered accuracy above 85%. It prints 98.2% filtered against 99.0% smoothed; the gap is the price of lateness, and only the filtered number is available to a trader. The fitted durations print as 21.9 and 5.7 months. Starting from stress with a 12-month horizon, the mixture still gives stress only 43% of the weight, because stress lasts under six months. At a 600-month horizon the weights must match the stationary distribution to within two points.

Filtered probabilities are for decisions and smoothed ones for research, which is the whole story of the beautiful backtest in Hana's vignette. Labeling is where the block can still bite. Sorting by mean return works when regimes differ in mean, as they do here, but when they differ mainly in dispersion, as in the CCC story of §12.9, the means can sit close together and the labels can flip between fits. The 20% start also happens to equal the planted stress share, which real data will not oblige. And a state that claims fewer months than there are sectors has a covariance the ridge keeps invertible but cannot make meaningful.

*The full listing is [Listing 12.4 in Appendix F](#code-12-4).*

Block 5 is the optimizers (§12.6–12.8): tangency and ERC unit tests, the flat frontier, Kaz's allocation on reported versus desmoothed risk, the tiered strategic allocation with shadow prices, and the tactical tilt.

The number Theo wanted for the investment committee was not a weight but a price: what the 15% cap was costing at the margin (§12.7). Listing 12.5 is where that price is computed. Everything so far produced inputs. The allocation is where inputs meet constraints, and where a desk discovers that the constraints make more of the decisions than the inputs do. Ines would say you cannot size a bet until you know what you are allowed to lose and how fast you can leave the table. The same problem has to be solved over and over: under reported risk and under desmoothed risk, under a 15% illiquid cap and under 16%, in calm and in stress. The desk automates it because a committee that asks "what if" expects the answer before the coffee cools, and because every answer must be checked against every constraint, every time.

The listing is a toolbox with one workhorse. `feasible_start` builds a point satisfying the budget and the bounds and refuses if the bounds cannot sum to one. `max_sharpe` and `min_var` wrap SLSQP with analytic gradients; `max_return_under_bounds` fills the highest-return sectors to their caps, which is the exact answer to a linear problem; `frontier` spaces six return targets from the minimum-variance return to 95% of the way to that maximum. `optimize_erc` solves the risk-budget problem by Newton's method with a backtracking line search on $\tfrac12 y^\top\Sigma y-b^\top\ln y$. `risk_contrib`, `beta_variance_share` and `utility` are one-liners the tests lean on.

`optimize_tiered` is the engine. It maximizes $w^\top\mu-\tfrac{\gamma}{2}w^\top\Sigma w$ subject to full investment, the bounds, the 15% illiquid cap, a 35% floor on highly and moderately liquid sectors, and a days-to-liquidate budget of 32, the constraint set of (12.4). Given a reference portfolio and a tilt budget, it adds a buy and a sell variable per sector, caps their total at the budget, and charges half the round-trip LCS on each unit traded. The script then runs the checks: tangency against the closed form, ERC to $10^{-8}$, and the beta share at 0.5. It prints the flat frontier, with Sharpe ratios from 0.21 to 0.35. It repeats Kaz's allocation on reported and desmoothed risk, where the reported-risk book pins direct lending at its 35% bound, claims 3.02% volatility and carries 4.56%. It takes shadow prices of the cap and the HY floor by finite difference, relaxing each by one point of NAV. Finally it applies the tactical tilt, using the annualized difference between the stress-mixture and stationary means as the overlay.

The trap here is that SLSQP does not promise feasibility and the result's success flag is not evidence. Hence the asserts: sums, bounds, caps and the liquid floor are re-checked directly on the weights. Two smaller traps travel with it. The finite-difference prices are one-point steps, not derivatives, and can straddle a change in which constraint binds. And a 10% $\ell_1$ tilt budget lets only 5% of NAV change hands, five out and five in.

*The full listing is [Listing 12.5 in Appendix F](#code-12-5).*

Two notes on reading the output. The asserts check what is a theorem or a tolerance: the frontier's volatility rises with its target, the reported-risk portfolio is riskier than it claims, relaxing a constraint cannot reduce utility, and the caps hold. The *weights* are printed rather than asserted, because they depend on illustrative inputs. The useful exercise is to change one expected-loss assumption by 25 bp and watch how far they move (§12.6).

## 12.11 Desk Debrief

**Finder.** Each tool the chapter builds, with the box that explains it, the scene that tests it and the listing that implements it.

| Regime persistence and fat tails | $1/(1-P_{kk})$; (12.2) | The weather coin and two bell curves (§12.4) | Kaz's "typo"; Twenty-Five Days, Beat 1 (§12.9) | [Listing 12.4](#code-12-4) |

| Desmoothing appraisal returns | $\xi = (1-\phi)/(1+\phi)$ | The thermometer with a lag (§12.5) | The listed twin (§12.5) | [Listing 12.2](#code-12-2) |
| Flat frontier and risk budgets | Mediant chain; $\text{RC}_i = b_i$ | Mixing lemonades (§12.6) | Kaz concedes the region, not the point (§12.6) | [Listing 12.5](#code-12-5) |
| Liquidity tiers, the gate, the shadow price | (12.4); $\eta$ | The price of a rule (§12.7) | The Queue (§12.7) | [Listing 12.5](#code-12-5) |
| Tactical tilt and the turnover budget | $\lVert w - w^{\text{SAA}}\rVert_1 \le \kappa$ | Jars and a kitchen scale (§12.8) | Twenty-Five Days (§12.9); the CCC/BB split (§12.9) | [Listing 12.5](#code-12-5) |

Friday, after the April replay. Kaz's direct-lending weight had fallen from the 35% bound to whatever the 15% cap and the days budget allowed. The PM's comment on the new spreadsheet said "Why?" Theo answered it with three numbers, and none of them was a yield.

- **The forward return is an identity with two measures in it.** Yield is a market ($\mathbb{Q}$-flavored) quantity; the loss term must be physical. A CDS-implied default probability in the loss term forecasts a zero risk premium by construction.
- **Expected credit loss is the restructuring banker's variable.** Set recovery by the seat in the waterfall (about 33% for direct loans, 52% for syndicated loans, 39% for HY bonds per FEDS 2024), not by a rating table. A 33% recovery has a 40% larger loss given default than a 52% one.
- **Rank sectors by spread per unit of something.** Break-even default $s/(1-R)$, carry per unit of DTS risk $(1 - \text{EL}/s)/(D^{\text{spr}}\sigma(\Delta s/s))$, and spread net of LCS. A wider spread is a bigger bet, not a better one.
- **Composition moves the mean, not the tail.** The HY index went from 37% BB to 51–54% BB. Z-scores against raw history mostly measure that change. Use fixed-mix spreads and bucket-level models.
- **Desmooth before you optimize.** $\sigma_{\text{true}} = \sigma_{\text{reported}}/\sqrt{\sum_j\theta_j^2}$; contemporaneous beta is understated by $\theta_0$. At AR(1) $\phi = 0.8$, volatility is understated threefold and beta fivefold.
- **The frontier is flat by the mediant inequality.** Long-only credit Sharpe ratios are weighted averages of sectors' systematic Sharpes. When the optimizer's choice sits inside the error bars, the constraints, not the objective, decide the allocation.
- **Liquidity tiers bind first.** The 15% illiquid cap, the liquid-sleeve minimum and the days-to-liquidate budget are known exactly; expected returns are not. Report shadow prices, and remember that a 5% quarterly gate is a queue position.
- **Regimes size the tilt; valuation directs it.** Trade on filtered probabilities with a delay, never smoothed ones. Expect the filter to be a month late into stress and a month late out of it, as in April 2025.

### The Spec You Hand the Robot

```text
ROBO: build mac_engine, a multi-asset credit allocator. Implement exactly this; where anything is
unspecified, stop and ask. Do not guess.

INPUTS (decimals per year; durations in years; point-in-time)
  sectors[n]: yld (yield-to-worst EX-DISTRESSED: drop constituents priced < 50, model them separately),
              pd (PHYSICAL annual default rate; never CDS-implied), rec (by seat in the waterfall),
              dmod, dspr (OAS duration for callables), spread, dspread_h (expected change over horizon),
              tier in {HL, ML, LL, IL} (Rule 22e-4 style), days (to liquidate), lcs_bp (round trip),
              w_min, w_max, smoothed (bool: appraisal-marked series?)
  R[T,n] monthly excess returns at bucket level (BB, B, CCC split); U[T,n] relative spread changes
  h horizon (years), cash rate, gamma (risk aversion)
PIPELINE
  1 mu_i = yld - pd*(1-rec) - dmod*d_rates/h - dspr*dspread_h/h   (eq. 12.1; raise on percent inputs)
  2 smoothed series: fit GLM theta (k=2, theta>=0, sum 1, invertible or REFUSE); vol /= sqrt(sum theta^2);
    covariances with others /= theta_0 (i.e. use the true-risk view, never the reported one)
  3 Omega = EWMA(U, lam chosen by out-of-sample likelihood), shrink to one-factor target (LW delta);
    Sigma = diag(DTS) Omega diag(DTS) + sig_y^2 dmod dmod'; assert min eigenvalue >= -1e-10
    (base case rho_ys = 0; total-return extension adds rho_k cross term inside each Sigma_k, section 12.5)
  4 HMM: K=2, full covariance, log-space forward-backward, EM; align labels (state 0 = higher mean);
    act on FILTERED probabilities with a one-month delay; never use smoothed ones in a backtest
  5 regime CMA: horizon-averaged mixture (eq. 12.2); overlay = mixture mean - stationary mean
  6 SAA: max w'mu - gamma/2 w'Sigma w  s.t. sum w = 1, w_min <= w <= w_max, sum_IL w <= 0.15,
    sum_{HL,ML} w >= liquid_min, w'days <= tau_max; report shadow prices of every binding constraint
  7 TAA: same, plus ||w - w_saa||_1 <= kappa via split variables, cost sum |dw| * lcs/2;
    kappa shrinks as the filtered stress probability rises
  8 single-issuer DTS share <= cap; report top-5 issuer yield contribution per sector
ACCEPTANCE TESTS: the asserts in Section 12.10, plus: every constraint re-checked after the solver
returns; weights printed with and without desmoothing; a 25bp perturbation to any el moves no
weight by more than the stated tolerance or the run is flagged "fragile".
```

### Exercises

1. **Read the chart.** Nuveen's Figure 3 prints 6.97, 2.55, 0.37, 0.49 and 3.56. Compute the default rate implied by each possible assignment of 2.55 and 0.49 to expected credit loss at 40% recovery. Which assignment survives? What would you need from the PDF itself to settle it without economics?
2. **The appraisal discount.** A perpetual BDC reports quarterly NAV returns with volatility 1.8% annualized and a lag-1 autocorrelation of 0.6. Under AR(1) smoothing, compute $\xi$, the true volatility and the factor by which its contemporaneous HY beta is understated. Then explain to the valuation committee, politely, why the annualization was the problem and not the arithmetic.
3. **Kaz's typo.** Kaz's HMM has $P_{11} = 0.97$ and $P_{22} = 0.10$. Compute the expected duration of each regime and the stationary distribution. Show that a filter acting with a one-month delay cannot, on average, act on this stress state at all. Then propose a reparameterization (weekly data, or a prior on $P_{22}$) and say what it costs.
4. **Two-asset ERC.** Show that for $n = 2$ the equal-risk-contribution weights are $w_i \propto 1/\sigma_i$ for any correlation. Apply this to HY (DTS 0.096) and CLO BBB to B (DTS 0.22) at a common $\sigma(\Delta s/s)$, and compare with 50/50 market-value weights.
5. **The gate as a queue.** A BDC has a 5% quarterly gate. Redemption requests are 15% of NAV this quarter and will be 10% of the remaining NAV in each later quarter. How many quarters until an investor who requested a full exit this quarter is fully paid, assuming pro-rata fills? What days-to-liquidate $\tau$ should the optimizer use, and why is a constant the wrong answer?
6. **ROBO literalism.** You tell ROBO to "minimize the number of regime switches the model reports." What does it build, and which single line in the spec above prevents it?
