A May 2023 super-priority deal had defined "Required Lender" as more than 50% of the first-out plus second-out loans, read from the agent's register. In July 2023 Invesco quietly bought enough of those loans to cross 50%, and became Required Lender without anyone calling it. An ad hoc group of the other lenders (Bain Capital Credit, Canyon and Eaton Vance) and the sponsor, One Rock, answered on December 11, 2023: they lent \$228.3mm to RS Funding, a vehicle the parent voted and Robertshaw economically owned, and the cash prepaid \$117.6mm of first-out loans. Invesco fell below 50%, and the other group became Required Lender in its place. Robertshaw filed for Chapter 11 on February 15, 2024, and on June 20, 2024, Judge Lopez held that the new group were the Required Lenders and that Invesco's remedy was a money claim against the company, not its control back. Required-Lender status is a position you can trade into and out of, at prices nobody publishes, so `holder_hhi` and every coalition input must be re-read from the register as often as the register can be had, not lifted from the last 10-Q or the last Rule 2019 statement. When the register is the battlefield, the knapsack is a snapshot of a fight, and the sponsor is only one of the people packing bags.

**Why prices drift before announcements.** One more refinement explains a pattern every loan trader has seen. Lenders do not observe $V$ exactly. Each gets a noisy signal $s_i = V + \sigma \epsilon_i$. In the global-games framework of Morris and Shin (*Unique Equilibrium in a Model of Self-Fulfilling Currency Attacks*, American Economic Review, 1998), a coordination game with noisy private signals has a unique threshold equilibrium: each player joins the coalition if and only if its signal falls below a cutoff $s^*$, so the coalition forms if and only if $V$ is below some $V^*$. The cutoff is common knowledge in equilibrium, which means *the act of organizing is itself a signal that the organizers' estimates of $V$ are low*. Loan prices drift down as groups organize, before anything is announced. For the desk, an organizing signal (counsel hired, a Rule 2019 statement, a co-op reported) is a downward update on $V$ and an upward update on the PRS at the same time.

> **Math, Gently.** *Global games in one picture.* Every lender in the class carries a thermometer, and every thermometer is slightly off. Nobody knows the company's true temperature, $V$. But each lender knows that everyone else's thermometer reads close to its own: if mine says "cold," yours probably says "cold-ish," and you know that mine does, and I know that you know. That chain of "I know that you know" collapses to a single cutoff reading. Below it you join a group; above it you don't. Nobody has to agree with anybody, and the cutoff still emerges from the noise. Tiny number: if the cutoff reading is 1,500 and thermometers err by about 100, a lender reading 1,400 joins, and it expects most others to have read below 1,500 too, which is why a group can form in a week once the first call is made.

Prices usually drift down as groups organize. Not always, and the exception teaches the rule. When the threshold is a supermajority and a minority can block it, the tranche that carries the blocking vote becomes a seat, and seats can be bid up. Wesco Aircraft's 2026 secured notes needed two-thirds consent for anything with "the effect of" releasing substantially all collateral. In February 2022 a minority group announced it held more than a third of the 2026s, enough to block the majority's plan, and the two sides raced for the marginal bond; by one market commentator's account the 2026 notes ran from about 85 to above par in the scramble. The price moved *up* because the seat, not the company, was being bought. A model that reads every organizing headline as bad news for the bond will get that tranche exactly backwards, and §13.9 tells the rest of that story.

> **Poker Table.** "The sponsor isn't a player," Ines says. "The sponsor is the dealer, and the dealer chooses who sees the flop. Every lender at the table thinks they're playing the other lenders. They're playing for a seat." She taps the screen. "So when that client offers the Larkspur loan at 78, I don't ask what the loan is worth. I ask which seat the seller has." Her hand history, replayed through markouts: suppose the desk had bought the \$15mm at 78, the uptier closed three weeks later, and the excluded tranche marked at 52 *(illustrative)*. The markout is $-26$ points, or $-\$3.9$mm, on one ticket. Across many such hands the average markout on "client sells after an organizing headline" is the market's estimate of $\Pr(\text{excluded}) \cdot \mathbb{E}[\Delta R^{\text{excl}}]$, which is exactly what §13.8 tries to forecast before the headline.

> **[SOURCE EXTRACTION]** *Moyer_Distressed_Debt_Analysis p.86:* "as in poker, which is analogous because the “multiple-hand” format of the game is similar to the series of transactions in the distressed marketplace, to be effective one must have a credible “bluff.”"
>
> **Annotation.** Moyer's point is about repeated play: an investor who never holds out cannot threaten to, so investors sometimes act against their immediate interest to keep the threat credible for future deals. The LMT era made this literal. A small set of sponsors and a small set of distressed funds meet across many capital structures, and a sponsor's history of non-pro-rata deals is a public record of its type. That is why `sponsor_repeat_lme` is a feature and why it carries a positive sign. Lenders have repeated-game reputations too, and the cooperation agreement (§13.5) is the institution they built to make their threats credible collectively when no single lender's bluff is large enough to matter.

## 13.5 Game Theory II: Cooperation Agreements as Commitment Devices

By Thursday the Larkspur lenders who have not been called have found each other, the way excluded lenders always do: by comparing notes on who has not been called. By Friday they have counsel, a financial advisor, and a forty-page document with a sunset clause. The Ad Hoc Group, represented by counsel, announces in unison that it has "organized." (Cooperation agreements signed in this book so far: 1.)

Mags reads it twice. "When I started, this was a steering committee and a handshake. Now it's a transfer restriction with a joinder." She puts it down. "It's better. Don't repeat that."

#### Lumen, 2023–2026: the co-op that became the deal

*A replay, run the Serta way. The cast and its dialogue are fictional; prices and dates come from the filings and the research note cited.*

Theo wants to know what "better" looks like when it works, so Mags pulls the second binder, the thin one, and they do it the way they did Serta, with Kaz's sheet of paper and nobody reading ahead. The case is Lumen, and it is the reason this section exists: the co-op that did not defend against the deal so much as become it.

**Autumn 2023: the wall.** Lumen Technologies and its subsidiary Level 3 had about \$10bn of debt due in 2027 and a market that did not want to refinance any of it. On October 31, 2023, the company signed a transaction support agreement, the TSA, with a group of creditors holding "over \$7 billion" of its debt. The first version of the deal had pieces for nearly every layer: \$1.2bn of new Level 3 first-lien money, exchanges of Level 3 first-lien notes that needed a 66.7% consent threshold, up to \$2bn of Level 3 unsecured notes moved into a second lien, and Lumen term loans into super-priority paper. The holders were not named in the company's 8-Ks. Guggenheim and Wachtell advised Lumen.

Kaz slides the sheet down to the week of November 9, 2023, where a research note has the prices for paper outside the TSA. Lumen's 4% secured notes due 2027 at 57, the 5.125% 2026s at 52, the term loan B at 75. Level 3's 3.4% first-lien 2027s at 83, the 3.875% first-lien 2029s at 73, its unsecured 2028s at 47. TSA paper traded about ten points above the same bonds outside it. About 49% of the Level 3 unsecured class, \$1.94–1.97bn, was being primed by its own classmates (CreditSights, week of Nov 9, 2023).

"Here is why this is fine," says Kaz, who has read ahead in this section to the paragraph with the inequality, and is visibly pleased about it. "The group holds more than $1-\theta$ of every class it cares about. So no coalition can form without it. So the game is bargaining, not an auction. So nobody gets dealt out, and the excluded do fine."

"The excluded are the people outside the agreement," says Mags. "Look at the Level 3 unsecured 2028s. Forty-seven. Half of its own class is about to sit ahead of it in a second lien, voted there by the other half. Your inequality protects the people who signed the inequality. 'Fine' is not the word."

"It's a ten-point word," says Ines. She has the same research note open and is doing what she always does with a spread, which is turn it into a bet. "TSA paper and non-TSA paper are the same bond with different seats. Ten points is the market's price of the seat. If being left out costs you something like twenty-five points of recovery, ten points says the market thinks there's about a forty percent chance you stay left out. If it costs forty, the market says one in four." She writes $\Pr(\text{excluded}) \times \text{loss} \approx 10$ on the whiteboard, under Kaz's flower and Theo's Serta options, which is getting to be a crowded whiteboard. "The ten points is the number. The argument is about which of the two factors is wrong."

#### Decision point: Friday, 10 November 2023

Theo sets the hand. "November 10, 2023. You hold \$25mm of Level 3 3.875% first-lien 2029s at 73. Suppose you're offered a joinder. The exchange for that series needs 66.7%. If you sign, you go restricted: you can't sell, any transfer to someone outside the agreement is void, and the deal won't close for months. If you stay out, you keep your liquidity and your 73, and you bet that whatever happens to the people outside, it happens later, and more kindly, than it did at Serta."

"Sign," says Mags, at once. "I've watched what happens to people who stay out."

"It depends what four months of not being able to sell is worth to you," says Ines. "For a fund with redemptions, a lot. For us, the question is whether ten points of seat beats four months of optionality. On a bond at 73 it usually does. But that's a price, not a principle."

Kaz, for once, says nothing. Kaz is waiting for the sheet.

**January to March 2024: the deal.** On January 22, 2024, the TSA was amended to cover "over \$12.5 billion" of debt, more than 70% of the Lumen and Level 3 debt due through 2027, with \$1.325bn of new money and a \$1bn revolver. The structure had a seam down the middle. The term-loan pieces were open to all lenders. The note pieces were privately negotiated and "not offered to all holders." The closing thresholds were written into the agreement: 66.7% for the Level 3 secured notes, 50.1% for the unsecured notes, 95% for Lumen's Term A and A-1 loans. Each subscriber's new money was capped at \$250mm, transfers to non-parties were void, and the outside date was February 29, 2024.

It closed on March 22, 2024, with participation of 94.4% in the Lumen Term A and A-1 loans, 98.5% in the Lumen Term B and 99.5% in the Level 3 Term B. More than \$15bn of debt and commitments were addressed. The 2027 maturities fell from about \$9.5bn to about \$800mm, and those due in 2025 and 2026 from about \$2.1bn to about \$600mm. (Cooperation agreements signed in this book so far: 2.)

**Mags was right about the mechanism.** The non-TSA noteholders were primed as she said, and no suit by excluded holders is reported; one research shop called the indenture claims "difficult." It was the Serta picture again: a digital put written by people who were not asked.

**Then the outcome.** On September 17, 2024, Lumen offered the holders who had been left out a follow-on exchange into new 10% secured and second-lien notes due 2032. It paid \$975 per \$1,000 for the 4% secured 2027s (80.8% tendered), \$700 for the 4.5% 2029s (20.9% tendered) and \$860 for the Level 3 4.25% 2028s. On February 2, 2026, Lumen closed the \$5.75bn sale of its consumer fiber business to AT&T and used about \$4.8bn to retire super-priority debt. On May 20, 2026, a cash tender took the Level 3 4.25% 2028s at about 99.4% of par (our arithmetic, early premium included). The bond Mags pointed at, 47 in November 2023, was taken out at about 99 thirty months later.

"So I was right," says Kaz.

"You were right about the number and wrong about the reason," says Mags. "You said bargaining would protect the people outside. It didn't. It protected the people inside, and then the company turned out to be worth a lot more than the people outside were pricing."

Here is the idea that reconciles them, and it arrives formally a few paragraphs below. The co-op's bargain decides the *seats*; enterprise value decides what the seats are *worth*. In Nash-bargaining terms, the joint surplus $\Pi$ was large, because there was a fiber business someone would pay \$5.75bn for, and the company's outside option $d_{\text{sp}}$ was small, because nobody else was offering to refinance \$10bn of 2027 maturities. Large $\Pi$ and small $d_{\text{sp}}$ put the deal deep inside the deal region and hand the co-op most of the surplus. But a large $\Pi$ also means the company comes out the other side with enough value to clean up its leftovers, and the cheapest way to clean up an orphaned bond is to buy it. The excluded holder's recovery was the waterfall of §13.3 evaluated at a $V$ far above $K_1$, plus a company that wanted a simpler balance sheet. Kaz's inequality had nothing to do with it.

Theo writes one line under the Lumen binder: *the seat sets the order; the asset sale sets the drawer.* Ines photographs it, which is the closest she comes to praise.

#### The co-op in the model

**What the document does to the game.** A cooperation agreement is a set of lenders $C$, with combined holdings $s_C = \sum_{i \in C} w_i$, who promise not to negotiate separately, require any buyer of their loans to sign on, and agree on a sunset date. The number that matters is $s_C$ against $1 - \theta$. If $s_C > 1 - \theta$, any coalition $S$ that avoids the co-op satisfies

$$
\sum_{i \in S} w_i \;\le\; 1 - s_C \;<\; \theta ,
$$

so it cannot pass the amendment. Every winning coalition must contain a co-op member, and the no-separate-deal covenant turns "contains a member" into "contains the co-op." The sponsor's knapsack from §13.4 has no feasible solution that leaves the group out. The $n$-lender game, with its invitation list and its prisoner's dilemma, collapses into bargaining between two players: the sponsor and $C$.

> **Poker Table.** "A co-op," says Ines, "is the players agreeing not to play heads-up against the house. One at a time, every one of them can be dealt out. Together they're a blocking stack, and the dealer has to deal with the stack." Her hand history: the Larkspur loan, bid 78 before the co-op headline, trades at 81 the morning after *(illustrative)*. The three points are the market repricing $\Pr(\text{excluded})$, not $V$.

> **Math, Gently.** *Nash bargaining.* Two people are splitting a pie, and each has a walk-away: what they get if the talks fail. Neither will accept less than its walk-away, so the only thing really being bargained over is the pie *left over* after both walk-aways are paid. Nash's answer is that each side gets its walk-away plus a share of the leftover, the share set by bargaining strength. Tiny number: the pie is $\Pi = 100$, the co-op's walk-away is $d_C = 20$, the sponsor's is $d_{\text{sp}} = 30$, and they are equally strong, $\eta = \tfrac12$. The leftover is $100 - 20 - 30 = 50$, so the co-op gets $20 + 25 = 45$. Now let the sponsor find a better walk-away, an outside lender who will do a deal at 40. The leftover shrinks to 40 and the co-op gets $20 + 20 = 40$. Ten dollars of sponsor walk-away cost the co-op five, which is $\eta$ per dollar. That is the whole of the comparative static below. The full version is "The Full Derivation" at the end of this section.

**Nash bargaining.** Let $\Pi$ be the joint surplus from a deal (avoided Chapter 11 costs, runway, the equity's option value from an extension), $d_C$ the co-op's disagreement payoff (its litigation value or its Chapter 11 recovery), and $d_{\text{sp}}$ the sponsor's (a third-party "deal away," or Chapter 11). With $\eta \in (0,1)$ the co-op's bargaining weight, the generalized Nash solution gives the co-op

$$
\Pi_C = d_C + \eta\,\big(\Pi - d_C - d_{\text{sp}}\big),
$$

with the symmetric split at $\eta = \tfrac12$. Two boundary conditions matter. A deal exists only if $\Pi \ge d_C + d_{\text{sp}}$; otherwise each side's outside option beats the deal, and that is when you see deals away and free-fall filings. Inside the deal region, the comparative static is linear and brutal:

$$
\frac{\partial \Pi_C}{\partial d_{\text{sp}}} = -\eta .
$$

Every dollar of credible outside financing the sponsor can line up costs the co-op $\eta$ dollars at the table. This is why deals away came back in 2025, often with six-month par calls (Wachtell, Feb 2026). The par call makes the threat cheap: if the co-op folds later, the sponsor refinances the outside money at par after six months, so the cost of *executing* the threat is roughly six months of excess spread plus fees, while $d_{\text{sp}}$ rises by the full value of the alternative. The co-op's counter is to be the cheapest financing in the room. Miller (SSRN abstract 5549919) finds that "by operating collectively, incumbent lenders outbid third-party financing offers."

**Carve-out premiums are Shapley values.** Inside the co-op, members bargain with each other, and small holders have more power than their size suggests. Treat the co-op's blocking power as a weighted majority game in which a subset $T \subseteq C$ blocks if $\sum_{i \in T} w_i > 1 - \theta$. The Shapley value of member $i$ is the probability, over random joining orders, that $i$ is the member who turns a non-blocking subset into a blocking one (the summation formula is in "The Full Derivation" at the end of this section).

> **Math, Gently.** *The Shapley value.* Line the co-op's members up at the door in a random order and let them walk in one at a time. At some moment the people in the room first hold enough to block; whoever walked in at that moment is the *pivot*. Do this for every possible order and count how often each member is the pivot. That fraction is its Shapley value: its share of the power, measured by how often the group's power depends on it. Four members can line up in $4! = 24$ orders, few enough to count on a napkin. In the example that follows, A is the pivot in 10 of them, B in 10, and C and D in 2 each, so the values are $\tfrac{10}{24}, \tfrac{10}{24}, \tfrac{2}{24}, \tfrac{2}{24}$. Size is not power; being indispensable is.

Take a lien release with $\theta = \tfrac23$, so blocking needs more than a third, and a co-op of four: A holds 25%, B 6%, C and D 3% each, 37% in all. The blocking subsets are $\{A,B,C\}$ and $\{A,B,D\}$ (34% each) and all four; $\{A,C,D\}$ reaches only 31%. A and B sit in every blocking subset, so both hold vetoes. Counting orderings gives $\phi = (\tfrac{5}{12}, \tfrac{5}{12}, \tfrac{1}{12}, \tfrac{1}{12})$. B holds a quarter of A's position and an equal share of the blocking power. When B asks for a carve-out premium (a larger new-money allocation, a bigger backstop fee), it is asking to be paid its Shapley value instead of its pro rata share, and the arithmetic is on its side. A steering committee's carve-out premium is a Shapley value with a law firm attached. The code in §13.8 checks these four numbers. Figure 13.3 plots both splits.

![Figure 13.3: Against the sponsor the co-op gives up η dollars for each dollar of the sponsor's outside option and the deal vanishes once the two outside options exhaust the surplus (left); inside the co-op, B's 6% of the class earns the same Shapley value as A's 25% because both sit in every blocking subset (right). Illustrative: Π = \$100mm and d_C = \$20mm in the left panel; Shapley values by enumeration for the §13.5 four-member co-op with θ = 2/3.](../assets/figures/ch13_coop_bargaining_shapley.png)

**Three flavours, one failure mode.** Co-ops come *open* (any holder of the class may join), *closed* (membership fixed at signing), or *tiered* (anyone may join; early signers get the premium). A closed co-op that clears $\theta$ on its own is no longer a defense against a non-pro-rata deal. It *is* one, waiting for a term sheet; Miller (2025) calls the pattern "inclusive, but unequal." This is why `coop_reported` carries the split sign in the §13.2.1 table: it lowers the probability of a deal that excludes the co-op and raises the probability of *some* LMT, because a co-op that can block can also deliver.

**The antitrust attack is an attack on the commitment device.** Wachtell reports that "antitrust challenges in connection with cooperation agreements (Optimum and Selecta) are in their early days." Issuers have also found a contractual route: Seaton (SSRN abstract 5247506) reports that Warner Bros. Discovery's 2025 bonds pioneered an "anti-cartel" provision, and that issuers' equity falls on co-op news. The second fact is the Nash solution showing up in a stock price: a co-op raises $d_C$, and the sponsor's share falls by $1 - \eta$ per dollar of it.

Mags keeps a printout of the Optimum complaint on her desk, held down by a mug, and on the Friday of the Larkspur week she hands it to Theo with the air of someone lending a horror novel. The first antitrust suit had come a month earlier: on October 28, 2025, excluded holders of Selecta, the European vending company, sued the favoured holders and the company in the Southern District of New York, alleging that a cooperation agreement had been used to collude (No. 1:25-cv-08956). Optimum was different, because the plaintiff was the borrower. On November 25, 2025, Optimum Communications, the former Altice USA, sued its co-op lenders, naming in the original complaint Apollo, Ares, GoldenTree, Loomis Sayles, Oaktree and PGIM (*Optimum Communications, Inc. v. Apollo Capital Management, L.P.*, S.D.N.Y. No. 1:25-cv-09785). The complaint alleges a group boycott and price fixing: a co-op holding about 99% of the company's debt, which had agreed among itself to act only on a two-thirds vote of its members, against documents that let a simple majority amend. Those are allegations, not findings (Hogan Lovells; Crowell, via Mondaq). Defendants moved to dismiss in February 2026. Judge Jeannette Vargas refused to stay discovery while the motions were pending, and on August 4, 2026, confined it to a court-set "phase one."

Theo reads the complaint the way a restructuring banker reads anything: for leverage. "The borrower is suing the people it needs to refinance it."

"The borrower is suing the commitment device," says Ines. "If the no-separate-deal covenant is unenforceable, the co-op is just a list of names, and every name on the list can be bid away one at a time. That's §13.4 again, with the auction back on."

"And meanwhile," says Mags, "discovery runs. Every email a co-op member sent about who to let in is now a document somebody can read." She taps the 10-Q stapled to the back. On June 30, 2026, Optimum's quarterly report carried a going-concern warning, with \$4.12bn due in April 2027. Whatever the court decides about the co-op, the maturity is not a legal theory.

For the model, a co-op under live antitrust attack is a weaker commitment: its effective $d_C$ falls, the sponsor's $d_{\text{sp}}$ rises by whatever a deal away is now worth, and `coop_reported` stops being a clean feature, because its value now depends on the forum and the docket (§13.9).

#### The Pair Book: the Monday the legs changed places

*Vantress Capital Management, Dov Adler's pod, Owen Achterberg's pod next door, Wen Zhao and Marcus Oyelaran are fictional composites; the positions, the prices marked illustrative and every P&L figure are invented. Serta, Lumen, Level 3, their instruments, the deal terms and the dates are real and come from §13.3.1, §13.5 and the sources cited there. Both pairs are replays, run the way Ines runs them at the desk across town that quotes Dov's pod most weeks: Owen's is cut off at Friday, 19 June 2020, Dov's at Friday, 10 November 2023.*

That same Friday of the Larkspur week, Marcus Oyelaran walked the credit corner of the Vantress floor with a question he had not asked before. Marcus runs the platform's overnight x-ray of the credit pods, and his usual question is what a book is long that it did not mean to be. None of his pods owned Larkspur. What bothered him was the shape of the headline. "Every pair on this floor is long the senior and short the junior, or long the strong name and short the weak one," he said. "Show me a pair whose legs a document could swap. Before it happens, if you can. After, if that's all you have."

Owen had the after.

**Friday, 19 June 2020.** His ledger page was the one Chapter 3 opened, PB-06: long \$20mm of the Serta first-lien term loan at 45, short \$22.4mm of the second lien at 15 *(illustrative)*, an outside holder's position with no seat in either group. The ratio came from the jump, not the spread. At recoveries of 31 and 2.5, a default costs the long \$2.8mm and pays the short \$2.8mm. What the hedge removed was default and the mattress business itself, because one enterprise value sat under both legs. What it left was the bet Owen meant to own: the gap between the two claims, which is to say the vote, and a first lien his analysts read as the fulcrum.

Wen Zhao, who keeps the borrow sheet for Dov's pod and reads Owen's when asked, put a finger on the second leg. "Nobody lends a term loan. This is a sale you cover before it settles, and distressed paper can take weeks to settle. It's a short with a fuse on it. Every time the fuse burns down you buy the loan back from whoever will sell it, and light another one." Under it Owen had written the carry: the long earns a floating coupon near 4.5% on \$20mm, \$0.90mm a year; the short owes the second lien's coupon, near 8.5% on \$22.4mm of face, \$1.90mm; financing \$9.0mm of loan at 3% costs \$0.27mm *(all illustrative)*. A short in paper at 15 owes a coupon worth more than half its price every year. The pair cost about \$1.27mm a year, \$3,500 a day, before the bid–ask on two legs, one of which is paid again every time the fuse is relit.

Then Owen lifted the sheet.

**Monday, 22 June 2020.** The uptier closed. The loan Owen was long now stood behind \$200mm of first-out new money and about \$875mm of second-out, §13.3's strike of $K_1 = 1{,}075$. The remand court would later value the excluded loans at 25 on that day, and Owen marked the long there: twenty points, $-\$4.0$mm. The second lien left outside now stood behind the super-priority debt and the \$895mm of excluded first lien; he marked it at 5 *(illustrative)*, ten points on \$22.4mm, $+\$2.24$mm. Net, $-\$1.76$mm, on a day when nobody defaulted. The whole loss sat on one line of the explain, the line that had been the thesis.

"That's the mark," said Marcus. "Run the jump again. Same enterprise value, new document."

Wen ran it through §13.3's waterfall. The risk model's default state had enterprise value covering 31 cents of the first lien's \$1,887mm, about \$585mm, and \$585mm no longer reached the strike. The excluded first lien's recovery in that state fell from 31 to the nuisance value a plan finds for a class that votes, and Wen wrote 2. Chapter 8-B's jump line, $N(P - R)$, now read $20 \times (0.25 - 0.02) = \$4.6$mm on the long against $22.4 \times (0.05 - 0.025) = \$0.56$mm on the short. The pair that was jump-neutral on Friday was \$4.0mm long default on Monday. To be flat again Owen would have had to be short \$184mm of second lien, eight times his position and about two-fifths of the whole \$450mm class, through sales he would have to cover from a float the exchange had just shrunk.

"So hedge it with what's actually ahead of you now," said Marcus.

"What's ahead of me is the first-out and the second-out," said Owen. "The participants hold them. Nobody is going to lend me those either." He tapped the exchange terms: the second-lien loans that joined the deal had gone in at 39 cents of super-priority face. "Part of the class I was short on Friday is senior to me on Monday. I built a pair that was long the senior claim and short the junior one. The document made my long the junior claim. My long leg became the short."

Marcus wrote on his pad the sentence the platform uses now: *seniority is a field with a date on it.* Seniority is a document variable. That is this chapter's argument in one line, and the Pair Book is where it costs money. A hedge ratio is a function of the ranks, and the ranks belong to a document that a majority can rewrite after the trade is on. Chapter 13-B closes PB-06 at the excluded holder's markout.

**Friday, 10 November 2023.** Dov had brought the before. On the Friday of the joinder card (§13.5) he had the same research note open as Ines: Level 3's 3.875% first-lien 2029s outside the TSA at 73, and Lumen's own parent-level unsecured notes in the high twenties. The pair everyone wanted was long TSA paper and short the same bond outside it, and only members could own that long; without a seat, Wen said, you only ever see the short leg. So Dov's thesis, dated the way he dates all of them, was about entities instead of seats: *by March 2024 the deal will protect the creditors whose collateral sits at Level 3 and leave the parent's unsecured holders behind them.* PB-08: long the Level 3 secured notes, short the Lumen unsecured notes, borrowed through the prime broker.

He put his hand over the rest of the page. Write down four things before he lifts it: the ruler, the size of each leg, what the ruler cannot see, and the size Marcus's \$5mm single-issuer jump line allows *(illustrative)*.

The ruler was market-value DTS inside the issuer family. At 73 the Level 3 note's spread was about 540 bp on a spread duration of 5.0; at 28, a point inside the research note's range, the Lumen note's was about 3,300 bp on 3.3 *(illustrative)*. A dollar of the short carried four times the market of a dollar of the long, so \$20mm face of long, \$14.6mm of market value, needed \$3.6mm of short, about \$13mm face. That removes the family's spread beta, the telecom factor and most of the rates. A family default, at risk-model recoveries of 55 and 8, would cost the pair about a quarter of what it would cost a naked long. What remains is the thesis: which entity's creditors the deal protects.

"What is it long that it didn't mean to be?" said Marcus.

Wen answered with §13.8's expected priming loss, one factor at a time. The deal was signed, so the first factor was one. The research note already had half the Level 3 unsecured class being primed by the other half, so the second was high. The third, $\Pr(\text{excluded} \mid \text{NPR})$, is a forecast for every holder except this one. "We don't sign," she said. "For us that isn't a probability. It's the mandate." Ines's ten points in §13.5 are $\Pr(\text{excluded}) \times \text{loss}$ for a holder who might still join. If being left out costs 25 points, the screen prices a 40% chance of staying out, and a holder who will certainly stay out owns a bond worth 15 points less than the screen says; if it costs 40, 30 points less. On \$20mm face that is \$3.0mm to \$6.0mm, a document jump the DTS ratio could not see, because the short's exclusion was already in its price for every holder and the long's was a private fact about the pod.

Owen, who had just shown the floor what a document does on a Monday, told him not to open it. "Your long is somebody else's seat."

"My long is a lien," said Dov. "The seat is a line on the ledger, not a reason to stay flat." He cut the long to \$15mm face, so that the worse case, 30 points or \$4.5mm, sat inside the line, and the short to \$10mm face by the same ruler. The seat became a line of its own on the ledger: *outside, by mandate; document jump \$2.25–4.5mm.* Wen's borrow call, made as if it were that morning, found the Lumen notes available from an asset manager at 150 bp on market value *(illustrative; Asquith, Au, Covert and Pathak's custodian data for 2004–2007 show a mean fee of 33 bp and 173 bp in the 30 days before a bankruptcy filing)*. The fee mattered less than the weather, which is what Wen calls a bond's recall history. A lender that signs a joinder cannot leave its bonds with a stranger when transfers to non-parties are void, so the recall arrives in the week of the vote, and the plan for it is to buy back, because no index shorts Lumen's parent instead. The carry, per year: plus \$581k of coupon on the long, minus \$450k owed on the short at a 4.5% coupon, minus a \$42k fee, minus \$539k to finance the long net of what the short's cash collateral earns *(all illustrative)*. Over the four months Dov wrote down that is a cost of about \$150k, and half a point on each leg in and out costs another \$250k. If the deal leaves the parent's notes ten points lower and the Level 3 note where it is, the short makes \$1.0mm. That is the bet, net of what it costs to hold.

What leaks is the document, three ways: the seat, now sized but not hedged; the recall; and the short itself, which is excluded paper, and excluded paper is a bet on a sale or a ruling. Theo's line under the Lumen binder applies to it: the seat sets the order, the asset sale sets the drawer, and a company that can later afford to tidy up its orphaned bonds can lift a short leg in a day (Chapter 14 prices that gap). Chapter 25 stresses PB-08 against the covenant text that decides which entity the collateral reaches, and Chapter 13-B closes it at the TSA close on 22 March 2024. The full menu of short legs this scene walked, from a loan sold before it settles to a borrowed bond with a recall on it, is Chapter 8-D's (§8D.2).

> **View From Another Seat.** *The opportunistic credit fund.* To this seat a bond is an option on a legal process. The fund reads the document for the clause that creates blocking power, a third, two-thirds, a majority, then buys the position that holds the veto, and treats the court as the final counterparty. A thirty-cent bond that a market maker models as a jump-to-default is, here, a claim whose value depends on a ruling, a sale order or a co-op's vote. The seat has long lock-ups, a legal budget, and the willingness to go restricted for months, which is exactly the cost the Lumen joinder imposed. It is the natural buyer when CLOs at the CCC limit and index funds are forced to sell, and the party most likely to turn "excluded lender" into "winning bidder." The seat's public footprints are in court records, not in quotes: in Incora, the district court described the majority group as "led by funds managed or advised by PIMCO and Silver Point Capital, L.P.—the two largest sets of holders of the 2024 and 2026 Notes" (*Wesco Aircraft Holdings v. SSD Investments*, S.D. Tex., Dec 8, 2025). The same houses join co-ops in one capital structure and lead uptiers in another. For the desk, a known blocking holder is a state variable: when one accumulates a position, the hazard of a deal that excludes it falls, and the variance of everyone else's recovery rises. The antitrust suits are an attempt to tax this seat's main tool, and the defence side's answer, in a Cleary Gottlieb note, is that co-ops "should generally withstand antitrust scrutiny."

> **Trend Watch.** *From auctions to bargaining, 2024–2026.* **Structures:** within a month of the Fifth Circuit's *Serta* ruling the market had a replacement, "amend-extend-and-exchange," which was "deployed throughout 2025"; deals away returned (Optimum/Altice USA, Altice International, Liberty Puerto Rico, KIK), often with six-month par calls (Wachtell Lipton, Feb 3, 2026). **Mix:** 25 LMEs closed in H1 2026 against 24 in H1 2025, but "the coercive uptier structures that defined 2025 have all but vanished," with equity handovers and consensual amend-and-extends dominating (9fin, Aug 28, 2026). **Hazard:** the Federal Reserve's *Financial Stability Report* of Nov 7, 2025 said the volume-weighted leveraged-loan default rate "stayed well below its historical median" while defaults including distressed exchanges "continued to be elevated relative to history"; the May 8, 2026 report repeated the point and added that in private credit "the elevated usage of payment-in-kind (PIK) provisions indicates some borrowers may face repayment difficulties." **Supply:** "\$580 billion of loans and \$625 billion of high-yield bonds mature between 2027 and 2029" (Wachtell). **What it means for the desk:** the modal 2026 game is the bilateral one of this section, not the auction of §13.4. Model `coop_reported` and deal-away capacity explicitly, let $\Pr(\text{non-pro-rata} \mid \text{LMT})$ fall with vintage, and keep the re-default hazard from the Desk Myth box: a maturity wall met by consensual extensions is a wall of candidates for a second LMT.

#### The Full Derivation: bargaining weights and pivots

**The Nash solution.** The generalized Nash solution maximizes $(\Pi_C - d_C)^{\eta}(\Pi_{\text{sp}} - d_{\text{sp}})^{1-\eta}$ subject to $\Pi_C + \Pi_{\text{sp}} = \Pi$, where $\eta \in (0,1)$ is the co-op's bargaining weight. Take logs and differentiate in $\Pi_C$:

$$
\frac{\eta}{\Pi_C - d_C} = \frac{1-\eta}{\Pi - \Pi_C - d_{\text{sp}}}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\Pi_C = d_C + \eta\,\big(\Pi - d_C - d_{\text{sp}}\big).
$$

Differentiating the solution in $d_{\text{sp}}$ gives $\partial \Pi_C / \partial d_{\text{sp}} = -\eta$, and the solution is interior only when $\Pi \ge d_C + d_{\text{sp}}$.

**The Shapley summation.** For the blocking game on the co-op $C$, member $i$'s Shapley value is

$$
\phi_i = \sum_{T \subseteq C \setminus \{i\}} \frac{|T|!\,(|C| - |T| - 1)!}{|C|!}\,\big(v(T \cup \{i\}) - v(T)\big), \qquad v(T) = \mathbf{1}\Big[\textstyle\sum_{j \in T} w_j > 1 - \theta\Big].
$$

The weight $|T|!\,(|C|-|T|-1)!/|C|!$ is the fraction of joining orders in which exactly the members of $T$ arrive before $i$, and $v(T \cup \{i\}) - v(T)$ is 1 exactly when $i$ is the pivot of such an order. For the four-member example, the 12 orders whose first three members include both A and B have their pivot in third place (A or B four times each, C or D twice each), and the other 12 orders have their pivot in fourth place (A six times, B six times), which gives $(\tfrac{10}{24}, \tfrac{10}{24}, \tfrac{2}{24}, \tfrac{2}{24}) = (\tfrac{5}{12}, \tfrac{5}{12}, \tfrac{1}{12}, \tfrac{1}{12})$.

## 13.6 Drop-Downs: Collateral Leakage Arithmetic

An uptier reorders the claims and leaves the assets where they are. A drop-down leaves the claims where they are and moves the assets. Same transfer, different mechanism, and a different payoff shape.

> **[SOURCE EXTRACTION]** *Moyer_Distressed_Debt_Analysis p.244:* "if the existing bank debt has a lien on substantially all the assets, there may be little or nothing to offer."
>
> **Annotation.** Moyer is describing the constraint on a classic coercive exchange: the issuer wants to offer bondholders secured paper, but the banks already hold the collateral. The drop-down is the modern answer to his problem. If nothing is unencumbered, *manufacture* unencumbered collateral by moving assets out of the restricted group through the investment and unrestricted-subsidiary baskets, then grant liens on them. Moyer's next item suggests offering "a structurally senior security"; the drop-down does both at once, because debt issued by the unrestricted subsidiary is structurally senior to the parent's lenders on the assets that moved. Where the desk departs: Moyer treats the absence of free collateral as a constraint. The 2026 desk treats it as a quantity, $C^{\text{unsub}}$, that a parser can measure and a model can rank.

**The arithmetic.** Let the collateral group be worth $V$ before the deal. The borrower moves assets worth $T$ to an unrestricted subsidiary, with $T \le C^{\text{unsub}}$ as declared at the time of the investment. (Agreements often let the borrower value the investment itself, in good faith, which makes $C^{\text{unsub}}$ a cap on the *declared* value of $T$, not its economic value. Read the valuation clause before you trust the cap.) The subsidiary borrows $D_u$ against the assets, structurally senior on them, and a fraction $\phi$ of the proceeds comes back into the collateral group as cash or debt paydown. The restricted group keeps the subsidiary's equity, worth $(T - D_u)^+$ at resolution. The existing lenders now recover

$$
R^{\text{post}}(V) = \frac{\min\!\big(V - T + \phi D_u + (T - D_u)^+,\; F\big)}{F}.
$$

Sanity checks: $T = 0$ returns $R_0(V) = \min(V,F)/F$. With $\phi = 1$ and $D_u = T$ the lenders keep every dollar but swap an asset for cash, and cash is the first thing a distressed company spends (the $\kappa$ of §13.3 again). The J.Crew trapdoor is the opposite corner, $\phi \to 0$ and $D_u \to T$: the asset leaves, is levered to the hilt, and the proceeds pay a different class. Then

$$
\Delta R(V) = R_0(V) - R^{\text{post}}(V) = \frac{\min(V, F) - \min(V - T, F)}{F} =
\begin{cases}
T/F, & V \le F, \\[1ex]
(F + T - V)/F, & F < V < F + T, \\[1ex]
0, & V \ge F + T.
\end{cases}
$$

Compare the shape with §13.3. The uptier's excluded lender wrote a *digital put*: it loses everything below $K_1$ and little above. The drop-down's victim sold a *forward*: it loses $T/F$ in every state where it matters. And for any $\phi \ge 0$ the loss is capped by capacity, because $V - T + \phi D_u + (T - D_u)^+ \ge V - T$ implies

$$
\Delta R(V) \;\le\; \frac{T}{F} \;\le\; \frac{C^{\text{unsub}}}{F}.
$$

That bound is why `unsub_capacity_pct_ev` is a feature, and why the IP blockers exist: a blocker sets $T$ to zero for the assets it names. It also tells you how the market prices the two species. A digital put is a tail problem that the market prices slowly, as the probability of a low $V$ rises. A forward is a level problem that the market prices on the day the investment is announced. Figure 13.4 puts the two shapes on one axis.

![Figure 13.4: The uptier's excluded lender loses most when enterprise value sits near K₁ and nothing once it is high, while a J.Crew-style drop-down takes a flat T/F = 20 points in almost every state. Illustrative: the §13.3 and §13.6 formulas with F = \$2,400mm, the Serta terms for the uptier, and T = \$480mm, φ = 0 and new debt equal to T for the drop-down (below V = T the loss is V/F).](../assets/figures/ch13_digital_put_vs_forward.png)

Kaz has been reading the J.Crew filings. "So the restricted subsidiaries are on probation."

"In a sense," says Theo.

"And the unrestricted subsidiary has been released. For good behavior?"

"Released, yes," says Mags. "Good behavior, never." She is right on the law: an unrestricted subsidiary sits outside the covenants, which is exactly why value parked there is beyond the lenders' reach.

> **Docket Diary.** *J.Crew, 2016–2020.* **Dec 5, 2016:** J.Crew discloses that it "invest[ed] certain intellectual property in the Company's wholly owned unrestricted subsidiary, J.Crew Domestic Brand, LLC," and says the step "fully complied with the Company's Term Loan Agreement." **Feb 1, 2017:** the company sues Wilmington Savings Fund Society, the successor term loan agent, to confirm that position (8-K Ex. 99.1). **July 13, 2017:** the exchange closes. \$565.7mm of 7.75%/8.50% PIK toggle notes due 2019, issued at a holding company and structurally junior to the term loans, are exchanged for \$249.596mm of 13% Senior Secured Notes due 2021 of J.Crew Brand, LLC and J.Crew Brand Corp., "secured on a first priority lien basis by a 72.04% interest in the Licensed Marks," plus \$189.688mm of preferred stock and about 15% of parent equity. \$150mm of term loans are repurchased; \$97mm of new-money notes are issued at a 3% discount; the marks are licensed back for \$42.5mm plus \$16.5mm per year; and the agent is directed "to dismiss, with prejudice, certain litigation" (8-K, July 2017). **May 4, 2020:** Chapter 11 (Bankr. E.D. Va., No. 20-32181); emergence in September 2020. *The Ad Hoc Group (this book's fictional chorus), represented by counsel:* "We note for the record that the junior class became the senior class on the brand." In the formula, the PIK holders were the "different class" that $\phi \approx 0$ funds, and the term-lender consent and dismissal were, in effect, bought with the \$150mm repurchase: the knapsack again.

**PetSmart and the guarantee lever.** BC Partners bought PetSmart in 2015 for about \$8.7bn and bought Chewy in May 2017 for \$3.35bn. In June 2018 PetSmart moved 20% of Chewy to its parent, Argos Holdings, and 16.5% to an unrestricted subsidiary, and sued the term loan agent, Citibank, that month, by contemporaneous press accounts. The lever was the guarantor-release clause: the position was that a guarantor that stops being wholly owned is released. Moving 36.5% of the shares was argued to release all of the guarantee, so the effective $T$ was the guarantee's value, not the shares'. That is leverage on the transfer, and it is why the code should compute $T$ from the release clause, not from the share count. Chewy's S-1 (Apr 29, 2019) records that "PetSmart settled existing litigation with the agent for its term loan lenders regarding these transfers in April 2019," and adds that "there can be no assurance that other PetSmart creditors may not seek to challenge these transfers." Chewy listed in June 2019 at \$22. The `chewy_blocker` (no release merely because a guarantor stops being wholly owned) exists because of those two sentences.

**When steps are judged together.** In *STG Logistics* (N.Y. Sup. Ct., Jan 3, 2026), the court viewed "amendments permitting a covenant strip, a drop-down exchange, and an intercompany loan – as a single integrated plan for purposes of analyzing 'sacred rights' (i.e., unanimous lender vote) claims," denied the motion to dismiss, and "shortly following the decision, the company filed for bankruptcy" (Wachtell, Feb 2026), on January 12, 2026. A drop-down that needs only majority votes step by step can need unanimity as a whole. Section 13.9 makes that precise.

## 13.7 Double-Dips and Pari-Plus: A Waterfall Engine That Conserves Value

"I'm told the new financing is a double-dip," says Kaz. "Is that a hygiene issue?"

"At a party," says Mags. "In a capital structure, it's a structure."

The desk's working definition: a guarantee and an intercompany loan walk into the same collateral pool and order twice. Pari-plus adds a foreign subsidiary that buys the first round.

> **[SOURCE EXTRACTION]** *Moyer_Distressed_Debt_Analysis p.165:* "Grants of security interests can similarly be viewed as provisions to override the general rule that property in an estate is shared pro rata among creditors."
>
> **Annotation.** Moyer frames liens (and, on the same page, guarantees and subordination) as overrides of the pari passu default. A double-dip is an override built from *claims* instead of liens: the new lender holds two claims of equal rank against the same obligor for one dollar of credit. Nothing about it is senior. It is counted twice in the pro rata denominator, and pro rata sharing does the rest. The desk's departure is computational. Moyer's overrides can be read off a priority chart. A double-dip can only be read off a *graph* of obligors, claims and equity ownership, which is why the engine below is a fixed-point solver rather than a lookup table.

**The closed form.** A special-purpose vehicle (SPV) borrows $F_2$ from new lenders and lends the cash to OpCo under an intercompany note that ranks pari passu with OpCo's existing first lien, $F_1$. OpCo also guarantees the SPV's debt, pari passu. In a pro rata distribution of OpCo's value $V$, three claims share: the first lien ($F_1$), the guarantee ($F_2$) and the note ($F_2$), at the rate $\rho = \min\big(1, V/(F_1 + 2F_2)\big)$. The new lenders collect $\rho F_2$ on the guarantee directly and, through the SPV, the $\rho F_2$ it collects on the note, capped at what they are owed. While $2\rho < 1$, that is, $V < (F_1 + 2F_2)/2$,

$$
R^{\text{DD}} = \frac{2V}{F_1 + 2F_2}, \qquad R^{\text{1L}} = \frac{V}{F_1 + 2F_2}.
$$

The double-dipper recovers exactly twice what the first lien recovers, from a claim of the same rank. With illustrative numbers $F_1 = 1{,}000$, $F_2 = 500$ (\$mm) and $V = 800$: without the dip both would get $800/1{,}500 = 53.3$ cents; with it, the first lien gets 40 and the new money 80. The \$133mm the first lien lost is exactly the \$133mm the new money gained, and on this desk that equality is the first thing anyone confirms, before the deal terms and long before the lawyers. Figure 13.5 draws the structure and the recoveries.

![Figure 13.5: Because the new lenders hold both a guarantee from OpCo and, through the SPV, an intercompany note against it, they recover twice what the first lien does below V = \$1,000mm (80 versus 40 cents at V = \$800mm, against 53 for each with no dip) and are paid in full from there. Illustrative: the §13.7 closed form with F₁ = \$1,000mm and F₂ = \$500mm, checked against the Listing 13.1 clearing engine.](../assets/figures/ch13_double_dip_structure_recovery.png)

Above the kink the arithmetic turns circular, and for once Kaz is the most comfortable person at the whiteboard. Once $V$ passes $F_2 + F_1/2$, the new lenders' two claims would collect more than they are owed, so the SPV ends up holding cash it does not need, and that excess is SPV equity. If OpCo owns the SPV, the equity flows back up into OpCo. A bigger OpCo pays more on every pro rata claim, the note included, so the SPV's excess grows, so OpCo grows again. Theo draws an arrow from OpCo to the SPV, another arrow back, and stares at the loop.

"It's a dog chasing its tail," he says.

"It's a dog that runs half as far each lap," says Kaz, and starts a column of numbers. Take $V = 1{,}200$ with the same $F_1 = 1{,}000$ and $F_2 = 500$, so OpCo's three pro rata claims add up to 2,000. Guess that OpCo pays 50 cents. Then the SPV collects 250 on its note, owes its lenders the 250 the guarantee did not cover, and has nothing left over, so OpCo has just its own 1,200, which pays 60 cents, not 50. Guess 60: the SPV collects 300, needs 200, returns 100; OpCo has 1,300 and pays 65. Guess 65: the SPV returns 150, and OpCo pays 67.5. The column reads 50, 60, 65, 67.5, 68.75, and the distance to 70 is cut in half on every line: 20, 10, 5, 2.5, 1.25.

"Seventy," says Kaz. "At seventy the SPV collects 350, needs 150, hands back 200. OpCo has 1,400, and 1,400 over 2,000 is seventy. Nothing moves."

"Back in my day," says Mags, "the circularity was resolved by whoever hung up the phone last." She studies the column. "This is better. It stays in this room that I said so."

Seventy cents is the fixed point, and it has a clean meaning. The first lien collects $0.70 \times 1{,}000 = 700$; the new lenders collect 350 on the guarantee and 150 through the SPV, which is exactly the 500 they lent. In general, above the kink,

$$
\rho = \frac{V - F_2}{F_1},
$$

so the new lenders take $F_2$ and the first lien takes everything else, as conservation demands. The regimes meet at $\rho = \tfrac12$, so recoveries are continuous and monotone in $V$. Kaz's halving is not luck, and the box says why; the algebra is in "The Full Derivation: the clearing map" at the end of this section.

> **Math, Gently.** *Fixed points, and why iteration converges.* A fixed point of a rule is an input the rule hands back unchanged: feed in 70 cents, get 70 cents out. When an answer depends on itself (a recovery that depends on equity that depends on the recovery), the honest way to solve it is Kaz's: guess, apply the rule, feed the output back in. Whether that settles down depends on one number, the rule's slope, which is how far the output moves when the input moves by one. A thermostat that closes part of the gap each cycle settles; one that overshoots by less each time still settles; one that overshoots by more each time swings the room between sauna and meat locker. Slopes between $-1$ and $1$ settle, and anything bigger in size does not. Here each lap moves the payment rate by $2F_2/(F_1 + 2F_2)$ times the last lap's move, which is below 1 whenever there is any first lien and exactly $0.5$ at $F_1 = 1{,}000$, $F_2 = 500$. Every step halves the error, so an error of a dollar per dollar of face falls below $10^{-10}$ in about 33 steps ($2^{33}$ is about 8.6 billion). A slope of 0.99 would need about 2,300 steps, which is why the engine allows 10,000 passes and raises an error, rather than quietly returning a number, when it runs out. For any number of entities the same map is Eisenberg and Noe's, next.

Real structures have more entities than one OpCo and one SPV, and the general tool is the clearing framework of Eisenberg and Noe (*Systemic Risk in Financial Systems*, Management Science, 2001), extended to priority classes. It is Kaz's whiteboard column, done for every entity at once. Each debtor has a pot: its external value, plus whatever its own intercompany claims were paid, plus whatever is left over at the subsidiaries it owns. Each debtor pays its claims rank by rank, senior first, and pays every claim within a rank the same fraction of what is still owed on it. The pots depend on the payments and the payments depend on the pots, so the engine guesses, pays, recomputes the pots, and pays again, until no payment moves by more than $10^{-10}$. The invariant is conservation: payments to outside creditors plus residual outside equity equal total external value, because every intercompany payment is one entity's outflow and another's inflow. The precise map is in "The Full Derivation: the clearing map."

**Pari-plus.** Add a non-guarantor foreign subsidiary worth $V_f$ that guarantees the new money directly. Before the deal, $V_f$ reached the first lien only as equity flowing up to OpCo. After it, the new lenders take $\min(F_2, V_f)$ first and double-dip OpCo for the deficiency, so the first lien loses the foreign value and is diluted on the rest. With $V_f = 0$ the structure collapses to the double-dip, which the code asserts. Sabre's May 2023 financing is the template: a "\$665 million new senior secured credit facility" from "lenders led by affiliates of Centerbridge Partners, L.P." to Sabre Financial Borrower, LLC, "a newly created wholly-owned subsidiary of Sabre GLBL," "secured by an intercompany loan by the Borrower to Sabre GLBL" and by "direct guarantees from, and security interest in assets of, certain foreign subsidiaries of Sabre," with proceeds funding capped tenders for three series of notes (8-K Ex. 99.1, May 25, 2023).

#### The Full Derivation: the clearing map

**The double-dip fixed point.** Above the kink, let $A$ be OpCo's distributable value including the returned SPV equity $(2\rho - 1)F_2$, with $\rho = A/(F_1 + 2F_2)$. Then

$$
A = V + \Big(\frac{2A}{F_1 + 2F_2} - 1\Big)F_2
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\rho = \frac{V - F_2}{F_1}.
$$

Written as a map on the payment rate, one pass sends $\rho$ to $\big(V - F_2 + 2\rho F_2\big)/(F_1 + 2F_2)$. Its slope in $\rho$ is $2F_2/(F_1 + 2F_2) < 1$, so the map is a contraction on the regime $\rho \ge \tfrac12$ and the iteration converges geometrically to the unique fixed point there. Kaz's column is this map at $V = 1{,}200$: $\rho \mapsto 0.35 + 0.5\rho$.

**The general map.** For a debtor $d$ with external value $e_d$, define its distributable value as external value plus intercompany receipts plus the residual equity $E_c$ of the subsidiaries $c$ it owns. A claim $j$ of rank $r$ owed by $d$ is then paid

$$
A_d(p) = e_d + \sum_{\ell:\ \text{cred}(\ell) = d} p_\ell + \sum_{c:\ \text{parent}(c) = d} E_c(p),
\qquad
p_j = \bar p_j \cdot \min\!\left(1,\ \frac{\big(A_d - \sum_{\text{rank}(m) < r} p_m\big)^+}{\sum_{\text{rank}(m) = r} \bar p_m}\right),
$$

where the sums in the fraction run over $d$'s own claims and $\bar p_j$ is the amount still owed on claim $j$ (face, less anything already collected from a co-obligor on the same debt). Iterate $p \mapsto \Phi(p)$ until $\|p^{(k+1)} - p^{(k)}\|_\infty < 10^{-10}$. Every payment is non-decreasing in every other payment, so $\Phi$ is monotone: iterating up from $p = 0$ climbs to the least clearing vector, and iterating down from face descends to the greatest. When every loop of ownership and claims has some outside value behind it, as in the structures of this chapter, the two meet; when they do not, the first item of "Ways This Blows Up" in §13.7.1 applies.

### 13.7.1 Case Study: Trinseo (2023–2026), the Double-Dip Meets Chapter 11

*A replay, docket cut off at Wednesday, June 24, 2026, three months before Theo's first day. The cast and the illustrative stack on the whiteboard are fictional; the filings, figures and dates come from the record cited.*

Theo meets Trinseo the way restructuring bankers meet most companies, through a disclosure statement. This one is dated Monday, May 25, 2026, which was Memorial Day, and was filed the next day as an exhibit to an 8-K, alongside the petitions; Ines hands it to him in the replay binder. He reads it with the pleasure of a man back in his native language. Then he reads the history, because the history is where the claims came from.

On September 8, 2023, Trinseo announced "a senior secured term loan facility of \$1,077 million" borrowed by two SPVs, Trinseo Luxco Finance SPV S.à r.l. and Trinseo NA Finance SPV LLC. Of that, \$948mm was on-lent to OpCo as "2023 Term Loans" under its 2017 credit agreement. The SPV loans paid Term SOFR + 8.50% and matured May 3, 2028; the intercompany loans paid Adjusted Term SOFR + 9.66% and matured May 3, 2030. Proceeds repaid the 2018 term loans and redeemed \$385mm of 5.375% notes due 2025 (8-K, Sept 2023). Note the design: the intercompany loan pays more and runs longer than the external loan it funds, so the claim that shares pro rata with OpCo's lenders grows faster than the debt behind it.

What the 8-K did not describe, the excluded lenders later did, and their account is an allegation rather than a finding. By their telling, \$125mm of the SPV money went to OpCo as equity, which manufactured enough basket room to move a 50% interest in the Americas Styrenics joint venture (AmSty, about \$100mm of EBITDA) into an unrestricted subsidiary, and that subsidiary guaranteed the new loan. No existing lender was asked to consent, because no clause required it. If the allegation holds, the double-dip of §13.7 had a pari-plus leg from its first day: value the new lenders could reach and the OpCo lenders could not.

Then came a second chapter, the one the stylized engine knows nothing about. On January 17, 2025, about \$447mm of Trinseo's unsecured notes became second-lien notes, the intercompany loan grew by about \$494.5mm to roughly \$1.5bn, a \$300mm super-priority revolver replaced the old one, and a \$115mm Tranche C joined the Super HoldCo term loans. The SPV's intercompany term loans counted as votes toward the majority that approved the changes (by Debtwire's account of the excluded lenders' complaint). Theo stops on that sentence and reads it twice. "The SPV lends to OpCo, it belongs to OpCo's group, and it votes on OpCo's amendments." It is the denominator question of §13.2 in its purest form: whose loans count toward "Required Lenders," and whether a document written to cap affiliated votes saw this kind of affiliate coming.

Trinseo filed for Chapter 11 on May 26, 2026 (Bankr. S.D. Tex., lead case No. 26-90545, Judge Christopher Lopez). Its disclosure statement (dated May 25, 2026, filed as 8-K Ex. 99.2) is the first full-cycle test of the closed form, and the closed form turns out to be conservative. Funded debt was about \$2.9bn. Estimated recoveries: revolver (\$348mm) 99–100%; Super HoldCo first-lien term loans (\$1,266mm, including a \$115mm Tranche C from January 2025) **60–78%**; OpCo 2028 term loans (\$716mm) **2–9%**; 7.625% notes due 2029 (\$390mm) 0%. The OpCo intercompany term loans, \$1,508mm, were pledged to the Super HoldCo lenders. The restructuring support agreement of May 13, 2026 had 100% of the revolver, about 99.9% of the Super HoldCo first lien and about 86% of the OpCo term loans; 2025 adjusted EBITDA was \$162.5mm; the plan contemplates an \$850mm exit term loan and a \$270mm rights offering for 47.73% of the new equity.

The stylized engine says the double-dipper recovers twice what the first lien does. Trinseo's estimated multiple is roughly 7 to 39 (60/9 to 78/2). Theo's first instinct is that the disclosure statement is wrong. His second, better instinct is that his model is too small. He goes to the whiteboard and tries the closed form straight: $F_1 = 716$ for the OpCo 2028 term loans, $F_2 = 1{,}266$ for the Super HoldCo loans, a guarantee and a note of equal size, all pari passu. Whatever $V$ he writes in, the Super HoldCo lenders recover exactly twice what the OpCo lenders recover, so if Super HoldCo gets 60 to 78 cents, OpCo would get 30 to 39. The disclosure statement says 2 to 9. He is off by a factor of somewhere between three and twenty, depending on which ends of the ranges he pairs.

Mags, passing with a coffee, looks at the board for about four seconds. "Where's the revolver?"

Theo adds \$348mm across the top, paid in full, and every recovery below it falls. Kaz, who has drifted over, points out that the ratio has not moved. Pro rata sharing is indifferent to the size of the pot, and a multiple of two is still a multiple of two.

"What's the note?" says Mags.

"Nine forty-eight. On-lent in 2023."

"Read the disclosure statement again."

The OpCo intercompany term loans, the claim the Super HoldCo lenders hold by pledge, are \$1,508mm. Later tranches, accrued interest and the make-wholes live in the gap over the original \$948mm; about \$494.5mm of it arrived with the January 2025 transaction, by the excluded lenders' account, and the rest we leave undecomposed. Theo rewrites the pari pool at OpCo as 716 of term loans, 1,266 of guarantee and 1,508 of note, 3,490 in all. Now the Super HoldCo lenders collect $(1{,}266 + 1{,}508)/1{,}266 \approx 2.19$ times the OpCo rate from OpCo. Better. Still nowhere near seven.

"And who guarantees Super HoldCo," says Mags, "that doesn't guarantee you?"

That is the pari-plus leg, the value upstairs. Theo puts it in as a single number he cannot verify, an illustrative \$735mm that only the Super HoldCo lenders can reach, and leaves OpCo \$175mm after the revolver *(illustrative)*. The OpCo pool now pays $175/3{,}490 \approx 5.0$ cents. The Super HoldCo lenders collect $2{,}774 \times 0.050 \approx 139$ from OpCo and 735 from upstairs, about 874 on 1,266 of face, or 69 cents. Both numbers sit inside the disclosure statement's ranges, and the multiple is about 14. Finding the whole region of values that does this is Exercise 4; one point is enough to show what the ranges are made of. Ines adds up the board: \$348mm plus \$175mm plus \$735mm, about \$1.26bn. "Under eight times the \$162.5mm of 2025 EBITDA, for a chemicals company coming out with an \$850mm exit loan. Not a crazy place to stand."

What Theo takes from the whiteboard is that the multiple was never a stable statistic. Once the revolver, the \$1,508mm note and the value upstairs are in, the OpCo recovery is a small number left over after large ones have been subtracted, and the ratio of 69 to 5 is mostly a statement about how small 5 is. Cut OpCo's residual from 175 to 70 and OpCo falls from 5 cents to 2, while Super HoldCo slips only from 69 to 62; the multiple jumps from 14 to 31. A pair trade sized on "the multiple" would be sized on the noisiest number in the room.

The make-wholes are where the fight went, and the fight is about the size of the 1,508. An "OpCo Investigation" flagged the intercompany make-whole claims, and the proposed settlement took the form of "a gift through a carve-out of the Collateral securing the Allowed OpCo Intercompany Term Loan Claims."

"A gift," says Kaz. "From the senior lenders. Is there a card?"

"In bankruptcy," says Mags, "a gift is value a senior class hands to a junior class so the plan gets confirmed without the junior class fighting it. The card is the disclosure statement."

Some of the junior class fought anyway. CastleKnight, holding OpCo 2028 loans and 2029 notes, objects, and with Elevation CLO 2013-1 brought an adversary proceeding (No. 26-03208) seeking declaratory judgment on lien validity, priority and subordination. The excluded lenders' complaint attacks both the 2023 and the 2025 steps, asks the court to recharacterize the \$1.5bn intercompany loan as something other than debt, and challenges about \$56mm of consideration offered only to signers of the restructuring support agreement, under section 1123(a)(4), the equal-treatment rule that *ConvergeOne* (§13.9) put back in the news. CastleKnight had also bid to provide an alternative debtor-in-possession loan; the court approved a \$427.5mm DIP on June 17, 2026. On June 23, 2026 the plaintiffs opposed judgment-on-the-pleadings motions by the debtors and the "Super HoldCo Lender Defendants."

Ines prices the lawsuit on the same whiteboard, with the same illustrative stack, one count at a time. If the court strikes the gap and allows the note only at \$948mm, the pool shrinks to 2,930 and OpCo gets about 6.0 cents. If it recharacterizes the whole intercompany loan as equity, the pool is 1,982 and OpCo gets about 8.8. Only if the guarantee falls too, and the 2023 steps unwind, does OpCo stand alone in its pool, at about 24 cents, with more to come if the value upstairs comes back down. "So the recharacterization count is worth about four points," says Ines, "and the count that unwinds the deal is worth twenty. They have different odds, so they get different prices." Kaz, who has watched the engine print each of those numbers in under a second, adds the part it cannot print: "It tells you what each allowed claim does to OpCo. It can't tell you which claim the judge allows."

How a systematic desk flags it: the September 2023 8-K is machine-readable evidence of the three ingredients (a new SPV obligor, an intercompany loan pari with the existing first lien, an upstream guarantee). The parser emits `double_dip_present = 1`, the clearing engine reprices every OpCo-level claim with the new denominator, and the trade is the pair: long the dip, short (or underweight) the claims it dilutes. The pair is a bet on the recovery multiple, which the engine computes across $V$.

#### Decision point: Wednesday, 24 June 2026

It is Wednesday, June 24, 2026, the morning after the opposition brief. You have no verified secondary price for either instrument, only the plan's estimates: OpCo 2028 term loans at 2 to 9 cents, Super HoldCo first lien at 60 to 78. Buying the OpCo loans is buying the lawsuit: a few cents of plan recovery plus a claim on the unwind, worth roughly $q$ times the twenty-odd points the whiteboard found, less the legal bill and the chance that the plan is confirmed over the objection. Buying Super HoldCo is the same lawsuit with the opposite sign, plus the plan. Mags would buy the litigation, on her old principle that losing bidders sue, and that an excluded lender willing to fund the estate believes its own complaint. Ines would rather own the house, or the pair, because she cannot see the judge's cards and the Super HoldCo lenders hold most of the others. Which would you do, at what size, and what entry on the docket would change your mind? If you want to grade yourself against the record, it kept moving: on July 30, 2026 Judge Lopez denied judgment on the pleadings on Counts I to III; the confirmation hearing closed on August 19 with the matter under advisement and the judge asking who would fund an alternative; and we had found no ruling by mid-October 2026.

> **Ways This Blows Up.** *Five ways a clearing engine lies.* (1) **Circular ownership with no outside value.** If entities own each other in a loop that has no external value, Eisenberg–Noe can have many clearing vectors: iterating down from face finds the greatest, up from zero the least. Run both. If they differ, the answer is a legal question, not a numerical one. (2) **Deficiency conventions.** The engine assumes a creditor may assert full face against each obligor until paid in full, collecting no more than face in total. Some documents and jurisdictions net co-obligor recoveries first, which shrinks the dip. Make it a parameter, never a constant. (3) **Substantive consolidation.** Moyer observes that "a substantive consolidation makes the two claims pari passu" (Moyer_Distressed_Debt_Analysis p.305). Consolidate OpCo and the SPV and the guarantee and the note become one claim; the dip disappears. (4) **The challenge list.** Moyer's checklist of attacks (p.351; list items joined) reads like an inventory of the engine's hidden parameters: "Invalidity of guarantees · Substantive consolidation · Critical creditor/vendor status · Interpretation of contractual subordination language · Violations of covenants · Transfers that might be deemed fraudulent conveyances." Each one deletes or resizes an edge in the claim graph. (5) **Claims at face plus premium.** Trinseo shows that the allowed amount of an intercompany claim is itself a litigated number. Price the dip over a range of allowed claims, not at one.

## 13.8 The Priming Risk Score

"You've told me how much I lose if I'm dealt out," says Ines. "Now tell me how often the dealer deals."

Theo's first answer is a banker's answer: it depends on the company, the sponsor, the advisors, and whether anyone has called sponsor counsel yet. Ines wants a trader's answer, a number per name per year that can be compared across the book on a Monday morning without anyone reading a credit agreement. Kaz has an answer that sounds like neither.

"Every loan has a clock on it," Kaz says. "It clicks when somebody does an LMT. We can't see the clock. We can see what the loan looked like each time it clicked."

Theo pulls up what there is to see. Roe and Rotaru hand-collected 89 coercive LMEs. The desk's universe is about 1,500 loans, the size of Noor's list in §13.2.1. The documents that produced most of the 89 were written before anyone had heard of a Serta blocker, and the documents the desk is pricing were written after.

"Eighty-nine," says Mags. "In my day we'd have called that a war story, not a dataset."

She is not wrong, and the section is built around her objection. It needs three ideas, each of them small: a hazard, to say exactly what "how often" means; a logistic link, to turn a row of features into a probability; and a prior, to stop 89 examples from saying something absurd.

**From hazard to a fixed-horizon score.** The template is the proportional-hazards model Bohn and Stein use for default (Bohn_Stein_Active_Credit_Portfolio_Management p.233), applied to the LMT event:

$$
\lambda^{\text{LMT}}_i(t) = \lambda_0(t)\,e^{\beta^{\top} x_i(t)}, \qquad
\text{PRS}_i(t, h) = 1 - \exp\!\Big(-\int_t^{t+h} \lambda^{\text{LMT}}_i(u)\,du\Big) \in [0,1].
$$

Kaz's clock is a hazard rate, the speed of a counter that clicks at random (Chapter 3 and Chapter 6, §6.1.4, build it; Chapter 5, §5.1.5, first turned the 13-week model into one). If the counter is expected to click $H$ times over the year, the chance of no click is $e^{-H}$, so a one-year PRS of 10% is a counter running at $H = -\ln 0.9 \approx 0.105$. Each feature turns a dial on that speed, and a coefficient of 0.69 doubles it, since $e^{0.69} \approx 2$. Mags's clock from §13.1 is the same counter, attached to a company after its LMT and clicking much faster.

($\lambda^{\text{LMT}}$ carries a superscript because $\lambda_t$ is reserved for default.) With the 89, a time-varying baseline is a luxury. Fit at a fixed horizon $h = 1$ year with a logistic link on standardized features $z_i$: $\text{PRS}_i = \sigma(\beta_0 + \beta^{\top} z_i)$, $\sigma(u) = 1/(1+e^{-u})$, the squasher that turns any score into a probability (the logit of Chapter 5, §5.5.3, run backwards). For small probabilities $1 - \exp(-e^{u}) \approx e^{u} \approx \sigma(u)$, so the logistic and the Cox model agree in the region where the desk lives: a score of $-2.2$ is 10.0% through the logistic and 10.5% through the clock. At a score of 0 they part, 50% against 63%, but a loan with a coin-flip chance of being primed has bigger problems than the choice of link.

**Priors, because 89 is not a sample size.** Mags's objection has a formal answer, and it is to say in advance what the desk believed before the data arrived. The desk puts $\beta \sim \mathcal{N}(\beta^{\text{prior}}, \tau^2 I)$ on the slopes and a Beta$(a,b)$ prior on the base rate $\pi_0 = \sigma(\beta_0)$, the base-rate framing of Bohn–Stein p.447. The maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimate is the coefficient vector that best balances the logistic likelihood against both priors, and two consequences carry all the intuition. The intercept's first-order condition says that the mean fitted PRS equals the observed event rate plus a correction of order $\max(a,b)/n$, so the base-rate prior nudges the level and does not overrule it. And each fitted slope is, to a good approximation, a weighted average of the prior's slope and the maximum-likelihood estimate (MLE), with the weight set by how much information the data carry relative to $1/\tau^2$. The boundary conditions are the sanity checks: as $\tau \to \infty$ the prior vanishes and the fit returns the MLE; as $\tau \to 0$ the data vanish and the fit returns the prior. The code tests both limits. The objective, the first-order condition and the shrinkage matrix are written out in "The Full Derivation: the MAP estimate and its two limits" at the end of this section.

A Beta$(a, b)$ prior behaves as if the desk had already seen $a$ events and $b$ non-events, with mean $a/(a+b)$ (Chapter 5, §5.5.2, has the shelf with two knobs; Chapter 3, §3.3.4, the batting average that shrinks). The listing's default, Beta$(2, 38)$, is a 5% base rate held with the confidence of forty observations. Against a thousand borrower-years it barely moves the estimate; against 30 borrower-years with 9 events it pulls the data's 30% down to $(2 + 9)/(40 + 30) \approx 16\%$. That pull is shrinkage, and $\tau$ is the same dial for the slopes.

> **[SOURCE EXTRACTION]** *Bohn_Stein_Active_Credit_Portfolio_Management p.447:* "the Bayesian approach answers the question, “Given that I know that I have already observed zero defaults, what is the highest probability of default that I could expect with 95 percent certainty?”"
>
> **Annotation.** Bohn and Stein pose this for portfolios with few or no defaults. LMTs are the same problem one level up: the event is rare, its definition changed in 2020, and the population that generated the history (pre-blocker documents) is not the population you are pricing. The Beta prior turns "we have seen few events like this" into an honest upper bound rather than a zero. Where the desk departs from them: the prior must be *vintage-aware*. A base rate estimated on 2020–2022 documents overstates the risk of a 2026 agreement with a Serta blocker (Trend Watch, §13.3), so the prior's mean should come from events in documents of the same vintage, and its width should admit that there are few of them.

**What the desk prices.** The score is one factor of the expected priming loss, in fraction of par:

$$
\text{EPL}_i = \underbrace{\Pr(\text{LMT})}_{\text{PRS}_i} \cdot \Pr(\text{non-pro-rata} \mid \text{LMT}) \cdot \Pr(\text{excluded} \mid \text{NPR}) \cdot \mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{P}}\big[\Delta R^{\text{excl}}\big],
$$

and the quote is approximately $P \approx P_{\text{no-LMT}} - 100\cdot\text{EPL}_i - \text{risk premium}$, in points. The last factor comes from §13.3 (or §13.6 for a drop-down), the third from the knapsack of §13.4, the second from the co-op state of §13.5. **Measure discipline:** PRS is a $\mathbb{P}$-forecast of an event. The price impact is $\mathbb{Q}$-flavoured, because the marginal holder is averse to exactly this jump, and the *Serta* damages award shows a court measuring it with a market price. Calibrating PRS to prices would bake the market's fear into the forecast and then subtract it a second time in the quote, so the desk keeps the two apart: it regresses price residuals on EPL and calls the slope the premium.

**The Monday printout.** On the Monday after the model goes live, Ines prints the top forty names by score and reads down the list the way she reads a hand history, looking for the one that does not belong. A packaging company the desk has never traded has jumped from 0.12 to 0.19 overnight *(illustrative)*. She asks why. Kaz pulls the attribution, and almost all of the move is `loan_px`, which fell three points on Friday afternoon. Nothing in the document changed. Nobody new signed a co-op. The runway did not shorten. "So the price fell," says Ines, "and the score told us the price fell. That's a mirror, not a forecast." It is her first check on any move, and the reason is circular in the plainest way. The score exists to explain the price, so a score that moves only because the price moved has added nothing, and an EPL built on it would take the same three points off the quote twice. A score that moves because the parser found a new incremental-debt basket, or because a new Rule 2019 statement landed, is telling the desk something the price may not know yet.

Ines keeps the printout anyway, because ranking is what the score does well: within one vintage of documents and one forum, a name at 0.19 is more likely to see an LMT next year than a name at 0.05, and the order survives most of the ways the model can be wrong. The level does not. Vintage moves it (the Bohn–Stein annotation above), forum flips its sign (§13.9), and the holder block arrives late and dirty (Noor's Tuesday in §13.2.1; Robertshaw's quiet month in §13.4). "Use it to choose which forty documents to read first," she tells Kaz. "Multiply 0.19 by three more factors and quote the product to the second decimal, and you've mistaken a ranking for a measurement."

> **Ways This Blows Up.** *Separation.* On the training data, `loan_px < 80` and `runway_months < 9` together nearly separate events from non-events. An unpenalized logistic responds by sending those coefficients toward infinity and reporting a PRS of 1.000 for every distressed name, which is confident and useless. The Gaussian prior keeps $\hat\beta$ finite. The covariate doing most of the separating is Theo's `runway_months` (§13.2.1); without the prior, his runway would earn an infinite coefficient.

#### The Full Derivation: the MAP estimate and its two limits

**The objective.** In $\beta_0$-space, including the Jacobian, the Beta$(a,b)$ prior on $\pi_0 = \sigma(\beta_0)$ has log density $a \ln \sigma(\beta_0) + b \ln(1 - \sigma(\beta_0))$. With the Gaussian prior on the slopes, the MAP estimate is

$$
\hat\beta = \arg\max_{\beta}\; \sum_{i=1}^{n}\big[y_i \eta_i - \ln(1 + e^{\eta_i})\big] - \frac{\lVert \beta_{1:k} - \beta^{\text{prior}} \rVert^2}{2\tau^2} + a \ln \sigma(\beta_0) + b \ln\!\big(1 - \sigma(\beta_0)\big), \qquad \eta_i = \beta_0 + \beta_{1:k}^{\top} z_i .
$$
