**The intercept.** The first-order condition in $\beta_0$ says exactly what the base-rate prior does: $\sum_i (y_i - \hat p_i) + a(1 - \sigma(\hat\beta_0)) - b\,\sigma(\hat\beta_0) = 0$, so the mean fitted PRS equals the observed event rate plus a correction of order $\max(a,b)/n$.

**The slopes.** A quadratic expansion of the log-likelihood around the MLE (information matrix $H$) gives the shrinkage form

$$
\hat\beta_{1:k} \approx \Lambda\,\beta^{\text{prior}} + (I - \Lambda)\,\hat\beta^{\text{MLE}}, \qquad \Lambda = (H + \tau^{-2} I)^{-1}\tau^{-2},
$$

with boundary conditions $\tau \to \infty \Rightarrow \Lambda \to 0$ (the MLE) and $\tau \to 0 \Rightarrow \Lambda \to I$ (the prior). ($\Lambda$ here is the shrinkage matrix of this subsection only; the order-arrival intensity $\Lambda(\delta)$ of Part V is a different object.) The code tests both limits.

### Specification for AI Implementation

*What ROBO built from the vague version.* Theo typed: "Flag every borrower that could be primed." ROBO returned the entire index, correctly: any agreement can be amended with 100% consent. The precise version names $\theta$ for the specific action, the `buyback_exception` enum, and a horizon. ROBO returned 11 names. One was the desk's own warehouse line. The precise version, with schemas and edge cases, is the Spec at the end of the chapter; the three listings below are what ROBO built from it.

At the Trinseo whiteboard every question Mags asked (where is the revolver, what is the note, who guarantees Super HoldCo) made Theo redraw the OpCo pool by hand, and the closed form of §13.7 knew about none of them. Listing 13.1 is that redraw done by a function. It takes whatever the parser pulled out of the documents (who owes whom, how much, at what rank, who owns which entity) and returns recoveries that add up to the value in the structure, every time. "Adds up" is the part ROBO can be tested on, so the listing is built around it.

`waterfall_clearing` takes `ents`, which maps each entity to its external `value` (\$mm) and its `parent` (`None` at the top of the tree), and `claims`, the claim rows of the Spec; `reduce_by` means that whatever a co-obligor has already paid on the same debt comes off what this claim may still assert. It returns payments by claim id and the equity left at the top.

Each pass is the guess, pay and recompute loop of §13.7, with one detail the prose there skipped: what a claim may still assert is its face less the `reduce_by` payments, floored at zero. The loop stops when nothing moves by more than 1e-10, and raises `RuntimeError` after 10,000 passes rather than return a number that merely looks settled.

`dd_recoveries` builds the stack of §13.7 (OpCo, the SPV, an optional foreign subsidiary) and returns first-lien and new-money recoveries per dollar of face. Every call asserts conservation of value and that no claim is paid above face. The checks below it reproduce the closed forms: $2V/(F_1 + 2F_2)$ for the double-dipper and half that for the first lien below the kink; 0.70 and 1.00 at \$1,200mm; monotone recoveries in $V$; and pari-plus collapsing to the plain dip when the foreign subsidiary is worth nothing.

The function computes faithfully from whatever claim list it is handed, so whether a guarantee survives challenge, or whether the court consolidates the entities, is an input and never an output; that was Kaz's point at the Trinseo whiteboard. It also iterates only upward from zero payments, so on a loop of ownership with no outside value it finds the least clearing vector and nothing else. The twin that iterates down from face, item (1) of the Ways This Blows Up box in §13.7.1, is not in the listing yet.

*The full listing is [Listing 13.1 in Appendix F](#code-13-1).*

Ines's question at 7:41 had two halves: if the dealer deals me out, what does it cost, and whom does the dealer invite instead? Listing 13.2 answers the first with the three-region transfer of §13.3 and the second with the knapsack and veto of §13.4 and §13.5. It is right when the pieces conserve value and the Monte Carlo agrees with the closed form. When they disagree, Kaz will suggest "let's just assume Gaussian," and someone will have to stop them.

`uptier(V, F, N, x, p)` takes an array of enterprise values and the deal terms (face $F$, new money $N$, exchange ratio $x$, participation $p$) and returns four arrays of per-dollar recoveries: the old pari passu class, first-out, second-out and excluded. `priming_loss` is the old recovery minus the excluded one. It is deliberately not floored at zero, because between $K_2$ and $F$ the excluded lender gains from the participants' face haircut. Calibrated to Serta ($F = 2{,}400$, $N = 200$, $p = 0.5$, $x = 875/1{,}200$, so $K_1 = 1{,}075$ and $K_2 = 2{,}275$), the checks are: face times recovery sums to $\min(V, K_2)$; the loss equals the old recovery wherever $V \le K_1$ and vanishes above $F + N$; and a degenerate deal ($x = 1$, $N = 0$, $p = 1$) transfers nothing.

The expected transfer comes from an illustrative lognormal for $V$ (median \$1,500mm, volatility 0.45). Quadrature with breakpoints at $K_1$, $K_2$ and $F$ gives about 0.22, or 22 cents per dollar of par. A 400,000-draw Monte Carlo must land within four standard errors of it, and the closed-form partial expectation of §13.3 must match its own Monte Carlo.

`min_cost_coalition(w, c, theta, eps, coop)` solves the sponsor's knapsack. It removes co-op members from the candidates, returns `None` if the rest cannot reach $\theta + \varepsilon$ (a veto, not an empty coalition), and otherwise picks the subset that clears the bar at the lowest $\sum c_i w_i$. Up to twelve candidates it enumerates every subset (at most 4,095) and is exact. Beyond that it takes the cheapest $c_i$ first, ignoring holding size, which is a heuristic only. In the demo, funds are cheap, CLOs dear and the litigator dearest: at $\theta = 0.5$ the chosen coalition (five holders, 54% of the class) leaves the litigator out, and a 36% co-op against $\theta = 2/3$ returns `None`. `shapley(w, quota)` enumerates every ordering and credits whoever tips the running total past the quota, reproducing the (5/12, 5/12, 1/12, 1/12) of §13.5. Because it visits $n!$ orderings, it suits a steering committee of eight, not a class of eighty.

One trap is silent. At $p = 1$ nobody is excluded, so `uptier` returns `nan` for the excluded recovery by design, and `priming_loss`, with any average taken over it, comes back `nan` without raising anything.

*The full listing is [Listing 13.2 in Appendix F](#code-13-2).*

Listing 13.3 is Mags's objection ("a war story, not a dataset") turned into code. With the 89 and a dozen features, an unpenalized logistic reports a PRS of 1.000 for every name the separation box describes, so the listing says in advance what the desk believed (a prior on each slope from the published studies, a Beta prior on the base rate), proves the shrinkage is a dial by turning it to each end, and finishes by multiplying the four factors into one number in points that Ines can hold up against a bid.

The listing runs on synthetic borrower-years so the fitter can be graded against known coefficients. `simulate` draws 400 rows of five features (blocker, unsub capacity, loan price, runway, repeat sponsor), `BETA_TRUE` generates the events, and `brentq` solves the intercept so that about 15% of rows come out positive. `BETA_PRIOR` is the "published" prior: right signs, smaller magnitudes. `runway_months` is the §13.2.1 definition, capped at 120 months when burn is zero or negative.

`fit_map(Z, y, prior, tau, a, b)` returns the intercept and slopes on standardized features. It maximizes the posterior of §13.8: the logistic likelihood, a Gaussian $\mathcal{N}(\text{prior}, \tau^2)$ on each slope, and a Beta$(a, b)$ on $\sigma(\beta_0)$, with defaults $a = 2$, $b = 38$, a 5% base rate worth forty pseudo-observations. Newton steps use an analytic gradient and Hessian, and each step is halved until it stops raising the negative log posterior. Setting `tau=np.inf` with `a=b=0` gives the plain MLE, which is how the listing proves both limits of the shrinkage formula: a huge `tau` reproduces the MLE, a tiny one returns the prior. The other checks: the intercept first-order condition holds to 1e-6; the mean fitted PRS stays within 1.5 points of the observed rate; a 200-resample bootstrap band covers the estimate; a blocker lowers the score and unsub capacity raises it; and on a fresh holdout the fit beats the constant base rate on Brier score.

`prs` is the one scoring entry point: it standardizes a raw feature row with the training means and standard deviations, then applies the logistic. `expected_priming_loss` multiplies the four factors of §13.8 and asserts each lies in $[0, 1]$. The last lines score the illustrative Larkspur row with 7 months of runway, a harsher burn than the eleven months Theo forecast in §13.2.1, using the excluded share from block (b), a placeholder 0.5 for the non-pro-rata probability, and the 0.22 expected transfer. On the seeded run: 70 events, PRS about 0.90, EPL about 4.6 points. The 0.90 says more about synthetic coefficients than about any real borrower.

Its one silent failure is `iters=100`: the loop returns after 100 passes without saying whether it converged. On this synthetic data that never matters. On real, nearly separated data with `tau=np.inf` it would, and the coefficients would be huge with no warning. The prior is the convergence guarantee, and a fit across document vintages needs a vintage covariate (the Bohn–Stein annotation above).

*The full listing is [Listing 13.3 in Appendix F](#code-13-3).*

The three blocks are cumulative: (c) composes the knapsack's participation share from (b) and the Serta-shaped expected transfer, and in production the drop-down and double-dip transfers from (a) slot into the same last factor.

## 13.9 Autopsies: The Court Is a Random Variable

The $q$ in the litigation option of §13.4 has been the most volatile parameter on the desk since 2023. Two features carry it: the clause and the doctrine.

#### The Incora board, 28 March 2022

*A replay. The cast is fictional and the dialogue is theirs; the steps, holdings and rulings come from the court opinions and the law-firm accounts cited.*

Mags tells the Incora story the way a chess columnist annotates a famous game: every move legal, and the position lost long before anyone resigned. Theo has the district court's opinion open. Kaz has the whiteboard.

The board, as of early 2022. Wesco Aircraft, owned by Platinum Equity, had raised over \$2bn in 2020 to finance Platinum's acquisition of Wesco and its combination with Pattonair: \$650mm of 8.5% secured notes due 2024, \$900mm of 9% secured notes due 2026, and \$525mm of 13.125% unsecured notes due 2027. Two clauses in the secured indentures matter. A majority could consent to issuing more notes, pari passu. Releasing substantially all the collateral, or anything with "the effect of" doing so, needed two-thirds. By late 2021 the company needed money badly enough that its UK auditors wanted \$150–200mm injected or the UK entity faced being struck off. In December 2021 PIMCO and Silver Point, the two largest holders of the 2024 and 2026 notes, proposed a rescue. In February 2022 a minority group, which the district court later identified as led by BlackRock and JPMorgan, announced that it held more than a third of the 2026 notes. That was a blocking position against any two-thirds vote, and it set off the race for the marginal bond described in §13.4. The minority offered about \$147.5mm of financing, then \$173mm. The board chose the majority's \$250mm.

"So the minority has a third," says Theo. "The majority can't release the liens."

"Can't release them *today*," says Mags. "Watch."

Then came March 28, 2022, four steps on one day.

*Step one.* Holders supporting the deal owned more than two-thirds of the 2024 notes, more than 59% of the 2026 notes and more than half of the 2027s. A majority is enough to add pari passu notes, so they signed the Third Supplemental Indentures, which permitted \$250mm of additional 2026 notes. Nobody's lien moved. Kaz writes $v_1 = 0.59 \ge \theta_1 = 0.5$ and a check mark.

*Step two.* The \$250mm was wired, and the new 2026 notes were issued to the majority group. Kaz does the arithmetic out loud. The class used to be \$900mm, of which the group held at least 59%, about \$531mm. Now it is \$1,150mm, of which the group holds about \$781mm, or 67.9%: two-thirds, with a point to spare. The minority's \$300mm-plus, a third of the old class, is about 26% of the new one. Its block has evaporated without a single minority bond changing hands.

"The least they could have walked in with," says Kaz, "is about 57.4% of the old class. They had 59. The whole lawsuit is in that point and a half."

*Step three.* With two-thirds in hand, the group signed the Fourth Supplemental Indentures, which released the liens securing the 2024 and 2026 notes.

Kaz, reading over Theo's shoulder: "The fourth supplemental indenture. Is that the one with the new teeth?"

"It's the one that pulled them," says Mags.

*Step four.* The participants exchanged their 2024 and 2026 notes into new super-senior first-lien notes, which press accounts put at about \$1.27bn, and participating 2027 holders exchanged into 1.25-lien notes. The non-participants woke up holding unsecured paper behind, by the same accounts, more than \$1.7bn of new debt. Milbank had given an opinion that the steps complied with the indentures.

Kaz steps back from the board. Every step has a check mark: 0.59 against a half for the first, a wire for the second, 0.679 against two-thirds for the third, a voluntary exchange for the fourth. "Each move is legal."

"Each move," says Mags. "Now look at the position before the first move and ask whether they could have done the whole thing in one go."

They could not. Measured on the morning of March 28, the group held about 59% of the 2026s against a two-thirds bar, and that gap is the whole of the litigation. The excluded holders sued in state court in October 2022. Wesco filed for Chapter 11 on June 1, 2023, with an adversary proceeding the same day. At closings in June 2024, Judge Isgur said he believed "with a high degree of certainty" that the \$250mm was unauthorized, two weeks before he ruled. The plan on file before the ruling had given the participants 96.5% of the equity; at emergence on January 31, 2025, the secured noteholders took 98.4% plus \$420mm of take-back notes. Then the district court took the steps one at a time, as Kaz had, and found each one compliant.

"So who was right?" says Theo. "The bankruptcy judge or the district judge?"

"For the desk that's the wrong question," says Ines. "The right one is what the clauses made the odds. The two-thirds bar was in the document. The pari passu basket was in the document. Anyone who read both in 2021 could see that a 57.4% holder could manufacture a two-thirds holder in a day, and that some court would one day have to choose between reading steps and reading plans. That choice is $q$. Both groups were pricing it in February, when they paid up toward par for the marginal 2026 bond."

#### Steps, plans and the scoreboard

**Steps versus plans.** Write an LMT as a composition of document moves $\mathcal{D}_0 \to \mathcal{D}_1 \to \cdots \to \mathcal{D}_m$, where step $k$ needs holders with share $v_k(\mathcal{D}_{k-1})$ of the class to clear $\theta_k$. A step-by-step court asks whether $v_k(\mathcal{D}_{k-1}) \ge \theta_k$ for every $k$. An integrated court treats the composite as one move and measures support before anything happened, $v(\mathcal{D}_0) \ge \max_k \theta_k$, plus unanimity for any sacred right the composite touches. The gap $g = \max_k \theta_k - v(\mathcal{D}_0)$ is the feature `integration_gap`. When $g > 0$ the deal works only in a step-by-step forum, and $q$ becomes a bet on doctrine. On the board's numbers Wesco/Incora had $v(\mathcal{D}_0) \approx 0.59$ of the 2026s against $\theta = \tfrac23$, so $g \approx 0.08$: each step cleared its own bar, and the composite did not. *STG Logistics* (§13.6) is the same test applied to a drop-down.

> **Docket Diary.** *Wesco Aircraft/Incora, 2022–2026.* **Mar 28, 2022:** the transaction closes, in four steps on one day. **Before the 2024 trial:** Judge Isgur (Bankr. S.D. Tex.) sends to trial whether the deal was an "open market purchase" or a "redemption" and whether it was a "single, integrated transaction" (Ropes & Gray via HLS Roundtable, May 21, 2024). **July 10, 2024:** oral ruling after a 35-day trial: no breach of the 2024 indenture, but a breach of the 2026 indenture, because the amendment that permitted the new notes was a "domino agreement" that needed two-thirds of the 2026s; under his "domino theory," "the majority group did not have the requisite two-thirds majority at the time of the first amendment" (Wachtell). **Dec 27, 2024:** a consensual plan is confirmed, premised on the rulings, with appellate rights preserved. **Jan 17, 2025:** the written report and recommendation on the contract claims: the 2026 liens restored, the \$250mm an unsecured claim only. **Jan 31, 2025:** emergence. **Dec 8, 2025:** District Judge Crane reverses, looking "no further than the language of the agreements, the sophistication of the parties, and the 'direct effect' of a specific amendment." **Early January 2026:** the minority noteholders seek review in the Fifth Circuit (Mayer Brown, Jan 21, 2026); the appeal is docketed on Jan 13, 2026 as *Wesco v. 2026 Noteholders*, No. 26-20018. **As of Oct 18, 2026:** we found no Fifth Circuit ruling. *The Ad Hoc Group (this book's fictional chorus), represented by counsel:* "We were two-thirds. Eventually." In the model, $g > 0$ and $q$ swung from high to low on doctrine alone; the excluded noteholders now hold an option on a Fifth Circuit panel.

**The company's clock runs faster than the court's.** Incora's litigation took longer than Incora's solvency, and Saks Global shows how short the company's clock can be. On December 23, 2024 Saks bought Neiman Marcus at a \$2.7bn enterprise value, funded in part by \$2.2bn of 11% senior secured notes due 2029, with Jefferies as initial purchaser. By May 16, 2025 the notes were at 47.5, a holder group of about half the class was weighing new money that could leapfrog the rest, and a \$121mm coupon was due at the end of June. The exchange launched on July 21, 2025 and priced the coalition in plain sight. Per \$1,000 of old notes, holders who had pre-funded the new money received \$106 of new SPV notes and \$894 of second-out notes; holders who funded new money in the offer received \$550 of second-out and \$250 of third-out; holders who did neither received \$750 of third-out. About 98% tendered by August 8, 2025. Saks filed for Chapter 11 on January 13, 2026 with about \$3.4bn of funded debt, and the plan confirmed on June 5, 2026 cut that by roughly two-thirds to three-quarters (one account puts the remainder near \$1.2bn) and left junior creditors owed about \$1.5bn with a litigation trust of \$20mm as reported before confirmation. From new issue to petition took about thirteen months; from exchange to petition, five. The exchange did not end the story. It reordered the queue for the next chapter, which is what Mags meant in §13.1 by a state with a clock on the wall. The eight cases the desk keeps on its scoreboard put numbers on the clock.

| Case | The deal | Excluded holders' fate | Endgame | Months, deal to filing |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Revlon | May 7, 2020: BrandCo drop-down plus roll-up | litigated, settled in the plan | Ch 11 June 15, 2022 | 25 |
| Boardriders | Aug 2020: uptier by "open market purchase" | repaid at par, Sep 2023 | sold to Authentic; no filing | none |
| Envision | Apr–Aug 2022: drop-down, then non-pro-rata uptier | "fourth-out"; some sued | Ch 11 May 15, 2023 | 9–13 |
| Incora | Mar 28, 2022: vote-dilution uptier | liens restored, then reversed | Ch 11 June 1, 2023 | 14 |
| Robertshaw | May 9 and Dec 11, 2023: uptier, then control flip | money claim only | Ch 11 Feb 15, 2024 | 9 |
| Lumen | Oct 31, 2023 to Mar 22, 2024: cooperation (TSA), partial priming | primed, later taken out near par | no filing | none |
| Trinseo | Sep 8, 2023 and Jan 17, 2025: double-dip, then exchange | est. 2–9% on OpCo term loans | Ch 11 May 26, 2026; ruling pending | 33 (16 from 2025) |
| Saks | Dec 23, 2024 and Aug 8, 2025: new issue, then non-pro-rata exchange | about 2% held out | Ch 11 Jan 13, 2026 | 13 (5 from exchange) |

The months are our own arithmetic on the deal and petition dates. The six filers' median is about 13.5 months, whichever end of Envision's range is used, and the two cases that never filed are the two that ended in a sale or a take-out at or near par.

**Forum is time-varying.** In 2023 a Texas bankruptcy court found *Serta*'s "open market purchase" "clear and unambiguous" in the borrower's favor. On Dec 31, 2024 the Fifth Circuit read the same words against the borrower, on the day New York upheld *Mitel* (§13.2); Mitel nonetheless filed a prepackaged Chapter 11 on Mar 10, 2025, had its plan confirmed by Judge Lopez on Apr 17, 2025, and by June 20, 2025 had emerged owned by its former lenders with about \$1.15bn less debt (Paul, Weiss, *Mitel Emerges from Chapter 11 with Less Debt*, June 20, 2025; Davis Polk's account of the participating lenders' appellate win). A legal win and a credit win turned out to be nearly independent. A PRS fitted with a static forum coefficient averages a sign flip, so interact `forum_ny_vs_tx` with `buyback_exception` and a post-2024 dummy. In the bankruptcy court itself the *Serta* rule keeps spreading: in *ConvergeOne* (S.D. Tex. district court, 2025, on appeal), backstop fees on a \$245mm exit rights offering were "a form of recovery on participating creditors' pre-bankruptcy debt claims, and therefore had to be open to all creditors in the applicable class, absent robust market testing" (Wachtell). The next observations are already docketed: *Invesco v. Robertshaw* (5th Cir. No. 26-20422) and the bond-side exit-consent fight over Lions Gate/Starz's 2024 exchange of \$389,861,000 of 5.500% notes due 2029 (*CPPIB Credit Investments II v. Deutsche Bank Trust Co. Americas*, Sup. Ct. N.Y. Cnty., Mar 17, 2026). IDO or it didn't happen: LMT P&L is the one place where "idiosyncratic" was defined by two courts, in two states, on the same day.

#### Theo's sheet, 4:50 p.m.

*Tuesday, 4:50 p.m. The same Tuesday.*

At 7:51 that morning Ines made the call Theo could not yet make. "Tell them 75, for five." The client did not hit it. At 7:58 sales reported, in the voice sales reserves for a lost trade, that the client had done all fifteen million away at 78. Loans do not print on TRACE, so the desk learned the level the way it learns most things about loans: from a salesperson who heard it from a client who wanted them to know.

Theo spent the day doing what this chapter just did. At 4:50 he stands at Ines's desk with one sheet of paper, which is a regression from the legal pad, which was a regression from the napkin.

"Four factors," he says. "The PRS first. With this morning's headline coded as a group organizing, the model says 0.35 for an LMT inside a year. I checked what moved it, the way you do. The price falling from 84 to 78 accounts for about four hundredths of that. The headline and the document account for the rest, so it isn't a mirror."

"What's in the document?"

"An agreement signed in early 2022, before the blockers became the norm later that year. No Serta blocker. A J.Crew blocker, no Chewy blocker. And 9.05(g) says 'open market purchase,' not bare 'purchase.' After the Fifth Circuit, that wording makes a straight Serta-style exchange harder to defend, but it does nothing against an amend-extend-and-exchange. So the second factor, the chance the deal is non-pro-rata given that there is a deal, is a half. Before December 2024 I'd have said seven in ten."

"Third."

"The knapsack. The group says it holds 51.3%, and the action it needs is a bare majority, so the bag is already full. Anyone who arrives today with fifteen million is outside it by construction, and fifteen million is too small to be worth a seat even if the bag weren't full: a one-percent holder adds almost nothing toward $\theta$ and costs a chair at the table. The only way in is a sponsor who opens the deal to everyone to keep the litigators quiet, which happens more often since *Serta* than it used to. Pr(excluded) is 0.85."

"Fourth."

"The Serta-shaped put. Twenty-two cents of expected transfer, from the illustrative lognormal in the §13.8 listing, because I don't have Larkspur's terms yet. It's the factor I trust least." He writes the product, $0.35 \times 0.5 \times 0.85 \times 0.22 \approx 0.033$, about 3.3 points.

"That's for a random holder," says Ines. "Who sold at 7:41?"

"That's the part I couldn't do this morning." Theo turns the sheet over. "If the seller was in seat two, they knew they were out and the deal was close. Then the PRS is more like 0.8, the non-pro-rata chance 0.8, and they're excluded for certain: $0.8 \times 0.8 \times 1 \times 0.22$, about 14 points. If it was seat three, the CLO, it's the random-holder number, 3.3. Seat one can't sell. Given that somebody offered at 78 within a minute of the headline, I'd put four in ten on seat two. That's about 7.6 points of expected priming loss. Without any LMT risk, Larkspur would trade around 86 *(illustrative, from comparable names)*, and our residual regression says the market charges about a third on top of EPL for bearing the jump, call it two and a half points. Eighty-six, less seven and a half, less two and a half: 76. And five million, not fifteen. If they hit 76 in four seconds, I've learned which seat they had, and I paid for the lesson on a third of the size."

"In my day," says Mags, "we'd have bid seventy, hung up, and called it judgment."

"It was judgment," says Ines. "It just didn't have units."

Kaz leans over from the next desk. "And my question from this morning? Why 'excluded' means 25 in one case and 99 in another?"

"Because 'excluded' was never the variable," says Theo. "The variable is where $V$ lands against the strike when the story ends, and who gets to say the story has ended: a court, a sale, or the next filing. Serta ended in a courtroom with $V$ below $K_1$. Lumen ended with an asset sale big enough to put $V$ above everybody's strike, and so did Boardriders. Same word, different $V$, different referee."

Ines pulls up the hand history for a trade she did not do. Larkspur is quoted 74–76 at the close *(illustrative)*. The other dealer's 78 marks out at about −3, roughly \$450,000 on fifteen million. Her 75 for five, had it traded, would be flat. Theo's 76 for five would be down about \$50,000, and the desk would know something it does not know now. "The markout says the seller had a reason," she says. "Nobody followed with another offer at 78, and the bid leaked all day. Seat two, or a very nervous seat three. Write it down."

She does not say whether 76 was right, because the hand is not over. Three days later the lenders who had not been called would find each other and organize, the loan would trade at 81 (§13.5), and the same 78 would mark out at +3. Ines keeps markouts at the close, at a day and at a week for exactly this reason, and she keeps all three.

Theo writes the card that goes on his monitor.

- **An LMT is the difference of two waterfalls.** In low states it is zero-sum among creditors; the liquidity story lives in high states. Compute $\Delta_j(V)$ before you read the press release.
- **Know your payoff shape.** Excluded from an uptier: short a soft digital put struck at $K_1$. Victim of a drop-down: short a forward capped at $C^{\text{unsub}}/F$. Diluted by a double-dip: someone is counted twice in your denominator.
- **The sponsor solves a knapsack** and leaves out the constrained, the fragmented and the litigious. Model your invitation probability, not your participation decision.
- **A co-op above $1 - \theta$ turns an auction into a bargain.** Deal-away capacity costs the co-op $\eta$ per dollar; carve-out premiums are Shapley values. (Cooperation agreements signed in this book so far: 2. Antitrust complaints about them: 2, and counting.)
- **One word can be the whole loss.** The court is a random variable with a clause, a forum, a doctrine and a vintage.
- **PRS is $\mathbb{P}$; the price is $\mathbb{Q}$.** Never calibrate the score to prices. The prior keeps $\hat\beta$ finite, and Theo's runway is the covariate that separates.
- **The LMT is not the terminal state.** Only 22% of coercive-LME firms avoided both re-default and bankruptcy within two years. Price the next event.

### The Spec You Hand the Robot

Build `lmt_engine.py` (numpy/scipy; `rng = np.random.default_rng(13)`; runs top to bottom; values in \$mm, recoveries in fraction of par, runway in months, PRS at a 12-month horizon). **Schemas:** `entities` rows are `id` (str), `value` (\$mm, $\ge 0$) and `parent` (entity id or `None`); `claims` rows are `id`, `creditor` (`"ext"` or an entity id), `debtor`, `face` (\$mm, $>0$), `rank` (1 = most senior) and `reduce_by` (ids of co-obligor claims on the same debt); `features` has one row per borrower-year with the §13.2.1 columns, `buyback_exception` one-hot, and `y` = 1 if an LMT closed within 12 months. (1) `waterfall_clearing(entities, claims)`: priority ranks, pro rata within rank, intercompany receipts and subsidiary equity routed to parents, `reduce_by` for co-obligor claims on one debt, all value residual at an entity with no claims; stop at $\lVert \Delta p \rVert_\infty < 10^{-10}$, raise a convergence error after 10,000 iterations rather than return silently; assert conservation to $10^{-8}$, no payment above face, monotonicity in $V$, the double-dip closed form, pari-plus collapse at $V_f = 0$. (2) `uptier`, `priming_loss`: guard $N = 0$ and $p = 1$; assert conservation, zero loss for $V \ge F + N$, full loss for $V \le K_1$; expected loss by quadrature checked against Monte Carlo and the lognormal partial expectation. (3) `min_cost_coalition`: brute force to 12 holders, greedy beyond, `None` (never an empty coalition) when a co-op exceeds $1 - \theta$; `shapley` by enumeration. (4) `runway_months`, capped at 120 when burn $\le 0$; `fit_map`: Newton with step-halving, `logaddexp` in the likelihood, an overflow-safe logistic via `tanh`, Gaussian slope prior, Beta base-rate prior, and the prior required under quasi-separation (never `tau=inf` in production); assert the intercept first-order condition, both $\tau$ limits, the bootstrap band, signs, and a holdout Brier score below the base rate. (5) `expected_priming_loss` $=$ PRS $\times$ P(NPR $\mid$ LMT) $\times$ P(excluded $\mid$ NPR) $\times$ $\mathbb{E}[\Delta R]$, inputs in $[0,1]$. Never fit PRS to prices.

### Exercises

1. **Unblend Serta.** Redo §13.3.1 with the \$1.95bn first lien and \$450mm second lien as separate classes. Parameterize the unknown lien split of the \$1.2bn exchanged, compute $K_1$ for the excluded first-lien lenders, and find the split at which the blended 44.8-point transfer at $V = \$1.075$bn is off by more than 10 points.
2. **The 5% veto.** A co-op holds A 20%, B 10% and C 5%, and the action needs $\theta = \tfrac23$. Show that each Shapley value is $\tfrac13$. Find the smallest block of C's loans that, sold to A, destroys C's veto, and explain why C will ask for more than par.
3. **Forward or digital?** For a drop-down with $T = 300$, $D_u = 280$, $\phi = 0.1$ and $F = 2{,}000$ (\$mm, illustrative), plot $\Delta R(V)$, verify $\Delta R \le T/F$, and compute its expectation under the lognormal in block (b). Then redo it with PetSmart-style leverage, where moving 36.5% of a subsidiary's shares releases its whole guarantee.
4. **Rebuild Trinseo.** From the figures in §13.7.1, build an entity graph for `waterfall_clearing` and find ranges of $V$ and of the allowed intercompany claim that reproduce both 60–78% and 2–9%. Which parameter matters most?
5. **ROBO minimizes priming loss.** Told to "build the portfolio with the lowest expected priming loss," ROBO bought only loans in which every amendment needs unanimous consent. Explain in one sentence why the portfolio is empty, then rewrite the objective with a carry constraint, a turnover limit and units.

# Chapter 14: The Default & Recovery Cycle in the LMT Era (TREND)

*Thursday, 2:40 p.m. The loan market is quiet in the way a card room is quiet right before somebody shoves.*

*(Quillfeather, its lenders, the client and every trade the desk does in it are fictional, and Quillfeather's history is a composite of real ones; the Serta figures are public record.)*

The RFQ arrives at 2:40: a client wants an offer on \$12mm of the Quillfeather Packaging first-lien term loan due 2029. Fourteen months ago Quillfeather's sponsor ran a non-pro-rata uptier. A 52% majority of the first-lien lenders exchanged into a new super-priority tranche and put in \$90mm of new money. The other 48% kept their old loans, which now sit behind more than a billion dollars of debt that did not exist the week before. The agencies called it a distressed exchange, counted it as a default, and a few weeks later re-rated the company out of default. The client wants the old, excluded first lien. It was marked at 41 last night.

It is a one-way request. The client has asked for an offer and not for a bid, which on a loan desk is the difference between "what is this worth?" and "I want it." The name on the ticket belongs to a special-situations fund that the coverage sheet lists as a buyer of stressed paper. As far as anyone can tell from the press reports and the cleansing materials published after the uptier, it was not in the June group.

Ines Okafor does not look up from her screen. "Hand history."

Theo Marsh pulls the markouts. The desk has traded the excluded Quillfeather loan nine times since the uptier, all in small size, almost all of it CLOs selling to the desk in the last week of a month, and the desk made money a week later on every one of those trades *(illustrative)*. "Nobody has ever asked us for an offer on this," he says. "Only bids."

"So this is the first hand where somebody is raising into us," says Ines.

"So it already defaulted," says Kaz Lind. "Is it immune now? Like chickenpox?"

"It's not immune," says Mags Dunleavy. "It's on parole."

"I don't understand why it trades at all." Kaz has the look of someone whose model just produced a negative variance. "In every model I have ever built, default is absorbing. The process stops. You collect $R$ and go home. This thing defaulted fourteen months ago and it was marked last night."

"That's a bankruptcy you're describing," says Mags. "This was a default the way a speeding ticket is a criminal record. The agencies wrote it down. The company kept paying interest. The loan is still outstanding, and the people who own it still have to decide every morning whether to keep owning it. Back in my day, default meant the phone stopped ringing. Now it means the phone starts." She does not reach for a terminal. She has been asked for this comparison often enough that she gives it from memory. "Serta. Twenty-second of June, 2020. A bare majority of the first lien, 52.6% of the class on the numbers the remand court eventually used, put in new money and swapped their loans into a super-priority tranche at 74. Everybody else in the same class stayed behind in loans the court later valued at about 25. Same loan, same Monday, forty-nine points apart, and the only difference was who had picked up the phone." She taps the 41 on Theo's screen. "That 41 is the 25 and the 74 averaged by someone who doesn't know which one they own."

Kaz takes the line literally, which is the most useful thing Kaz does. "If the only two outcomes are 25 and 74, a price of 41 puts weight $(41-25)/(74-25) = 16/49 \approx 0.33$ on the good one. So the market thinks a holder of this loan has about a one-in-three chance of being in the room next time."

"Or of a court putting them there," says Mags. "Ask the Serta excluded lenders how long that takes. And your arithmetic ignores time, which is the expensive part."

Theo has the 13-week cash flow model open, the one he still carries on a USB stick for emotional support. He rolled it forward last night out of habit, the way some people check the weather, and he reads the bottom line off the screen. "The new money buys them runway to about the third quarter of next year. After that, the interest bill comes back." He scrolls. "Liquidity crosses the revolver's minimum-availability test somewhere in that quarter, unless they sell something or get another deal done."

"Another deal," says Kaz, "meaning another default."

"Meaning another default by the agencies' definition, possibly," says Theo. "Or a filing. Those are different events with different recoveries, and the 41 doesn't tell you which one it's pricing."

Ines turns her chair a quarter turn. "What's the pot, what are the odds, and who at this table was in the majority group?"

"The pot is about \$4.9mm at 41. The odds..." Theo stops. "The odds are the problem. In 2015 I'd have looked up a recovery for a defaulted first lien and called it forty cents. But this loan has already defaulted once and it isn't in bankruptcy. Its next default could be a filing or another exchange. And its recovery depends less on the word 'first' in its name than on which side of the table its holders were sitting on in June."

"And the buyer?" Ines asks.

"Either they think the parole ends well, or they want to be inside the room for the next deal." Theo looks at the ticket again, and the thing he had been circling lands. "And they weren't inside the room last time. A fund that wasn't in the June group, asking only for an offer, in a loan that has only ever traded one way. They're not buying a recovery. They're buying a seat."

"Then the flow is the information," says Ines. "If they're assembling a block for the next negotiation, every piece they buy is a piece the sponsor will have to call, and 41 is too cheap to be short to them. If they just like the runway, 41 is fine and we're a normal dealer having a normal Thursday. Which hump our \$12mm ends up in depends on who is buying it, and that isn't on the term sheet."

From offstage, the Ad Hoc Group speaks in unison, through counsel: *"We are not sellers. We neither confirm nor deny that we are buyers."*

Ines lets that go by. "Three things before you answer. Which of the two default rates is that 41 pricing, the one that counts this exchange or the one that pretends it didn't happen? How fast does a loan on parole go back to jail, on Moody's numbers and not your gut? And how much of the spread in recoveries is nothing but which side of the room you sat on? Then I want ROBO to be able to build all of it without asking you a single question, because it won't ask. It'll just build the wrong thing."

**The question this chapter answers: what is the joint law of (time to the next default, recovery) for a credit that has already been restructured once, and how is it different from the law we all learned in 2015?**

The chapter answers her three questions, then the co-op, the courts and the regime they sit in, and comes back to this minute in §14.9. It is 2:41. Do you offer \$12mm at 41, and what would make you offer 38 or 44?

## 14.1 Two Default Rates, Two Recovery Rates

In the RSSG seat, "default" had a clear meaning. It was the day the company filed, or the day it missed a coupon and the forbearance agreement ran out. Everything before that was positioning. Everything after was a plan of reorganization, a valuation fight, and eighteen months of fee applications. Default was one absorbing state, and the recovery was whatever the plan said your class got.

The systematic desk inherits a different definition, and the gap between the two is now the most important footnote in credit.

Before the definition fight starts, one piece of vocabulary. The number in a rating agency's headline is a *rate*; the number a model wants is an *intensity*, or *hazard*, $\lambda_t$. Theo met the second in Chapter 5, when his 13-week model became a hazard, and here the two are about to be asked to do the same job.

> **Math, Gently.** *A default rate is an odometer; a hazard is a speedometer.* An odometer tells you how many miles the car covered this year; a speedometer tells you how fast it is going right now. A twelve-month default rate is an odometer reading: of the companies alive last June, 5.8% had defaulted by this June. A hazard rate $\lambda$ is the speedometer: the rate, per year, at which the companies still alive are defaulting at this instant. If the speed held constant all year, the share surviving the year is $e^{-\lambda}$, so a 5.8% rate means $e^{-\lambda} = 0.942$, a speed of $\lambda = -\ln(0.942) \approx 0.0597$ per year. The two numbers are close when they are small and drift apart as they grow, because a company that defaulted in March cannot default again in October; the survivors are a shrinking base. At that same speed, three years of survival is $e^{-3 \times 0.0597} = e^{-0.179} \approx 0.84$, so about 16% of the cohort is gone, not the $3 \times 5.8\% = 17.4\%$ you get by adding up odometer readings. A constant speed is the memoryless exponential clock of §1.5 and §6.1.4, the Poisson count seen from the other end. Most of this chapter is about what happens when the speed is not constant and there are two engines instead of one, which is where §14.2 starts.

With the vocabulary in hand, here is the sentence that makes one company's speedometer show two different speeds at once.

> **[SOURCE EXTRACTION]** *Schmid_Credit_Risk_Pricing_Models p.336:* "Distressed exchanges, on the other hand, are considered defaults whenever the debtholders are offered substitute instruments with lower coupons, longer maturities, or any other diminished financial terms."
>
> **Annotation.** Schmid is paraphrasing S&P's definition, and it was a sensible rule when distressed exchanges were rare, voluntary bond swaps that a creditor committee negotiated with the company. The rule is unchanged. What it now catches is not. An uptier, a drop-down financing, an amend-and-extend at a discount, and a PIK toggle forced through a majority vote can all be "substitute instruments with diminished terms," so all of them can be defaults, even though no court is involved, often no payment is missed, and the company is usually re-rated out of default within weeks. On a 2026 desk this sentence is the reason one company can be "in default" for Moody's, performing for its CDS, and current for its CLO manager's interest-coverage test, all on the same Tuesday. The modern desk departs from the textbook by refusing to collapse those into one flag. It carries two event types, two hazards and two recovery laws, and decides only at the end which one a given contract pays on.

Kaz, who has been reading the S&P rating scale, raises a hand. "What is a 'selective default'? Does the issuer get to pick which quarter?"

"Close," says Mags. "It gets to pick which creditors." That is the correct reading. S&P's SD, like Moody's "/LD" suffix, marks an issuer that has defaulted on a particular issue or class while it keeps paying the rest. It is the rating system's way of saying the company chose its victims.

Here is the fork the rest of the chapter is built on.

| Who is counting | Hard default (bankruptcy, missed payment) | Distressed exchange / LME | What the number is used for |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Rating agencies (Moody's, S&P, Fitch) | Default | Default (S&P SD, Moody's /LD, Fitch RD) | Default studies, CLO tests, PD model training labels |
| Standard North American corporate CDS (traded without restructuring as a credit event) | Credit event (bankruptcy, failure to pay) | Generally *not* a credit event | $\mathbb{Q}$-hazards from CDS spreads (Chapter 24) |
| Bankruptcy and restructuring studies | Filing | Not counted until a filing | Legal research, "Chapter 22" counts |
| Index default trackers (e.g., LCD-style "with and without LMEs") | Default | Shown both ways | Cycle commentary |

Moody's now publishes the gap directly. In June 2025 the trailing twelve-month speculative-grade default rate for bonds and loans combined was 5.8% including distressed exchanges. Removing the 51 distressed restructurings brought it to 2.1%, "almost one-third" of the headline (Moody's Asset Management Research, *Corporate Credit Risk Looking for a Catalyst to Break Out*, 7 August 2025). Same issuers, same twelve months, a factor of almost three, and the difference is a definition. Figure 14.1 sets that gap beside the soft share of defaults behind it.

![Figure 14.1: Counting distressed exchanges multiplies the headline default rate by almost three (left), because soft defaults have grown from about a third to about two-thirds of all defaults (right). Source: Moody's Asset Management Research (6 March 2025, 7 August 2025), Moody's (28 April and 18 May 2026) and S&P (15 August 2024, as cited by FTI Consulting, 9 October 2026), as quoted in §14.1; shares are rounded as published, S&P's are for US defaults, and the agencies' definitions differ.](../assets/figures/ch14_two_default_rates.png)

The punchline for a model builder is uncomfortable. A probability-of-default model trained on pre-2020 labels ("filed or missed a payment") and scored against today's agency default rate will look as if it under-predicts by roughly that factor of three. It isn't miscalibrated. It is answering a different question. Mixing Moody's DE-inclusive counts, S&P's SD, Fitch's RD and a vendor's "excluding LMEs" series in one training set produces label noise that no amount of gradient boosting will find, because it isn't noise in $X$. It is noise in the definition of $y$.

Here are the same years seen from a chair that has to live with both numbers. Picture a CLO manager *(a fictional composite)* running a dozen vehicles of broadly syndicated loans from an office where the most important document is the monthly trustee report. Her job is not to beat an index. It is to keep seven numbers inside their lines, above all a CCC share under its limit, "typically set to 7.5%," and overcollateralization and interest-coverage cushions above theirs; the median CLO, by one European Systemic Risk Board study, runs "within 4% of the most stringent covenant threshold" (Kundu, ESRB Working Paper 141, March 2023).

2024 was the record year for liability management, and for her it was a parade of phone calls she was not on. A sponsor's advisers would call a few large holders, a deal would close, a press release would arrive. If her vehicles were in the group, she came out with a first-out loan she could hold. If they were not, she came out with a loan rated SD for a few days and then CCC, and once her CCC bucket overflowed, the excess was marked at the lowest price in the bucket, straight out of her OC numerator. Either way the agencies' count ticked up, because an exchange is a default whichever side of it you sat on.

In 2025 the count fell, and a consultant's deck called it the year LMEs peaked. Her trustee reports said otherwise: fewer deals, the same soft share of defaults. By 2026 the coercive uptier had all but gone, replaced by equity handovers and consensual amend-and-extends, and a discounted version of either is still a default to the agencies and still a CCC in her bucket. The technique had changed clothes, not careers, and the number on her monthly report depended on which of the two default rates the trustee read. (Her ledger, with its sources, closes this section.)

How strange is a world in which most defaults happen out of court? Very, by the standards of the shelf.

> **[SOURCE EXTRACTION]** *Moyer_Distressed_Debt_Analysis p.87:* "Given the relative simplicity of the out-of-court restructuring, one might well wonder why it is successfully employed less than 10% of the time."
>
> **Annotation.** Moyer was writing in 2004, and his answer was the holdout problem: an exchange offer needed very high participation (he cites thresholds of 85–90% elsewhere in the book), and any holder who refused kept a full claim against a company that the others had just de-levered. Twenty years later, out-of-court restructuring is the *majority* outcome. The holdout problem was not solved by better persuasion. It was solved by contract technology that turned holdouts into victims: if a bare majority can amend the credit agreement, subordinate the minority, or move the collateral to an unrestricted subsidiary, then holding out stops being a free option and becomes a short put. That inversion is the whole LMT era in one sentence, and it is why the 2004 base rates in every distressed textbook are the wrong prior for 2026.

Mags, who remembers 2004 as "recent," takes the long view. "We used to call it a coercive exchange, and it needed ninety percent to work. Now it needs fifty point one percent and a dictionary." She pauses. "The Fifth Circuit, to its credit, eventually bought a dictionary too." (We get to that ruling in §14.6.)

**Quant-shop life (fictional composite): forty-one issuers that cannot agree.** The platform's risk-data team, the Tuesday of the week a new vendor default file arrives. Nobody announces the file. It lands in a storage bucket at 6:12 a.m., the ingestion job picks it up at 6:15, and by 9:30 there is a ticket in the queue, DATA-2291, titled "default_flag mismatch, 2023 cohort," assigned to Hana, the junior quant who owns the risk-data pipeline (Chapter 5). Hana has learned that tickets with the word "mismatch" in the title never close on the day they open.

The PD model's training set carries three default columns, because three sources sell default histories and the firm licenses all of them. `default_flag_mdy` is Moody's, with distressed exchanges counted. `default_flag_sp` is S&P's, where an SD counts. `default_flag_vnd` is a vendor's "ex-LME" series, which counts a default only on a filing or a missed payment. On most rows the three agree, because most companies either pay or do not. On the 2023 rows they disagree about 41 issuers *(an invented count for this composite; the real number depends on the vendor and the universe)*. Hana sorts the 41 by date, and the pattern is not subtle. Nearly every one is an uptier, a drop-down or a discounted amend-and-extend. Moody's and S&P say default; the vendor says performing. The model, trained on a column called `y`, has been told both on alternate refreshes, depending on which source a configuration file written in 2021 happened to point at.

The meeting about it lasts fifty minutes, and forty of them are about names. One researcher wants a single `default_flag` with a documented precedence rule. Another wants the three source columns kept forever and a fourth, `default_type`, taking the values `HARD`, `DE` and `NONE`. Someone proposes `default_flag_v2`, and the room goes quiet the way rooms do when everyone remembers `vol_60d_v2`. Theo, invited because he "knows the restructuring side," asks the question he always asks: "What does the credit agreement call it?" Nobody knows, and it turns out to be the right question, because the credit agreement does not call it anything. The exchange was done *under* the agreement, by amendment, and on the company's own documents nothing ever went wrong. The agencies called it a default. The lenders left outside called it something that does not go in a schema.

Then the point-in-time problem arrives, the one Hana already met in Chapter 5 when a vendor restated its marks. Call it *what we knew when*. One of the 41 was rated SD by S&P for nine days and then B-. The current file shows B-. A back-test run on the current file never sees the SD, and treats a company the market spent nine days pricing as a defaulter as a clean B- credit all along. The fix is dull and correct: store both ratings, each with the time it took effect and the time the firm received it, and make the training job ask for the state *as known* on each date. Hana writes it into the ticket as a schema change, a `rating_event` table keyed on issuer, agency, rating, effective time and received time, and it takes the rest of the week.

By Friday the training set has a `default_type` column, three source flags, and a precedence rule written down where the risk committee can read it. Not one line of the model's own logic has changed, and its validation accuracy has moved by a few points anyway *(illustrative)*, because for two years it had been graded against an answer key that changed with the configuration. That is the "noise in the definition of $y$" from earlier in this section, seen from the desk where somebody has to fix it.

The recovery side has forked the same way. Measured *at the exchange*, recoveries on distressed exchanges look excellent: Moody's put first-lien DE recoveries at 71% at end-2024, up from 55% in 2023 (as reported by Bloomberg Law, *Distress Exchange Leads to Re-Default Half the Time*, 23 April 2025). Measured *at the eventual bankruptcy*, first liens of companies that had done an LME recovered far less. PitchBook, summarizing a Fitch study of 2024 emergences, reported weighted-average first-lien recoveries of 23% for issuers with a prior LME against 53% for those without. We could not open the Fitch original, so treat the pair as indicative rather than gospel. The two numbers are not contradictory. The first is measured at a moment chosen by the borrower, for holders who were in the deal. The second is measured at the next event, which is where the excluded holders' losses and the participants' second haircut actually show up. A recovery database that records only the first number has a survivorship bias with a lawyer.

So "the default rate" is now two numbers, and "the recovery rate" is now at least two distributions. The rest of the chapter builds the machinery to carry both.

> **Trend Watch.** *The soft-default takeover, 2010–2026.*
> - **Baseline.** S&P counted distressed exchanges at roughly one-third of US defaults over 2010–2023 and about half in the years to mid-2024 (S&P, *Distressed Exchanges Reached Their Highest Level Since 2009*, 15 August 2024, as cited by FTI Consulting, 9 October 2026; we could not open the S&P original).
> - **2024.** Distressed exchanges were roughly three in five Moody's-rated defaults, a record share (Moody's AMR, 6 March 2025). LMT counts hit a high-water mark of 38 (Wachtell Lipton, *Liability Management 2026*, 3 February 2026).
> - **H1 2025.** About 60% of defaults in the first half of 2025, similar to 2024, concentrated in loan-only, private-equity-backed capital structures (Moody's AMR, 7 August 2025).
> - **2025.** About 65% of all defaults were distressed restructurings (Moody's, 28 April 2026). LME counts fell to 24, yet LMEs were still about two-thirds of default activity by issuer count and exceeded payment defaults and bankruptcies on a rolling twelve-month basis every month of the year (Wachtell, 3 February 2026). In Moody's direct-lending proxy, the default rate was 1.6% excluding distressed exchanges and 4.7% including them.
> - **2026.** The Federal Reserve's May 2026 *Financial Stability Report* notes that defaults including distressed exchanges "remained relatively high" even as volume-weighted loan default rates sat below their median. 9fin counted 25 completed LMEs in H1 2026, against 24 in H1 2025, with coercive uptiers having "all but vanished" in favor of equity handovers and consensual amend-and-extends (9fin, 28 August 2026).
> - **What it means for the desk.** The *level* of the headline default rate is now a weak cycle signal, while the *mix* is a strong one. The count of LMTs fell after 2024; the share of defaults that are soft did not. The technique migrated rather than retreating. Any feature called `default_rate` in your warehouse needs a sibling called `default_rate_ex_de`, and the spread between them is itself a regime variable (§14.7).

### Deep-Dive Resource Graph (§14.1)
