The Markov-switching fit must return valid probabilities that sum to one and call the regime correctly in more than 85% of 80 simulated years. Last come arithmetic tripwires: the P-versus-Q ratio, three co-op cases, and two Serta dollar identities, such as \$484.88mm less \$895mm of face at 25 cents equaling \$261.13mm.

The desk runs it after every edit and before any refactor merges. A green run proves that the code implements the stated math and says nothing about whether the math describes the market, since no real data touch it. It is also silent in one place inside the code: every closed-form comparison runs with regime switching turned off, the cohort simulator's regime transitions are never checked against a closed form, and the Markov-switching test uses a separate generator, so nothing tests how the two interact.

*The full listing is [Listing 14.5 in Appendix F](#code-14-5).*

The tests double as documentation. If a later contributor "simplifies" `aalen_johansen` into one minus Kaplan–Meier, the trap test fails. If someone replaces the cure model with an exponential, the fourteen-month test prints ROBO's answer next to the truth.

### Deep-Dive Resource Graph (§14.7)

- **Academic Papers.** Hamilton (1989), *A New Approach to the Economic Analysis of Nonstationary Time Series and the Business Cycle*, Econometrica. Fine & Gray (1999), *A Proportional Hazards Model for the Subdistribution of a Competing Risk*, JASA 94(446). Aalen & Johansen (1978), *An Empirical Transition Matrix for Non-homogeneous Markov Chains Based on Censored Observations*, Scandinavian Journal of Statistics.
- **Data & Code.** Moody's and S&P annual default studies (vendor) for DE counts by year; Federal Reserve FSR Figure 2.9 for a public DE-inclusive series.

## 14.8 Case Studies: Three Clocks

### 14.8.1 Case Study: Serta Simmons Bedding, 2020–2026 (the whole regime in one name)

*A replay, cut off at Wednesday, 8 July 2026, 7:20 a.m.* *(The bank, Mags's position at it and every line of dialogue are fictional; everything Serta did, and everything the courts and the parties said, is public record and cited.)* The remand opinion came out the previous afternoon, and by that morning the desk had two client requests asking what an excluded Serta claim was worth. Mags priced them before Theo arrived; now she runs the morning again for him, starting six years earlier, with a spiral notebook that has a coffee ring on the cover and "2020 Q2" written on the spine in marker. In 2020 she ran the distressed loan book at a bank, and by 22 June the book held \$15mm face of the Serta first-lien term loan *(illustrative)*: \$5mm bought the previous autumn on a thesis she now summarizes as "a mattress is the last thing people stop buying, which turned out to be wrong," and the ten million she bought from a CLO the week before the deal, which Chapter 1 tells from the trading side.

"Before anybody prices anything," she says, "you're going to live through it. Three stops. At each one I tell you what we knew, you tell me what you'd do, and then I tell you what happened."

"Like Ines's Lumen replay," says Kaz.

"Ines's replays come out of a folder. This comes out of a notebook. The notebook has my mistakes in it."

#### Act I: the phone that did not ring (June 2020)

The capital structure was ordinary. In 2016 Serta Simmons Bedding had put in place a \$1.95bn first-lien term loan and a \$450mm second lien (Duane Morris, February 2025), the sort of sponsor-backed loan that sat in many CLOs in small pieces. In the spring of 2020 the stores that sold its mattresses closed their showrooms, and by June the market knew that the company was negotiating for liquidity with some of its lenders, and knew that it was not negotiating with all of them. Mags opens the notebook at a page dated 15 June. The entry, in full: *"Phone hasn't rung. Called two dealers. Both 'can't talk about it.' Asked which group. 'Which group?'"*

Theo does what he was trained to do, which is to read the credit agreement before forming a view, and in June 2020 the agreement's text was public. He finds section 9.05(g) in a few minutes. It lets the borrower buy back loans from some lenders and not others in two ways: through a Dutch auction open to all lenders, which the agreement defines meticulously over a page of mechanics, or through "open market purchases," which it does not define at all. "That's the door," he says. "If an exchange with half the class counts as an open market purchase, the pro rata sharing protection doesn't bite, and the agreement lets a bare majority subordinate everyone else's liens." He keeps reading, out of RSSG habit, and passes section 2.18(c), a sharing clause that says a lender receiving a disproportionate payment has to buy participations from the others, for cash at face value, so that the benefit is shared ratably. He reads it as boilerplate, notes it in the margin as "standard," and moves on. Mags watches him do it and says nothing.

Kaz approaches it from the other end. "Two humps," Kaz says, pointing at Figure 14.4. "Inside and outside. For a holder whose phone hasn't rung, the coin has landed. Not calling you is a measurement. Your $\pi$ is about zero."

"And it isn't an accident," says Ines. "The majority needs 50.1% to amend. Every lender it adds to the group is another mouth sharing what gets taken from the outside. A coalition that can close at 52% has no reason to be 70%. You aren't being left out because they forgot you. You're being left out because you're expensive." Kaz writes $\pi \approx 0$ on the whiteboard and then, after a moment, writes "by design" next to it.

"So," says Mags. "It is the week of 15 June 2020. You hold \$15mm of the first lien. The phone has not rung. What do you do?"

The desk works through the options, and each is less attractive than it sounds. Theo's instinct is to call the company's advisers and offer to join, or to bring a competing proposal, which is what he would have advised a client to do. Ines points out that the group has every reason to keep the door shut, and that a competing proposal from a \$15mm holder does not get a meeting. Kaz proposes selling before the deal closes. "To whom?" asks Ines. "The only people bidding for this loan that week are people who think they know whether they're getting in. If they're bidding, they know more than you." The fourth option is to go to court, and that is the one somebody took. Apollo, Angelo Gordon and Gamut, first-lien lenders outside the negotiating group, asked a New York state court to stop the transaction. Justice Andrea Masley declined to enjoin it; at that stage she was not persuaded that the exchange violated the lenders' sacred rights, the short list of terms that no majority can change without each affected lender's consent. Mayer Brown's June 2020 note adds that she also found no irreparable harm, because money damages were available; Bloomberg Law reported the plaintiffs' names.

"Which," says Kaz, "I now understand does not involve a priest."

"It involves a list," says Mags. "If the thing being done to you isn't on the list, the majority can do it. Subordination wasn't on Serta's list. The sharing clause was, and the open-market-purchase exception was the way around it." She turns the page. "What I did was hold. I called everyone I knew, nobody called back, and I decided that 'open market purchase' could not possibly mean a private deal with half the lenders. I was right about the words. I was wrong about the year."

The deal closed on 22 June 2020. It brought \$200mm of new-money first-out super-priority debt, and the participating lenders exchanged about \$1.2bn of first- and second-lien loans into about \$875mm of second-out super-priority debt, first liens at 74 and second liens at 39 (Proskauer, 2 January 2025; Jones Day, March 2025). On the remand court's findings years later, the participants held about 52.6% of the first-lien class, and the excluded loans were worth about \$0.25 at the closing. Mags's \$15mm was still called a first lien. It now sat behind more than a billion dollars of debt that had not existed the week before. "Same loan, same Monday," she says, as she did in the cold open. "Forty-nine points apart."

#### Act II: parole (2021 to mid-2023)

The next page Mags opens is dated January 2021. The excluded loan is quoted around 20 *(illustrative)*, and the sellers are the ones §14.1 would predict: CLOs, for whom a loan fresh from a distressed exchange counts against a CCC bucket already swollen by the pandemic's downgrades *(the seller mix is the pattern §14.1 describes, not a sourced list)*. They were selling not because they had a view, but because their trustee reports did. "January 2021," she says. "Excluded paper at 20. Do you buy, and what's the thesis?"

Kaz reaches for the remand number first. "The court said 25. So 20 is five points cheap."

"Nobody in January 2021 had heard of the 25," says Mags. "That's a number a court found in 2026, looking back with experts. In 2021 the only number was the screen."

Kaz regroups, and the regrouping is useful, because it forces the thesis into the open. A buyer at 20 owns three things at once: the runway, because the \$200mm of new money bought the company time and, if the business recovers, the excluded loan is still a claim for par at maturity, behind the new layers but not erased; the bankruptcy option, which is mostly a cost, because in a filing the new super-priority debt is paid first; and the claim, the excluded lenders' argument that the exchange was never an open market purchase at all. Theo, who has now read 9.05(g) more times than he would admit, thinks the argument is good. "A defined Dutch auction next to an undefined 'open market purchase' reads like the drafters meant two different things. A private exchange with a hand-picked majority isn't any market I've ever heard of."

"Then what's the claim worth?" asks Ines. "Not the argument. The money."

Theo stops, because he does not know. A breach of contract is worth whatever a court decides the damages are, and in January 2021 he has no way to say whether that would be the difference between 74 and 25, or the market value of what was lost, or nothing at all because the excluded lenders could have sold. He writes "remedy?" on his pad and underlines it twice, and he still does not go back to 2.18(c).

Mags reads her own January 2021 entry aloud. *"Sold 7.5 at 20. Keep 7.5. Litigation = lottery ticket. Runway = hope."* "I halved it," she says, "to somebody who had read the remedy clause more carefully than I had. I didn't know that at the time. I thought he was a tourist."

The selling was real, and years later it was entered into evidence. At the remand, the participating lenders' mitigation expert testified that up to \$186mm face of the first-lien loans traded between June 2020 and the end of 2021, and constructed hypothetical sales of \$62mm to \$94mm, the argument being that excluded lenders who held on had chosen not to cut their losses. The court recited Bloomberg chats with a dealer's loan market maker. "That's my markout," says Ines. "Entered into evidence." It is the most useful hand history in the book: a public court record of a dealer making a market in a loan whose priming a court would later hold to be a breach of the agreement.

Then the parole ran out. Serta filed for Chapter 11 in the Southern District of Texas on 23 January 2023, about 31 months after the uptier. On the clock of §14.3.2, that is a late failure: most post-exchange re-defaults arrive within two years. The court case turned against the outside lenders too. On 28 March 2023 the bankruptcy court granted partial summary judgment that the exchange was an "open market purchase." The plan was confirmed on 14 June 2023, and it carried an indemnity for the participating lenders against claims arising from the 2020 transaction.

"That was the bottom," says Mags. "Not the price. The feeling. We'd lost on the words, and the plan promised to cover the other side for the cost of having beaten us." She closes the notebook on her thumb. "If you'd asked me in June 2023 whether the excluded hump was ever going to move right, I'd have told you to go and price something with a future."

#### Act III: the words come back (2024 to 2026)

The last section of the notebook is not in the notebook. Mags left the bank a few weeks after that January entry, the fund she moved to wound down in 2022, and what she kept after that she kept in a folder of court opinions and law-firm memos, printed out, because she does not trust a PDF she cannot write on.

The appeal was argued in the Fifth Circuit on 10 July 2024 and decided on 31 December 2024, five and a half months later. The court reversed. An open market purchase, it held, "occurs on the secondary market for syndicated loans," and a privately negotiated exchange with a subset of lenders is not one; it read the "deafening silence" of an undefined phrase sitting next to a meticulously defined Dutch auction as meaning what Theo had thought it meant on the first morning. It also struck the plan's indemnity for the participating lenders (§14.6). The opinion was revised on 14 February 2025, rehearing was denied on 18 February, and Barings, one of the participating lenders, asked the Supreme Court to review the indemnity ruling. On 10 November 2025 the Court declined (No. 24-1322; Law360, November 2025; Furniture Today, December 2025).

"Thirty-one December," says Kaz. "That's the Mitel day."

"Same day," says Theo. "A different court in Manhattan read different words in Mitel's agreement and came out the other way." The two words that separated them are in §14.6.

Then the case went back down. In November 2025 Serta itself, the reorganized debtor, won summary judgment on discharge grounds, which left the participating lenders as the only defendants. The damages trial was held in March 2026. On 7 July 2026, the day before the replay's cut-off, the court awarded \$261.13mm, the gap between a but-for value of about \$484.88mm and an actual value of \$223.75mm, which is the excluded lenders' \$895mm of face at \$0.25. On top of that it awarded 9% New York prejudgment interest from 22 June 2020, with the award allocated severally by each defendant's holdings (Mayer Brown, July 2026).

Theo reads the remedy section of the opinion summary twice, and then he goes back to his own annotated copy of the 2016 agreement, the one he marked up on the first morning of the replay, and finds his margin note next to section 2.18(c). It says "standard." The court's measure of damages ran through that clause: a lender that receives a disproportionate payment has to "purchase (for Cash at face value) participations" so that the benefit is shared ratably, a non-cash exchange counts as a payment, and so damages run on face value, not on whatever the excluded loan would have fetched in the market. The participating lenders' defences, ratification, unclean hands and failure to mitigate (the \$186mm of trading from Act II), all failed. The clause Theo had waved past as boilerplate was the one that turned a lawsuit into a number. It is the same lesson as Robertshaw's in §14.6, from the other side: the remedy is where the money is, and it was printed in the agreement in 2016.

Kaz does the arithmetic that the opinion leaves to the reader. From 22 June 2020 to 7 July 2026 is about 6.04 years, so 9% simple interest adds roughly 54% to the award, about \$142mm, for a total near \$403mm *(approx.; before allocation, collection risk, or appeal)*; Law360 later put it at "roughly \$400 million" (22 July 2026). On \$895mm of face, that is about 45 points of par, *on top of* whatever the excluded loans recovered in the plan. Add it to the 25 the court said the loans were worth at the closing and the excluded lender's dollar is back to about 70 cents on face, before allocation, collection and appeal. Our "illustrative" $\mu_{\text{out}} = 0.25$ was the value at closing. Six years later, the excluded hump had a litigation tail worth more than the loan had been worth on the day of the exchange. Kaz reads Mags's own line from §14.6.1 back to her, about the best-performing tranche in the Serta capital structure being New York prejudgment interest. "Not entirely a joke," she says.

"Last stop," says Mags. "It is 8 July 2026. Two clients want a price on the excluded claim. Price it."

Kaz builds a three-branch tree, because that is what a contingent claim with a dated path is, and labels every branch *(illustrative)*. In the first branch, with probability 0.55, the award is paid in full in about a year: 45 points, discounted at a litigation-finance hurdle of 12%, is worth about 40.2 today. In the second, with probability 0.30, it settles at 70 cents on the dollar after two years: 31.5 points, discounted, about 25.1. In the third, with probability 0.15, it is reversed or never collected, and it is worth nothing. The probability-weighted value is $0.55 \times 40.2 + 0.30 \times 25.1 \approx 29.6$ points per 100 of excluded face, for the claim alone.

"So thirty," says Kaz.

"Thirty to whom?" says Ines. "What's the pot, what are the odds, and who at this table knows more than you? The defendants know whether they're appealing. The holders know what their counsel told them about timing. We know the arithmetic. That's three people who know more than we do about two of the three branches." She widens the market Kaz was about to quote to something she describes as "honest," which in practice means wide.

Theo's list of what a buyer of the claim would want to know first comes out as questions, not rules, because none of them has a general answer. Can the claim be transferred at all, and on what documents, which is the first question any claims trader asks? Several liability means each defendant pays its own share, and the defendants named in the opinions, among them Barings, Boston Management and Research, Credit Suisse Asset Management, Eaton Vance and Invesco, are large institutions, so the risk sits in time and appeal far more than in anyone's solvency. Will anyone appeal? As of the morning after, nobody had said. And how does interest run between judgment and payment? Kaz's tree ignores that, which is a choice and not an answer.

Mags closes the folder. "The half I sold at 20 in January 2021," she says, "is, for whoever bought it, the best trade in the capital structure. Exercise 4 makes you work out how good." She stands up. "The half I kept belongs to people I don't work for any more. Back in my day, a lawsuit was where a position went to die." She considers that. "This one took six years to come back to life. I'll grant it that."

A fortnight later Law360's write-up of the ruling drew the lesson in a sentence: holding and preserving claims can beat selling at a loss (22 July 2026).

**How a systematic desk flags it.** Read back through the chapter's instruments, Mags's notebook records four signals that were on the table before 22 June 2020: the undefined "open market purchase" Theo found on the first morning (a Priming Risk Score input, Chapter 13); a fragmented, CLO-heavy holder base with no co-op ($c \approx 0$ in §14.5); the dealers' "which group?", which out of court is the substitute for a Rule 2019 statement; and RFQ flow one-sided by holder type, the cold open's lesson six years early. After the closing the trade was the inside/outside spread, after 31 December 2024 it was the excluded claim, a contingent asset with a dated appellate path, and on 8 July 2026 it was Kaz's three-branch tree.

### 14.8.2 Case Study: Mitel Networks, 2022–2025 (win the case, lose the credit)

The facts are short. In October 2022 participating lenders provided about \$156mm of new-money first-out debt, exchanged first-lien loans into second-out at a 5% discount, that is at 95, and exchanged second-lien loans into third-out at an 18% discount, at 82 (Paul Weiss, 10 January 2025). The excluded lenders were left behind about \$857mm of priming debt. On 31 December 2024 the First Department held the deal permitted. On 10 March 2025 Mitel filed a prepackaged Chapter 11 in the Southern District of Texas, about 29 months after the uptier, and the plan was confirmed on 17 April 2025 before Judge Lopez.

What makes Mitel worth a scene is the ten weeks between the ruling and the filing, because that is where Kaz was wrong, out loud, in a meeting.

*A replay, cut off at Thursday, 2 January 2025, 8:05 a.m.* *(The desk's dashboard, its hazards and all the dialogue are fictional; Mitel's dates and terms are public record and cited.)* Kaz was on the desk that morning and made the call; in Ines's replay Kaz makes it again, for Theo's benefit. The first desk meeting of the year is mostly people reading the holiday's rulings off their phones. Serta has gone one way in New Orleans and Mitel the other way in Manhattan, on the same afternoon, and Kaz has already updated the dashboard. "Mitel won," Kaz says. "The uptier stands. No unwind, no damages, no cloud over the capital structure. So I've taken its hazard down."

"Down why?" asks Ines.

"Because the biggest risk to the company was losing the case. If the court had unwound the deal, the new money would have been in question and the priming would have been reversed. That risk is gone. Fewer bad states means a lower hazard."

It is a reasonable sentence, and it is the kind of sentence a model builder writes when every input to the model lives in one table. Mags does not argue with it. She asks a different question. "Did the ruling put any money in the bank?"

Theo already has the answer, because he worked it in §14.3.2 for a different reason. The \$156mm of new money in October 2022 was the company's runway, and on the reading this chapter uses it bought about two and a half years, which puts the cliff somewhere in the spring of 2025. "The court decided who gets what if things go wrong," he says. "It didn't decide whether things go wrong. The cash burn is the same this morning as it was last week. The clock is still running, and by my count it's close to the end."

Kaz looks at the dashboard for a while. Then Kaz does the thing that makes Kaz worth having on a desk, which is to change position completely and say why. "I put the ruling into the wrong parameter. A ruling on the words moves $\theta_w$, the chance that the next deal written in those words gets done, for every agreement with a bare 'purchase' in it. For Mitel's own excluded lenders it moves $\mu_{\text{out}}$, and it moves it nowhere good, because they lost. It doesn't touch the company's re-default hazard at all. The hazard runs on runway." Kaz restores the old number and adds a note to the change log, which says, in full, "Reverted: ruling ≠ cash."

"So the people who won the case," says Ines, "own a company that's ten weeks from running out of money."

Ten weeks, it turned out, was about right. The ruling preceded the filing by about 2.3 months. Mitel filed its prepack on 10 March 2025, and on Paul Weiss's account the plan cut about \$1.15bn of debt, lowered annual interest by about \$135mm, and brought in about \$125mm of new money, converting secured debt into equity along the way. The lenders who had won the right to prime their colleagues in Manhattan spent the spring in a Texas bankruptcy court anyway. In the mixture-cure model Mitel was one of the susceptible 25%, failing inside the high-hazard window that the $k > 1$ calibration predicts, and the desk's model now keeps legality and survival in different columns on purpose.

### 14.8.3 Case Study: Del Monte Foods, 2024–2026 (the fast clock)

Here we keep to the dockets, and the reason we do is itself a story about judgment.

The public record that this book has checked is a list of dates. A 2024 financing, reported as a non-pro-rata deal in August 2024 (a date and a set of terms this book has not verified against the documents), was followed by Chapter 11 on 1 July 2025 (Bankr. D.N.J. 25-16984), about eleven months later and well inside Moody's two-year window. Litigation between lender groups followed: an adversary proceeding naming members of the Ad Hoc Term Lender Group and of the Ad Hoc Group of Minority Secured Lenders (23 January 2026), a district-court action by the minority group (6 March 2026), and a bankruptcy appeal (28 May 2026). The deal terms, recoveries and holdings are in the first-day declaration and the complaints.

*A Tuesday in October 2026, the quarterly refresh.* *(The desk, its event table and the dialogue are fictional; the Del Monte dates and docket numbers are public record.)* Once a quarter the desk adds the new names to the event table that trains the re-default engine of §14.3: one row per LME, with the exchange date, the type, the new money as a fraction of debt, the exchange ratios, the filing date if there is one, and the recoveries if they are known. It is a dull job, done in an afternoon with the door closed, and this quarter Kaz has the keyboard. Del Monte is the interesting row, because eleven months is the shortest clock in the table and one short clock moves the fitted scale $\eta$ more than three long ones.

Kaz has the numbers half-typed from a news summary: a size for the 2024 financing, an exchange ratio, an estimate of how much of the class was inside. "It's all in the press," Kaz says. "I'll mark the source as press."

"Which press?" asks Mags.

Kaz names a newsletter. Mags asks whether the newsletter read the first-day declaration, and Kaz does not know. Theo knows what a first-day declaration is, because he has drafted parts of them: the company's own account, filed on the first day of the case and sworn to by an officer, of how it got there, with the capital structure, the prepetition transactions and the reasons for filing laid out in an order somebody's lawyers argued over for a week. "That's where the terms are," he says. "Along with the complaints, which are the other side's account. If the two disagree, that's the litigation. Nobody on this desk has read either."

"Then we have dates," says Mags. "Put in the dates."

Kaz objects, reasonably. A row with dates and no terms is a row the model can only half use. The exchange ratio and the new-money fraction are the covariates that move $p$ and $\eta$, and leaving them blank throws away the most informative short clock in the sample. Ines settles it with the oldest move in the card room. "Folding is a play. A wrong number in a training set doesn't look wrong. It looks like data, and in a year nobody will remember it came from a newsletter. A blank looks like a blank, and somebody fills it properly." The row goes in with the exchange date marked "reported, unverified," the filing date and docket number, the three litigation dates, and every term field set to missing with a flag, `terms_unread = TRUE`. The engine treats the row as a dated event with unknown covariates, which is a smaller piece of information than Kaz wanted and a truer one.

From the corner of the room, the book's recurring chorus splits in two, each half speaking through its own counsel, and the only sentence they share is the one every ad hoc group shares: *"We reserve all rights."* (The chorus is this book's device. The two groups named in the Del Monte dockets have said nothing to us.)

The refusal is a judgment call, not a rule, and it could have gone the other way. A desk with a position in the name, or a client asking for a price, would read the declaration that afternoon, because the cost of not knowing would be a trade rather than a slightly worse fit. For a training row, the cost of a wrong number is larger and slower: it bends the clock for every future name that looks like this one, and nobody sees it happen. What the desk does know is already instructive. Del Monte's shape is a short $\eta$, then a second fight about $\pi$ inside the bankruptcy itself, two ad hoc groups of the same company's lenders litigating against each other in three forums. The two humps of §14.4 did not collapse when the company filed; they went to court.

## 14.9 Trading the Regime

*Thursday, 2:41 p.m., again.* The chapter has taken the long way round to come back to one minute. The Quillfeather RFQ is still on the screen: \$12mm of the excluded first lien, one-way, an offer wanted, from a special-situations fund that was not in the June group. Ines's question has not changed. Do you offer at 41, and what would make you offer 38 or 44? The answer arrives the way most answers on this desk arrive, as five lines from five voices, and each line is a feature with a timestamp rather than an opinion.

Kaz goes first, with the clock. "Fourteen months since the exchange. That's inside the hump. Six to 24 months after an exchange is where the susceptible names fail, and the rating hasn't moved since the agencies re-rated it out of default, which is normal; agency ratings often stay flat after LMEs (Roe & Rotaru, 2026). Read the 41 with a post-LME recovery instead of 40% and the hazard it implies is well below what the cure model says." Across a book, that gap between the cure-model hazard and the hazard implied by the loan price, computed with the *post*-LME recovery rather than 40%, is the systematic underweight that defensive high-yield books run (Chapter 11). "On the clock alone," says Kaz, "the loan is rich. For an ordinary buyer I'd offer lower. Thirty-eight."

"It isn't an ordinary buyer," says Mags, with the register. Stage 0 of §14.4 is who sits inside, and on a systematic desk it is scored from Rule 2019 statements, co-op announcements, CLO trustee holdings, and the adviser-hire headlines that Chapter 25's NLP pipeline extracts. "This fund wasn't in the June group, it's asking only for an offer, and the only people who've ever traded this loan with us are CLOs selling at month-end. That's a seat being assembled." The systematic version of her point is a trade: long likely-inside, short likely-outside in the same class, where the document score is high and the holder base fragmented. Here the buyer is trying to move its own paper from one side of that line to the other.

Theo, with the documents, says why the seat is worth assembling. Quillfeather's agreement *(fictional, like the company)* was written in 2021, before the blockers. Buccola and Nini (2024) find that most new loans blocked uptiers by mid-2022 while the legacy stock stayed loose, and that stock decays only as it matures or is amended. "So the next deal can be done the way the last one was," Theo says. "And it isn't just Quillfeather. Every loan written before the blockers carries the same exposure until it rolls off. It's a factor, not a one-off."

ROBO says nothing, because nobody asked it a question, but it has put a line on the dashboard: the dual default-rate spread, headline minus ex-DE default rate, which feeds the high-yield beta and the Hamilton filter of §14.7. The filter reads 0.88, the number the risk committee argued about. The desk is, with reasonable confidence, in the world where second deals happen.

Ines, with the calendar, has the last line. Pending appellate decisions (Wesco and ConvergeOne in the Fifth Circuit, the first co-op antitrust ruling) are known catalysts with direction-dependent jumps in $\theta_w$ and $\mu_{\text{out}}$, and none of them falls this month. "Nobody gets to be surprised by a date," she says. "You price each outcome before the ruling, so that on the day you're executing, not thinking. Nothing's due. So the calendar doesn't move this price."

From somewhere off the desk the Ad Hoc Group, through counsel, *"continues to monitor the docket."*

Then Ines adds up the hand. "If a tourist wanted this paper with no seat to build, the clock says 38. If it were a CLO buying back in, which they almost never do, 41 would be fine. A fund assembling a block before the next deal is paying for a seat, and a seat is worth more to them than this loan is to us." She types the offer: 44 for the full \$12mm *(illustrative)*. The client lifts it inside a minute, which tells her she was not wrong, and very possibly not high enough.

Three weeks later the trade press reports that a new ad hoc group of Quillfeather first-lien lenders has hired counsel, and the cleansing materials that follow list the special-situations fund among its members *(fictional, like everything about Quillfeather)*. The desk's markout on the trade at 44 is flat.

"Flat is a win," says Ines, replaying the hand. "At 41 it would have been the hand history of a lesson."

> **View From Another Seat.** *The dealer desk: a co-op'd loan is inventory you may not be allowed to sell.* A bank's loan-trading desk, described generically, sees a Quillfeather-type name as a balance-sheet problem with a calendar attached. The sellers are CLOs near month-end, ahead of their test dates (§14.1), and if the loan sits under a co-op with Lumen-style transfer restrictions, the buyers thin out in the same week (§14.5.1). A market maker that buys a block from a CLO on the 28th may find the natural buyers either inside the co-op and restricted or outside it and uninterested, so the dealer widens, or passes, or works the order, looking for the other side before taking the risk. Legal bills sit in the same calculation, because the LMT era's creditor-on-creditor fights generate costs that any holder, dealer inventory included, may end up sharing; the Financial Times' Sujeet Indap gave the general-audience account on *Odd Lots*, "Inside the Blood Sport of Creditor-on-Creditor Violence" (25 November 2024). For the dealer, the question is less which hump the loan lands in than whether it can hand the loan to someone before it lands.

> **[SOURCE EXTRACTION]** *BlackRock_Systematic_High_Yield_Credit p.6:* "Our proprietary probability of default signal that has underpinned all of our credit strategies for over 20 years has successfully identified 77% of the defaulted bonds in the ICE BofA High Yield Index within 24 months of its default since 2010."
>
> **Annotation.** A strong claim, and the right kind of signal to own. The question this chapter teaches you to ask is: *which* default? A bond-index default definition, a structural model built on asset value and volatility, and a sample mostly from before the LMT era were all built to catch hard defaults. A soft default is a negotiation over runway and coalition, and asset value is only one input to it. A 2026 default-avoidance signal should be scored separately on $F_H$ and $F_D$, and its hit rate on distressed exchanges reported on its own line.

"IDO or it didn't happen," says Ines, closing the hand. "Knowing that distressed exchanges are 65% of defaults is beta. Everyone has the Moody's report. Knowing which 52.6% of the class you're in is alpha."

#### The Pair Book: Carvana, and the short leg that gapped up

*Vantress Capital Management, Owen Achterberg's pod, Dov Adler's pod next door, Wen Zhao and Marcus Oyelaran are fictional composites; the positions, share counts, the pod's probabilities and every P&L figure are illustrative. Carvana, its notes, its exchange, its fair-value marks and its stock closes are real and sourced in Chapters 5 and 6. Pair Book entry PB-05 is a replay, run the way Ines runs them at the desk across town: Chapter 5 cut it off at the close on Friday, 2 June 2023, and this folder runs to the September 2023 quarter-end, the first mark after the exchange settled.*

Owen Achterberg's capital-structure pod closes its replays on Friday afternoons, and this Friday it is closing PB-05: long Carvana's 5.875% senior notes due 2028, short Carvana's common stock. The folder holds nothing that was not public by its date, with one declared exception: the models are allowed to be today's. Dov Adler has come over from the next pod because short legs are what keep him awake. Wen Zhao, who keeps Dov's borrow sheet and reads Owen's when asked, has brought both. Marcus Oyelaran, who runs the overnight x-ray for the credit pods, is there because the replays that lose money are the only ones he is invited to.

Owen puts up the card he wrote at the cut-off, the card of Chapter 5's cold open seen from a pod. Long \$10mm face of the 2028s at 55; short 128,000 shares, 0.30 of the bonds' \$5.5mm market value at the May close of \$12.92, sized by the structural model's equity delta *(illustrative)*. The card does not ask whether Carvana will default. It asks which door, writes each leg's one-year P&L behind each door, and weights the doors by Owen's own cumulative incidences:

| Door | Owen's CIF | Long \$10mm 2028s at 55 | Short 128,000 shares at \$12.92 | Pair |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Hard default (filing), $F_H$ | 0.25 | to 40: −\$1.50mm | to \$0.25: +\$1.62mm | +\$0.12mm |
| Distressed exchange, $F_D$ | 0.60 | to 62 in new paper: +\$0.70mm | "up a bit," to \$16: −\$0.39mm | +\$0.31mm |
| No event in the year, $S$ | 0.15 | to 75: +\$2.00mm | to \$25: −\$1.55mm | +\$0.45mm |

$$
\mathbb{E}[\Pi] = F_H\,\Pi_H + F_D\,\Pi_D + S\,\Pi_S \approx +\$0.28\text{mm},
\qquad
F_H + F_D + S = 1 .
$$

The second equation is the identity of §14.2.1, and the card passes it. The 62 is Owen's guess at a deal better than the March offer the holders had just refused. "Hedged behind the door I feared," he says, "and long the door I believed in. That was the trade."

Marcus reads the middle row twice. "Who wrote 'up a bit'?"

"I did. It's the only number on the card I didn't derive."

Chapters 5 and 6 tell what came through door D, so the replay needs only the marks. The 2028s received 66.6 cents of new secured par per dollar, near the bottom of the allocation table (§5.6.2), and the company marked its note stack, by then mostly the new secured paper, at 77.7 at the September quarter-end. Owen's long finished near 51.7, down 3.3 points: −\$0.33mm, against the card's +\$0.70mm *(the stack ratio stands in for any single bond)*. The door was right and the coupon was wrong. Then the short. The stock did not go up a bit. It closed June at \$25.92 and September at \$41.98 (vendor closes, approximate). At the June month-end Owen resized to the model's new delta, 0.25 of the long's value at the company's June mark, which came to about 71,000 shares: fewer shares, more dollars. On 19 July the support agreement was announced and the stock went from about \$39.80 to \$55.80, the 40.2% session of §6.10.1, and 71,000 shares lost \$1.14mm before the close. Marcus called at 4:10. The pod's practice is that a line under a risk call does not resize until the call is closed, and this one stayed open until the exchange settled, so the July and August resizes never happened. The short lost \$1.66mm in June and \$1.14mm from the June mark to the September one, nearly all of it in that one session: \$2.80mm in four months.

Wen has the frictions. The folder has no borrow tape for the stock, so the replay assumes a fee of 15% a year on the short's market value *(illustrative; with close to half the float short, on the S3 Partners count Chapter 6 cites, she calls the assumption polite)*: about \$0.14mm, less about \$0.05mm earned on the short's cash collateral. Carvana paid no dividend, so the short owed nothing else. Financing the long at 7% all-in cost about \$0.12mm, and half-spreads on two legs, one resize and the close about \$0.10mm. The long's coupon, accrued from the cut-off and paid in cash at settlement, brought in \$0.15mm. Owen writes the explain the way Chapter 8-C would, with the card's middle row standing in for start-of-day betas:

| Line | \$mm | What it is |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Idio | −0.33 | the exchange path: the door, and where the 2028s landed in it |
| Hedge cost the card budgeted behind door D | −0.39 | "up a bit" |
| Leak | −2.41 | the restrike: the short's real cost behind door D, less the budget |
| Carry | +0.15 | the 5.875% coupon, cut-off to settlement |
| Friction | −0.31 | borrow fee net of rebate, financing, half-spreads |
| **Net** | **−3.29** | no capture ratio: the idio itself was negative |

"Right about the door, wrong about the coupon," says Owen, "and the hedge lost seven times what the thesis did."

"Then say what the hedge removed," says Marcus, who says it to everyone.

Owen answers in the Pair Book's order. *What the hedge removed:* direction, as it is felt behind door H, where at the opening ratio a filing would have left the pair \$0.12mm up while the long lost \$1.50mm. *What idio remained:* the exchange path, which door and where in it the 2028s landed, 66.6 against 89.3 for the 2030s. *What leaked:* the short leg itself. Behind door D the stock was not the residual claim on a firm drifting toward a barrier. It was the security the exchange restrikes. A support agreement that cuts face, pushes out maturities and is conditioned on new equity lifts the stock by more than it lifts the bonds, so behind the door Owen believed in, his hedge was a second position against his own thesis.

Dov has been reading his own card while Owen talks. PB-01's short is a bond, not a stock: Halvorsen's 7.25% 2029s, borrowed. "Same table, different instrument," he says. "Behind door H my short makes 78 less the recovery. Behind door D, if the unsecured are offered an exchange at a premium, it loses ten points: the \$3.9mm on my card in 1-B." DTS sized PB-01 on spread, and a spread is one number for both taps. Behind door H the short's price falls to recovery; behind a premium door D it rises to the exchange value. The arithmetic that makes a DTS-neutral pair jump-neutral in expectation holds door by door only when both doors move the short's price the same way; that arithmetic, and the menu of short legs with what each costs, are Chapter 8-D's (§8D.4 and §8D.2). At the market's average soft hazard from §14.2.1, $\lambda_D \approx 0.038$, the one-year $F_D$ is about 3.7%, so $0.037 \times \$3.9$mm is about \$0.14mm a year of expected cost the DTS ratio never sees, on an issuer whose lender call makes it anything but average. Carvana ran the same sum on anyone short its bonds: a pod short the 10.25% 2030s from the 2022 year-end mark paid their climb from the mid-40s to an exchange worth about 69, 89.3 cents of new par at 77.7 *(illustrative)*, and its lender, owning a bond with a consent attached, would have wanted it back before the deadline.

Wen adds a column while he says it: recalls in the days before a consent record date. The soft tap announces itself first to the one person in the pod who talks to lenders every morning. She does not call it a signal yet. She calls it weather. Single-name CDS, the usual answer when a bond cannot be borrowed, does not rescue the short either: the standard North American contract has no Restructuring credit event (Chapter 24), so protection pays through door H and not through door D. Every short on the menu hedges one tap.

#### Decision point: the parole long, 29 September 2023

*The exchange has settled. Owen holds about \$6.66mm face of new senior secured notes, paying in kind in their first year and marked near 78, and 71,000 shares short. In this chapter's terms the issuer is on parole. Write down three things: keep the long or sell it; if you keep it, the short leg and the ratio; and the hazard you would ask the risk manager to charge.*

The clock of §14.3.2 answers the third question first. The lightbulb box's 0.175 is the base-rate chance of a hard default within two years of a soft event, and among the issuers that are going to fail the hazard rises at first, because a PIK coupon buys runway out of recovery. Marcus has a different number. "My x-ray reads the rating and the new capital structure. It has no state called parole. Keep it, and I charge you the hazard of whatever the agencies say it is now, not the hazard of a name four weeks out of an exchange."

The second question goes down the menu, and every answer is a refusal. The stock is short the cure, and the cure is three-quarters of the mass, $1 - p = 0.75$: the same mistake behind a different door. CDS pays on one tap, if a contract on the name can be traded at all; only about a hundred US names trade regularly, on one quantitative manager's own count (Man Group, *Quantitative Credit: Alpha Opportunities for Early Movers*, 2022). The \$205mm of old notes left outside the exchange, stripped of their covenants (§6.10.1), are a different claim with no lender worth calling. CDX HY takes out the cycle and none of Carvana. "Nothing on the menu isolates the parole," Owen says. "Without a short, that long isn't a pair. It's a position in $1 - p$, and I don't run positions." He closes both legs at the September mark. The ledger records PB-05 as closed and adds a line underneath it: post-exchange long, no short leg, declined.

Grade the cards. Keeping the long against the stock would have lost again: the stock closed 2023 at \$52.94 and 2024 at \$203.36 (§6.10.1). Keeping the long naked would have paid, because Carvana turned out to be one of the three-quarters: the stack was marked at 84.7 by December, the new 2028s were bought back above par, and the 2030s were refinanced in August 2026 (§5.6.2). It would also have meant carrying a hazard the risk model could not see through a cohort that ran hot: about 46% of 2023's distressed exchanges had re-defaulted by April 2025, reportedly counting repeat exchanges (the re-default ledger, §14.3.2), and in September 2023 nobody could know which side of that line Carvana would land on. Closing earned nothing more and kept the mandate. Owen's card is graded on the explain, not the outcome, and the explain says the door was right, the coupon was wrong, and the hedge was the bigger trade. He writes one sentence at the bottom, the one the Pair Book now carries on every name inside a liability-management window: *in an exchange, the short leg gets the premium.*

## 14.10 Desk Debrief

**Finder.** Each idea once, with where its intuition, its judgment and its code live.

| Concept | Equation | Intuition | Judgment (scene) | Code |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Two default rates | $\lambda = -\ln(1-\text{rate})$ (§14.2.1) | Odometer and speedometer (§14.1) | Read the label dictionary before the likelihood: Hana's 41 issuers (§14.1) | Listing 14.1 (`LMEParams`) |
| Competing risks and CIFs | $F_k(t) = \int_0^t S\,\lambda_k$; $\sum_k F_k + S = 1$ (§14.2.1) | Bucket with two taps (§14.2); attendance register (§14.2.2) | CIFs for what happens, Fine–Gray for which features, never one minus KM: Kaz's shortcut (§14.2.2) | Listing 14.2 |
| Re-default clock | Mixture-cure Weibull, $h_H(u)$ (§14.3.2) | Lightbulbs and LEDs (§14.3.2) | $k \gtrsim 1$; censored names are unplugged bulbs: Kaz's three worries (§14.3.2) | Listing 14.3 (`fit_cure_weibull`) |
| Runway as a covariate | $\operatorname{logit} p_i$, $\ln \eta_i$ (§14.3.2) | Betting line (§14.3.2; box in §5.5.3) | A PIK toggle buys $\eta$ with $L$; the runway was Mitel's clock (§14.3.2, §14.8.2) | Schema covariates (§14.7) |
| Expected loss with a soft default | $\mathrm{EL}(T)$ integral (§14.3.3) | Envelope table (§14.3.3) | Late exchanges have little time to re-default: Kaz's month thirty-five (§14.7) | Listing 14.3 (`expected_loss`) |
| Recovery as two humps | Beta mixture; between part $\pi(1-\pi)\Delta^2$ (§14.4.1) | School hall (§14.4.1; box in §5.1.2) | Membership belongs to the holder: Mags reads Rule 2019 (§14.4.2); Lumen's ten points (§14.5) | Listing 14.3 (`coalition_mixture_moments`) |
| Co-op threshold game | $d^\ast(c)$, $\Pi(c)$, $\lambda_{\text{NPR}}$ (§14.5.1) | Jury (§14.5.1; box in §8B.8) | Coverage moves risk to deals away; legality is a dated scenario: Lumen's card, Optimum's row (§14.5) | Listing 14.3 (`coop_break_prob`) |
| Rulings as jumps | $\operatorname{logit}\theta_w(t)$ (§14.6.1) | Betting line (§14.3.2) | Words, not conduct; remedy before merits; measure from the announcement: Robertshaw, Lions Gate (§14.6) | None (elicited priors) |
| Regime filter | Hamilton update and prediction (§14.7.1) | Umbrellas at the door (§14.7.1) | Publish filtered, not smoothed; refit on a schedule; check the switch date by dropping a source: risk committee (§14.7.1), Ines (§14.7.2) | Listing 14.4 |
| $\mathbb{P}$ versus $\mathbb{Q}$ | $s \approx \lambda^{\mathbb{Q}}(1-R^{\mathbb{Q}})$ (§14.7.2) | Stewards' room (§14.7.2; boxes in §1.5, §5.1.1) | Take out $\lambda_D$ and the 40% before comparing: the 7:10 note (§14.7.2) | Listing 14.5 (P-vs-Q tripwire) |
| A pair across competing risks | $\mathbb{E}[\Pi] = F_H\Pi_H + F_D\Pi_D + S\,\Pi_S$ (§14.9) | Three doors (§5.6.1); bucket with two taps (§14.2) | Write each leg behind each door; in an exchange the short leg gets the premium: Owen's Carvana replay, PB-05 (§14.9) | Listing 14.2 (the CIFs) |

- **"The default rate" is two numbers.** Headline and ex-DE rates differed by a factor of almost three in June 2025 (5.8% vs. 2.1%). Carry $\lambda_H$ and $\lambda_D$ separately, and name the definition in the column.
- **Use cumulative incidence, not 1 − Kaplan–Meier.** Censoring the competing cause overstates the probability of the cause you care about, and the bias grows with horizon.
- **A distressed exchange is parole, not immunity.** About a quarter of soft events end in hard default, more than 70% of those within two years. The hazard among the susceptible *rises* at first, because the deal bought runway. Calibrate $k \gtrsim 1$, not $k < 1$.
- **Recovery is two humps.** Membership alone can generate a 24-point standard deviation. Stage 0 of the LGD model is $\mathbb{P}(\text{in majority})$, and it belongs to the holder, not the loan.
- **Co-ops move risk; they don't remove it.** Coverage above the blocking line crushes the uptier hazard and raises the drop-down and deal-away hazard. The co-op's own legality is a dated scenario.
- **Rulings are regime switches with timestamps.** Encode them as documented log-odds jumps by wording class. Serta and Mitel, decided the same day, are the proof that tokens beat economics.
- **Never compare a CDS hazard with an agency default rate** without removing $\lambda_D$ and replacing the 40% convention. Most "the market is underpricing default" notes are units errors.
- **In an exchange, the short leg gets the premium.** A hedge sized on one hazard, by spread, DTS or equity delta, hedges the sum of the taps, and the LMT era makes the taps pay the short leg with opposite signs. After the exchange, a long with no short leg that isolates the parole is a position in $1-p$, not a pair.

**The Spec You Hand the Robot.** "Build `lme_cycle_engine.py` per §14.7. Inputs: an event table with the schema given, or `LMEParams` for simulation. Hazards are per year under $\mathbb{P}$, recoveries are fractions of par, and the DE recovery is the value held immediately after the exchange. Estimate cause-specific Nelson–Aalen and Aalen–Johansen CIFs on first events only, and assert $S + \sum_k F_k = 1$ to 1e-10. Fit the post-DE clock as a mixture-cure Weibull with right-censoring. Never fit an exponential or set the hazard to zero after the last observed event. Report EL by coalition side (`in`, `out`, `blend`) by quadrature, and check it against Monte Carlo within 0.005. Fit the two-state binomial Markov-switching model on DE *counts*, with ordered shares and a log-space filter, and accept time-varying $P$ as a $(T,2,2)$ array. Never delete DE rows to 'exclude' them: report the ex-DE rate as a second output. Seed every generator. Raise on a horizon beyond `T_max`. Print PASS/FAIL for every check in block 5."

## Exercises

1. **Two rates, two hazards.** Moody's reports 5.8% including and 2.1% excluding distressed exchanges. Convert both to intensities, compute $\lambda_D/\lambda_H$, and compute the three-year $F_D$ and $F_H$. Then explain, in one paragraph a PM would read, why a CDX-implied hazard should be compared with only one of them. *Where this came up:* the odometer-and-speedometer box in §14.1, and the 7:10 a.m. research note that Kaz deletes in §14.7.2.
2. **Kaz's parole question.** Using the mixture-cure model with $p = 0.25$, find $\eta$ for $k = 0.8, 1.0, 1.2, 1.5$ from the 70%-within-two-years condition. For each, compute the population hazard $h_H(u)$ at $u = 0.5, 2, 6$ years and the year-six increment in cumulative incidence. Which shapes satisfy all four Moody's facts? What does your answer say about when to short a post-LME loan? *Where this came up:* Mags's "parole" in the cold open, the lightbulb box and Moody's four facts in §14.3.2, and Mitel's 29-month clock in §14.8.2.
3. **Which hump are you in?** You own \$10mm of a first-lien loan in a class where a co-op covers 70% and you are not in it. Under the §14.5.1 game ($m = 0.501$, $n = 10$, $\varphi = 0.10$), compute the probability of a non-pro-rata deal. Then let the sponsor buy defectors so that $\varphi = 0.35$. Using the coalition mixture with $\mu_{\text{in}} = 0.74$ and $\mu_{\text{out}} = 0.25$, what is the most you would pay to join the co-op, in points? *Where this came up:* Ines's Poker Table in §14.5 and the jury in §14.5.1, and the holdout's question on 10 November 2023 in the Lumen replay of §14.5.
4. **The best-performing tranche.** An excluded Serta lender bought \$5mm face of the excluded first lien at 20 in January 2021. Using the July 2026 award, 9% simple prejudgment interest from 22 June 2020, a 60% probability that the award is collected in full by July 2027 and zero otherwise, and ignoring plan recoveries, compute the expected multiple and IRR. Then state every assumption a litigation-finance desk would attack. *Where this came up:* Mags's January 2021 sale in Act II of §14.8.1, and Kaz's three-branch tree on 8 July 2026 in Act III.
5. **Fix ROBO.** Rewrite the instruction "exclude distressed exchanges from the default rate" as a spec of no more than 120 words that ROBO cannot misread. Include units, the output columns, what happens to the excluded issuers' future events, and one assert. *Where this came up:* Hana's forty-one issuers in §14.1, and the zero-and-one `regime` column ROBO built from a vague spec in §14.7.1.
6. **Regime detection.** Simulate 40 years of DE counts with $\rho_0 = 0.30$, $\rho_1 = 0.63$, and mean defaults 90 per year, with a switch in year 30. Fit `fit_ms2` and report the first year in which the filtered LME-regime probability exceeds 0.9. Repeat with mean defaults of 12 per year (a private-credit-sized sample). How many years of "it's just noise" does the small sample buy you? *Where this came up:* the umbrella box and the "regime explain" risk committee in §14.7.1, and Ines's switch-date check at the end of §14.7.2.
