## 15.5 Antitrust and Regulatory Timelines as Survival Analysis

### 15.5.1 Desk framing: the regulator counts in working days

Every payoff in §15.2–15.4 fires on a date. The date is set by a process the RSSG reader knows as a sequence of filings: HSR notification and a 30-day initial waiting period (15 days for a cash tender offer), which a Second Request extends until 30 days after the parties certify "substantial compliance" (15 U.S.C. §18a); a European Phase I of 25 working days and a Phase II of 90 working days, extendable by 15 or 20 (European Commission merger procedures page); CFIUS, the Surface Transportation Board, state attorneys general, and a district judge with a calendar. The desk's job is to turn that sequence into a survival curve.

The base rates are lopsided in the way that makes survival analysis worth doing. Almost every HSR filing clears in the initial period; the event risk lives in a few dozen deals a year.

| FY | Adjusted transactions | Second Requests (FTC + DOJ) | Share of adjusted | Early terminations granted |
| :-- | --: | --: | --: | --: |
| 2016 | 1,772 | 54 | 3.0% | 1,102 |
| 2018 | 2,028 | 45 | 2.2% | 1,170 |
| 2020 | 1,580 | 48 | 3.0% | 861 |
| 2021 | 3,413 | 66 | 1.9% | 417 |
| 2022 | 3,029 | 47 | 1.6% | 5 |
| 2023 | 1,735 | 37 | 2.1% | 0 |
| 2024 | 1,973 | 59 | 3.0% | 3 |
| 2025 | 1,944 | 41 | 2.1% | 265 |

*Source: FTC/DOJ Hart-Scott-Rodino Annual Reports, FY2023–FY2025, Appendix A. FY2021 Second Requests per the FY2025 table (the FY2023 table shows 65).*

> **[SOURCE EXTRACTION]** *Bohn_Stein_Active_Credit_Portfolio_Management p.232:* "But what happens if some of the firms drop out of the sample due to, say, a merger or acquisition? In this case, adjustments can be made to sample survival functions of the sort shown in Figure 4.3 to account for this censorship. This results in a particular form of survival function estimator called the Kaplan-Meier (sometimes called the product limit) estimator"
>
> **Annotation.** In default modelling a merger is a nuisance: it removes a firm before you learn whether it would have defaulted, so you censor it. In this chapter the roles reverse. The merger *is* the event, and the nuisances are the deals still pending at the data cutoff, the deals whose outside date was extended, and the deals that died for reasons other than the one you are modelling. The estimator is the same; the bookkeeping is inverted. Where the desk departs from the textbook: in deal data, censoring is often *informative*. An outside date gets extended precisely when a deal is in trouble, so "still pending" is not independent of the hazard, and a naive Kaplan–Meier is optimistic about closing.

#### The clock comes to the desk: ICE–MarketAxess, September 29 to October 18, 2026

*The deal, the filings, the bond terms, the fees and the regulators are real and cited; the desk's feed and dashboard, its position in the 2036s and all dialogue are invented.*

**Tuesday, September 29, 2026, 7:20 a.m.** For once the deal on Theo's screen is about the desk's own plumbing. At the end of July, Intercontinental Exchange agreed to buy MarketAxess, the electronic bond venue through which the desk answers a large share of its client RFQs every day, for \$167 a share in cash: a 33% premium, about \$6.0bn of equity value and about \$5.7bn of enterprise value, all of it debt-funded, with opening leverage of 3.4x and a close expected in the first half of 2027 (ICE 8-K, Ex. 99.1, July 2026, EDGAR). The morning's alert is a MarketAxess 8-K. The parties had filed their HSR notification on August 26. On September 25, the day the initial 30-day waiting period would have run out, they withdrew it, and this morning they refiled it, in the filing's words, "to provide the DOJ with additional time." The new expiry is October 29, which is also the day of the MarketAxess stockholder vote (MarketAxess DEFM14A and 8-K, Sept. 2026, EDGAR).

Kaz reads it twice. "They withdrew it so that it would take longer. Is that a legal term or a confession?"

"It's called pull-and-refile," Theo says. "The initial waiting period is thirty days. When it runs out, the agency either lets the deal through or issues a Second Request, which means months of documents and depositions. If the staff isn't ready to do either, the parties can withdraw and refile, and the clock starts again. Thirty more days, and no Second Request yet."

"So it's a Second Request in disguise."

"Or it's a staff that wants to say yes and needs another month to write down why. That's the trade."

Ines has a different question, and she has had it since July. "I'll get to the bonds. First tell me what happens to my feed." The desk's quoting engine lives inside the RFQ protocols that MarketAxess runs. Its hit rates, its response times and its markouts, Ines's beloved hand history, are all computed from messages that arrive through that venue. ICE frames the purchase as joining MarketAxess's "trading data and analytics" to its own pricing, reference-data and index businesses, and it has made no public commitment on fees or competition (ICE 8-K, Ex. 99.1). "I'm not asking for a forecast," Ines says. "I'm asking which of our numbers depend on a contract that's about to have a new counterparty." The operations team takes a week to compile the answer, and the first item is mundane. On July 30, MarketAxess had announced that it was "suspending its practice of issuing monthly volumes press releases" (MarketAxess Q2-2026 release). The desk's market-share dashboard, which had scraped those releases every month since 2021, has been showing June's number all summer, because nobody told it the series had ended. It had not crashed. It had simply stopped learning, and it had kept reporting with the same confidence.

**9:40 a.m.** Mags has been through this before, and says so. "Back in my day you filed, you asked for early termination, and if the deal was clean you had it in two weeks. A thousand deals a year got that." She is not exaggerating by much: the agencies granted 1,102 early terminations in FY2016. Then they suspended the practice, and the count fell to 5 in FY2022 and 0 in FY2023 before coming back to 265 in FY2025 (FTC/DOJ HSR Annual Reports; the table above). "Kroger took twenty-six months from signing to ruling. ICE has ten months left before its first outside date. You tell me which clock is the normal one."

Theo, who spent the summer listening to merger podcasts on the train, offers one data point on the regime: a live *Odd Lots* episode, "FTC Chief Andrew Ferguson on the Trump Vision for Antitrust" (Mar. 17, 2025), on the new FTC's decision to keep the previous administration's merger guidelines. It is about the FTC, and a deal between two market operators sits with the DOJ, but it makes the HSR table's point more bluntly: the baseline hazard is a policy variable, and a model fitted to the early-termination world of 2016 is fitted to a world that ended.

Theo opens the USB stick. He renames the 13-week model's columns from "Week 1 ... Week 13" to "weeks since signing," deletes the cash rows, and keeps one: "Regulatory." It is now a Kaplan–Meier curve with a spreadsheet's personality.

He fills in the row from the filings. Signing at the end of July. HSR filed August 26. Pulled September 25, refiled September 29. Expiry October 29. Then the dates further out: an outside date of July 29, 2027, with two automatic extensions that can carry it to July 29, 2028. And then a block he has never had to fill in before, the other consents: FINRA; CIRO and the Ontario Securities Commission in Canada; the Dutch central bank and the AFM in the Netherlands; the FCA in the UK; the Monetary Authority of Singapore (DEFM14A). Each regulator that licenses a subsidiary runs its own change-in-control clock, some in calendar days and some in working days; the UK's assessment runs on working days and can pause while the regulator asks questions. Theo writes "working days?" next to four of the seven. The section heading was understating the problem: the regulators do not count in working days. They each count in their own.

**10:30 a.m.** Kaz has been building a model. "Days to clearance," they announce. "Normal distribution, mean 270 days, standard deviation 120. I fitted it to the deals in our database."

Mags looks at the screen for a long time. "What does it say about the chance that a deal clears before it files?"

Kaz checks. Zero days is $270/120 = 2.25$ standard deviations below the mean, so the bell puts about 1.2% of its weight on clearing at a negative number of days. "That's small."

"It's impossible. Now what does it say about clearing in the first thirty days?"

Thirty days is two standard deviations below the mean, so the bell puts about 2.3% of its weight below it, and once the impossible 1.2% below zero is taken out, about 1% between zero and thirty days. The HSR table says something very different. In FY2025 the agencies issued 41 Second Requests against 1,944 adjusted transactions, so about 98% of filings never got one, and nearly all of those were through by the end of their initial waiting period. Kaz's database is skewed toward the large, contested deals the desk cares about, so its share of quick clearances is lower than the HSR universe's, but it is nowhere near 1%. The real distribution is a spike near one month and a long, lumpy tail of deals that went to a Second Request, a lawsuit or both. A bell centred at nine months has no spike and no tail. It is wrong at both ends and roughly right only in the middle, where hardly any deals actually live.

"Two populations," Mags says. "The ones that clear and the ones that fight. You've averaged a sprinter and a marathon runner and called it a jogger." Exercise 5 makes the argument with a log-likelihood; Mags makes it with a napkin. Kaz deletes the Gaussian, then quietly restores it, because it is the only model on the desk that runs in under a second.

**11:15 a.m.** The question then arrives in its trading form. ICE is not only an acquirer; it is an issuer, and two weeks after signing it sold bonds to pay for the purchase. Theo pulls the prospectus supplement, dated August 11, 2026. Four series, \$3.75bn in all: \$1.25bn of 4.700% notes due 2029, \$1.1bn of 4.900% notes due 2031, \$650mm of 5.150% notes due 2033 and \$750mm of 5.400% notes due 2036. The rest of the money is to come from a new term loan, commercial paper, the revolver and cash, with a 364-day bridge facility of up to \$6.20bn standing behind it all (ICE 424B5, Aug. 11, 2026, EDGAR). The special mandatory redemption is the reverse of Kroger's. It sits on the 2033s and 2036s, \$1.4bn of the long money, and not on the 2029s or 2031s. If the deal dies, ICE hands back its long bonds at 101 and keeps the short ones.

"So the gauge is in the long end this time," Kaz says. "And every non-SMR bond from the new deal is shorter than the SMR bonds."

"Which makes it an extrapolation problem again," Theo says, "unless we use ICE's older long bonds as nodes." He has learned that one already, from Kroger, the other way round.

The sentence that stops him is the trigger. The SMR fires if ICE does not consummate the acquisition on or before July 29, 2027 "(subject to two automatic extensions of six months each, to January 29, 2028 and to July 29, 2028, respectively," if U.S. antitrust clearance, another required regulatory approval or a court order restraining the merger "remains outstanding and all other conditions to closing are satisfied"), or if the merger agreement is terminated before the outside date. ICE then has five business days to send the notice, and the redemption date falls no earlier than three business days and no later than 30 days after the notice (ICE 424B5).

Theo reads the extension clause aloud, because it is the Tapestry parenthesis grown up. Tapestry's outside date could move if two parties agreed to move it. ICE's moves by itself, and it moves in exactly one circumstance: when a regulator or a court is the only thing still in the way. "The date extends precisely when the deal is in trouble," he says. "So the deals still pending on July 29, 2027 will be the ones in trouble. If this deal is still running in a year and I put it into a Kaplan–Meier, it goes in as 'censored, still pending,' and the estimator treats it like a random deal that happened not to have finished yet. It won't be one. It'll be a deal whose own contract says it's stuck."

That is the Bohn–Stein annotation above, written into an indenture: informative censoring with a CUSIP.

#### Decision point: ICE–MarketAxess, Tuesday 29 September 2026

A pull-and-refile has just extended the clock by a month. Write three things: whether that is a Second Request in disguise, how you move $\pi_d$, and what a 5.5% reverse regulatory fee tells you that the equity spread does not.

**Wednesday, September 30 to Friday, October 16.** The desk argues about it for two and a half weeks, mostly at the coffee machine, which remains the desk's most important risk forum.

Ines takes the first question and declines to answer it. "A pull-and-refile is a tell. It says the staff wanted more time than the statute gave them. It doesn't say what they'll do with the time. Some staffs use the month to get comfortable; some use it to draft the Second Request." Theo goes looking for a public base rate, how often a pull-and-refile ends in a Second Request, and does not find one he trusts. He writes that down as a gap instead of inventing a number, which Mags describes as the most mature thing she has seen him do.

Kaz takes the second. In the language of §15.5.2, the refile is a covariate, not an outcome. It does not move the deal into the Second Request population; it moves it into a smaller one that the database has never tagged, the deals that asked for more time. The honest adjustment is modest: nudge $\pi_d$ down a little, stretch the expected time to resolution by at least the month that has just been added, and mark October 29 as a milestone that will carry information whichever way it goes. If the new period expires quietly, Bayes' rule in §15.5.2 says the deal probability rises, and the first sign of good news will be nothing at all.

Mags adds the check she runs on every curve Kaz shows her, and it is not statistical. "For every deal still pending in your sample, tell me why. Waiting for a vote, under a timing agreement, extended, in court. If the answers bunch up, your curve is optimistic about closing, by about as much as they bunch." Kaz's database has eleven deals still at risk in month fourteen. "That's not a curve," she says. "That's eleven anecdotes with error bars."

Theo takes the third, because it is a contract question and he has read the contract. The merger agreement carries two termination fees. In the cases where MarketAxess owes one, it owes ICE \$148.8m, about 2.5% of the equity value; if the deal fails on regulatory grounds, ICE owes MarketAxess \$327.4m, about 5.5% (DEFM14A). The second number is more than twice the first, and the proxy adds that ICE has no duty to divest assets to win approval. A reverse regulatory fee is a put the buyer writes to the target's holders on the regulator, and its size is the buyer's own revealed view of where the risk lives. The equity arbitrage spread blends all of this into one number together with financing, market beta and MarketAxess's standalone value. The fee schedule pulls the regulatory piece out by itself and puts a dollar figure on it. "The equity spread tells you how worried the market is," Theo says. "The fee tells you how worried the buyer was when it signed, and the buyer had read the lawyers' memo."

"The buyer also had a reason to make it look big," Ines says. "Bigger fee, more credible commitment, easier signing. A tell can be a bluff."

"Then it's an expensive bluff. Three hundred and twenty-seven million is real money, even at ICE."

Ines concedes the point the way she concedes all points, by changing the subject to sizing.

**Sunday, October 18.** As this chapter goes to press, nothing has happened, which is the point. The vote and the HSR expiry are eleven days away. The 2033 and 2036 notes carry their SMR toward an outside date that can stretch to July 2028. The desk owns a small position in the 2036s, sized, in Ines's phrase, "for a deal we don't understand yet," and a much larger list of questions about its own feed. Theo's "weeks since signing" column has reached eleven, and the "Regulatory" row holds seven regulators, at least two ways of counting days, and one cell that just says *quiet*. The next section turns that cell into a number.

### 15.5.2 Derivation: Kaplan–Meier to competing risks

Put $t=0$ at signing (or at HSR filing; say which). Each deal ends in one of three causes, $k=c$ (close), $a$ (abandon), $b$ (litigated block), or is right-censored at the cutoff. Let $t_1 < t_2 < \dots$ be the distinct event times, $n_i$ the number of deals pending just before $t_i$, $d_{k,i}$ the number ending in cause $k$ at $t_i$, and $d_i = \sum_k d_{k,i}$.

> **Math, Gently.** *Censoring is leaving the stadium before the race ends.* Survival analysis (built from scratch for defaults in §7-B.4) asks what fraction of a group is still waiting at time $t$, the survival $S(t)$, and what fraction of those still waiting finish in the next short interval, the hazard. Take 100 signed deals. Five resolve in month one: a hazard of 5%, survival 0.95. Ten resolve in month two out of the 95 still at risk, so survival is $0.95 \times 85/95 = 0.85$. That multiplication is Kaplan–Meier, and its value is that it keeps working when the group shrinks for other reasons. You are timing a marathon, and at the four-hour mark you have to leave to catch a train. Some runners have finished; of the rest you know only that each took *more* than four hours. Throwing them away makes the race look fast, and recording them at four hours is just as wrong. The honest move is to count them as at risk for every minute up to the moment you left and then drop them, which is why the $n_i$ below shrinks both when deals end and when they are censored. The trick has one condition: your leaving must have nothing to do with how the runners were doing. If you left *because your runner was losing*, the runners you stopped watching are not a random sample of the field, and the estimate is biased. That is *informative* censoring, and it is the ICE extension clause of §15.5.1.

**All-cause survival.** The Kaplan–Meier estimator walks through the event dates in order and, at each one, multiplies in the fraction of still-pending deals that did not end that day:

$$
\hat S(t) \;=\; \prod_{t_i \le t}\Big(1 - \frac{d_i}{n_i}\Big),
$$

and the Nelson–Aalen cumulative hazard adds the same fractions instead of multiplying their complements, $\hat\Lambda(t) = \sum_{t_i\le t} d_i/n_i$. (We write $\Lambda$ for a cumulative deal hazard only inside this section; $\lambda$ stays reserved for default intensity.) Greenwood's formula puts a standard error around $\hat S$, and it grows as the number still at risk shrinks; it is written out in "The Full Derivation" at the end of this section.

**Cause-specific hazards with covariates.** For each cause, $h_k(t\mid x) = h_{0,k}(t)\,e^{x'\beta_k}$: every deal's hazard has the same shape over time, the same rhythm of filing, review and decision, and its covariates only stretch that shape up or down by the always-positive multiplier $e^{x'\beta_k}$ (the Cox model; §7-B.4 has the gentle version). Bohn and Stein state the restriction exactly: "the shape of the hazard function (and the corresponding survival function) is arbitrary, but the impact ratio of the hazards over time is constant" (Bohn_Stein_Active_Credit_Portfolio_Management p.233). The coefficients are fit by Breslow's partial likelihood, which never estimates the baseline at all: at each date on which a deal ended in cause $k$, it asks how surprising it was that *this* deal ended rather than any of the others still pending, given their covariates, and chooses $\beta_k$ to make the realized sequence of endings least surprising, the way you can tell that one runner is twice as fast as another without knowing the course. A Second Request coefficient of $-1.2$ says a deal under a Second Request closes at $e^{-1.2} \approx 0.30$ times the rate of an otherwise identical deal. What that does to the clock depends on the baseline's shape. With a constant hazard, the memoryless exponential wait that fits radioactive atoms and not mergers, the deal would take $1/0.30 \approx 3.3$ times as long. Deals ripen instead, their hazard rising as they move from filing through review to a decision, and with a Weibull of shape 1.6 the median stretches by $0.30^{-1/1.6} \approx 2.1$, so a six-month median becomes about thirteen (Chapter 5 owns the distributions; Kaz's bell from §15.5.1 belongs nowhere here, because waiting times cannot be negative). If a covariate's effect changes over the life of a deal, the proportional assumption is false and the coefficient averages things that are not alike. And with 41 Second Requests in FY2025 and far fewer litigated blocks, a hazard for blocks is fitted on a handful of events, with error bars wide enough to drive a merger through. Deals ending in other causes are censored for cause $k$; that is correct for cause-specific hazards and wrong for anything else. The partial likelihood and its gradient are in "The Full Derivation."

> **Math, Gently.** *Competing risks are three doors out of one room.* Every pending deal sits in a waiting room with three doors, marked close, abandon and block. Each door has its own hazard, the rate at which deals walk through it. Once a deal goes through one door it cannot use another: a blocked deal never closes. So the chance of eventually leaving through the close door depends on the other doors too, because every deal that leaves through "block" was not around to close. The tempting shortcut, $1 - e^{-\Lambda_c(t)}$, computes the chance of closing in an imaginary room where the other two doors are bricked up, and it overstates closing. Tiny number: in each month, 10% of waiting deals close and 5% are blocked. Ignore the blocks and after two months $0.10 + 0.90 \times 0.10 = 19\%$ have closed. Count them, and only 85% are left to try again in month two, so $0.10 + 0.85 \times 0.10 = 18.5\%$ have closed. The gap is half a point after two months and compounds every month after that; by a year and a half it is the eighteen points of Figure 15.4. The Aalen–Johansen estimator does the honest bookkeeping, and the fact that the three doors' totals add up to everyone who left the room is its unit test. The full version is in "The Full Derivation."

**Cumulative incidence.** The probability of ending in cause $k$ by $t$ is not $1 - e^{-\Lambda_k(t)}$, because a deal that is blocked cannot later close. The Aalen–Johansen estimator respects that: at each event date it takes the probability of still being pending just before it and multiplies by the fraction of pending deals that ended in cause $k$ on that date, then adds those pieces up. Because every deal that ends must end through exactly one door, the three incidences sum exactly to the probability of having ended at all, $\sum_k \hat F_k(t) = 1 - \hat S(t)$, which makes that identity the best unit test in the chapter. The estimator itself is in "The Full Derivation." Figure 15.4 shows the three incidences on the Listing 15.4 cohort, and how far the cause-specific shortcut overstates closing.

![Figure 15.4: By about 1.5 years the cause-specific shortcut (dashed) says 90% of deals have closed, while the competing-risks estimate says 72%, because 14% were abandoned and 9% blocked, and the three incidences sum exactly to total exits. Illustrative: Aalen–Johansen estimates from the seeded 600-deal synthetic cohort of Listing 15.4 (Weibull cause-specific hazards with planted coefficients, independent censoring), stopped where fewer than 20 deals remain at risk.](../assets/figures/ch15_competing_risks_incidence.png)

**From clocks to PnL.** For a position whose price jumps by $\Pi_k(t)$ on outcome $k$ at $t$, under $\mathbb{P}$,

$$
\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{P}}[\text{PnL}] \;=\; \int_0^{\infty} e^{-rt}\,S(t)\,\big[h_c(t)\Pi_c(t) + h_a(t)\Pi_a(t) + h_b(t)\Pi_b(t)\big]\,dt \;+\; \text{carry}.
$$

**Silence is data.** Each milestone that passes quietly (the 30-day wait expires with no Second Request; Phase I ends without Phase II; a complaint deadline passes) updates the deal probability by Bayes' rule (Chapter 1's odds box), with $q_d$ and $q_b$ the probabilities of a quiet milestone under "deal" and "break," conditional on quiet so far:

$$
\pi_d^{+} \;=\; \frac{\pi_d\, q_d}{\pi_d\, q_d + (1-\pi_d)\, q_b},
$$

which rises whenever $q_d > q_b$. Picture 100 deals at $\pi_d = 0.80$, with $q_d = 0.90$ and $q_b = 0.60$, because dying deals tend to make noise. Eighty will close, and 72 of those pass quietly; twenty will break, and 12 pass quietly; of the 84 quiet deals 72 are closers, so $\pi_d^{+} = 72/84 \approx 0.857$. Nothing happened, and the probability moved by almost six points. When $q_d = q_b$, silence carries no information, and a model that updates anyway is inventing news. Giglio & Shue (2014) show that equity markets underreact to the information in the passage of time during pending mergers. If the credit market does the same, a target bond's spread should drift tighter through silent milestones; that is Chapter 10's trend signal with a legal calendar for a clock.

> **Poker Table.** Ines on the Second Request: "It's a tell, but a cheap one. In FY2024 the agencies issued 59 Second Requests and brought 32 merger enforcement actions, most of them consents and abandonments; the FTC litigated six. A Second Request means the hand goes to the river, not that you lose it. The expensive tell is the one nobody announces: the timing agreement with the agency, which you infer when the parties stop guiding to a close date." Replay the hand: markouts on the target's bonds over the ten days after each Second Request, split by eventual outcome. If the bonds that eventually closed sold off as hard as the ones that were blocked, the market was paying you to know the base rate.

> **Trend Watch.** *Regulatory regime as a shift in the baseline hazard, 2016–2026.* Early terminations of the HSR waiting period, the fast lane for clean deals, ran at 1,102 in FY2016 and 1,220 in FY2017, fell to 417 in FY2021 after the agencies suspended the practice, to 5 in FY2022 and 0 in FY2023, and came back to 265 in FY2025 (FTC/DOJ HSR Annual Reports, Appendix A). The second-request rate meanwhile oscillated between 1.6% and 3.0% of adjusted transactions. In procedure, the new HSR form took effect February 10, 2025; a federal district court vacated it on February 12, 2026 (FTC notice dated February 13, 2026); the Fifth Circuit granted an administrative stay on February 19 and then denied a stay pending appeal on March 19, 2026, and the agencies now accept filings on either form (FTC Premerger Notification Program page). What it means for the desk: the baseline $h_{0,c}(t)$ in the first 30 days is not stationary across administrations, so never pool FY2016–2019 clocks with FY2022–2024 clocks without a regime covariate, and expect the first month of every filing in 2025–26 to carry procedural variance that had nothing to do with antitrust.

#### The Full Derivation: Greenwood, Breslow and Aalen–Johansen

With $t_i$, $n_i$, $d_i$ and $d_{k,i}$ as defined at the start of §15.5.2, the Kaplan–Meier estimator and Greenwood's variance are

$$
\hat S(t) \;=\; \prod_{t_i \le t}\Big(1 - \frac{d_i}{n_i}\Big),
\qquad
\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}\big(\hat S(t)\big) \;=\; \hat S(t)^2 \sum_{t_i \le t} \frac{d_i}{n_i(n_i - d_i)} .
$$

For the cause-specific Cox model, with $R_i = \{j: t_j \ge t_i\}$ the risk set, the Breslow partial log-likelihood for cause $k$ is

$$
\ell_k(\beta) \;=\; \sum_{i:\,\text{cause}_i = k}\Big[x_i'\beta - \log\!\sum_{j\in R_i} e^{x_j'\beta}\Big],
\qquad
\nabla \ell_k \;=\; \sum_{i:\,\text{cause}_i = k}\big(x_i - \bar x_w(t_i)\big),
$$

with $\bar x_w(t_i)$ the $e^{x'\beta}$-weighted mean of the covariates in $R_i$. The gradient reads as the sum, over the deals that ended in cause $k$, of how far each one's covariates sat from the risk-weighted average of those still pending; the maximum is where those gaps cancel. Deals ending in other causes are censored for cause $k$.

The Aalen–Johansen estimator of cumulative incidence is

$$
\hat F_k(t) \;=\; \sum_{t_i \le t} \hat S(t_{i}^{-})\,\frac{d_{k,i}}{n_i},
\qquad
\sum_k \hat F_k(t) \;=\; 1 - \hat S(t),
$$

and the identity on the right is exact: summing over $k$ replaces $d_{k,i}$ by $d_i$, and $\hat S(t_i^-)\,d_i/n_i$ is precisely the drop in $\hat S$ at $t_i$, so the sum telescopes to $1 - \hat S(t)$.

### Specification for AI Implementation

**What ROBO built from the vague version.** "Estimate how long the deal will take." ROBO averaged signing-to-close times over closed deals and returned seven months. Every deal that had been blocked, abandoned or was still pending had been dropped as "missing data." Survivorship bias, delivered with confidence.

*The precise spec for Listing 15.4 (estimators, array shapes and return values) is in [The Engine: Full Specifications](#ch15-engine-specs) before §15.9's Spec You Hand the Robot.*

ROBO's seven months described the winners and nothing else. The fix is textbook statistics, and Theo's renamed 13-week columns are already most of the way there. The trouble is that each estimator is ten lines long and fails without a sound when the bookkeeping slips: a tied date, a pending deal counted as an event, a competing cause treated as if it never happened. A desk that will mark hundreds of deal clocks every morning cannot eyeball those, so it writes the estimators itself, bolts each to an identity or to an answer planted in advance, and only then points them at real deals.

Listing 15.4 builds the toolkit from scratch, then proves it on data whose answers are planted. `synthetic_deal_cohort` draws 600 deals with six covariates, generates a latent clock for each of the three causes from a Weibull proportional-hazards model with known coefficients, keeps the earliest as the outcome, and censors at an independent cutoff between half a year and four years; cause 0 means still pending. `_risk_table` does the bookkeeping everything else relies on: the distinct event times, the number at risk just before each, and the number of events, with ties kept in the risk set. `kaplan_meier` adds Greenwood bands (plain Wald intervals, clipped to the unit interval) and `nelson_aalen` the cumulative hazard. `aalen_johansen` computes all-cause survival and then, for each cause, the running sum of the previous step's survival times that cause's events over the number at risk. `cox_ph` maximizes the Breslow partial likelihood for one cause, treating the others as censored, with an analytic gradient and Hessian; it returns coefficients, standard errors, a baseline cumulative hazard, a convergence flag, and the correlation of Schoenfeld residuals with time as a proportional-hazards smell test. `bayes_deal_prob_path` applies the silence update one milestone at a time, taking the quiet probabilities as inputs.

The checks are identities wherever identities exist. With no censoring, Kaplan–Meier equals one minus the empirical distribution function. The three cumulative incidences sum to one minus survival to twelve decimals, and that survival matches the Kaplan–Meier curve. The close-hazard coefficients land within four standard errors of the planted ones. The Bayes path starts at 0.80 and rises through three quiet milestones.

Every check passes in a world real data will not give you, because the cohort censors independently by construction and the ICE indenture does not: run the toolkit on real deals only after Mags's question about why each one is still pending. Its other use is as an audit, running any library the desk adopts later on the same cohort. The failure Hana hit first was a constant column. She fitted a sample drawn from a single regulatory regime, `regime` never varied, the information matrix was singular, and `cox_ph` raised a `LinAlgError` instead of returning a standard error. The column came out.

*The full listing is [Listing 15.4 in Appendix F](#code-15-4).*

The printed Second Request coefficient lands near the planted $-1.2$, which is the 2.1-fold stretch of the median from the cause-specific paragraph, and the 30-days-versus-a-year gap in the HSR data, recovered from a seeded cohort. That is the point: before you fit real deals, prove the engine finds the parameters you planted.

- **Academic Papers:** Giglio & Shue (2014), *No News Is News: Do Markets Underreact to Nothing?*, Review of Financial Studies, DOI 10.1093/rfs/hhu052; Dikova, Sahib & van Witteloostuijn (2010), *Cross-Border Acquisition Abandonment and Completion*, Journal of International Business Studies, DOI 10.1057/jibs.2009.10; Wollmann (2019), *Stealth Consolidation: Evidence from an Amendment to the Hart-Scott-Rodino Act*, AER: Insights, DOI 10.1257/aeri.20180137.
- **Data & Code:** FTC/DOJ HSR Annual Reports, FY2023 https://www.ftc.gov/system/files/ftc_gov/pdf/fy2023hsrreport.pdf and FY2024 https://www.ftc.gov/system/files/ftc_gov/pdf/FY24-HSR-ANNUAL-REPORT-FOR-TRANSMITTAL-TO-CONGRESS.pdf ; European Commission merger procedures, https://competition-policy.ec.europa.eu/mergers/procedures_en ; CourtListener REST API, https://www.courtlistener.com/help/api/ ; ICE–MarketAxess announcement (ICE 8-K, Ex. 99.1, July 2026), https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001571949/000119312526324909/d116245dex991.htm ; MarketAxess definitive proxy (termination fees, consents, outside date), https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1278021/000119312526395678/d171374ddefm14a.htm ; MarketAxess 8-K on the HSR withdrawal and refiling, https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1278021/000119312526407834/d142535d8k.htm .

## 15.6 Target vs. Acquirer: Spread Compression, Acquirer Widening, and Event Momentum

The morning after a deal is announced, the target's bonds and the acquirer's bonds start telling two different stories, and twenty years of research has checked which story usually comes true. Billett, King & Mauer (2004) find that target bondholders gain on average, with the gains concentrated in below-investment-grade targets bought by better-rated acquirers, while acquirer bondholders do not share in them. Furfine & Rosen (2011) find that mergers raise the acquirer's default risk on average. Anyone who has sat on the sell side of a pitch will recognize the shape: the target is lent the acquirer's balance sheet, and the acquirer pays for the privilege with its own.

Ines tells the third result as a hand she has replayed many times. Acharya & Johnson (2010) asked what the equity and CDS of LBO targets did in the days before anyone announced anything. They moved before the announcement, and they moved more when more insiders were involved, more parties brought inside the deal before it was public. For Ines that is adverse selection reduced to one regression. "Every seat you add to the financing is another player who has seen the cards. The tape doesn't care how the information got out. It shows you that somebody was buying protection, or buying the bonds, before you knew there was a hand." Her replay is the one she runs after every take-private: pull the markouts on the target's bonds and CDS for the ten trading days before the press release, line them up against the desk's own fills, and see which side of each trade the desk was on. If the desk sold protection to a client three days before an LBO, the hand history says so. Her response is never outrage. It is a smaller quote size, the next time, on the next name that looks like a sponsor's target, which is the only lesson the market lets you keep.

Theo builds the trade the chapter's machinery suggests, event momentum, and the building takes a morning. He runs `bayes_deal_prob_path` on each pending deal and looks for target bonds whose $\pi_d(t)$ is rising through silent milestones faster than their spread is tightening toward the acquirer's curve, the deals where the market is slower than Bayes. For sizing he borrows Paleologo's rule that a shorter runway to the event means a smaller position, because "there is less time to build it" (Paleologo_Advanced_Portfolio_Management p.152). The first backtest is glorious. Ines asks it one question: how much of that is the acquirer? Theo strips the acquirer's own spread change, the rates leg, carry and the market factor from the target's return, and most of the glory leaves with them. Most of what a target bond does after announcement is the acquirer's beta wearing the target's CUSIP. What is left is smaller, steadier and real. IDO or it didn't happen.

> **View From Another Seat.** *The multi-strategy relative-value pod (a generic description; no firm is named).* Inside a multi-strategy platform the same event-momentum book lives under two constraints that matter more than the model. One is factor neutrality: the platform's risk team sums spread beta across hundreds of portfolio managers and treats it as a firm exposure, so the PM hedges the acquirer's beta with index CDX or the acquirer's own bonds and is paid on the residual, the long-target, short-acquirer pair that isolates the event. The other is the drawdown stop. A PM two-thirds of the way to a capital cut sizes down before the risk manager calls, so a deal that goes quiet for two months, good news under Bayes, can be closed out for budget reasons just as its probability is rising. The pod's edge is speed and hedging discipline; its weakness is that it cannot always afford to be patient with a clock a regulator sets.

> **View From Another Seat.** *The dealer desk on the other side of the target's bonds (a generic description).* For a bank's credit-trading desk the morning after an announcement is a flow problem before it is a view. Clients who own the target call to sell into the rally or to buy more for the change-of-control put, holders of the acquirer call about the new supply, and the trader has to reprice the target off the acquirer's curve before the acquirer's own bonds have finished moving. The bank's financing arm may be arranging the acquirer's bridge, so the trading desk can be the one part of the building walled off from the deal it is making markets in. And the clients who call first are often the ones who have read the indenture, which makes the morning's first quote the one most likely to show up later in somebody's hand history.

## 15.7 When the Deal Dies: The Merger as the Credit

For a weak target, the bond price before resolution is a mixture of two curves:

$$
P^{\text{tgt}}_t \;=\; \pi_d(t)\,P^{\text{acq}}_t \;+\; \big(1-\pi_d(t)\big)\,P^{\text{sa}}_t,
\qquad
\Delta P^{\text{tgt}}\big|_{\text{block}} \;=\; -\,\pi_d(t^-)\,\big(P^{\text{acq}}_t - P^{\text{sa}}_t\big),
$$

where $P^{\text{sa}}$ is the standalone value. A block is a jump of known sign and estimable size on a date the court publishes: a staircase, not the ramp of small random steps a diffusion risk model assumes, and its size has nothing to do with how volatile the price was yesterday. A target bond priced at $\pi_d = 0.7$, with a 15-point gap between the acquirer leg and the standalone leg, falls $0.7 \times 15 = 10.5$ points on the day of a block, while a one-day 99% VaR estimated over the quiet months before the ruling might read 1.5 *(illustrative)*. The VaR is not wrong about the ramp; it cannot see the stair, because the stair was never in its data (Chapter 5's mixtures; Chapter 14's distress dynamics). The desks that survive these days carry the jump as its own line in the risk report, sized by the mixture and dated by the court's calendar.

*The Spirit, JetBlue and court facts are real and cited; the telling and the dialogue are invented.*

Mags tells the Spirit story standing up, in the order it happened, which is how she tells every story that cost somebody money. It is a slow Thursday in October 2026, Theo has asked why the chapter's mixture formula has a minus sign in front of it, and Mags has decided that the answer is an airline.

"July 2022," she begins. "JetBlue agrees to buy Spirit. From that day the Spirit bonds stop being Spirit bonds. Nobody prices an ultra-low-cost carrier with a fleet problem anymore; they price a JetBlue credit with an asterisk, times whatever you think the odds of closing are, plus a little bit of Spirit for the bad case. Nobody bothers to work out that little bit carefully, because nobody needs it. For eighteen months the standalone leg is a number in a footnote." In the chapter's notation, the market was pricing $\pi_d\,P^{\text{acq}}$ with care and $P^{\text{sa}}$ with a shrug, and the shrug was weighted by $1-\pi_d$, which made it look small.

"Meanwhile the company is waiting. A target that has signed a merger agreement is a company in a holding pattern. Merger agreements typically restrict what the target can do while the deal is pending: no big new financings, no dramatic strategy changes, operate in the ordinary course. Which is fine if you're going to be bought. If you're not, you've spent a year and a half not fixing yourself."

Kaz asks the obvious question. "Didn't the stockholders mind waiting?"

"The stockholders were being paid to wait. That's the part I want you to remember." The deal paid Spirit's stockholders prepayments while the agreement was in effect, about \$425mm by the time it ended. Nobody paid the bondholders anything for the same eighteen months.

Then the dates, and Mags slows down for them, because these are the facts and the rest is her opinion.

Spirit Airlines is the template. On January 16, 2024 the District of Massachusetts enjoined the JetBlue merger; three days later Spirit reported \$1.3bn of liquidity at year-end and sale-leasebacks of 25 aircraft. On March 4, 2024 the parties terminated by mutual agreement; JetBlue paid Spirit \$69mm. On November 18, 2024 Spirit filed a prearranged Chapter 11 with a restructuring support agreement signed by a supermajority of its loyalty-program and convertible noteholders: a \$350mm backstopped equity investment, equitization of \$795mm of funded debt, and a \$300mm DIP from existing bondholders (Spirit 8-Ks and releases, EDGAR). Signing to block took about 18 months; block to bankruptcy took about ten.

Mags comes back to the prepayments. "The ticking money went to the equity. The ticking clock went to the bonds."

Theo maps the dates onto the formula. On January 15, 2024, the day before the ruling, the bonds sat at $\pi_d P^{\text{acq}} + (1-\pi_d)P^{\text{sa}}$, with the standalone leg priced from a footnote. On January 16 the judge set $\pi_d$ close to zero in a single afternoon, and the price stepped down to $P^{\text{sa}}$, whatever that was. The trouble was that nobody knew what it was, because nobody had needed to, until three days later the company published the inputs. "That press release," Mags says, "was the standalone leg being priced for the first time in eighteen months. In public. By the company that most needed it to look good."

"So the jump was really two jumps," Kaz says. "One for the probability and one for discovering what the bad state was worth."

"And the second one didn't have a court date."

The ten months after the termination are, in Mags's telling, the part a model handles worst. The deal was dead, so the merger arbitrage community left and took its liquidity with it. The bonds now traded on the standalone airline, a company that had spent eighteen months in a holding pattern, and the prearranged restructuring that followed was the bondholders' answer to a clock they had never been paid for. Chapter 16 picks the story up from there (§16.7): emergence in March 2025, a second filing less than six months later, and a coda that *The Octus Download* covered in its EP 29, "Spirit's Final Flight, AMC Hangs On & The Parent Trap" (May 7, 2026): Spirit ceased operations on May 2, 2026, after a floated federal rescue fell through.

Theo writes the lesson on a sticky note, and for once it is not a rule but a question for the next pending deal. *Who is being paid to wait, and who is waiting for free?* In Spirit the answer was on the face of the merger agreement: the equity had a ticking payment, and the bonds had a mixture formula with a minus sign and a standalone leg nobody had priced, because the probability in front of it had been large.

## 15.8 Case Study: Warner Bros. Discovery 2025–26, the Covenant Strip and the Ticking Fee

*A replay, dealt on Monday, October 5, 2026, the day before the deal closed; Ines breaks her Friday rule because the river is dealt tomorrow. The WBD filings, deal terms, indenture clauses, podcasts and dates are real and cited; the desk's position in the Historic TW notes, held since before Theo arrived, and all dialogue are invented.*

**Cut one: Tuesday, June 10, 2025, 8:05 a.m.** The offer documents arrive the way they always do, as a long PDF and a short press release that disagree about what matters. On Monday, WBD launched tender offers and consent solicitations for substantially all the notes of four entities in its family: Discovery Communications, WarnerMedia Holdings, Warner Media LLC and Historic TW. The coverage is about strategy. WBD plans to split itself in two, and its debt is being rearranged to fit (press reports, June 2025). The desk holds a position in the Historic TW notes, old Time Warner paper that has already survived two mergers and has the documentation to show for it.

Theo reads the consent solicitation first, because that is where restructuring bankers live. "It's an exit consent," he says. "You tender, you get paid, and on your way out of the door you vote to strip the covenants from the bonds that stay behind. Delaware's Court of Chancery blessed the technique in *Katz v. Oak Industries* in 1986. I've worked on three of these."

"Is that legal?" Kaz asks.

"It's been legal for longer than you've been alive. The question is never whether it's legal. The question is whether you'd rather be the holder who tenders or the holder who's left behind."

Ines likes it already. "Threshold game. If enough holders consent, the ones who didn't are left owning a bond with no rules. So everybody consents, including the ones who would rather keep the covenants, because nobody wants to be the last holder of a stripped bond. Section 13.4 has the math. What I want to know is what we're being paid for what we're giving up."

That is the question, and on June 10 nobody on the desk can answer it. The offer documents set out what a consenting holder receives. The covenants have a value too, and that value depends entirely on what the issuer will do with its new freedom, which is the one thing the documents do not say. On June 10 there is no buyer. There is a plan to split the company, a set of indentures written for a company that was not planning to split, and an issuer that wants the covenants gone before anything else happens.

Mags has seen the move before, in a different neighbourhood. "Back in my day you stripped covenants when you were in trouble. Distressed exchange, exit consents, and the bonds left behind traded at forty. Now an investment-grade company does it on a Monday, with a press release about strategy." She flips through the Historic TW indenture, which is older than some of the desk. "Ask why they want it now. Covenants are cheapest to buy when nobody can see what they'll be needed for."

Kaz reaches for the framing the chapter has been building. "So consenting is selling an option. What's the underlying?"

"Everything the company might do next," Theo says. "That's the problem. I can price the option the moment you tell me the underlying."

#### Decision point: Historic TW, Tuesday 10 June 2025

You hold Historic TW notes. The consent solicitation is open and no buyer exists. Write it on the card: do you consent, and what exactly are you selling?

**The strip came first.** Requisite consents arrived on June 16, and the supplemental indentures "eliminate substantially all of the restrictive covenants" and certain events of default once operative (WBD 8-K, June 13, 2025, EDGAR). Which protections survived in each series, the change-of-control offer among them, is a question for each supplemental indenture; the structural lesson does not wait for the answer. The issuer exercised its counter-option *before* the put could be in the money, when consent was cheap.

The same week brought a smaller clause with a long future. The Twenty-Third Supplemental Indenture for the Discovery Communications notes, dated June 13, 2025, carries a section titled "Non-Boycott" that bars holders and their non-screened affiliates from agreements that would restrict them from buying the group's new debt or lending it cash (WBD 8-K, Exhibit 4.1, June 2025, EDGAR). It is a borrower writing a rule against creditor cooperation agreements into its own bonds, the counter-technology to the co-ops of §13.5, and the European Leveraged Finance Association warned publicly that such clauses were risky (Bloomberg Law, "Europe's ELFA Warns Warner Bros. Non-Boycott Clauses Are Risky," 2025).

**The loan said what it was.** A \$15bn bridge was documented as the "Non-Investment Grade Leveraged Bridge Loan Agreement" (June 26, 2025). Kaz: "They named the loan after its rating?" Theo: "It's the only honest title in the data room." It was refinanced on June 4, 2026 with a \$13bn term loan B at SOFR+250 and a €1,717mm term loan B at EURIBOR+250 at Discovery Global Holdings, maturing June 4, 2033, whose change of control, "such as the consummation of the previously disclosed proposed acquisition of the Company by Paramount Skydance Corporation," permits acceleration (WBD 8-K, June 2026). Entry 5 of the §15.1 table, with the trigger named in advance.

**Cut two: Friday, December 19, 2025.** Two weeks after Netflix signs, Ines deals the episode the desk listened to that afternoon, *Money Stuff: The Podcast*, "Good Game: WBD, Tricolor, TAE" (Dec. 19, 2025), in which Matt Levine and Katie Greifeld spend part of the episode on closing certainty in merger agreements: the break fees and conditions that decide how likely a signed deal is to close. "Closing certainty is what an SMR prices and what a ticking fee charges for," Ines says. "Somebody's going to put a number on the calendar." Theo hears it with a different ear. By this cut the Historic TW holders who consented in June own bonds with almost nothing left to enforce, and the question for them is no longer who wins WBD. It is how much debt the winner will put where, and which subsidiaries will guarantee it.

**Three suitors, one clock.** WBD signed with Netflix in early December 2025, amended on January 19, 2026 to \$27.75 a share in all cash, and then signed with Paramount Skydance on February 27, 2026 at \$31.00 in cash plus "Ticking Consideration" of \$0.00277778 per share per day after September 30, 2026, capped at \$0.25 per 90 days. Stockholders approved on April 23, 2026. The deal closed on October 6, 2026 at \$31.01666668 a share: exactly six days of ticking ($6 \times 0.00277778$), or \$41,886,975.78 in aggregate. At closing WBD repaid the June 2026 term loans and its October 2024 revolver, and WBD subsidiaries guaranteed Skydance's new notes and credit agreement (WBD 8-Ks, EDGAR). Figure 15.5 puts every date on one axis.

![Figure 15.5: The covenant strip on the legacy notes came eight months before the winning bidder signed and sixteen months before the deal closed. Source: WBD 8-Ks (June 2025 to October 2026), EDGAR, as cited in Section 15.8; the December 4, 2025 Netflix signing date is from the EDGAR 8-K filed December 5, 2025 for that agreement.](../assets/figures/ch15_wbd_timeline.png)

> **Math, Gently.** *The expected positive part is a parking meter with a grace period.* The ticking consideration works like a parking meter that does not start running until September 30, 2026. Close before then and the meter reads zero. Close after and it charges \$0.00277778 a share for every day past the grace period. The expression $(\tau_c - t^{*})^{+}$, read "the positive part of $\tau_c - t^{*}$," is that meter: the number of days past the grace period if there are any, and zero if there are not. Its expected value is not the meter read at the expected closing date, because the meter never runs backwards. An early close contributes zero, not a refund, so the average reading is at least the reading at the average date, and usually more. Tiny number: suppose the deal is sure to close sometime in the 60 days after September 30, each day equally likely. The meter reads anywhere from 1 to 60 days, about 30 on average, and the expected ticking is about $30 \times 0.00277778 \approx \$0.083$ a share. Now suppose instead that the close is equally likely on any day of the 60 centred on September 30. The expected closing date is September 30 itself, and a careless calculation says zero ticking. But in the half of outcomes that land late, the meter runs 15 days on average, so the expected ticking is about 7.5 days, roughly \$0.021 a share. The real answer replaces these toy windows with the closing-time curve of §15.5; that is exercise 4. The actual deal closed six days past the grace period, for about \$0.0167 a share.

**Pricing the ticking fee.** Annualized, $0.00277778 \times 365 \approx \$1.014$, about 3.3% a year on \$31. That compensates shareholders for time, not for break risk, which they still carry. A survival model prices the rest: the expected ticking payment is $0.00277778 \times \mathbb{E}\big[(\tau_c - t^{*})^{+}\big]$ in days, with $t^{*}$ = September 30, 2026, and the competing-risks curve of §15.5 supplies the law of $\tau_c$.

**Cut three: Thursday, May 7, 2026.** Theo has heard this one already, on a PJT commute in May: *Cloud 9fin Syndication Nation*, "The \$81bn HY/IG jigsaw puzzle behind Paramount-WBD" (May 7, 2026), in which William Hoffman and Sunny Oh walk through the financing, about \$32bn of existing bonds and about \$49bn of new syndicated debt split across asset classes. He sketches it on the back of a printout, a box for each market, and Ines asks the only question that matters to the desk: "Where does our Historic TW paper sit in your jigsaw?" Theo does not know, and says so. The answer will be in the guarantee documents at closing, and he has learned to wait for the document rather than the headline.

> **View From Another Seat.** *The dealer's syndicate desk (a generic description, grounded in the 9fin episode above).* To the banks arranging it, \$49bn of new debt is not a credit view; it is a placement problem. No single market absorbs that much at once, so the syndicate desk cuts it into pieces each market can digest: secured term loans for the loan market and the CLOs behind it, high-yield bonds for one set of accounts, investment-grade bonds for another, with the rating on each piece deciding which buyers may even look. The weeks before launch are boring and decisive: soundings with anchor accounts, a book that fills or does not, price talk that moves, and a running tally of what is left on the banks' balance sheet if a piece does not clear. Every protection the old bonds lost in June 2025 is room the new money can use, and the syndicate desk prices the new pieces knowing exactly how much room there is.

> **View From Another Seat.** *The CLO manager holding the SOFR+250 term loan (a generic description).* The June 4, 2026 term loan B at Discovery Global Holdings is an unusual asset: a loan whose change-of-control clause names its own likely trigger in advance. The manager buys it knowing the probable path is a par repayment at closing, months rather than years later, which is good news for credit risk and a nuisance for everything else: the spread is earned briefly, and the cash comes back in whatever market prevails on closing day, to be reinvested inside the spread, rating-factor, CCC and overcollateralization tests, which care nothing for the merger. The repayment arrived on October 6, 2026 (WBD 8-K). To the CLO the deal was a reinvestment date.

**Tuesday, October 6, 2026.** The deal closes at \$31.01666668 a share, six days into the meter. Kaz computes the ticking to the penny and is faintly disappointed that the 8-K has already done it. Theo takes out his card from the June cut and answers it out loud, sixteen months after the fact.

"On our reading, we were selling the covenants that would have policed where acquisition debt could sit and which of the issuer's subsidiaries could guarantee it," he says. "We sold them in a week when there was no buyer, which is the week their value was hardest to see. I couldn't price the option because I couldn't see the underlying. The issuer didn't need to see it. It only needed the option gone before anyone could. Once WBD's subsidiaries guarantee the acquisition debt, the new money has claims at the same entities as our notes, and a stripped indenture doesn't police it. That's our reading; the guarantee documents will say."

"So the consent was the credit event," Kaz says.

"The consent was the credit event. The merger was just the day we found out."

### Quant-Shop Life: The Security Master Has Forty New Columns

*(A fictional composite. The shop, its people, its tickets and its numbers are invented; the market events and the regulatory order cited are real.)*

The systematic asset manager, a different shop from the desk, occupies two floors of a converted warehouse, and on Tuesday, December 10, 2024, Noor, a data engineer eight months into the job, spends the whole of it on a ticket titled "Add M&A contingency fields to secmaster." Research has asked for forty new columns. Noor has learned that requests for forty columns are really requests for six, plus thirty-four that someone thought of in the meeting, so she starts with the six: `coc_double_trigger`, `agencies_required`, `defeasance_releases_coc`, `portability_window_end`, `smr_outside_date` and `smr_date_extendable`.

Every one of them starts a definitional argument. `coc_double_trigger` was going to be a yes-or-no flag until a covenant analyst points out that some ratings triggers need a downgrade by two of three agencies and some by all of them, which is how `agencies_required` becomes an integer. `defeasance_releases_coc` is worse. Whether an indenture's covenant-defeasance article releases the issuer from the repurchase covenant is a question for a lawyer, and the shop has one lawyer and three hundred issuers, so the field gets three allowed values, TRUE, FALSE and UNREAD. By lunch UNREAD is the most common value in the table, which Noor considers the first honest thing the security master has ever said.

The backfill runs through the morning. Her scripts pull registered prospectuses from EDGAR for the three hundred issuers on research's list and search them for the defined terms. The double-trigger language comes back clean for most investment-grade names. `portability_window_end` comes back empty almost everywhere, and at first she suspects her parser before realizing that it is telling the truth: investment-grade bonds rarely port, and the high-yield bonds that do are sold under Rule 144A and never filed. A null that means "not applicable" and a null that means "we cannot see it" look identical in a database, so she adds a second column to tell them apart. By three o'clock 212 of the 300 issuers are done, and the column count is up to seven.

At eleven, the point-in-time archive catches a vendor in the act. Overnight, the reference-data feed changed the maturity on one bond in the universe and overwrote the old value, as if it had always been the new date. The archive, which stores what arrived and when rather than what is true now, still holds the old record. Without it, every later backtest would have used the corrected maturity on dates when nobody knew it, a small leak of the future into the past. Noor files a ticket with the vendor and loses forty minutes to a call in which the vendor explains that the correction is a correction.

The worst find of the day is a single hand-keyed date. Someone had typed the European Commission's Phase I deadline for a pending deal as 25 calendar days after notification, instead of 25 working days. The deal-probability model, which treats a deadline that passes quietly as good news, had registered the milestone as passed more than a week early and nudged the deal probability up on a silence that had not yet happened. Nobody traded on it, probably. Noor adds a `clock_basis` column, CAL or WORK or BUS, with a holiday calendar per regulator, and the column count reaches eight.

In the late afternoon the Kroger ruling comes in: the court grants the preliminary injunction. Around six a portfolio manager updates the `ruling_date` and `ruling_outcome` fields on the Kroger 2027s himself, because the ticket queue is slow and the fix is obvious.

At 7:30 the next morning the risk report goes out, and the Kroger 2027s' spread duration has fallen from about 2.3 to 0.25 overnight *(illustrative)*, dragging the portfolio's spread duration with it. The risk committee, three people on a call, asks the question every risk committee asks: why is this number different from yesterday? The answer is that the number is right. The bond is no longer a three-year Kroger bond with a deal attached; it is a 101 claim that will settle within a month. The committee accepts that in two minutes and spends the next twenty on the question it actually cares about: who changed the field, when, and who reviewed it? The change log shows a live field edited by a PM outside the ticket process. That is the meeting's real finding, and it goes in the minutes.

Noor ends Wednesday by sorting the open-ticket queue by age. The oldest is from 2020, four years old, filed by a researcher who has since left: "SMR tranches carry call-schedule duration, not probabilistic duration." It is, she realizes, the bug the risk report just exposed, described in one line four years earlier. A month later the SEC will publish an order against a systematic manager whose employees had identified model vulnerabilities "in or before March 2019" that the firm waited until August 2023 to address (SEC Press Release 2025-15, Jan. 16, 2025). Noor reads it in January and closes her four-year-old ticket the same afternoon.

Her tally for the two days: eight new columns of the forty, 212 issuers backfilled, one vendor correction caught, one hand-keyed clock fixed, one governance finding, and no trades. By the standards of the job it was a very good day.

**Friday, October 16, 2026, 6:10 p.m.** The desk has a ritual for the end of a long case: whoever ran it says what they learned, out loud, to people who are allowed to heckle. Theo stands by the whiteboard. The sticky note from the Kroger replay three weeks ago is still there, curling at the corners, stuck to the Tapestry 8-K: *Who actually owns this option, and who owns the clock?*

"The holder owns the option on paper," he says. "Every clause in the §15.1 table is drafted that way: the 101 put, the SMR, the change-of-control acceleration in a loan. But every one of them was lived as the issuer's counter-option. Kroger chose which tranches got the SMR. EA's new owner chose to deposit Treasuries instead of paying 101. WBD stripped the covenants before there was a buyer to need them. Portability lets a sponsor choose the leverage that decides whether the put exists at all. So the holder owns the option, and the issuer owns the right to decide whether it is still there when it matters."

"And the clock?" Ines asks.

"Nobody at this table. A judge in Portland. A DOJ staff that asked for thirty more days. A regulator in London counting working days, and a contract that extends its own outside date whenever the deal is stuck. The SMR is the one place the market prices the clock honestly, and it goes blind when its two legs meet. Everything else is survival analysis on a sample that won't tell you why it's still pending unless you ask."

"So what do we own?" Kaz asks.

"The reading," Theo says. "The paragraph nobody read. Kroger's tranche list, EA's defeasance article, the WBD consent. Three cases, and the credit event was a paragraph every time. That's the only edge in the chapter that's ours."

Mags has been quiet, which is how she prepares a verdict. She has the EA closing 8-K open, the one with the deposit of U.S. Government Obligations. "I said I hated it," she says. "I still do. But look at what the holders who stayed were left with: a 2051 bond backed by Treasuries sitting with a trustee. Back in my day you'd have traded your firstborn for collateral like that. We used to fight for months over a second lien on a warehouse in New Jersey." She closes the file. "They took away a put and handed over the best collateral in the world. It's a robbery with excellent manners." A pause. "Grudging respect."

Theo takes the sticky note down and puts it in his wallet, next to the USB stick. Then he tries to fit the chapter onto a fresh one, fails, and uses the whiteboard.

> **Taped to the Monitor.** *The chapter in seven lines.*
>
> - **Every deal clause is a payoff function.** Write it as (outcome, trigger, price at trigger), and store the issuer's counter-options (consent strip, defeasance, exchange offer) next to it in the security master.
> - **CoC moneyness is coupon vintage.** The put cares about $101 - P$, not the credit story. The IG double trigger needs both inspectors, and for LBOs the trigger and the payoff covary ($M > 1$).
> - **Portability is a short digital on a number the sponsor chooses.** Every point of permitted add-back lowers the odds that your put survives.
> - **The SMR is a $\mathbb{Q}$ break gauge inside the acquirer's curve.** Its resolution is $|P^{\text{close}} - G_f|$, its control group is contaminated, and its duration jumps on ruling day.
> - **Regulatory clocks are competing-risks survival data.** Censoring is informative, regimes shift $h_0$, and $\sum_k F_k = 1 - S$ is your unit test.
> - **Silence is data, and beta is not alpha.** Update $\pi_d$ through quiet milestones, then strip the acquirer's beta before claiming the event. IDO or it didn't happen.
> - **The most expensive three words have a cousin:** "defease certain obligations."

### The Engine: Full Specifications {#ch15-engine-specs}

The three listings of this chapter were explained where the story needed them. Their precise specifications, the part ROBO actually reads, are collected here so that they stop interrupting the derivations. Each is the contract the corresponding listing in Appendix F was written against.

**Listing 15.1, the change-of-control put ([Appendix F](#code-15-1)).** Implement `price_coc_put` with the payoff conditional on deal × trigger, the post-close bond priced on the post-close curve, the trigger allowed to depend on the post-close spread (to capture $M>1$), and an optional issuer counter-option (defeasance or strip) that may depend on how far in the money the put is.

- **Inputs.** `deal_prob` $\pi_d\in[0,1]$ (state the measure); `trigger_prob_given_deal`, a float or a callable mapping spreads (decimal, shape `(n,)`) to per-path probabilities; `post_spread_sampler(rng, n)` returning decimal spreads of shape `(n,)`; `coupon` in percent of par; `maturity_years` and `t_close` in years (ACT/365 clock; coupons 30/360 semiannual, valued on a coupon date so accrued is zero); `defeasance_prob`, a float or a callable of intrinsic value.
- **Outputs.** A dict with `value` (points per 100 face at signing), `stderr`, `moneyness_ratio` $M$, and `mean_intrinsic`.
- **Edge cases.** `deal_prob == 0`, a scalar trigger probability of 0, or a scalar defeasance probability of 1 returns exactly 0. A bond maturing before `t_close` returns 0 with a warning. Spreads are clipped at 0. $M$ is `nan` when intrinsic value is zero everywhere.
- **Variance reduction.** Integrate the deal and trigger Bernoullis analytically (Rao–Blackwellization): simulate only the spread.

**Listing 15.3, the SMR break gauge ([Appendix F](#code-15-3)).** Fit a Z-spread curve through the issuer's non-SMR tranches by maturity (PCHIP, flat beyond the last node, with an `extrapolated` flag), price each SMR tranche on that curve to get $P^{\text{close}}$, compute the fail leg $G_f$ with accrued interest and the acquirer's short yield, invert for $\hat\pi_f$ with a denominator guard and clipping report, and return the value-weighted probabilistic duration. Schema: a DataFrame with columns `tranche_id` (str), `coupon` (percent), `maturity` (years, on the half-year grid so that `bond_price` values on a coupon date), `price` (full price per 100), `is_smr` (bool). Raise if fewer than two non-SMR tranches or duplicate non-SMR maturities.

**Listing 15.4, the deal clock ([Appendix F](#code-15-4)).** From-scratch estimators (no `lifelines`): `kaplan_meier` with Greenwood bands, `nelson_aalen`, `aalen_johansen` for cumulative incidence, `cox_ph` by Breslow partial likelihood with analytic gradient and Hessian through `scipy.optimize`, a seeded synthetic cohort with known cause-specific Weibull hazards, and the Bayesian milestone path. Shapes: `times (n,)` in years ACT/365, `event (n,)` in $\{0,1\}$, `cause (n,)` in $\{0,1,2,3\}$ with 0 = pending, `X (n,p)`. Cox returns `beta (p,)`, `se (p,)`, baseline cumulative hazard `(m,2)` at $x=0$, and Schoenfeld-residual time correlations (reported, not asserted). Working-day calendars are converted to years by the caller, never inferred.

**The Spec You Hand the Robot.** "Build `event_credit_engine.py` (numpy, scipy, pandas; seeded). (1) `price_coc_put`: Monte Carlo over post-close spreads (decimal), deal × trigger × issuer-counter-option probabilities integrated analytically, bond priced on the post-close curve, return value in points per 100, stderr and $M$; exact zeros for degenerate inputs. (2) `curve_match_close_price`, `smr_fail_leg`, `smr_implied_break_prob`, `smr_duration`: PCHIP Z-spread curve over non-SMR tranches with an extrapolation flag; accrued to the redemption date; raise when $|P^{\text{close}} - G_f| < 10^{-6}$; clip and report. (3) `kaplan_meier`, `nelson_aalen`, `aalen_johansen`, `cox_ph` (Breslow, log-sum-exp, analytic gradient and Hessian), `bayes_deal_prob_path`. Assert: closed-form match for a constant spread; SMR round trip to $10^{-10}$; KM equals $1-$ECDF without censoring; CIFs sum to $1-\hat S$ within $10^{-12}$; Cox recovers planted $\beta$ within four standard errors. Units: years ACT/365 for clocks, 30/360 accrued, spreads decimal, prices per 100 face. Never pool regimes without a regime covariate. Never mix $\mathbb{P}$ and $\mathbb{Q}$ without saying so."

### Exercises

1. **The defeasance arithmetic.** With block 1, price the put on 1.85% and 2.95% bonds with 4.5 and 24.5 years remaining under an LBO spread of 350bp *(illustrative)*. Then compute what a sponsor saves per 100 face by depositing Treasuries instead of paying 101. Explain why 95% of EA's legacy holders declined the tender, and whether they were right.
2. **The blind thermometer.** Find the parallel Treasury move after issue at which a 4.60% three-year SMR tranche has $P^{\text{close}} = G_f$. Explain why $\hat\pi_f$ is undefined there and which instrument you would use instead.
3. **The vintage anomaly.** For an IG issuer on a take-private watch list, regress same-issuer Z-spreads on coupon with maturity controls. Derive the sign the embedded put predicts for the coupon coefficient, and design the test that tells the put apart from the low-coupon bonds' lower convexity and better index eligibility.
4. **Was the ticking fee generous?** Fit a Weibull to time-to-close from the Paramount Skydance signing with a median of seven months *(illustrative)*, and compute the expected ticking consideration per share. Compare it with the \$0.0167 realized and with a 2026 cash yield. Who wrote the better option?
5. **Kaz assumes Gaussian.** Kaz proposes a normal distribution for days-to-clearance. Using the HSR table, show that a two-component mixture (cleared in the initial period versus Second Request) beats every Gaussian on log-likelihood, and explain what the Gaussian implies about deals clearing before they file.
