## 16.8 Putting It Together: A Post-Reorg Book

### 16.8.1 The distribution you are actually trading

*(The desk's week, its whiteboard, Kaz's vendor file and the packaging company in Ines's ticket are fictional; the published studies are not.)*

Monday, 8:10 a.m. Ines's Friday question is still on the whiteboard in her handwriting, under the word *airlines*: cut both, hedge the pair with the sector, or keep the second carrier and buy the next one smaller. Somebody has added, in Kaz's handwriting, "define 'smaller'," which Ines has decided to treat as a contribution.

Theo spent part of the weekend on the question and has come in with an answer he likes, which in his experience is the first sign that something is wrong with it. "Cut both," he says. "We just watched a post-reorg equity go to zero in five months. The second carrier is the same instrument, in the same sector, born out of the same kind of plan. If I were still the banker on the second one, I'd be worried."

"You'd be worried about the company," Mags says. "Is the company the trade?"

Theo opens his mouth and closes it again, because that is the question. On Friday the desk spent four pages on one position. A strategy is not one position. It is a bet that a population of positions, each of which looks a little like Spirit on the morning it is bought, will on average pay for the few that turn into Spirit. Whether to cut the second carrier depends less on the second carrier than on what that population looks like, and the population is something the desk can write down.

Kaz writes it down, on the half of the whiteboard nobody has claimed. They combine §16.1's Trend Watch with §16.7's left tail. Over a 200-day horizon a single post-reorg equity's return $R$ is roughly a lognormal with median zero and mean +40% (the Jiang–Wang–Yang shape) with a jump to $-100\%$ mixed in (the Spirit shape). Write $X \sim N(0, s^2)$ and a jump indicator $J$ with $\Pr(J=1) = p_J$:
$$R = (1 - J)\left(e^{X} - 1\right) - J, \qquad \mathbb{E}[e^X] = e^{s^2/2} = 1.4 \;\Rightarrow\; s = \sqrt{2\ln 1.4} \approx 0.82 .$$

"How does a median of zero go with a mean of forty?" Theo asks. "That's the line I'd have circled in a fairness opinion."

"Because the exponential bends," Kaz says, and for once the explanation is short. They write a coin on the board: a 200-day log return of $+0.82$ or $-0.82$, average zero, gives price multiples of $e^{0.82} \approx 2.27$ and $e^{-0.82} \approx 0.44$, which average 1.36, not 1. A full bell curve of the same spread has tails beyond the coin and lifts the mean to $e^{s^2/2} = e^{0.336} \approx 1.40$. "Same $\tfrac12\sigma^2$ as Chapter 6," Kaz says. "Wearing your numbers. The more volatile the ticket, the more of its average lives in a few draws, and the worse its typical draw looks."

Then $\mathbb{E}[R] = (1-p_J)(1.4) - 1$, which is +33% for $p_J = 5\%$ *(illustrative)*, while the median is slightly *negative*: solving $p_J + (1-p_J)\Phi(\ln(1+m)/s) = \tfrac12$ gives $m \approx -5\%$. This is Chapter 5's mixture (§5.1.1): a weighted coin picks the deck, five times in a hundred the one-card deck at $-100\%$ and otherwise the survivor deck, so the mean is just $0.95 \times 1.40 = 1.33$, while the five cards at the far left push the middle draw a little inside the survivor deck's lower half. A small lump at zero barely dents the mean and quietly drags the median below water.

"So the typical name loses money," Theo says, "and the average name makes a third."

Mags writes that sentence on a sticky note: **the typical single name loses money; the average name makes a third.** She puts it on the bottom edge of Theo's second monitor, under the Wolfspeed chart, where anyone proposing a concentrated post-reorg book will have to read it on the way to proposing it. Figure 16.5 shows the single-name distribution beside a 20-name book.

![Figure 16.5: A single post-reorg name has a mean return of +33% but a median of −5%, while an equal-weighted book of 20 names has a median of +29%, close to its mean, so the premium is a portfolio property. Illustrative: 400,000 simulated draws per panel from the §16.8.1 jump-lognormal mixture (s = 0.82, jump probability 5%, seed 16); the right panel groups them into 20,000 books of 20 names.](../assets/figures/ch16_post_reorg_return_distribution.png)

Diversification turns the mean into the median. For an equal-weighted book of $N$ independent names, the book return has the same mean, standard deviation reduced by $\sqrt N$, and skewness reduced by $\sqrt N$, so its median moves toward its mean. With $N = 20$ (about the size of Jiang, Wang & Yang's portfolio) the median book return is comfortably positive, as Block 5 confirms by simulation.

Theo looks at the right-hand panel for a long time. "So Spirit wasn't a mistake in the strategy. It was one of the five cards."

"It was one of the five cards," Ines says. "Now read the word you skipped."

He reads the paragraph again. *Independent.* The $\sqrt N$ only works if the twenty names fail for twenty different reasons. Two airline equities that emerged within months of each other share fuel prices, leisure demand, aircraft lessors and, as of this summer, a card-processing industry that has learned to hold back receipts from carriers in trouble. If their returns move together with a correlation of 0.5, two names diversify like about one and a third ($N_{\text{eff}} = N/(1 + (N-1)\rho) = 2/1.5$) *(illustrative correlation)*, and the book's median does not get the help the figure promises. That is the honest answer to the whiteboard, or most of it. Spirit going to zero says little about the second carrier's own coin. It says a great deal about whether the desk's "twenty names" are really twenty. The sector hedge is the tool for the part the two carriers share, and the "buy the next one smaller" option is the tool for the part they do not, which leaves Kaz's question, *define smaller*, as the only thing left on the board.

### 16.8.2 Sizing: Kelly with a trapdoor, then a liquidity ceiling

Kaz answers their own whiteboard question before lunch, which is how Kaz answers most questions: by computing something. "Smaller," they announce, "is the growth-optimal fraction. I ran Kelly on our post-reorg history. For a single name it says about half the book."

Nobody says anything for a moment. Mags puts her coffee down.

"Half," Ines says. "Of the book. In one OTC stock."

"That's what the sample says." Kaz turns their screen around. "It's the vendor's post-reorg universe, 2005 to 2024, two hundred-odd names, 200-day returns from the effective date."

"How did the vendor build the universe?"

Kaz scrolls to the methodology note, which they have not read, and reads it now, aloud, at a speed that slows as they go. The universe was assembled from tickers with a price history in the vendor's equity database. A company that emerged, filed again and was cancelled had its new ticker retired, and a retired ticker with no successor fell out of the history file the following year. "So the names that went to zero," they say, "are not in the names."

"So your sample has no Spirits in it."

"My sample has no Spirits in it." Kaz looks at the number again. "And with no Spirits in it, half the book is exactly what the model says, if you take the jumps out. I can show you why."

> **Math, Gently.** *Kelly in one coin flip.* Somebody offers you a coin that lands heads 60% of the time and pays even money: bet a dollar, win a dollar or lose it. You will play hundreds of times, and each bet is a fraction $f$ of whatever you have at that moment. What fraction makes your wealth grow fastest? Not 100%. Bet everything and you are wiped out the first time the coin lands tails, which it will, usually within the first few flips; one zero multiplies everything after it by zero. Not 0% either, since you have an edge. The answer, from maximizing the average *log* of each flip's wealth multiple, is $f = 0.6 - 0.4 = 20\%$, and it grows your wealth by about 2.0% per flip ($0.6\ln 1.2 + 0.4\ln 0.8 \approx 0.020$). Its two neighbors tell the rest of the story. Half-Kelly, 10%, earns about 1.5% a flip, three-quarters of the growth for half the swings, which is why desks that are unsure of their odds use it. Double-Kelly, 40%, earns about $-0.2\%$ a flip: twice the optimal bet on a *winning* coin loses money over time. The log is what makes the trapdoor visible: $\ln 0 = -\infty$, so a bet that can lose everything at full size scores minus infinity however good the odds, and in this chapter the trapdoor is §16.8.1's five-in-a-hundred card at $-100\%$. Chapter 28 (§28.4) carries the full treatment, with jump-to-default for bonds.

For a single name held as a fraction $f$ of capital, growth-optimal sizing maximizes $g(f) = \mathbb{E}[\ln(1 + fR)]$. The jump to $-100\%$ makes $g(f) \to -\infty$ as $f \to 1$, so the Kelly fraction is always strictly less than one, and the first-order condition
$$g'(f) = \mathbb{E}\!\left[\frac{R}{1 + fR}\right] = 0$$
has a neat check point at $f = \tfrac12$, where the survivor half of $R$ contributes exactly nothing and the jump half contributes $-2p_J$ (the short calculation is in the Full Derivation below). So $g'(\tfrac12) = -2p_J$, and two things follow at once. With any jump risk at all, full-name Kelly is below one half. And with $p_J = 0$, which is what a sample with no Spirits in it estimates, Kelly is *exactly* one half, which is Kaz's number, reproduced by a formula that believed everything it was told.

"So the formula is fine," Theo says, "and the data is lying."

"The data is telling the truth about a different population," Ines says. "The population of companies that survived long enough to be in a database. That's not the population you buy on effective date."

The afternoon brings the second half of the lesson, and it arrives as a ticket. Theo, who has been convinced by the morning that the strategy is a portfolio and that the next post-reorg name is worth owning, puts in a request to buy \$5mm of a small-cap packaging company that emerged last week and trades over the counter. It is the kind of name §16.2 is built for: a CLO-heavy fulcrum, an overhang the model can schedule, a discount to the rights price. Ines declines the ticket from her phone and walks over.

"What does it trade?"

"About two hundred thousand dollars a day."

"If the trucking company calls us tomorrow and says it needs the risk budget, or if the packaging company's first 10-Q has a going-concern paragraph in it, how fast can you get out?"

Theo does it on a legal pad, because some habits survive the move to a systematic desk. If a position must be exitable at participation rate $\pi$ of average daily dollar volume $\text{ADV}$ within $d$ days, its size is capped at $\pi \cdot \text{ADV} \cdot d$. At a 10% participation, which is about as much of an OTC stock's volume as a desk can be before it *is* the volume, and a 20-day exit, the cap is $0.10 \times \$200\text{k} \times 20 = \$400\text{k}$.

"Four hundred thousand," he says.

"That's your size. Kelly's a ceiling on a ceiling. We use half-Kelly (Chapter 28), because if you've overestimated the edge by a factor of two, full Kelly is double-Kelly, and double-Kelly on a winning coin grows nothing. And in this corner of the market we never get anywhere near even half, because the constraint that actually binds is the door." She turns to go, then turns back. "This is why the surviving post-reorg alpha, the part Jiang, Wang and Yang found still lives in the OTC names, doesn't scale. It's real. And a \$500mm book can own about four hundred thousand dollars of it per name."

Theo does the second piece of arithmetic in his head and does not enjoy it: \$400k is 0.08% of a \$500mm book. Twenty such names are 1.6% of the book. Mags, passing behind him, reads the number over his shoulder. "Back in my day," she says, "we did this trade with the whole book and three phone numbers, and the risk committee met once a quarter. One of those was a mistake."

#### The Full Derivation

The check point at $f = \tfrac12$ takes two lines. On the survivor branch, $R = e^X - 1$, so
$$\frac{R}{1 + \tfrac12 R} = \frac{2(e^X - 1)}{e^X + 1} = 2\tanh(X/2),$$
and since $X \sim N(0, s^2)$ is symmetric about zero and $\tanh$ is an odd function, $\mathbb{E}[2\tanh(X/2)] = 0$. On the jump branch, $R = -1$ and the integrand is $(-1)/(1 - \tfrac12) = -2$. Weighting the branches by $1 - p_J$ and $p_J$ gives $g'(\tfrac12) = -2p_J < 0$: with any jump risk at all, full-name Kelly is below one half. Because $g''(f) = -\mathbb{E}[R^2/(1+fR)^2] < 0$, $g$ is concave, so $g'(\tfrac12) < 0$ puts the maximum to the left of one half, and $g'(\tfrac12) = 0$ when $p_J = 0$ puts it exactly there.

### 16.8.3 The pair trades

By Thursday the whiteboard has filled up with a different kind of list: the questions people asked that week, written down by whoever was nearest the marker. On Thursday afternoon Ines notices that every one of them has the same kind of answer, two positions, one long and one short, chosen so that everything cancels except the thing the person was asking about.

Tuesday's was Mags's. A vendor was offering its trade claim at 30 because payroll is on Friday, while the senior unsecured bonds that will share the same distribution were quoted at 38 *(illustrative)*. "Which price is wrong?" she asked. Neither, about enterprise value, since the two claims share it. The eight points are the vendor's forced-seller discount, and owning the claim against a short in the bond collects them while leaving the valuation fight to somebody else (Moyer p.269). The other four came from Theo (the claims pool, without the timing), Kaz (the warrants' volatility, without an opinion on the company), the operations analyst who books new-issue settlements (why a name is cheapest weeks after delivery) and Harlan (the seat against the plain rights). Ines copies the five answers into a table so that nobody has to stand at the whiteboard to read them:

| Pair | What it isolates | Section |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Long 503(b)(9) / short GUC (or the reverse) | Pool-size risk, holding timing fixed | §16.5.3 |
| Long trade claim / short senior unsecured bond | The forced-seller discount on the claim, holding enterprise value fixed | §16.5.1, Moyer p.269 |
| Long warrant / short stock at the dilution-adjusted delta | Volatility and survival, holding direction fixed | §16.4.2 |
| When-issued vs. regular-way stock | Settlement and delivery timing, i.e. the $\alpha$ of §16.2.2 | §16.2.2, Moyer p.370 |
| Backstop seat vs. plain rights | The put premium plus exclusivity | §16.3.2 |

> **Poker Table.** Ines replays the cold open's hand through the model, assuming most of the CLO's allocation had not yet settled (delivery rate $\alpha = 5$ per year, execution rate $\theta \approx 3.4$, total discount $\kappa Q_0/M = 15\%$, all *illustrative*). Buying the CLO's first offer at the open marks out at about −4.4% after one month and about −6.6% at the three-month trough, then climbs back to about −1.2% after a year: the open was the first card of a long deal, not the end of the hand. Buying at the trough instead earns about +5.4% to the one-year mark from the flow alone, before anyone has an opinion about trucking. "You didn't lose because the stock was bad," Ines says. "You lost because you called before the seller had finished getting chips." The hand history is in Block 5.

Ines's hand assumes the CLO sells into the screen, a few thousand shares at a time. Some mornings it calls a dealer instead.

> **View From Another Seat.** *The dealer desk.* (A generic seat; no real firm is described.) Where the systematic desk sees the CLO's day-one offer as a supply schedule to wait out, a bank's distressed or special-situations trading desk sees a client asking for an exit, and its question is not "what is this stock worth?" but "how long will I hold it, and who takes it off me?" On day one the dealer may bid for a block from the CLO manager at a discount and then work it out over days to hedge funds, crossover accounts and, quite possibly, the systematic desk. In §16.2's language the block bid is a moment when $\theta$ jumps: weeks of drain compressed into an afternoon, the overhang moved onto a balance sheet whose clock is set by inventory limits and the capital held against an illiquid equity position. Months later, around day 130 *(illustrative)*, when the largest holders' lock-ups have rolled off and, if the plan granted them registration rights, a registered secondary becomes possible, the same bank may be on the cover of the prospectus, pricing a marketed offering at a discount to the last trade and allocating it to long-only funds that would not have touched the stock on effective date. From that seat the post-reorg discount is the fee for warehousing a stock between the holders the waterfall chose and the holders who want it, and the dealer is the one participant who can be paid at both ends. For the systematic desk the dealer's flow is information: a block that clears a CLO's position early is §16.2.4's expiry date arriving ahead of schedule, and a secondary is a second overhang with a date printed on it.

### Specification for AI Implementation

**The Spec You Hand the Robot.** *Vague version:* "Size the post-reorg book." *What ROBO built:* full Kelly on the sample mean, which put 100% of capital into the single name with the highest historical return, a stock that had since gone through Chapter 22. *Precise version:* simulate 200-day returns from the jump-lognormal mixture, verify the mean–median gap and its disappearance under diversification, compute the single-name Kelly fraction on a grid strictly below one, apply half-Kelly and a liquidity cap, and replay the cold-open hand through `ForcedSellerOverhang` markouts.

Kaz's vendor file is why the listing simulates rather than samples. Every number in §16.8 is one you can check, so the listing draws from the jump-lognormal mixture, asserts the mean-median gap and its disappearance in a 20-name book, finds the Kelly fraction by grid search over simulated returns, caps the size by liquidity, and replays Ines's hand as three markouts through the §16.2 overhang model. Its Kelly fraction is still an in-sample maximum that inherits whatever jump probability it was given, one more reason the liquidity cap, not Kelly, decides the size in OTC names.

*The full listing is [Listing 16.5 in Appendix F](#code-16-5).*

Friday, 6:40 p.m. The trucking company's stock is still on Theo's first monitor, where it has been, in one window or another, since the 9:31 a.m. open that started all this. Beside it is a draft of eight sentences for the desk wiki, where the desk keeps the things it means to remember and then forgets to read. Ines has agreed to hear them before he posts them, on one condition: he reads them out loud, "because a sentence that sounds fine in your head is how ROBO ends up in cash."

He reads the first. "**The plan value is a negotiated number.**"

"Negotiated by whom?"

"The controlling creditors."

"Who wanted it where?"

"Low," Theo says. He sat in the rooms: a low plan value means more of the new company per dollar of claim and a cheaper rights price for the people buying the rights. "Low, because they were on both sides of it."

"Then say that. 'Negotiated' sounds like a handshake. It was a price set by the buyer." He rewrites the line on the spot, and it goes up on the wiki this way: **The plan value is a number the controlling creditors negotiated, and they negotiated it down.** The honest anchor for every post-reorg instrument is the price insiders actually pay in the same plan, the rights price or the direct-investment price, and not the disclosure statement's midpoint.

The second sentence is Mags's, and she says so from across the aisle without looking up. **Forced selling is a supply schedule, not a mood.** The man at the regional bank becomes three parameters: an overhang $Q_0$, an execution rate $\theta$ (about 3.4 a year, a 2.4-month half-life, from the fallen-angel aggregates), and capital $M_t$ that arrives slowly. With staggered delivery, as across the eleven vehicles, the discount peaks *after* the event, and the signal expires when the 13G says the constrained holders are out. "And when he stops calling," Mags adds. "Put that in a footnote."

The third is Monday's whiteboard. **The post-reorg premium is a portfolio property.** Mean +40%, median zero, and no alpha after 2010 for listed names. Only a diversified book harvests the right tail, and the surviving OTC alpha does not scale past a few hundred thousand dollars a name, which Theo learned from a declined ticket and a legal pad.

The fourth he reads for Harlan, who is not there. **A backstop is a short put, and the fee is its smallest leg.** At a 25% discount and 70% volatility the fair fee is about 6%; the discount, the fee paid in shares and the exclusivity option take the all-in transfer to about 20% of the raise. Since *ConvergeOne*, an exclusive backstop without a market test also carries legal reversal risk.

The fifth makes Kaz wince, which Theo takes as confirmation that it is right. **Price warrants with dilution, and never charge for the funeral twice.** With a market spot, jump-to-default enters through $r + \lambda$, not as an $e^{-\lambda T}$ haircut. And the plan's own warrant valuation tells you the volatility the other side assumed, which is the closest a post-reorg desk ever gets to reading the other player's cards.

The sixth is the claims desk in one line. **A claim is long a ratio and short a call at par.** Near par, pool uncertainty costs recovery (about 8 points at a 30% log-sd); deep out of the money, it helps. The whole trade depends on knowing which side of the kink you are on.

The seventh Theo is pleased with, and reads with a little flourish. "**The 503(b)(9)/GUC pair isolates pool risk.** The person who has counted the leases, applied the §502(b)(6) cap and struck the duplicate claims should be long the GUC against the 503(b)(9). That person used to work at PJT."

Ines lets the flourish land and then takes it apart. "What did that person bring from PJT?"

"The ability to count leases."

"And what didn't they bring?"

He thinks about the October memo to compliance and the wall that is exactly as thick as the manual says. "Anything they learned there about a specific company."

"So the sentence is half right. The skill travels. The files don't." She nods at the USB stick, which is on his desk, as it always is. "The template on that stick is yours. The data rooms it was filled from never were." The line goes up as: **That person used to work at PJT, and brought the method, not the files.** It is less funny. Ines says that is how you can tell it is better.

The eighth needs no correction, because it came out of a four-page post-mortem and has the scar tissue to prove it. **Check the 13-week model before the multiple.** Spirit's first post-reorg equity lasted under six months; Hertz's warrants run to 2051 and the company was back in the room in 2026. Runway drives the jump term.

"Now the screen," Ines says.

Theo looks at the trucking company and answers the first morning's question. Part of that 11% discount was flow: eleven vehicles on eleven clocks, four of them amortizing and with nowhere to put a share, a supply schedule with a half-life of about two and a half months and a trough that the staggered deliveries pushed weeks past the open. That part needed no view on trucking, only patience and a registry that tied: the trade was not to lift the 9:31 offer but to let the seller finish getting chips and buy near the trough, at a size the door allowed. The rest of the discount was value, and that part was the old job: what a trucking-and-warehousing business is worth with its debt cut, whether its own plan's projections turn into cash on schedule, and what the rights price said about what the creditors really thought. "The flow I can schedule," he says. "The value I have to underwrite. And the plan value was never the answer to either. It was the opening bid."

"Post it," Ines says, and goes home.

*One subject the week never reached is the plumbing of actually buying a claim rather than pricing it: LSTA par and distressed confirms, assignment versus participation, disqualified-lender lists, delayed compensation, and the §502(d) taint that can follow a claim to its buyer. That is the claims desk's business, and it gets its own chapter (Chapter 16-B).*

**The Spec You Hand the Robot.** Build `post_reorg_engine.py` with five modules, each under $\mathbb{P}$ unless labeled, each carrying the asserts in Blocks 1–5 as unit tests. (1) `overhang`: `ForcedSellerOverhang(Q0, theta, M0, M_star, rho, kappa, alpha=None)` with `Q`, `discount`, `drift`, `half_life`, `peak_time`; inputs from a holder registry (plan schedule, Rule 2019, 13D/13G, Form 4, 13F, trustee reports); output a daily expected-excess-drift signal per name that is exactly zero once executed fraction reaches one. (2) `rights`: `RightsOffering(n0, m, K)` with `post_money`, `right_value_per_plan_share`, `backstop_payoff`, `fair_fee(x0, sigma, T)`; plus an all-in transfer with fee in shares, reserved fraction `a`, unexercised-in-the-money fraction `eta`, and a fee-survival probability by circuit and market test. (3) `warrants`: `warrant_price(S, K, T, sigma, r, omega, lam)` as the dilution fixed point with jump via $r+\lambda$; `implied_vol_warrant` by bracketed root-finding; spot must be labeled `market` or `going_concern`, and only the latter may take a survival haircut. (4) `claims`: register ingestion (drop superseded and withdrawn claims, apply §502(b)(6)/(b)(7) caps, separate 503(b)(9) by receipt evidence), `expected_recovery_lognormal`, `price_claim` for `GUC` and `503b9`, the priority-spread decomposition, and `in_kind_recovery` for claims fixed in petition-date dollars. (5) `book`: jump-lognormal return simulation, Kelly on a grid strictly below one, half-Kelly, a liquidity cap of participation × ADV × exit days, and a runway-driven jump intensity $\lambda_t = \lambda_0 e^{-\beta L_t/B_t}$. Units: shares in millions, money in USD millions unless a field says per share, rates and intensities per year, time in years. Seed every simulation with `np.random.default_rng(16)`. ROBO should refuse, not guess, when a required field is missing.

### Exercises

1. **The CLO that wanted a term loan.** A plan gives a fulcrum class 100% of the new equity; CLOs hold 30% of the class, a sponsor holds a locked 35%, and the rest is free. (a) Compute $\phi^{\text{OH}}$. (b) Using Block 1 with $\theta = 3.4$, $\kappa = 0.3$ and capital equal to twice the overhang, compute the expected total abnormal return. (c) The plan is amended to let CLOs elect take-back term loans instead, and 80% of them do. Recompute (a) and (b), and explain why the CLO managers' election improved the stock for everyone else.
2. **Two speeds.** Simulate a panel with Block 1 using $\rho = 0.5$, $M_0 = 30$ and $M^* = 60$, then fit $(\theta, \rho)$ jointly with `scipy.optimize.least_squares`. Show that a single exponential fitted to the first two six-month windows underpredicts the third, as the single-exponential fit to Dynkin's 5.75/1.04/0.86 does, and report which parameter the third window identifies.
3. **Four legs of the seat.** For a \$500mm rights offering at a 30% discount to fair value, 65% volatility, a 0.3-year commitment window, a dilution factor of 0.6, a 10% fee paid in shares, 20% of the offering reserved for the backstop parties and 15% of in-the-money rights left unexercised, compute each leg of $\Pi^{\text{BP}}$ in expectation. Which leg is largest? Now apply a 60% probability that the fee survives an equal-treatment challenge, and say which legs a court can and cannot reach.
4. **Kaz's funeral, formally.** Show that $C_{\text{BS}}(S, K, T, \sigma, r + \lambda) > C_{\text{BS}}(S, K, T, \sigma, r)$ for $\lambda > 0$. Then find the going-concern spot $S^{\text{GC}}$ at which Kaz's haircut price $e^{-\lambda T}C_{\text{BS}}(S^{\text{GC}}, K, T, \sigma, r)$ equals the correct jump price at the market spot $S$, for the Hertz warrant inputs. Interpret $S^{\text{GC}}/S$ in one sentence a restructuring banker would accept.
5. **The boat and the truck.** Vendor A shipped \$2mm of goods by sea 25 days before the petition, free on board at the shipping point; they were unloaded at the debtor's warehouse 18 days before the petition. Vendor B's truck delivered \$2mm of goods 22 days before the petition. Under *World Imports*, which vendor holds a 503(b)(9) claim? Price both claims with Block 4 (use $h = 1.5$, $r = 4\%$, $\psi = 8\%$, a GUC class with $\mu_Y = \ln 0.4$ and $s_Y = 0.35$) and compute the dollar value of having hired a slower ship.
6. **Short a call, paid nothing.** An FTX-style customer held 1 BTC, dollarized at about \$17k at the petition date, and received 120% of that in cash about 2.5 years later. Using Black–Scholes with 60% volatility, value the call on 1.2 BTC struck at the petition-date dollar amount that the dollarization clause implicitly made the customer write. Compare it with what a claims buyer at 15 cents paid for the claim, and explain who was really short volatility.

# Chapter 17: Private Credit & the Public–Private Convergence

> *"Middle market direct lending (Private Credit): Proxy Index using S&P UBS Leveraged Loan B Index."* (Nuveen_Multi_Asset_Credit_Quant_Framework p.9)
>
> And, two pages earlier in the same framework's sector table, in the volatility column for middle-market direct lending: "N/A". (Nuveen_Multi_Asset_Credit_Quant_Framework p.2)

## Cold Open: Volatility N/A

*(A replay. The desk, its dialogue, the listed BDC, its notes and the \$25mm RFQ are fictional, and every price the desk sees on its own screens is illustrative. The fund in the headline and its numbers are real: InvestmentNews, June 23, 2026.)*

The desk keeps a folder called "Replays": real credit events cut off at a minute, with nothing inside that was not public by then. Ines runs one on a Friday afternoon every few weeks, and the rule never changes: nobody mentions anything that happened after the cut-off. This Friday in October, the week the Fed finally put private credit into its Financial Accounts, the folder on the big screen is labeled *Tuesday 23 June 2026, 2:40 p.m.* Mags and Kaz were on the desk that day. Theo was at RSSG, where the same headline arrived as somebody else's problem and stayed that way until dinner.

Ines starts the clock.

**2:40 p.m.** The headline crosses the news screen in the clipped grammar of a wire: Apollo Debt Solutions, a \$26 billion non-traded private credit fund, has received repurchase requests for 16.8% of its shares this quarter, about \$2.4 billion, and will pay 5%, which the story calls "the standard limit for such vehicles." Two other sponsors' funds appear further down the piece; the desk will get to them in §17.6.

Kaz reads it twice, the way Kaz reads anything with a percentage in it, and shrugs. "That's their fund. It isn't our bond. Their investors want out of a vehicle that only lets five in a hundred leave each quarter. Our bonds don't have investors who want out. They have a price."

It is a reasonable sentence, and Mags lets it sit on the desk for a while, the way you let a junior's bid sit on a screen to see who hits it.

**3:05 p.m.** The desk makes markets in the unsecured notes of a listed BDC that lends to the same kind of borrower as the fund in the headline: sponsor-backed, middle-market, heavy in software. The run sheet shows the 2029 notes quoted where they were at lunch, because nothing has printed since. The BDC's shares are down a little more than 2% since the headline, which is the only price anywhere on the screen that has moved.

Theo opens the BDC's last 10-Q, skips everything a normal person would read, and goes looking for the credit agreement behind the revolver, which the 10-Q mentions in two sentences and files as an exhibit to a different document. It takes him twenty minutes to find the definition of the borrowing base, and another ten to find the paragraph that matters, which is about what the bank will lend against and what it will not. Loans on non-accrual drop out. Loans that have been amended to pay in kind, interest that accrues as more debt instead of arriving as cash, are "Eligible Investments" only at a haircut, and the haircut gets worse the longer the PIK runs.

He reads it out loud, which is what he does when he finds the paragraph that matters. "What does the revolver say about borrowing-base eligibility for PIK loans? If the bank haircuts anything that's been amended into PIK, and a fifth of the book is software that's been amended into PIK, then the borrowing base shrinks exactly when the fund needs it. And these notes sit behind that line."

Nobody answers, because the question is a good one and the 10-Q does not say how much of the book is PIK by amendment rather than by design. Theo writes a sticky note and puts it under the one from Chapter 4 (*"price" = as of when, in what size, from whom?*): *whose number is it?*

**4:10 p.m.** Kaz has pulled the BDC's NAV history and the history of a loan index beside it, and is quietly pleased with the first chart and quietly annoyed with the second, because the second one moves.

**4:40 p.m.** The RFQ arrives: a client wants to sell \$25mm of the BDC's senior unsecured notes due 2029, two hours after the headline, twenty minutes before the close, from an account the desk sees about once a quarter.

Kaz has the NAV chart up. "I don't see the problem. NAV per share has moved less than one percent all quarter. I tried to pull the volatility of the loan book and the vendor field says N/A."

"N/A isn't zero," Ines says. "N/A means nobody looked. What's the pot, what are the odds, and who at this table knows more than we do? Somebody wants out of the bond of a vehicle that owns the same kind of loans as the fund that just got a run. They want out at 4:40 today, not at 9:30 tomorrow. That's the hand."

"In my day," Mags says without looking up, "we called a bond with no price a bond. You found out what it was worth when you tried to sell it. Then you found out who else was trying."

"Are you saying the NAV is wrong?" Kaz asks.

"I'm saying the NAV is a mark," Theo says. "It's marked quarterly, by the manager, who earns fees on it. The bond price is a price. Underneath, it's the same loans."

Ines nods at the screen. "Then the question isn't what the bond is worth. It's what the loans are worth, and which of the things we *can* trade already knows."

She stops the clock there, at 4:41, with the RFQ still blinking, and hands out index cards, because a replay is worthless if people get to answer after they have heard each other. "Write three things: what you bid, how much of the \$25mm, and which public thing you'd hedge it with. Then put the card face down. We turn them over at the end of the chapter."

Kaz writes quickly. Mags writes one line and folds the card. Theo looks at his sticky note for longer than he looks at his card, which is, Ines notes without saying so, the right order.

Four prices will be attached to the same loans before this chapter is done: the manager's NAV, the listed sibling's share price, a pension fund's bid at par, and a secondary buyer's bid for a fund's units at two-thirds of NAV. Each is honest about a different question, which is why Theo's sticky note is the right one.

The question this chapter answers: **what are the true value and risk of a portfolio whose only published price is set by its owner, and which public instruments let us trade our answer?**

By the end of this chapter you will be able to: write a private mark as a moving-average filter of an unobserved return and derive what that filter does to volatility, correlation, beta and Sharpe ratio; estimate the smoothing kernel from a few dozen quarterly marks without fooling yourself; turn a listed BDC's price-to-NAV ratio into an implied markdown on its loans, and its non-accrual disclosures into an implied carrying value for bad loans; forecast the direction of private-to-public refinancing flow from a public regime variable; price a semi-liquid fund's redemption queue as a run with a pro-rata cap; and assemble the book of public instruments that expresses all of it.

## 17.1 One Borrower Pool, Two Pricing Regimes

### 17.1.1 Desk framing: the same credit, measured twice

Start with the definitional trap, because every number in this chapter has to survive it. "Private credit" ranges from about \$1.3 trillion to more than \$3 trillion depending on whether you mean loans or assets under management, the US or the world, and whether you include dry powder. On October 16, 2026 the Federal Reserve settled the US loan number by putting private credit into the Financial Accounts (Z.1): \$1,493.5 billion of private-credit loans at the end of 2025, held by private debt funds (\$532B), BDCs (\$456B), the rest of the world (\$376B), interval and tender-offer funds (\$76B) and middle-market CLOs (\$54B) (Brinkman et al., FEDS Note, October 16, 2026). When someone tells you the size of private credit, ask which of those numbers they mean. It is the "but what does the credit agreement say?" of market sizing. Figure 17.1 shows who holds the \$1,493.5 billion and how fast each holder has grown since 2023.

![Figure 17.1: Private debt funds still hold the most (\$532B at the end of 2025), but BDCs and interval and tender-offer funds, the two holder types that reach retail investors, grew fastest, 1.9 and 2.2 times in two years. Source: Brinkman et al., FEDS Note (16 October 2026), Table F4.4.s of the Federal Reserve's Financial Accounts (Z.1), holder-side values in \$ billions at year-end; the borrower-side split in the same table is estimated.](../assets/figures/ch17_z1_holders.png)

Now the fact that organizes the chapter. Private credit and public leveraged finance are not two asset classes. They are **one borrower pool with two pricing regimes**. A Fed study of the two markets finds that 41% of large middle-market borrowers have used both, that switching from leveraged loans to private credit peaked near half of leveraged-loan borrowers in early 2023, and that the borrowers in each market look like this:

| 2025 issuance (medians unless stated) | Private credit | Leveraged loans |
| :--- | ---: | ---: |
| Borrower revenue | \$223M | \$902M |
| Debt / EBITDA | 5.0x | 3.2x |
| Interest coverage | 2.2x | 3.7x |
| Spread | S+500 | S+400 |
| Rated BB or better | 0% | 28% |
| CCC or below | 15% | 9% |
| Software share of issuance | 21% | 16% |

*Source: Banegas et al., "Private Credit and Leveraged Loan Markets: Similarities, Differences, and Substitution," FEDS Note, August 11, 2026.*

The private borrower is smaller, more levered and more software-heavy. It pays about 100bp more for the privilege. None of that makes it a different kind of credit; it is the bottom-left of the same scatter plot. The same sponsor, the same software company and the same five turns of leverage can sit in a CLO as a daily-priced syndicated loan or in a BDC as a quarterly-marked unitranche. **What differs is not the credit. It is the measurement.**

Mags has heard this argument before, in a different decade. "When I started, loans were priced by phone and by grudge. The bid you got depended on whether the man on the other end had been stuck with your last one. Terrible system. But every one of those numbers came from somebody who'd lose money if it was wrong."

"Who loses money if a private mark is wrong?" Theo asks. He means it as a real question: in a restructuring, the first thing anyone asks about a valuation is who paid for it.

Kaz starts to answer and then stops, because the honest answer is *nobody, this quarter*. If the manager carries a loan at 97 and it is worth 85, no trade happens at 97, no one is filled at the wrong price, and the fee is still charged on 97. The error does not show up as a loss to anyone; it shows up as a mark that is twelve points too high and a volatility series that is too smooth, and it gets corrected later, by a committee, in an amount and at a speed the committee chooses.

"Oh," Kaz says. "That's the whole problem. A public loan is *priced*: daily, noisily, by people who lose money when they're wrong, so the error is roughly mean zero. A private loan is *marked*: quarterly, from a model, smoothed, by the party that owns it and earns a fee on the number. Nobody is paid to make the error go away, so it doesn't go away. It just arrives late."

Everything in this chapter is the mathematics of that difference. Ines gives Theo the one sentence for his monitor, and he tapes it under the sticky note: *private credit is public credit with the price removed, and our job is to put the price back and get paid by whoever still believes it was never there.*

Theo will find the structure familiar, because he has seen it on the other side of the table. A BDC is, in the Boston Fed's phrase, "a CLO in which banks hold the top tranche" (Fillat, Landoni, Levin and Wang, Boston Fed Current Policy Perspectives 25-8, May 21, 2025): a bank revolver on top, unsecured notes in the middle, listed or non-listed equity at the bottom, and a manager who both picks the collateral and marks it. The redemption queue that made the cold open's seller nervous turns that structure into a borrower with a maturity wall, and §17.6.1 is where Theo's USB stick gets its next job. And "selective default" (PIK amendments, amend-and-extends, covenant holidays) is the bilateral market's liability management transaction: the same redefinition of default Theo watched in Serta and Incora, done quietly, with one lender and no docket.

### 17.1.2 What "private" actually buys: access and patience

There is an honest case for private credit, and it is worth stating before we spend thirty pages being rude about marks. The post-crisis evidence says borrowers went to nonbanks for *access*, not price. In 2010–2015 about one-third of middle-market loans came directly from nonbanks, those loans priced about 190bp above comparable bank loans after controls, and the probability of borrowing from a nonbank rose sharply when EBITDA turned negative (Chernenko, Erel and Prilmeier, NBER w26458; RFS 2022). Private lenders write cash-flow loans that banks will not, with real maintenance covenants (Block, Jang, Kaplan and Schulze, NBER w30868). The lender is paid for underwriting what the syndicated market won't take, and for holding what nobody can sell.

> **[SOURCE EXTRACTION]** *Ben_Dor_Quantitative_Credit_Portfolio_Management p.166:* "Long-term investors, with reduced mark-to-market constraints, can choose to provide liquidity to the market and buy the bond, comfortable with the low default risk."
>
> **Annotation.** This is the respectable theory of the illiquidity premium: patient capital that does not have to mark to market earns a premium for absorbing assets that forced sellers must dump. Ben Dor and coauthors are writing about public bonds after downgrades, but the logic is the original pitch for private credit, and it has two conditions. The investor must have *reduced mark-to-market constraints*, and the default risk must be *low*. The 2020s growth of semi-liquid retail vehicles quietly removed the first condition: a fund that promises quarterly liquidity at NAV has re-imported the mark-to-market constraint while keeping the mark smoothed. The 2025–26 cycle tested the second, through software borrowers exposed to AI disruption. The modern desk departs from the shelf here. It treats the illiquidity premium as real but *conditional* on the holder's liability structure, and it prices the premium separately for a drawdown fund (patient), an insurer (patient but rating-constrained) and a perpetual BDC (patient until the redemption queue says otherwise).

Ben Dor's patient investor has a modern name, and it holds earnings calls. Theo reads one of them the way he used to read a lender presentation: for what the lender says it will refuse to do.

> **View From Another Seat.** *The direct lender.* From the chair of Ares Capital, one of the largest listed BDCs, the edge is documents and patience, and the managers say so in public. On Ares Capital's fourth-quarter 2025 call (4 February 2026), its president Jim Miller said, "We will walk away from transactions based on documentation terms," put the portfolio's first-lien loan-to-values "in the high 30% to low 40% range," and reported non-accruals of 1.8% at cost against a 3.8% average for BDCs. A loan with sixty cents of equity value under it and a covenant package negotiated line by line does not need a daily price to be a good loan, and a lender that can hold it to refinancing does not need to sell it to anyone. The same seat is candid about where the weakness lives, and it is not in the loans. On the Ares Management call of 31 July 2026, chief executive Michael Arougheti said "there is a risk that some of the wealth flows could be more pro-cyclical than people thought they were." That sentence is the hinge of this chapter. The direct lender's assets are patient; a growing share of its liabilities, the retail money in perpetual vehicles, is not, and the place where a public desk meets the private lender is the funding side, where §17.6's queue lives. (Quoted words are the speakers' own, from the calls cited; the reading of them is ours.)

The dishonest version of the case is the one the Nuveen table hints at. If the volatility cell says "N/A," an optimizer that needs a number will use whatever is smoothest, and the smoothest series in the world is one nobody updates. Cliffwater's direct lending index (CDLI), which aggregates BDC portfolio marks, returned 9.3% in 2025, 10.4% of it from interest income, with a 20-year average of 9.5% and one negative year (Cliffwater release, March 31, 2026). Those are real returns to real loans. The question §17.2 answers is how much real *risk* sits behind them, and why the reported series cannot tell you.

> **Trend Watch.** *From niche to a Z.1 line item, 2010–2026.* Private-credit vehicle AUM grew from about \$350 billion in 2012 to more than \$2.6 trillion (Brinkman et al., FEDS Note, October 16, 2026). The number of loans held by private-credit BDCs rose from roughly 1,400 in 2010 to roughly 20,000 in 2022 (Ellias and de Fontenay, *The Credit Markets Go Dark*, 134 Yale L.J., January 2025). On the Fed's new Z.1 basis, US private-credit loans were \$1,042.6B (2023), \$1,253.6B (2024) and \$1,493.5B (2025), growth of about 20% a year, and private credit is now 6% of nonfinancial business debt against 3% for syndicated loans (Brinkman et al.). The retail channel grew fastest: semi-liquid fund net assets rose from about \$15B in 2018 to \$388B in 2025 (George and Shin, FEDS Note, October 14, 2026). Globally, AUM passed \$2.2T in March 2025 with a \$4.5T forecast for 2030 (BlackRock *Private Credit Primer*, January 2026). **What it means for the desk:** private credit now has official holder-level series (Z.1 codes FL893167205 for the total, FL453067203 for BDCs, FL443067205 for private debt funds, FL673067205 for middle-market CLOs; see Appendix B), which makes it a flow-of-funds variable like any other. The forced-seller graph in Chapter 1 needs five new nodes, and the largest of them, BDCs, files a schedule of every loan it owns every quarter.
